problem:
Let \( N \) be a positive integer, and consider an \( N \times N \) grid. A right-down path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell below the previous cell in the sequence. A right-up path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell above the previous cell in the sequence.

Prove that the cells of the \( N \times N \) grid cannot be partitioned into less than \( N \) right-down or right-up paths.
solution:
We define a good parallelogram to be a parallelogram composed of two isosceles right-angled triangles glued together as shown below.

Given any partition into $k$ right-down or right-up paths, we can find a corresponding packing of good parallelograms that leaves an area of $k$ empty. Thus, it suffices to prove that we must leave an area of at least $N$ empty when we pack good parallelograms into an $N \times N$ grid. This is actually equivalent to the original problem since we can uniquely recover the partition into right-down or right-up paths from the corresponding packing of good parallelograms.

We draw one of the diagonals in each cell so that it does not intersect any of the good parallelograms. Now, view these segments as mirrors, and consider a laser entering each of the $4 N$ boundary edges (with starting direction being perpendicular to the edge), bouncing along these mirrors until it exits at some other edge. When a laser passes through a good parallelogram, its direction goes back to the original one after bouncing two times. Thus, if the final direction of a laser is perpendicular to its initial direction, it must pass through at least
one empty triangle. Similarly, if the final direction of a laser is opposite to its initial direction, it must pass though at least two empty triangles. Using this, we will estimate the number of empty triangles in the $N \times N$ grid.

We associate the starting edge of a laser with the edge it exits at. Then, the boundary edges are divided into $2 N$ pairs. These pairs can be classified into three types:
(1) a pair of a vertical and a horizontal boundary edge,
(2) a pair of boundary edges from the same side, and
(3) a pair of boundary edges from opposite sides.

Since the beams do not intersect, we cannot have one type (3) pair from vertical boundary edges and another type (3) pair from horizontal boundary edges. Without loss of generality, we may assume that we have $t$ pairs of type (3) and they are all from vertical boundary edges. Then, out of the remaining boundary edges, there are $2 N$ horizontal boundary edges and $2 N-2 t$ vertical boundary edges. It follows that there must be at least $t$ pairs of type (2) from horizontal boundary edges. We know that a laser corresponding to a pair of type (1) passes through at least one empty triangle, and a laser corresponding to a pair of type (2) passes through at least two empty triangles. Thus, as the beams do not intersect, we have at least $(2 N-2 t)+2 \cdot t=2 N$ empty triangles in the grid, leaving an area of at least $N$ empty as required.

problem:
Let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\) be real numbers. Let \(A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}\) be the matrix with entries

\[
a_{ij} = 
\begin{cases} 
1, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} \geq 0 \\ 
0, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} < 0 
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose that \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix whose entries are \(0,1\) such that the sum of the elements in each row and each column of \(B\) is equal to the corresponding sum for the matrix \(A\). Prove that \(A = B\).
solution:
Denote by $b_{i j}$ the entries of the matrix $B$. Suppose the contrary, i.e., that there is a pair $\left(i_{0}, j_{0}\right)$ such that $a_{i_{0}, j_{0}} \neq b_{i_{0}, j_{0}}$. We may assume without loss of generality that $a_{i_{0}, j_{0}}=0$ and $b_{i_{0}, j_{0}}=1$.
Since the sums of elements in the $i_{0}$ th rows of the matrices $A$ and $B$ are equal, there is some $j_{1}$ for which $a_{i_{0}, j_{1}}=1$ and $b_{i_{0}, j_{1}}=0$. Similarly, from the fact that the sums in the $j_{1}$ th columns of the matrices $A$ and $B$ are equal, we conclude that there exists $i_{1}$ such that $a_{i_{1}, j_{1}}=0$ and $b_{i_{1}, j_{1}}=1$. Continuing this procedure, we construct two sequences $i_{k}, j_{k}$ such that $a_{i_{k}, j_{k}}=0, b_{i_{k}, j_{k}}=1, a_{i_{k}, j_{k+1}}=1, b_{i_{k}, j_{k+1}}=0$. Since the set of the pairs $\left(i_{k}, j_{k}\right)$ is finite, there are two different numbers $t, s$ such that $\left(i_{t}, j_{t}\right)=\left(i_{s}, j_{s}\right)$. From the given condition we have that $x_{i_{k}}+y_{i_{k}}<0$ and $x_{i_{k+1}}+y_{i_{k+1}} \geq 0$. But $j_{t}=j_{s}$, and hence $0 \leq \sum_{k=s}^{t-1}\left(x_{i_{k}}+y_{j_{k+1}}\right)=$ $\sum_{k=s}^{t-1}\left(x_{i_{k}}+y_{j_{k}}\right)<0$, a contradiction.

problem:
Let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\) be real numbers. Let \(A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}\) be the matrix with entries

\[
a_{ij} = 
\begin{cases} 
1, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} \geq 0 \\ 
0, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} < 0 
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose that \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix whose entries are \(0,1\) such that the sum of the elements in each row and each column of \(B\) is equal to the corresponding sum for the matrix \(A\). Prove that \(A = B\).
solution:
We will in fact prove by induction on the number of rows $m$ the following more general statement:

  “Let $m,n$ be positive integers, let $x_{1},\dots,x_{m}$ and $y_{1},\dots,y_{n}$ be real numbers, and define the $m\times n$ “threshold matrix” $A=(a_{ij})$ by
  \[
    a_{ij} \;=\;
    \begin{cases}
      1,&x_{i}+y_{j}\ge0,\\
      0,&x_{i}+y_{j}<0.
    \end{cases}
  \]
  Suppose $B=(b_{ij})$ is any $m\times n$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ having the same row‐sums and the same column‐sums as $A$.  Then $B=A\,$.”

The original problem is the special case $m=n$.  We now carry out the induction.

Base case ($m=1$).  Then $A$ is a $1\times n$ row whose $j$th entry is $1$ if and only if $x_{1}+y_{j}\ge0$, and $0$ otherwise.  Any other $1\times n$ $\{0,1\}$–matrix $B$ with the same row‐sum and the same column‐sums must agree entry‐wise with $A$, so $B=A$.  This settles the base.

Inductive step.  Fix $m\ge2$ and assume the claim true for all matrices with fewer than $m$ rows.  Now let
\[
  A=(a_{ij})_{1\le i\le m,\;1\le j\le n},\quad
  B=(b_{ij})_{1\le i\le m,\;1\le j\le n}
\]
be as in the statement, and suppose $B$ has the same row‐sums and column‐sums as $A$.

1.  Choose an index $i_{0}$ with
\[
   x_{i_{0}} \;=\;\min\{\,x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m}\}.
\]
Define the set
\[
   J \;=\;\{\,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}:\;a_{i_{0}j}=1\}
         \;=\;\{\,j:\;x_{i_{0}}+y_{j}\ge0\}.
\]
Since row $i_{0}$ of $A$ has exactly $|J|$ ones, row $i_{0}$ of $B$ must also have exactly $|J|$ ones.  We claim in fact
\[
   b_{i_{0}j} \;=\;a_{i_{0}j}
   \quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Suppose, to the contrary, that there is some column $j_{0}\notin J$ with
\[
   b_{i_{0},j_{0}}=1\quad\text{but}\quad a_{i_{0},j_{0}}=0.
\]
Since row $i_{0}$ of $B$ has only $|J|$ ones whereas row $i_{0}$ of $A$ has its $|J|$ ones exactly on $J$, there must exist $j_{1}\in J$ with
\[
   b_{i_{0},j_{1}}=0
   \quad\text{but}\quad
   a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1.
\]
We now look at column $j_{1}$.  In $A$ the ones in column $j_{1}$ occur precisely at those rows $i$ for which
\[
   a_{i,j_{1}}=1
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   x_{i}+y_{j_{1}}\ge0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   x_{i}\;\ge\;-\,y_{j_{1}}.
\]
In particular $a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1$ shows $x_{i_{0}}\ge -y_{j_{1}}$.  Since $B$ has the same column‐sum as $A$ in column $j_{1}$ but $b_{i_{0},j_{1}}=0<a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1$, there must be some other row $\ell\neq i_{0}$ with
\[
   b_{\ell,j_{1}}=1
   \quad\text{but}\quad
   a_{\ell,j_{1}}=0.
\]
However
\[
   a_{\ell,j_{1}}=0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}<0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}< -y_{j_{1}}.
\]
Combining
\[
   x_{\ell} \;>\; x_{i_{0}}
     \quad\text{(since }x_{i_{0}}\text{ is minimal)}
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   x_{i_{0}}\;\ge\;-y_{j_{1}}
\]
yields
\[
   x_{\ell} \;\ge\; x_{i_{0}}\;\ge\;-y_{j_{1}}
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}\;\ge\;0,
\]
contradicting $x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}<0$.  This contradiction shows no such $j_{0}$ can exist, and hence
\[
   b_{i_{0}j}=a_{i_{0}j}
   \quad\text{for all }j.
\]

2.  Having established that row $i_{0}$ of $B$ agrees exactly with row $i_{0}$ of $A$, we now delete that row from both $A$ and $B$.  We are left with two matrices of size $(m-1)\times n$, and since row $i_{0}$ was identical in $A$ and $B$, those two smaller matrices still have the same row‐sums (for the remaining $m-1$ rows) and the same column‐sums.  Moreover, those two smaller matrices are again of the “threshold form’’ defined by the same $y_{1},\dots,y_{n}$ and the $m-1$ numbers $x_{i}$ with $i\ne i_{0}$.  By the induction hypothesis (applied to $m-1$ rows), the two smaller matrices must coincide entry‐wise.  Reattaching the common row $i_{0}$ we conclude $B=A$ as claimed.

This completes the induction and hence the proof in the square case $m=n$ as well.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle with circumcircle \(\Omega\). Let \( B_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AC \) and \( C_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( D \) be the foot of the altitude from \( A \), and let \( G \) be the centroid of the triangle \( ABC \). Let \(\omega\) be a circle through \( B_0 \) and \( C_0 \) that is tangent to the circle \(\Omega\) at a point \( X \neq A \). Prove that the points \( D, G, \) and \( X \) are collinear.
solution:
If $A B=A C$, then the statement is trivial. So without loss of generality we may assume $A B<A C$. Denote the tangents to $\Omega$ at points $A$ and $X$ by $a$ and $x$, respectively.

Let $\Omega_{1}$ be the circumcircle of triangle $A B_{0} C_{0}$. The circles $\Omega$ and $\Omega_{1}$ are homothetic with center $A$, so they are tangent at $A$, and $a$ is their radical axis. Now, the lines $a, x$, and $B_{0} C_{0}$ are the three radical axes of the circles $\Omega, \Omega_{1}$, and $\omega$. Since $a \nmid B_{0} C_{0}$, these three lines are concurrent at some point $W$.

The points $A$ and $D$ are symmetric with respect to the line $B_{0} C_{0}$; hence $W X=W A=W D$. This means that $W$ is the center of the circumcircle $\gamma$ of triangle $A D X$. Moreover, we have $\angle W A O=\angle W X O=90^{\circ}$, where $O$ denotes the center of $\Omega$. Hence $\angle A W X+\angle A O X=180^{\circ}$.

Denote by $T$ the second intersection point of $\Omega$ and the line $D X$. Note that $O$ belongs to $\Omega_{1}$. Using the circles $\gamma$ and $\Omega$, we find $\angle D A T=\angle A D X-\angle A T D=\frac{1}{2}\left(360^{\circ}-\angle A W X\right)-\frac{1}{2} \angle A O X=$ $180^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2}(\angle A W X+\angle A O X)=90^{\circ}$. So, $A D \perp A T$, and hence $A T \| B C$. Thus, $A T C B$ is an isosceles trapezoid inscribed in $\Omega$.

Denote by $A_{0}$ the midpoint of $B C$, and consider the image of $A T C B$ under the homothety $h$ with center $G$ and factor $-\frac{1}{2}$. We have $h(A)=A_{0}, h(B)=B_{0}$, and $h(C)=C_{0}$. From the
symmetry about $B_{0} C_{0}$, we have $\angle T C B=\angle C B A=\angle B_{0} C_{0} A=\angle D C_{0} B_{0}$. Using $A T \| D A_{0}$, we conclude $h(T)=D$. Hence the points $D, G$, and $T$ are collinear, and $X$ lies on the same line.

Solution 2. We define the points $A_{0}, O$, and $W$ as in the previous solution and we concentrate on the case $A B<A C$. Let $Q$ be the perpendicular projection of $A_{0}$ on $B_{0} C_{0}$.

Since $\angle W A O=\angle W Q O=\angle O X W=90^{\circ}$, the five points $A, W, X, O$, and $Q$ lie on a common circle. Furthermore, the reflections with respect to $B_{0} C_{0}$ and $O W$ map $A$ to $D$ and $X$, respectively. For these reasons, we have

$$
\angle W Q D=\angle A Q W=\angle A X W=\angle W A X=\angle W Q X
$$

Thus the three points $Q, D$, and $X$ lie on a common line, say $\ell$.

To complete the argument, we note that the homothety centered at $G$ sending the triangle $A B C$ to the triangle $A_{0} B_{0} C_{0}$ maps the altitude $A D$ to the altitude $A_{0} Q$. Therefore it maps $D$ to $Q$, so the points $D, G$, and $Q$ are collinear. Hence $G$ lies on $\ell$ as well.

Comment. There are various other ways to prove the collinearity of $Q, D$, and $X$ obtained in the middle part of Solution 2. Introduce for instance the point $J$ where the lines $A W$ and $B C$ intersect. Then the four points $A, D, X$, and $J$ lie at the same distance from $W$, so the quadrilateral $A D X J$ is cyclic. In combination with the fact that $A W X Q$ is cyclic as well, this implies

$$
\angle J D X=\angle J A X=\angle W A X=\angle W Q X
$$

Since $B C \| W Q$, it follows that $Q, D$, and $X$ are indeed collinear.

problem: To each side \(a\) of a convex polygon, we assign the maximum area of a triangle contained in the polygon and having \(a\) as one of its sides. Show that the sum of the areas assigned to all sides of the polygon is not less than twice the area of the polygon.
solution:
Lemma. Every convex $(2 n)$-gon, of area $S$, has a side and a vertex that jointly span a triangle of area not less than $S / n$.
Proof. By main diagonals of the ( $2 n$ )-gon we shall mean those which partition the ( $2 n$ )-gon into two polygons with equally many sides. For any side $b$ of the $(2 n)$-gon denote by $\Delta_{b}$ the triangle $A B P$ where $A, B$ are the endpoints of $b$ and $P$ is the intersection point of the main diagonals $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$. We claim that the union of triangles $\Delta_{b}$, taken over all sides, covers the whole polygon.

To show this, choose any side $A B$ and consider the main diagonal $A A^{\prime}$ as a directed segment. Let $X$ be any point in the polygon, not on any main diagonal. For definiteness, let $X$ lie on the left side of the ray $A A^{\prime}$. Consider the sequence of main diagonals $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}, C C^{\prime}, \ldots$, where $A, B, C, \ldots$ are consecutive vertices, situated right to $A A^{\prime}$.

The $n$-th item in this sequence is the diagonal $A^{\prime} A$ (i.e. $A A^{\prime}$ reversed), having $X$ on its right side. So there are two successive vertices $K, L$ in the sequence $A, B, C, \ldots$ before $A^{\prime}$ such that $X$ still lies to the left of $K K^{\prime}$ but to the right of $L L^{\prime}$. And this means that $X$ is in the triangle $\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}, \ell^{\prime}=K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$. Analogous reasoning applies to points $X$ on the right of $A A^{\prime}$ (points lying on main diagonals can be safely ignored). Thus indeed the triangles $\Delta_{b}$ jointly cover the whole polygon.

The sum of their areas is no less than $S$. So we can find two opposite sides, say $b=A B$ and $b^{\prime}=A^{\prime} B^{\prime}$ (with $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$ main diagonals) such that $\left[\Delta_{b}\right]+\left[\Delta_{b^{\prime}}\right] \geq S / n$, where $[\cdots]$ stands for the area of a region. Let $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$ intersect at $P$; assume without loss of generality that $P B \geq P B^{\prime}$. Then

$$
\left[A B A^{\prime}\right]=[A B P]+\left[P B A^{\prime}\right] \geq[A B P]+\left[P A^{\prime} B^{\prime}\right]=\left[\Delta_{b}\right]+\left[\Delta_{b^{\prime}}\right] \geq S / n
$$
proving the lemma.
Now, let $\mathcal{P}$ be any convex polygon, of area $S$, with $m$ sides $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{m}$. Let $S_{i}$ be the area of the greatest triangle in $\mathcal{P}$ with side $a_{i}$. Suppose, contrary to the assertion, that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{S_{i}}{S}<2
$$

Then there exist rational numbers $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}$ such that $\sum q_{i}=2$ and $q_{i}>S_{i} / S$ for each $i$.
Let $n$ be a common denominator of the $m$ fractions $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}$. Write $q_{i}=k_{i} / n$; so $\sum k_{i}=2 n$. Partition each side $a_{i}$ of $\mathcal{P}$ into $k_{i}$ equal segments, creating a convex ( $2 n$ )-gon of area $S$ (with some angles of size $180^{\circ}$ ), to which we apply the lemma. Accordingly, this refined polygon has a side $b$ and a vertex $H$ spanning a triangle $T$ of area $[T] \geq S / n$. If $b$ is a piece of a side $a_{i}$ of $\mathcal{P}$, then the triangle $W$ with base $a_{i}$ and summit $H$ has area

$$
[W]=k_{i} \cdot[T] \geq k_{i} \cdot S / n=q_{i} \cdot S>S_{i}
$$
in contradiction with the definition of $S_{i}$. This ends the proof.

problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral with no two sides parallel. Let \(K, L, M\), and \(N\) be points lying on sides \(AB, BC, CD\), and \(DA\), respectively, such that \(KLMN\) is a rhombus with \(KL \parallel AC\) and \(LM \parallel BD\). Let \(\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}\), and \(\omega_{4}\) be the incircles of triangles \(ANK\), \(BKL\), \(CLM\), and \(DMN\), respectively. Prove that the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{3}\) and the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{2}\) and \(\omega_{4}\) are concurrent.
solution:
Let $I_{i}$ be the center of $\omega_{i}$, and let $r_{i}$ be its radius for $i=1,2,3,4$. Denote by $T_{1}$ and $T_{3}$ the points of tangency of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ with $N K$ and $L M$, respectively. Suppose that the internal common tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ meet at point $S$, which is the center of homothety $h$ with negative ratio (namely, with ratio $-\frac{r_{3}}{r_{1}}$ ) mapping $\omega_{1}$ to $\omega_{3}$. This homothety takes $T_{1}$ to $T_{3}$ (since the tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ at $T_{1}$ to $T_{3}$ are parallel), hence $S$ is a point on the segment $T_{1} T_{3}$ with $T_{1} S: S T_{3}=r_{1}: r_{3}$.

Construct segments $S_{1} S_{3} \| K L$ and $S_{2} S_{4} \| L M$ through $S$ with $S_{1} \in N K, S_{2} \in K L$, $S_{3} \in L M$, and $S_{4} \in M N$. Note that $h$ takes $S_{1}$ to $S_{3}$, hence $I_{1} S_{1} \| I_{3} S_{3}$, and $S_{1} S: S S_{3}=r_{1}: r_{3}$. We will prove that $S_{2} S: S S_{4}=r_{2}: r_{4}$ or, equivalently, $K S_{1}: S_{1} N=r_{2}: r_{4}$. This will yield the problem statement; indeed, applying similar arguments to the intersection point $S^{\prime}$ of the internal common tangents to $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{4}$, we see that $S^{\prime}$ satisfies similar relations, and there is a unique point inside $K L M N$ satisfying them. Therefore, $S^{\prime}=S$.

Further, denote by $I_{A}, I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ and $r_{A}, r_{B}, r_{C}, r_{D}$ the incenters and inradii of triangles $D A B, A B C, B C D$, and $C D A$, respectively. One can shift triangle $C L M$ by $\overrightarrow{L K}$ to glue it with triangle $A K N$ into a quadrilateral $A K C^{\prime} N$ similar to $A B C D$. In particular, this shows that $r_{1}: r_{3}=r_{A}: r_{C}$; similarly, $r_{2}: r_{4}=r_{B}: r_{D}$. Moreover, the same shift takes $S_{3}$ to $S_{1}$, and it also takes $I_{3}$ to the incenter $I_{3}^{\prime}$ of triangle $K C^{\prime} N$. Since $I_{1} S_{1} \| I_{3} S_{3}$, the points $I_{1}, S_{1}, I_{3}^{\prime}$ are collinear. Thus, in order to complete the solution, it suffices to apply the following Lemma to quadrilateral $A K C^{\prime} N$.
Lemma 1. Let $A B C D$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, and define $I_{A}, I_{C}, r_{B}$, and $r_{D}$ as above. Let $I_{A} I_{C}$ meet $B D$ at $X$; then $B X: X D=r_{B}: r_{D}$.
Proof. Consider an inversion centered at $X$; the images under that inversion will be denoted by primes, e.g., $A^{\prime}$ is the image of $A$.

By properties of inversion, we have

$$
\angle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle X I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle X D I_{A}=\angle B D A / 2=\angle B C A / 2=\angle A C I_{B}
$$

We obtain $\angle I_{A}^{\prime} I_{C}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle C A I_{B}$ likewise; therefore, $\triangle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime} \sim \triangle A C I_{B}$. In the same manner, we get $\triangle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} B^{\prime} \sim \triangle A C I_{D}$, hence the quadrilaterals $I_{C}^{\prime} B^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}$ and $A I_{D} C I_{B}$ are also similar. But the diagonals $A C$ and $I_{B} I_{D}$ of quadrilateral $A I_{D} C I_{B}$ meet at a point $Y$ such that $I_{B} Y$ :
$Y I_{D}=r_{B}: r_{D}$. By similarity, we get $D^{\prime} X: B^{\prime} X=r_{B}: r_{D}$ and hence $B X: X D=D^{\prime} X$ : $B^{\prime} X=r_{B}: r_{D}$.

Comment 1. The solution above shows that the problem statement holds also for any parallelogram $K L M N$ whose sides are parallel to the diagonals of $A B C D$, as no property specific for a rhombus has been used. This solution works equally well when two sides of quadrilateral $A B C D$ are parallel.

Comment 2. The problem may be reduced to Lemma $1$ by using different tools, e.g., by using mass point geometry, linear motion of $K, L, M$, and $N$, etc.

Lemma $1$ itself also can be proved in different ways. We present below one alternative proof.
Proof. In the circumcircle of $A B C D$, let $K^{\prime}, L^{\prime} . M^{\prime}$, and $N^{\prime}$ be the midpoints of arcs $A B, B C$, $C D$, and $D A$ containing no other vertices of $A B C D$, respectively. Thus, $K^{\prime}=C I_{B} \cap D I_{A}$, etc. In the computations below, we denote by $[P]$ the area of a polygon $P$. We use similarities $\triangle I_{A} B K^{\prime} \sim$ $\triangle I_{A} D N^{\prime}, \triangle I_{B} K^{\prime} L^{\prime} \sim \triangle I_{B} A C$, etc., as well as congruences $\triangle I_{B} K^{\prime} L^{\prime}=\triangle B K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$ and $\triangle I_{D} M^{\prime} N^{\prime}=$ $\triangle D M^{\prime} N^{\prime}$ (e.g., the first congruence holds because $K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$ is a common internal bisector of angles $B K^{\prime} I_{B}$ and $\left.B L^{\prime} I_{B}\right)$.

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{B X}{D X}=\frac{\left[I_{A} B I_{C}\right]}{\left[I_{A} D I_{C}\right]}=\frac{B I_{A} \cdot B I_{C} \cdot \sin I_{A} B I_{C}}{D I_{A} \cdot D I_{C} \cdot \sin I_{A} D I_{C}}=\frac{B I_{A}}{D I_{A}} \cdot \frac{B I_{C}}{D I_{C}} \cdot \frac{\sin N^{\prime} B M^{\prime}}{\sin K^{\prime} D L^{\prime}} \\
& =\frac{B K^{\prime}}{D N^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{B L^{\prime}}{D M^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{\sin N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}}{\sin K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}}=\frac{B K^{\prime} \cdot B L^{\prime} \cdot \sin K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}}{D N^{\prime} \cdot D M^{\prime} \cdot \sin N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{\sin ^{2} N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}}{\sin ^{2} K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}} \\
& \quad=\frac{\left[K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}\right]}{\left[M^{\prime} D N^{\prime}\right]} \cdot \frac{N^{\prime} M^{\prime 2}}{K^{\prime} L^{\prime 2}}=\frac{\left[K^{\prime} I_{B} L^{\prime}\right] \cdot \frac{A^{\prime} C^{\prime 2}}{K^{\prime} L^{\prime 2}}}{\left[M^{\prime} I_{D} N^{\prime}\right] \cdot \frac{A^{\prime} C^{\prime 2}}{N^{\prime} M^{\prime 2}}}=\frac{\left[A I_{B} C\right]}{\left[A I_{D} C\right]}=\frac{r_{B}}{r_{D}},
\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

problem: Given that \( \triangle ABC \) is a triangle where \( AB < AC \). On the half-lines \( BA \) and \( CA \), we take points \( F \) and \( E \) respectively such that \( BF = CE = BC \). Let \( M, N, \) and \( H \) be the midpoints of the segments \( BF, CE, \) and \( BC \) respectively, and let \( K \) and \( O \) be the circumcenters of the triangles \( \triangle ABC \) and \( \triangle MNH \) respectively. We assume that line \( OK \) cuts \( BE \) and \( HN \) at the points \( A_1 \) and \( B_1 \) respectively, and that \( C_1 \) is the point of intersection of \( HN \) and \( FE \). If the parallel line from \( A_1 \) to \( OC_1 \) cuts the line \( FE \) at \( D \) and the perpendicular from \( A_1 \) to the line \( DB_1 \) cuts \( FE \) at the point \( M_1 \), prove that \( E \) is the orthocenter of the triangle \( \triangle A_1OM_1 \).
solution:
The circumcenter of the triangle $\triangle M N H$ coincides with the incentre of the triangle $\triangle A B C$ because the triangles $\triangle B M H$ and $\triangle N H C$ are isosceles and therefore the perpendiculars of the $M H, H N$ are also the bisectors of the angles $\angle A B C, \angle A C B$, respectively.

Let $G, I$ be the points of tangents of the incircle $(O, r)$ of the triangle $\triangle A B C$ with the sides $A B$ and $A C$ respectively. Now if $a, b, c$ are the sides of the triangle $\triangle A B C$ and $s$ the semiperimeter of the triangle , we have

$$
O F^{2}=O G^{2}+F G^{2}=r^{2}+(a-s+b)^{2}
$$
and
$$
O E^{2}=O I^{2}+E I^{2}=r^{2}+(a-s+c)^{2}
$$

Then

$$
O F^{2}-O E^{2}=\alpha(b-c)
$$

Applying two times the theorem of Stewarts at the triangles $\triangle K F B$ and $\triangle K A C$ we get

$$
F A \cdot K A^{2}+c \cdot K F^{2}=a \cdot K A^{2}+a c \cdot F A \quad \text { or } \quad K F^{2}=K A^{2}+a(a-c)
$$
and
$$
E A \cdot K E^{2}+\alpha \cdot K A^{2}=b \cdot K E^{2}+a b \cdot E A \quad \text { or } \quad K E^{2}=K A^{2}+a(b-a)
$$

From (2) and (3) we have

$$
K F^{2}-K E^{2}=a(a-c)-a(b-a)=\alpha(b-c)
$$

From (1),(4), because $O F^{2}-O E^{2}=K F^{2}-K E^{2}$ we have that $F E \perp O K$.

Let $J$ the point of intersection of $F E, O K$.
Because $A_{1} D / / O C_{1}$ we have

$$
\frac{J O}{J A_{1}}=\frac{J C_{1}}{J D}
$$

And since $A_{1} E / / H N$ we get

$$
\frac{J E}{J A_{1}}=\frac{J C_{1}}{J B_{1}}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\frac{J O}{J E}=\frac{J B_{1}}{J D}
$$

Thus, from the inverse of Thales theorem we have that $E O / / D B_{1}$, So

$$
A M_{1} \perp E O
$$

Consequently, the point $E$ is the orthocenter of the triangle $\triangle A_{1} O M_{1}$
Remark(PSC): Here in the solution the side $B C$ has been referred as $\alpha$ and $a$, which are equivalent.

problem:
Prove that there is no function from positive real numbers to itself, \( f:(0,+\infty) \rightarrow(0,+\infty) \) such that:

\[
f(f(x)+y)=f(x)+3x+yf(y) \quad \text{for every} \quad x, y \in(0,+\infty)
\]
solution:
First we prove that $f(x) \geq x$ for all $x>0$.
Indeed, if there is an $a>0$ with $f(a)<a$ then from the initial for $x=a$ and $y=a-f(a)>0$ we get that $3 a+(a-f(a)) f(a-f(a))=0$. This is absurd since $3 a+(a-f(a)) f(a-f(a))>0$.
So we have that

$$
f(x) \geq x \quad \text {,for all } \quad x>0
$$

Then using (1) we have that $f(x)+3 x+y f(x)=f(f(x)+y) \geq f(x)+y$, so

$$
3 x+y f(y) \geq y \quad, \text { all } \quad x, y>0
$$

Suppose that $y f(y)<y$ for a $y>0$ and let $-y f(y)=b>0$ then for $x=\frac{b}{4}$ we get $\frac{3 b}{4}-b \geq 0$ so $b \leq 0$, absurd. So we have that $y f(y) \geq y$, for all $y>0$, and so

$$
f(y) \geq 1 \quad \text {,for all } \quad y>0
$$

Substituting $y$ with $f(y)$ at the initial we have that

$$
f(x)+3 x+f(y) f(f(y))=f(f(x)+f(y))
$$
and changing the roles of $x, y$ we have that:
$$
f(y)+3 y+f(x) f(f(x))=f(f(x)+f(x))
$$

So we have $f(x) f(f(x))-f(x)-3 x=f(y) f(f(y))-f(y)-3 y$, which means that the function $f(x) f(f(x))-$ $f(x)-3 x$ is constant. That means that there exist a constant $c$ such that

$$
f(x) f(f(x))=f(x)+3 x+c \quad \text {,for all } \quad x>0
$$

So we can write (6) in the form $f(x)(f(f(x))-1)=3 x+c$ and since $f(f(x))>1$ we have that $3 x+c \geq 0$, for all $x>0$. if $c<0$ then for $x=-\frac{c}{4}>0$ we get that $c>0$ which is absurd. So $c \geq 0$.
We write (6) in the form

$$
f(f(x))=1+\frac{3 x}{f(x)}+\frac{c}{f(x)}
$$

Since $c \geq 0$ then from (7) with the help of (1) and (3) we have that $f(f(x)) \leq 4+c$.
But from (1) we have that $f(f(x)) \geq f(x) \geq x$, for all $x \geq 0$, and so

$$
4+c \geq f(f(x)) \geq x \quad \text {,for all } \quad x>0
$$

Taking $x=5+c$ we get that the last one cannot hold. So there is no such a function.

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive real numbers such that \(abc = 1\). Prove that

\[
\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+a^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+b^{2}} \leq 1.
\]
solution:
First we remark that

$$
a^{5}+b^{5} \geq a b\left(a^{3}+b^{3}\right)
$$

Indeed

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{5}+b^{5} \geq a b\left(a^{3}+b^{3}\right) & \Leftrightarrow a^{5}-a^{4} b-a b^{4}+b^{5} \geq 0 \\
& \Leftrightarrow a^{4}(a-b)-b^{4}(a-b) \geq 0 \\
(a-b)\left(a^{4}-b^{4}\right) \geq 0 & \Leftrightarrow(a-b)^{2}\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)(a+b) \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the inequality as

$$
\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+a b c^{3}}+\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+b c a^{3}}+\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+c a b^{3}} \leq 1 .
$$

On the other hand the following inequality is true

$$
a^{5}+b^{5}+a b c^{3} \geq a b\left(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\right)
$$
and similar for the other two.
Finally, using AM-GM we get:
\$\$\begin{aligned}

\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+a^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+b^{2}} \& \leq \frac{1}{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}\left(\frac{1}{a b}+\frac{1}{b c}+\frac{1}{c a}\right)=\frac{a+b+c}{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}} 
\& \leq \frac{a+b+c}{\frac{(a+b+c)^{3}}{9}}=\frac{9}{(a+b+c)^{2}} \leq \frac{9}{(3 \sqrt[3]{a b c})^{2}}=1

\end{aligned}\$\$

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive real numbers such that \(abc = 1\). Prove that

\[
\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+a^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+b^{2}} \leq 1.
\]
solution:
Let  

\[
S=\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+a^{2}}+\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+b^{2}},
\qquad a,b,c>0,\;abc=1 .
\]

We prove that \(S\le 1\) and that equality is attained only at \(a=b=c=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  An algebraic lemma  

For every positive numbers \(x,y\) we have  
\[
x^{5}+y^{5}\ge xy\bigl(x^{3}+y^{3}\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

Indeed
\[
x^{5}+y^{5}-xy\left(x^{3}+y^{3}\right)
      =x^{5}-x^{4}y+y^{5}-xy^{4}
      =(x-y)(x^{4}-y^{4})
      =(x-y)^{2}\!\left(x^{3}+x^{2}y+xy^{2}+y^{3}\right)\ge 0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A bound for each summand of \(S\)

Apply (1) with \(x=a,\;y=b\).  
Because \(abc=1\), i.e. \(ab=\dfrac1c\), we obtain
\[
a^{5}+b^{5}\;\ge\;\frac{1}{c}\bigl(a^{3}+b^{3}\bigr),
\]
hence
\[
a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}\;\ge\;\frac{a^{3}+b^{3}}{c}+c^{2}.
\]

Taking the reciprocal of both sides (quantities are positive) and multiplying numerator and denominator by \(c\) gives

\[
\frac{1}{a^{5}+b^{5}+c^{2}}
      \le\frac{c}{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}.
\tag{2}
\]

By cyclic permutation we analogously have

\[
\frac{1}{b^{5}+c^{5}+a^{2}}\le\frac{a}{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}},\qquad
\frac{1}{c^{5}+a^{5}+b^{2}}\le\frac{b}{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}.
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Summing the three inequalities  

Adding (2) and (3) yields  

\[
S\le\frac{a+b+c}{\,a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}.
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  A comparison of the two symmetric sums  

We claim that
\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\;\ge\;a+b+c.
\tag{5}
\]

Because \(abc=1\), by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality we know  
\(a+b+c\ge 3\).  For every positive \(t\) we have \(t^{3}+1+1\ge 3t\)
(AM–GM on the three numbers \(t^{3},1,1\)).
Applying this to \(t=a,b,c\) and summing, we get  

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+6 \;\ge\; 3(a+b+c).
\]

Since \(a+b+c\ge 3\), we can subtract \(a+b+c\) from the right–hand side
without reversing the inequality:
\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}\;\ge\;a+b+c,
\]
which is exactly (5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Completion of the proof  

Inequality (5) implies that the right–hand side of (4) does not exceed \(1\);
hence  

\[
S\le 1.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Equality case  

All inequalities used become equalities simultaneously only when  
\(a=b=c=1\) (then \(abc=1\) and every step above is tight).  
Therefore \(S=1\) exactly for \(a=b=c=1\).

problem: Given a positive odd integer \( n \), show that the arithmetic mean of fractional parts \(\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}\), \( k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \), is the same for infinitely many primes \( p \).
solution:
We show that the arithmetic mean in question is $\frac{1}{2}$ for infinitely many primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$.
Notice that $\left\{\frac{k^{2 n}}{p}\right\}=\frac{r_{k}}{p}$, where $r_{k}$ is the remainder $k^{2 n}$ leaves upon division by $p$. Clearly, the $r_{k}$ are quadratic residues modulo $p$.
If $p$ is prime, and $p-1$ and $n$ are relatively prime, then the $r_{k}, k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}$, are pairwise distinct, since the $k^{2 n}, k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}$, are pairwise distinct modulo $p$, by Fermat's little theorem. In this case, the $r_{k}, k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}$, form the set $R$ of all $\frac{p-1}{2}$ quadratic residues modulo $p$ in the range $1$ through $p-1$.
If, in addition, $p$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, then $-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$, and the assignment $r \mapsto p-r, r \in R$, defines a permutation of $R$. In this case,

$$
\sum_{r \in R} r=\sum_{r \in R}(p-r)=\frac{p(p-1)}{2}-\sum_{r \in R} r
$$
so
$$
\sum_{r \in R} r=\frac{p(p-1)}{4},
$$

and the arithmetic mean in question is $\frac{1}{2}$.
Finally, since $n$ is odd, infinitely many primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ are also congruent to $2$ modulo $n$, by Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic sequences of integers; for such a prime $p$, the numbers $p-1$ and $n$ are clearly relatively prime. This completes the proof.

problem: Given a positive odd integer \( n \), show that the arithmetic mean of fractional parts \(\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}\), \( k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \), is the same for infinitely many primes \( p \).
solution:
We are given a fixed positive odd integer $ n $, and we are to show that the arithmetic mean of the fractional parts $ \left\{ \frac{k^{2n}}{p} \right\} $, for $ k = 1, 2, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2} $, is the same for **infinitely many primes $ p $**.

---

### Step 1: Understanding the Structure of the Problem

We are interested in the arithmetic mean of the fractional parts:

$$
\text{Mean} = \frac{1}{(p-1)/2} \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} \left\{ \frac{k^{2n}}{p} \right\}
$$

Recall that the fractional part $ \left\{ x \right\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor $, and for $ x = \frac{k^{2n}}{p} $, this becomes:

$$
\left\{ \frac{k^{2n}}{p} \right\} = \frac{k^{2n} \bmod p}{p}
$$

So the sum becomes:

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} \left\{ \frac{k^{2n}}{p} \right\} = \frac{1}{p} \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} (k^{2n} \bmod p)
$$

Hence, the arithmetic mean is:

$$
\text{Mean} = \frac{1}{(p-1)/2} \cdot \frac{1}{p} \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} (k^{2n} \bmod p)
$$

---

### Step 2: Using Number-Theoretic Properties

Let us analyze the structure of the sum $ \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} k^{2n} \bmod p $. Since $ n $ is fixed and odd, the exponent $ 2n $ is even. This implies that the function $ f(k) = k^{2n} $ is **even**, i.e., $ f(k) = f(-k) $, and since $ -k \equiv p - k \mod p $, we have:

$$
k^{2n} \equiv (p - k)^{2n} \mod p
$$

This symmetry implies that the values of $ k^{2n} \mod p $ are the same for $ k $ and $ p - k $, and hence, the values of $ k^{2n} \mod p $ are symmetric about $ p/2 $.

Therefore, the set $ \{ k^{2n} \mod p : k = 1, 2, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2} \} $ is exactly the set of **quadratic residues modulo $ p $**. This is because the exponentiation map $ k \mapsto k^{2n} \mod p $ has image equal to the quadratic residues when $ \gcd(2n, p-1) = 2 $, which we will ensure.

---

### Step 3: Ensuring the Mapping is Onto the Quadratic Residues

Let us suppose that $ \gcd(2n, p-1) = 2 $. Then, the mapping $ k \mapsto k^{2n} \mod p $ is a 2-to-1 map from the multiplicative group $ \mathbb{F}_p^* $ to the subgroup of quadratic residues. Since we are summing over $ k = 1 $ to $ \frac{p-1}{2} $, and the mapping is symmetric, this sum will exactly cover each quadratic residue **once**.

So, the sum $ \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} k^{2n} \bmod p $ is equal to the **sum of all quadratic residues modulo $ p $**.

---

### Step 4: Sum of Quadratic Residues Modulo $ p $

A key result from number theory is that **when $ p \equiv 1 \mod 4 $**, the quadratic residues modulo $ p $ can be paired as $ (a, p - a) $, each summing to $ p $. There are $ (p-1)/4 $ such pairs, so the total sum of all quadratic residues is:

$$
\sum_{\text{QR}} a = p \cdot \frac{p - 1}{4}
$$

Thus, the sum of the fractional parts is:

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} \left\{ \frac{k^{2n}}{p} \right\} = \frac{1}{p} \cdot \sum_{\text{QR}} a = \frac{1}{p} \cdot \frac{p(p-1)}{4} = \frac{p-1}{4}
$$

Then, the arithmetic mean is:

$$
\text{Mean} = \frac{1}{(p-1)/2} \cdot \frac{p-1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}
$$

---

### Step 5: Ensuring Infinitely Many Such Primes Exist

We now need to show that there are **infinitely many primes $ p $** such that:

- $ p \equiv 1 \mod 4 $,
- $ \gcd(2n, p-1) = 2 $, which implies $ \gcd(n, (p-1)/2) = 1 $.

Let us define a modulus $ M = 4 \cdot \text{lcm}(2, n) $, and consider the congruence:

$$
p \equiv 1 \mod 4, \quad \text{and } p \not\equiv 1 \mod 2q \text{ for each prime } q \mid n
$$

This ensures that $ \gcd(n, (p-1)/2) = 1 $. By the **Chinese Remainder Theorem**, there exists a unique congruence class modulo $ M $ satisfying these conditions. Since the modulus is fixed and the congruence class is non-empty, **Dirichlet's Theorem** guarantees that there are **infinitely many primes** in this congruence class.

Thus, there are **infinitely many primes $ p $** such that $ p \equiv 1 \mod 4 $ and $ \gcd(2n, p-1) = 2 $, and for each such prime, the arithmetic mean of the fractional parts is exactly:

$$
\frac{1}{2}
$$

problem: Given a positive odd integer \( n \), show that the arithmetic mean of fractional parts \(\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}\), \( k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \), is the same for infinitely many primes \( p \).
solution:
Let $S_p$ be the arithmetic mean of the fractional parts $\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}$ for $k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}$.
Let $m = (p-1)/2$. So $S_p = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^{m} \left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}$.
The fractional part $\left\{\frac{x}{p}\right\}$ is $\frac{x \pmod p}{p}$. Let $r_k = k^{2n} \pmod p$.
Then $S_p = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{r_k}{p} = \frac{1}{mp} \sum_{k=1}^{m} r_k$.

Let $X_p = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} (k^{2n} \pmod p)$.
Since $2n$ is an even exponent, we have $(p-k)^{2n} \equiv (-k)^{2n} \equiv k^{2n} \pmod p$.
The sum $\sum_{k=1}^{m} r_k = \sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} (k^{2n} \pmod p)$.
The sum $\sum_{k=(p+1)/2}^{p-1} (k^{2n} \pmod p) = \sum_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} ((p-j)^{2n} \pmod p) = \sum_{j=1}^{(p-1)/2} (j^{2n} \pmod p)$.
So $X_p = 2 \sum_{k=1}^{m} r_k$.
Therefore, $\sum_{k=1}^{m} r_k = X_p/2$.
Substituting this into the expression for $S_p$:
$S_p = \frac{X_p/2}{mp} = \frac{X_p/2}{((p-1)/2)p} = \frac{X_p}{(p-1)p}$.

Let $H$ be the image of the map $x \mapsto x^{2n}$ from $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$ to $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$. $H$ is a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$.
The elements $k^{2n} \pmod p$ for $k=1, \ldots, p-1$ are exactly the elements of $H$, where each element $y \in H$ appears $d = \gcd(2n, p-1)$ times.
So $X_p = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} (k^{2n} \pmod p) = d \sum_{y \in H} y$.
Thus, $S_p = \frac{d \sum_{y \in H} y}{(p-1)p}$.

This formula is valid unless $p-1$ divides $2n$.
If $p-1 | 2n$, then $k^{2n} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for all $k \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$.
In this case, $r_k=1$ for all $k=1, \ldots, m$.
Then $\sum_{k=1}^m r_k = m$.
So $S_p = \frac{m}{mp} = \frac{1}{p}$.
The condition $p-1 | 2n$ can only hold for a finite number of primes $p$ (namely $p \le 2n+1$). We are looking for a value that $S_p$ takes for infinitely many primes. $S_p=1/p$ is different for different $p$. So we will focus on primes $p$ such that $p-1 \nmid 2n$.

Let $k_H = |H|$ be the order of the subgroup $H$. We know $k_H = (p-1)/d$.
Substituting $d=(p-1)/k_H$ into the expression for $S_p$:
$S_p = \frac{((p-1)/k_H) \sum_{y \in H} y}{(p-1)p} = \frac{\sum_{y \in H} y}{k_H p}$.
We want to show $S_p$ is constant for infinitely many primes $p$. Let's test if $S_p=1/2$ is possible.
If $S_p=1/2$, then $\frac{\sum_{y \in H} y}{k_H p} = \frac{1}{2}$, which implies $\sum_{y \in H} y = \frac{k_H p}{2}$.

Consider the properties of $H$.
If $-1 \pmod p \in H$, then for any $y \in H$, its inverse $y^{-1} \in H$, and also $p-y \equiv -y \pmod p \in H$.
If $y \in H$, then $p-y \in H$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, $y \neq p-y$ (otherwise $2y=p$, which is impossible as $y$ is an integer).
Thus, elements of $H$ can be paired up $(y, p-y)$. There are $k_H/2$ such pairs. The sum of elements in each pair is $p$.
So, if $-1 \in H$ and $k_H$ is even, then $\sum_{y \in H} y = \frac{k_H}{2} \cdot p$.
In this case, $S_p = \frac{k_H p/2}{k_H p} = 1/2$.

The condition for $-1 \in H$ is that the congruence $x^{2n} \equiv -1 \pmod p$ is solvable.
This is true if and only if $(-1)^{(p-1)/d} \equiv 1 \pmod p$, where $d=\gcd(2n, p-1)$.
Since $p$ is an odd prime, $(-1)^{(p-1)/d}=1$ if and only if $(p-1)/d$ is even.
Note that $k_H = (p-1)/d$. So the condition is that $k_H$ must be even.
This is consistent with the pairing argument for $\sum_{y \in H} y$, which requires $k_H$ to be even.
If $k_H$ is odd, then $k_H p/2$ is not an integer (since $p$ is odd). But $\sum_{y \in H} y$ must be an integer.
So if $k_H$ is odd, $\sum_{y \in H} y \neq k_H p/2$, and thus $S_p \neq 1/2$.
Therefore, $S_p=1/2$ if and only if $k_H = (p-1)/d$ is even. (Assuming $p-1 \nmid 2n$. If $p-1|2n$, $k_H=1$, which is odd, and $S_p=1/p \neq 1/2$ for $p \neq 2$.)

Let $v_2(x)$ be the exponent of the highest power of 2 dividing $x$.
Let $2n = 2^s t_0$ where $t_0$ is an odd integer. Since $n$ is a positive odd integer, $n=2j+1$ for some $j \ge 0$.
So $2n = 2(2j+1)$. Thus $s=v_2(2n)=1$.
Let $p-1 = 2^r t_1$ where $t_1$ is an odd integer. Since $p$ is an odd prime, $p-1$ is even, so $r \ge 1$.
$d = \gcd(2n, p-1) = \gcd(2^s t_0, 2^r t_1) = 2^{\min(s,r)} \gcd(t_0, t_1)$.
Then $k_H = \frac{p-1}{d} = \frac{2^r t_1}{2^{\min(s,r)} \gcd(t_0, t_1)} = 2^{r-\min(s,r)} \frac{t_1}{\gcd(t_0, t_1)}$.
Since $t_1$ and $\gcd(t_0,t_1)$ are both odd, the fraction $\frac{t_1}{\gcd(t_0, t_1)}$ is an odd integer.
Thus, $k_H$ is even if and only if $2^{r-\min(s,r)}$ is even, which means $r-\min(s,r) \ge 1$.

We have $s=v_2(2n)=1$.
If $r \le s$, then $r=1$ (since $r \ge 1$). In this case, $\min(s,r)=r=1$. So $r-\min(s,r)=0$.
Then $k_H$ is odd. This happens when $v_2(p-1)=1$. This means $p-1 = 2 \cdot (\text{odd number})$, so $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
For $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ (and $p-1 \nmid 2n$), $S_p \neq 1/2$.

If $r > s$, then $\min(s,r)=s=1$. So $r-\min(s,r)=r-s = r-1 \ge 1$ (since $r>s=1$ means $r \ge 2$).
Then $k_H$ is even. This happens when $v_2(p-1) > v_2(2n)=1$, i.e. $v_2(p-1) \ge 2$.
This means $p-1$ is divisible by $2^2=4$. So $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
For these primes, $S_p=1/2$, provided $p-1 \nmid 2n$.

We need to find infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
By Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions, there are infinitely many primes in the arithmetic progression $4k+1$ for $k \ge 1$.
For each such prime $p$, we have $S_p=1/2$, unless $p-1 | 2n$.
The condition $p-1 | 2n$ implies $p-1 \le 2n$, so $p \le 2n+1$. This condition holds for only a finite number of primes.
Since we have an infinite list of primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, we can choose those $p > 2n+1$. There are still infinitely many such primes.
For these primes $p$, $p-1 \nmid 2n$ is satisfied, and $v_2(p-1) \ge 2 > v_2(2n)=1$, which implies $k_H=(p-1)/d$ is even.
Therefore, for these infinitely many primes $p$, the arithmetic mean $S_p$ is equal to $1/2$.

To summarize:
1.  The arithmetic mean is $S_p = \frac{d \sum_{y \in H} y}{(p-1)p}$, where $d=\gcd(2n,p-1)$ and $H=\{k^{2n} \pmod p : k \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*\}$. This formula is valid as long as $p-1 \nmid 2n$.
2.  If $k_H = |H| = (p-1)/d$ is even, then $-1 \in H$. This implies that the elements of $H$ can be paired as $(y, p-y)$, so $\sum_{y \in H} y = (k_H/2)p$.
3.  If $k_H$ is even, $S_p = \frac{d(k_H p/2)}{(p-1)p} = \frac{d((p-1)/d)p/2}{(p-1)p} = \frac{(p-1)p/2}{(p-1)p} = 1/2$.
4.  If $k_H$ is odd, then $k_H p/2$ is not an integer (as $p$ is an odd prime). Since $\sum_{y \in H} y$ is an integer sum of residues, $\sum_{y \in H} y \neq k_H p/2$. So $S_p \neq 1/2$.
5.  The integer $n$ is odd, so $2n=2(2j+1)$ for some integer $j \ge 0$. Thus $v_2(2n)=1$.
6.  $k_H$ is even if and only if $v_2(p-1) > v_2(2n)$. Given $v_2(2n)=1$, $k_H$ is even iff $v_2(p-1) > 1$, which means $v_2(p-1) \ge 2$. This is equivalent to $p-1$ being divisible by 4, i.e., $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
7.  By Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions, there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
8.  We must exclude primes $p$ for which $p-1 | 2n$. These are primes $p \le 2n+1$, which is a finite set. All primes $p > 2n+1$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ satisfy $p-1 \nmid 2n$ and $k_H$ is even.
9.  Thus, for infinitely many primes $p$ (namely, those $p > 2n+1$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$), the arithmetic mean $S_p$ is equal to $1/2$.

This shows that the arithmetic mean of the given fractional parts is the same (equal to $1/2$) for infinitely many primes $p$.

problem: Given a positive odd integer \( n \), show that the arithmetic mean of fractional parts \(\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}\), \( k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \), is the same for infinitely many primes \( p \).
solution:
Fix a positive odd integer \(n\), and set 
\[
m = 2n.
\]
We will show that for every prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
p \;\equiv\; 1 \pmod{4n},
\]
the arithmetic mean
\[
A_p \;=\;\frac{1}{\frac{p-1}{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
\]
equals \(1/2\).  Since by Dirichlet’s theorem there are infinitely many primes \(p\equiv1\pmod{4n}\), it will follow immediately that \(A_p\) takes the same value \(1/2\) for infinitely many primes \(p\), as required.

---

1.  **Grouping full residues.**  
    First we show that the average of the fractional parts \(\{k^m/p\}\) over the full reduced residue system \(\{1,2,\dots,p-1\}\) is \(1/2\).  Then we will deduce the same for the half–range \(k=1,\dots,\tfrac{p-1}{2}\).

    Because \(m\) is even, for each \(1\le k\le p-1\) the two integers \(k\) and \(p-k\) satisfy
    \[
    (p-k)^m \;=\; (-\,k)^m
    \;=\; k^m
    \quad(\bmod\;p).
    \]
    More precisely, by the binomial expansion,
    \[
    (p-k)^m
    \;=\;
    \sum_{i=0}^m\binom{m}{i}p^i(-k)^{\,m-i}
    \;=\;
    k^m \;+\; p\cdot Q
    \]
    for some integer \(Q\).  Hence
    \[
    \frac{(p-k)^m}{p}
    \;=\;
    \frac{k^m}{p} \;+\; Q,
    \]
    and taking fractional parts gives
    \[
    \Bigl\{\frac{(p-k)^m}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    \bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}+Q\bigr\}
    \;=\;
    \Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}.
    \]
    It follows that in the sum
    \(\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\{k^m/p\}\) the terms come in identical pairs \(\{k^m/p\}=\{(p-k)^m/p\}\).  Therefore
    \[
    \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    2\sum_{k=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\},
    \]
    and hence
    \[
    \frac{1}{\,p-1\,}\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    \frac{2}{\,p-1\,}\sum_{k=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    A_p.
    \]
    In particular, once we show the left–hand side equals \(1/2\), it will follow that \(A_p=1/2\).

2.  **Sum over a subgroup of \(m\)th powers.**  
    Since \(p\equiv1\pmod{4n}\), we have \(m=2n\mid p-1\).  Hence the map
    \[
      f: (\Bbb Z/p\Bbb Z)^\times\longrightarrow(\Bbb Z/p\Bbb Z)^\times,
      \quad
      f(k)=k^m,
    \]
    is a homomorphism of the cyclic group of order \(p-1\) onto its subgroup
    \[
      H \;=\;\{x^m: x\in(\Bbb Z/p\Bbb Z)^\times\}.
    \]
    Standard group theory tells us that \(\#H=(p-1)/m\).  Moreover each element \(h\in H\) has exactly \(m\) preimages under \(f\).  Hence when we sum the fractional parts \(\{k^m/p\}\) over all \(k=1,\dots,p-1\), the value \(\{h/p\}\) appears exactly \(m\) times for each \(h\in H\).  But for \(0<h<p\) we have
    \[
    \Bigl\{\frac{h}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    \frac{h}{p},
    \]
    so
    \[
    \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
    \;=\;
    \sum_{h\in H}
    m\;\frac{h}{p}
    \;=\;
    \frac{m}{p}\sum_{h\in H}h.
    \]
    Thus it remains only to compute the integer sum \(\sum_{h\in H}h\).

3.  **Pairing in \(H\) gives the exact sum.**  
    Write
    \[
    t \;=\;\#H \;=\;\frac{p-1}{m}.
    \]
    Because \(p\equiv1\pmod{4n}\) and \(m=2n\), we see
    \[
      t \;=\;\frac{p-1}{2n}
      \quad\text{is even.}
    \]
    Equivalently, \(-1\) belongs to the subgroup \(H\) (since in the cyclic group of order \(p-1\), \(-1\) is \(g^{(p-1)/2}\), and \((p-1)/2\) is a multiple of \(m\) exactly when \(4n\mid(p-1)\)).  Therefore whenever \(h\in H\), also
    \[
      -h\;(\bmod p)
      \;=\;
      p - h
    \]
    lies in \(H\).  Since \(H\subset\{1,2,\dots,p-1\}\) has even cardinality \(t\), we can partition \(H\) into \(t/2\) disjoint pairs \(\{h,p-h\}\).  Each such pair sums to
    \[
      h + (p-h)
      \;=\;
      p.
    \]
    Hence
    \[
      \sum_{h\in H}h
      \;=\;
      \frac{t}{2}\times p
      \;=\;
      p\;\frac{p-1}{2m}.
    \]
    Substituting back,
    \[
      \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
      \;=\;
      \frac{m}{p}\;\Bigl(p\,\frac{p-1}{2m}\Bigr)
      \;=\;
      \frac{p-1}{2}.
    \]
    Therefore
    \[
      \frac{1}{p-1}\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
      \;=\;
      \frac{p-1}{2(p-1)}
      \;=\;
      \tfrac12,
    \]
    and as observed in step 1 this forces
    \[
      A_p
      \;=\;
      \frac{1}{\frac{p-1}{2}}
      \sum_{k=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\Bigl\{\frac{k^m}{p}\Bigr\}
      \;=\;
      \tfrac12.
    \]

4.  **Conclusion via Dirichlet’s theorem.**  
    We have shown that whenever
    \[
      p\equiv1\pmod{4n},
    \]
    the arithmetic mean of the fractional parts \(\{k^{2n}/p\}\) over \(k=1,\dots,(p-1)/2\) is exactly \(1/2\).  Since there are infinitely many primes in the arithmetic progression \(1\pmod{4n}\) by Dirichlet’s theorem, it follows that this mean value is the same (namely \(1/2\)) for infinitely many primes \(p\).  This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem: Given a positive odd integer \( n \), show that the arithmetic mean of fractional parts \(\left\{\frac{k^{2n}}{p}\right\}\), \( k=1, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \), is the same for infinitely many primes \( p \).
solution:
Let  

m = (p-1)/2, R(p) = {k² (mod p) : 1 ≤ k ≤ m}                (1)

and for an odd integer n put  

Sₙ(p)=∑_{k=1}^{m}(k^{2n} mod p),  Aₙ(p)= 1 m · 1 p Sₙ(p).             (2)

Aₙ(p) is exactly the required arithmetic mean

Aₙ(p)= 1 m ∑_{k=1}^{m}{k^{2n}/p}= 1 m ∑_{k=1}^{m} (k^{2n} mod p)/p= Sₙ(p)/(mp).   (3)

The proof proceeds in four steps.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The set R(p) and its sum  

Because (−k)² = k², every quadratic residue modulo p occurs
exactly once among the numbers k² , 1 ≤ k ≤ m; hence

R(p) = {k² mod p : 1 ≤ k ≤ m} and |R(p)| = m.                 (4)

----------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The sum of quadratic residues for p ≡ 1 (mod 4)

Introduce the Legendre symbol (a/p) and write the indicator of
“quadratic residue’’ as (1+(a/p))/2.  Then

∑_{a=1}^{p-1} a · (1+(a/p))/2
      = ½∑_{a=1}^{p-1} a + ½∑_{a=1}^{p-1} a(a/p).             (5)

The first sum equals p(p−1)/4.  
For p ≡ 1 (mod 4) we have (−1/p)=1; pairing a with p−a gives

∑_{a=1}^{p-1} a(a/p)=0.                                       (6)

Consequently  

Σ_R(p) := ∑_{r∈R(p)} r = p(p−1)/4  when p ≡ 1 (mod 4).      (7)

----------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Raising quadratic residues to an odd power

The multiplicative group of quadratic residues,  
G = R(p)\{0}, has order m.  
For fixed odd n, the map  

φ_n : G → G ,  r ↦ r^n                                       (8)

is a group endomorphism.  If gcd(n,m)=1 the map is an
automorphism, hence a permutation of R(p).  Therefore

gcd(n,m)=1 ⇒ {r^n : r∈R(p)} = R(p)                           (9)

and

Sₙ(p)  = ∑_{k=1}^{m}(k^{2n} mod p)
        = ∑_{r∈R(p)} r^n
        = ∑_{r∈R(p)} r = Σ_R(p).                             (10)

----------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Primes for which Aₙ(p) is constant

Take any odd n.  Choose one reduced residue class a (mod

M = 4⋅∏_{q|n} q), for instance

a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a ≡ 2 (mod q) for every prime factor q of n. (11)

Because gcd(a,M)=1, Dirichlet’s theorem on arithmetic progressions
furnishes infinitely many primes

p ≡ a (mod M).                                                (12)

For such p we have p ≡ 1 (mod 4), hence (7) is valid, and moreover

(p−1)/2 ≡ (a−1)/2 ≡ 1 (mod q) for every q|n,                 (13)

so no prime divisor of n divides m; i.e. gcd(n,m)=1.  
Applying (10) and (7) we obtain

Sₙ(p) = Σ_R(p) = p(p−1)/4,                                   (14)
Aₙ(p) = Sₙ(p)/(mp) = [p(p−1)/4] / [m p] = ½.                 (15)

Thus the arithmetic mean equals the constant value 1/2 for every
prime in the infinite set (12).  In particular, the mean is the
same (namely 1/2) for infinitely many primes, which completes the
proof.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle. Variable points \( E \) and \( F \) are on sides \( AC \) and \( AB \) respectively such that \( BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA \). As \( E \) and \( F \) vary, prove that the circumcircle of \( \triangle AEF \) passes through a fixed point other than \( A \).
solution:
Let $H$ be the ortocenter of $A B C$ and $K, L, M$ be the feet of perpendiculars respectively from $A, B, C$ to their opposite sides of $A B C$. Also let $D$ be the intersection point of lines $B E$ and $C F$. From power of point we have

$$
B A \cdot B M=B C \cdot B K
$$
and
$$
C A \cdot C L=C B \cdot C K
$$

Adding (1) and (2) we have:

$$
C A \cdot C L+B A \cdot B M=B C \cdot B K+C B \cdot C K=B C(B K+C K)=B C^{2}
$$

Combining (3) with the problem statement $B C^{2}=B A \cdot B F+C E \cdot C A$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& B A \cdot B F-B A \cdot B M=C A \cdot C L-C E \cdot C A \\
& B A(B F-B M)=C A(C L-C E) \\
& B A \cdot F M=C A \cdot L E \\
& \quad \frac{L E}{F M}=\frac{A B}{A C}=\frac{B L}{C M}
\end{aligned}
$$

Where the last equality follows from $\triangle A M C \sim \triangle A L B$. Now since $\frac{L E}{F M}=\frac{B L}{C M}$ and $\angle F M C=\angle E L B=90^{\circ}$ we get that triangles $\triangle F M C \sim \triangle E L B$. From this similarity we get

$$
\measuredangle A E D=\measuredangle A E B=\angle L E B=\measuredangle M F C=180^{\circ}-\angle A F C=180-\angle A F D,
$$
meaning points $A, D, E, F$ are concylic.
Since both pairs $\{E, F\}$ and $\{M, L\}$ satisfy the problem condition, we must have this fixed point we are looking for is the second intersection of the circumcircles around $A F D E$ and AMHL. Let this point be $X$. We now prove that $X$ is fixed on the circumcircle of $A M H L$ (which would imply $X$ is fixed).
From the concylicity we have
$$
\angle X L E=180^{\circ}-\measuredangle X L A=\measuredangle X M A=\angle X M F \text { and } \measuredangle X E L=\measuredangle X E A=180-\measuredangle X F A=\measuredangle X F M
$$

and from here we get $\triangle X L E \sim \triangle X M F$. This similarity gives us

$$
\frac{X L}{X M}=\frac{L E}{M F} .
$$

Now combining (4) and (5) we get $\frac{X L}{X M}=\frac{A B}{A C}$ which is a fixed quantity. Since points $M, L$, the circumcircle of $A M L$, and ratio $\frac{X L}{X M}$ are fixed, this implies that point $X$ is fixed.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle. Variable points \( E \) and \( F \) are on sides \( AC \) and \( AB \) respectively such that \( BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA \). As \( E \) and \( F \) vary, prove that the circumcircle of \( \triangle AEF \) passes through a fixed point other than \( A \).
solution:
We proceed with a coordinate geometry approach. Place \(\triangle ABC\) in the coordinate plane with \(A\) at the origin \((0,0)\) and \(B\) at \((c,0)\), where \(AB = c\). Let \(C\) be at \((p,q)\), with \(AC = b\) and \(BC = a\). Since \(\triangle ABC\) is acute, all angles are less than \(90^\circ\), so \(p\) and \(q\) satisfy \(p^2 + q^2 = b^2\) and \((p - c)^2 + q^2 = a^2\). Solving these equations, we obtain:
\[
p = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2c}, \quad q = \sqrt{b^2 - p^2}.
\]
The condition \(BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA\) translates to \(a^2 = c \cdot BF + CE \cdot b\). Since \(F\) is on \(AB\), let \(AF = x\), so \(BF = c - x\). Similarly, since \(E\) is on \(AC\), let \(AE = y\), so \(CE = b - y\). Substituting, we have:
\[
a^2 = c(c - x) + b(b - y) = c^2 - cx + b^2 - by,
\]
which rearranges to:
\[
by + cx = b^2 + c^2 - a^2.
\]
From the law of cosines, \(b^2 + c^2 - a^2 = 2bc \cos A\), and since \(\cos A = p/b\) (as the dot product of vectors \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (c,0)\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC} = (p,q)\) is \(cp\), so \(\cos A = \frac{cp}{c b} = \frac{p}{b}\)), we have:
\[
by + cx = 2bc \cdot \frac{p}{b} = 2cp.
\]
Thus, the constraint is:
\[
by + cx = 2cp. \quad (1)
\]

Now, the coordinates of the points are \(A(0,0)\), \(F(x,0)\), and \(E\left(\frac{y}{b}p, \frac{y}{b}q\right)\). The circumcircle of \(\triangle AEF\) has the general equation \(x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0\). Since it passes through \(A(0,0)\), substituting gives \(F = 0\), so the equation simplifies to:
\[
x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey = 0. \quad (2)
\]
Substituting \(F(x,0)\) into (2):
\[
x^2 + Dx = 0.
\]
Since \(x \neq 0\) (as \(F\) is not \(A\)), we solve for \(D\):
\[
D = -x. \quad (3)
\]
Substituting \(E\left(\frac{y}{b}p, \frac{y}{b}q\right)\) into (2) and using (3):
\[
\left(\frac{y}{b}p\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}q\right)^2 + (-x)\left(\frac{y}{b}p\right) + E\left(\frac{y}{b}q\right) = 0,
\]
which simplifies to:
\[
\frac{y^2}{b^2}(p^2 + q^2) - \frac{x y p}{b} + \frac{E y q}{b} = 0.
\]
Since \(p^2 + q^2 = b^2\) and \(y \neq 0\) (as \(E\) is not \(A\)), divide by \(y/b\):
\[
y b + E q - x p = 0,
\]
solving for \(E\):
\[
E = \frac{x p - y b}{q}. \quad (4)
\]

We now find a fixed point \((s,t)\) that lies on the circumcircle for all \(x\) and \(y\) satisfying (1). Substituting (3) and (4) into (2) for \((s,t)\):
\[
s^2 + t^2 + (-x)s + \left(\frac{x p - y b}{q}\right)t = 0.
\]
From (1), \(by = 2cp - cx\), so \(y = \frac{c(2p - x)}{b}\). Substituting:
\[
s^2 + t^2 - x s + \frac{1}{q} \left( x p - b \cdot \frac{c(2p - x)}{b} \right) t = s^2 + t^2 - x s + \frac{1}{q} \left( x p - c(2p - x) \right) t.
\]
Simplifying the expression inside:
\[
x p - c(2p - x) = x p - 2c p + c x = x(p + c) - 2c p.
\]
Thus:
\[
s^2 + t^2 - x s + \frac{1}{q} \left( x(p + c) - 2c p \right) t = s^2 + t^2 + x \left( -s + \frac{(p + c)t}{q} \right) - \frac{2c p t}{q} = 0.
\]
This must hold for all \(x\), so the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant term must separately be zero:
\[
-s + \frac{(p + c)t}{q} = 0, \quad (5)
\]
\[
s^2 + t^2 - \frac{2c p t}{q} = 0. \quad (6)
\]
From (5):
\[
s = \frac{(p + c)t}{q}. \quad (7)
\]
Substitute (7) into (6):
\[
\left( \frac{(p + c)t}{q} \right)^2 + t^2 - \frac{2c p t}{q} = 0,
\]
\[
t^2 \left( \frac{(p + c)^2}{q^2} + 1 \right) - \frac{2c p t}{q} = 0.
\]
Since \(t \neq 0\) (as the fixed point is not \(A\)), divide by \(t\):
\[
t \left( \frac{(p + c)^2}{q^2} + 1 \right) - \frac{2c p}{q} = 0.
\]
Simplify:
\[
t \left( \frac{(p + c)^2 + q^2}{q^2} \right) = \frac{2c p}{q},
\]
\[
t \cdot \frac{(p + c)^2 + q^2}{q^2} = \frac{2c p}{q},
\]
\[
t = \frac{2c p}{q} \cdot \frac{q^2}{(p + c)^2 + q^2} = \frac{2c p q}{(p + c)^2 + q^2}. \quad (8)
\]
From (7):
\[
s = \frac{(p + c)}{q} \cdot \frac{2c p q}{(p + c)^2 + q^2} = \frac{2c p (p + c)}{(p + c)^2 + q^2}. \quad (9)
\]

The denominator \((p + c)^2 + q^2\) is fixed for \(\triangle ABC\), as \(p\) and \(q\) are fixed. Thus, \((s,t)\) is a fixed point. It is not \(A(0,0)\) since, in an acute triangle, \(q > 0\) and \(p\) and \(c\) are positive, so \(t \neq 0\) in general. Therefore, for all positions of \(E\) and \(F\) satisfying the given condition, the circumcircle of \(\triangle AEF\) passes through the fixed point \((s,t)\) other than \(A\).
author: llm

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle. Variable points \( E \) and \( F \) are on sides \( AC \) and \( AB \) respectively such that \( BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA \). As \( E \) and \( F \) vary, prove that the circumcircle of \( \triangle AEF \) passes through a fixed point other than \( A \).
solution:
Let \(A\) be the origin \((0,0)\) in the Cartesian plane. Let the line \(AB\) be the x-axis. Then the coordinates of the vertices are \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(c,0)\), and \(C=(b\cos A, b\sin A)\), where \(c=AB\), \(b=AC\), and \(A=\angle BAC\).
The point \(F\) is on side \(AB\), so its coordinates are \((x,0)\) where \(x=AF\).
The point \(E\) is on side \(AC\), so its coordinates are \((y\cos A, y\sin A)\) where \(y=AE\).
The given condition is \(BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA\).
Let \(a=BC\). So \(a^2 = c \cdot BF + b \cdot CE\).
Since \(F\) is on \(AB\), \(BF = AB - AF = c-x\).
Since \(E\) is on \(AC\), \(CE = AC - AE = b-y\).
Substituting these into the condition:
\(a^2 = c(c-x) + b(b-y)\)
\(a^2 = c^2 - cx + b^2 - by\)
Rearranging this equation, we get \(cx + by = b^2+c^2-a^2\).
By the Law of Cosines in \(\triangle ABC\), we have \(a^2 = b^2+c^2 - 2bc\cos A\).
Therefore, \(b^2+c^2-a^2 = 2bc\cos A\).
So the condition on \(x=AF\) and \(y=AE\) becomes \(cx + by = 2bc\cos A\).

Let \(\Omega\) be the circumcircle of \(\triangle AEF\). We are looking for a fixed point on \(\Omega\) other than \(A\). Let this point be \(K=(x_K, y_K)\).
Since \(A=(0,0)\), \(F=(x,0)\), and \(E=(y\cos A, y\sin A)\) lie on \(\Omega\), the equation of \(\Omega\) can be found.
Any circle passing through the origin \(A\) has an equation of the form \(X^2+Y^2+DX+GY=0\).
Since \(F(x,0)\) lies on \(\Omega\), we have \(x^2+Dx=0\). Since \(F \neq A\), \(x \neq 0\), so \(D=-x\).
Since \(E(y\cos A, y\sin A)\) lies on \(\Omega\), we have:
\((y\cos A)^2 + (y\sin A)^2 + D(y\cos A) + G(y\sin A) = 0\)
\(y^2(\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A) + Dy\cos A + Gy\sin A = 0\)
\(y^2 + Dy\cos A + Gy\sin A = 0\).
Since \(E \neq A\), \(y \neq 0\), so we can divide by \(y\):
\(y + D\cos A + G\sin A = 0\).
Substitute \(D=-x\):
\(y - x\cos A + G\sin A = 0\).
Since \(\triangle ABC\) is acute, \(A \in (0, \pi/2)\), so \(\sin A \neq 0\).
Thus, \(G = \frac{x\cos A - y}{\sin A}\).
The equation of the circumcircle \(\Omega\) of \(\triangle AEF\) is \(X^2+Y^2 - xX + \left(\frac{x\cos A - y}{\sin A}\right)Y = 0\).

Let \(K=(x_K, y_K)\) be a point on this circle, other than \(A\). So \((x_K,y_K) \neq (0,0)\).
Then \(x_K^2+y_K^2 - x x_K + \left(\frac{x\cos A - y}{\sin A}\right)y_K = 0\).
This equation must hold for any \(x,y\) satisfying \(cx+by=2bc\cos A\) and the conditions for \(E,F\) being on the sides (i.e. \(0 \le x \le c\) and \(0 \le y \le b\)).
From \(cx+by=2bc\cos A\), we can express \(y\) in terms of \(x\): \(y = \frac{2bc\cos A - cx}{b}\).
Substitute this expression for \(y\) into the equation for \(K\):
\(x_K^2+y_K^2 - x x_K + \left(\frac{x\cos A - \frac{2bc\cos A - cx}{b}}{\sin A}\right)y_K = 0\).
Multiply by \(\sin A\) (which is non-zero):
\((x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - x x_K \sin A + \left(x\cos A - \frac{2bc\cos A - cx}{b}\right)y_K = 0\).
\((x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - x x_K \sin A + \left(\frac{bx\cos A - 2bc\cos A + cx}{b}\right)y_K = 0\).
\((x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - x x_K \sin A + \frac{(b\cos A+c)x - 2bc\cos A}{b} y_K = 0\).
Rearrange the terms to group by powers of \(x\):
\(x \left[-x_K \sin A + \frac{b\cos A+c}{b} y_K\right] + \left[(x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - \frac{2bc\cos A}{b} y_K\right] = 0\).
\(x \left[-x_K \sin A + \frac{b\cos A+c}{b} y_K\right] + \left[(x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - 2c\cos A y_K\right] = 0\).
The problem states that \(E\) and \(F\) are variable points. This means that there is more than one pair \((x,y)\) satisfying the condition, so there is more than one value of \(x\). For this linear equation in \(x\) to hold for multiple values of \(x\), the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant term must both be zero.
So we have a system of two equations for \(x_K, y_K\):
1) \(-x_K \sin A + \frac{b\cos A+c}{b} y_K = 0\)
2) \((x_K^2+y_K^2)\sin A - 2c\cos A y_K = 0\)

Since \(K \neq A\), \((x_K,y_K) \neq (0,0)\).
If \(y_K=0\), then from (1), \(-x_K \sin A = 0\). Since \(\sin A \neq 0\), this implies \(x_K=0\). So \((x_K,y_K)=(0,0)\), which is point \(A\). We are looking for a point other than \(A\), so we must have \(y_K \neq 0\).
From (1): \(x_K \sin A = \frac{b\cos A+c}{b} y_K\).
So \(x_K = \frac{b\cos A+c}{b\sin A} y_K\). (Equation 1')
From (2), since \(y_K \neq 0\), we can divide by \(y_K\):
\(\frac{x_K^2+y_K^2}{y_K} \sin A - 2c\cos A = 0\), so \(x_K^2+y_K^2 = \frac{2c\cos A}{\sin A} y_K\). (Equation 2')
Substitute \(x_K\) from (1') into (2'):
\(\left(\frac{b\cos A+c}{b\sin A}\right)^2 y_K^2 + y_K^2 = \frac{2c\cos A}{\sin A} y_K\).
Since \(y_K \neq 0\), divide by \(y_K\):
\(\left[\left(\frac{b\cos A+c}{b\sin A}\right)^2 + 1\right] y_K = \frac{2c\cos A}{\sin A}\).
\(\left[\frac{(b\cos A+c)^2 + (b\sin A)^2}{(b\sin A)^2}\right] y_K = \frac{2c\cos A}{\sin A}\).
The numerator of the fraction in the square brackets is:
\((b\cos A+c)^2 + (b\sin A)^2 = b^2\cos^2 A + 2bc\cos A + c^2 + b^2\sin^2 A = b^2(\cos^2 A+\sin^2 A) + c^2 + 2bc\cos A = b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A\).
So, \(\frac{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A}{b^2\sin^2 A} y_K = \frac{2c\cos A}{\sin A}\).
Since \(A \in (0, \pi/2)\), \(\sin A \neq 0\). We can multiply by \(\sin A\).
\(\frac{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A}{b^2\sin A} y_K = 2c\cos A\).
As \(\triangle ABC\) is acute, \(A, B, C \in (0, \pi/2)\). Thus \(\cos A > 0\).
Also, \(b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A > 0\).
So, \(y_K = \frac{2c\cos A \cdot b^2\sin A}{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A} = \frac{2b^2c\sin A\cos A}{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A}\).
Now substitute \(y_K\) into Equation 1' to find \(x_K\):
\(x_K = \frac{b\cos A+c}{b\sin A} y_K = \frac{b\cos A+c}{b\sin A} \cdot \frac{2b^2c\sin A\cos A}{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A}\).
\(x_K = \frac{(b\cos A+c)2bc\cos A}{b^2+c^2+2bc\cos A}\).
The coordinates \((x_K, y_K)\) are uniquely determined by the side lengths \(b,c\) and the angle \(A\) of \(\triangle ABC\).
Thus, \(K=(x_K, y_K)\) is a fixed point. Since \(y_K \neq 0\) (because \(\cos A > 0, \sin A > 0, b,c > 0\)), this point \(K\) is distinct from \(A\).

The range of permissible values for \(x\) and \(y\) needs to allow for \(E,F\) to be "variable". The condition \(cx+by = 2bc \cos A\) defines a line in the \(xy\)-plane. The constraints \(0 \le x \le c\) and \(0 \le y \le b\) define a rectangle. The intersection of this line and rectangle is a line segment. As long as this segment is not a single point, there are infinitely many pairs \((x,y)\) satisfying the condition, and the argument that the coefficients in the polynomial in \(x\) must be zero holds. The problem states \(E\) and \(F\) vary, which implies the segment is not a point.

Therefore, the circumcircle of \(\triangle AEF\) passes through a fixed point \(K\) (with coordinates derived above) other than \(A\).
author: llm

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle. Variable points \( E \) and \( F \) are on sides \( AC \) and \( AB \) respectively such that \( BC^2 = BA \cdot BF + CE \cdot CA \). As \( E \) and \( F \) vary, prove that the circumcircle of \( \triangle AEF \) passes through a fixed point other than \( A \).
solution:
Throughout the proof we use the usual notation  
\(BC=a,\;CA=b,\;AB=c\) and we denote by \(M\) the midpoint of the side
\(BC\).

Step 1.  Setting up a convenient coordinate system  
Put the origin at \(A\).
Put the \(x\)-axis along the ray \(AB\); then \(B(c,0)\).
Because the triangle is acute the point \(C\) is situated above the
\(x\)-axis.
Using the law of cosines we may write  

\[
C\bigl(b\cos A,\;b\sin A\bigr),\qquad
\cos A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc},\qquad 
\sin A>0 .
\]

Step 2.  Coordinates of the variable points \(E\) and \(F\)  
Take  

\[
F(t,0)\quad (0<t<c),\qquad 
E(\lambda\,b\cos A,\;\lambda\,b\sin A)\quad (0<\lambda<1),
\]

so that  
\[
AF=t,\;BF=c-t,\quad AE=\lambda b,\;CE=(1-\lambda)b .
\]

Step 3.  Translating the given condition  
The given relation

\[
BC^{2}=BA\cdot BF+CE\cdot CA
\]

becomes, with the above notations,

\[
a^{2}=c(c-t)+b\bigl[(1-\lambda)b\bigr]
        =b^{2}+c^{2}-\bigl(ct+b^{2}\lambda\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\, ct+b^{2}\lambda = 2bc\cos A \,.
\tag{1}
\]

Step 4.  The equation of the circumcircle \((AEF)\)  
Because \(A\) is at the origin, every circle through \(A\) has an
equation

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}+ux+vy=0                                      \tag{2}
\]

with real constants \(u,v\).
Substituting first \(F(t,0)\) and then \(E(\lambda b\cos A,\lambda
b\sin A)\) into (2) we obtain

\[
u=-t,\qquad
\lambda b^{2}+u\lambda b\cos A+v\lambda b\sin A=0,
\]

that is  

\[
\, v=\dfrac{t\cos A-\lambda b}{\sin A}\,.        \tag{3}
\]

Consequently the circumcircle \(\omega\) of \(\triangle AEF\) is  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}-tx+\frac{t\cos A-\lambda b}{\sin A}\;y=0.    \tag{4}
\]

Step 5.  Looking for a point \(P(x_{0},y_{0})\)
common to all such circles  
The point \(P\) is required to satisfy equation (4) for every pair
\((t,\lambda)\) that fulfils (1).  Insert $(x_{0},y_{0})$ into (4),
multiply by \(\sin A\) and use (3):

\[
\sin A\bigl(x_{0}^{2}+y_{0}^{2}\bigr)
      -tx_{0}\sin A+(t\cos A-\lambda b)y_{0}=0.          \tag{5}
\]

Eliminate \(\lambda\) from (5) with the help of (1):

\[
\lambda=\frac{2bc\cos A-ct}{b^{2}} ,
\]

which gives after simplification

\[
t\bigl(-x_{0}\sin A+y_{0}\cos A+\frac{c}{b}y_{0}\bigr)
      -2cy_{0}\cos A+\sin A\bigl(x_{0}^{2}+y_{0}^{2}\bigr)=0. \tag{6}
\]

Because \(t\) can vary freely (choose \(F\) first, then define \(E\)
from (1)), both the
coefficient of \(t\) and the free term of (6) must vanish:

\[
\begin{cases}
-x_{0}\sin A+y_{0}\cos A+\dfrac{c}{b}y_{0}=0,\\[4pt]
\sin A\bigl(x_{0}^{2}+y_{0}^{2}\bigr)-2cy_{0}\cos A=0.
\end{cases}                                              \tag{7}
\]

Step 6.  Solving the system  
From the first equation of (7)

\[
x_{0}=y_{0}\,\dfrac{\cos A+\dfrac{c}{b}}{\sin A}.        \tag{8}
\]

Insert (8) into the second equation of (7):

\[
\sin A\,y_{0}^{2}\!\left[
\frac{\bigl(\cos A+\dfrac{c}{b}\bigr)^{2}}{\sin^{2}A}+1
\right]
      =2cy_{0}\cos A.
\]

Since \(y_{0}\neq 0\) (otherwise \(x_{0}=0\) and the point would be
\(A\) itself) we can divide by
\(y_{0}\) obtaining

\[
y_{0}= \frac{2bc\cos A\sin A}{b^{2}+c^{2}+2bc\cos A},     \tag{9}
\]

and, using (8),

\[
x_{0}=\frac{2c(c+b\cos A)\cos A}{b^{2}+c^{2}+2bc\cos A}.  \tag{10}
\]

Both coordinates depend only on the sides (actually on
\(a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A\)) and therefore describe a
fixed point \(P\).

Step 7.  Barycentric description of \(P\)  
Let us convert \(P\) to barycentric coordinates.
Because

\[
\frac{x_{0}}{y_{0}}
   =\frac{c+b\cos A}{b\sin A}
   =\frac{c}{b\sin A}+\cot A
   =\frac{c}{b\sin A}+\frac{\cos A}{\sin A},
\]

while  

\[
\frac{B_y-C_y}{B_x-C_x}= \frac{0-b\sin A}{c-b\cos A}
                       =-\frac{b\sin A}{c-b\cos A},
\]

one finds \(B\) and \(C\) to be symmetric with respect to the vertical
line through \(P\); hence
the two last barycentric coordinates of \(P\) are equal:
\(P=(k:1:1)\).
To determine \(k\) we use the well–known conversion
\((x,y)=\bigl( (k+2)^{-1}(c+b\cos A),\;(k+2)^{-1}b\sin A \bigr)\),
compare with (9)–(10), and obtain

\[
k=\frac{a^{2}}{2bc\cos A}.                                \tag{11}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\,P=(\,a^{2}:1:1\,)                                \tag{12}
\]

in barycentric coordinates.
Because its second and third barycentric coordinates coincide,
\(P\) lies on the median \(AM\); because all three are positive
(triangle \(ABC\) is acute, so \(\cos A>0\)), \(P\) is an interior
point.

Step 8.  Verification  
We already derived (5)–(7) under the sole assumption that \(P\) is
fixed.  
Conversely, for the particular values (9)–(10) (equivalently (12))
both equations (7) are fulfilled; hence every circle (4) indeed passes
through this \(P\).

Therefore the circumcircle of every triangle \(AEF\) satisfying
\(BC^{2}=BA\cdot BF+CE\cdot CA\) contains the fixed interior point

\[
P=(a^{2}:1:1),
\]

i.e. the unique point situated on the A-median \(AM\) which divides it
in the constant ratio  

\[
AP:PM = 4bc\cos A : a^{2}.
\]

Because \(A\neq P\), this finishes the proof.
author: llm

problem: Let \( ABC \) be an acute triangle and \( D \) a variable point on side \( AC \). Point \( E \) is on \( BD \) such that \( BE = \frac{BC^2 - CD \cdot CA}{BD} \). As \( D \) varies on side \( AC \), prove that the circumcircle of \( ADE \) passes through a fixed point other than \( A \).
solution:
Let the circumcircle of triangle $C E D$ intersect $B C$ at point $G$. From power of point we have

$$
B G \cdot B C=B E \cdot B D .
$$

Combining (1) with the problem statement we get

$$
\frac{B C \cdot B C}{B D}=B E=\frac{B C^{2}-C D \cdot C A}{B D}
$$
and from here we get
$$
C D \cdot C A=B C(B C-B G)=B C \cdot C G .
$$

(2) implies that $D, A, B, G$ are concyclic as well. This gives us

$$
\angle B E C=\measuredangle B G D=180^{\circ}-\measuredangle B A D=180-\measuredangle C A B .
$$

Now let the circumcircle of $A D E$ and $B E C$ intersect again at $X$. Since

$$
\angle X C B=\angle X E B=180^{\circ}-\measuredangle X E D=\angle X A D=\angle X A C
$$
and
$$
\angle B X C=\angle B E C=180^{\circ}-\angle B A C
$$

we have that $X$ is on the unique circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to side $B C$ at point $C$ and circumcircle of $B H C$ where $H$ is the ortocenter of triangle $A B C$. This intersection is unique and we are done.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( AB < AC \) inscribed in a circle \( c \). The tangent to \( c \) at point \( C \) meets the parallel from \( B \) to \( AC \) at point \( D \). The tangent to \( c \) at point \( B \) meets the parallel from \( C \) to \( AB \) at point \( E \), and the tangent to \( c \) at point \( C \) at point \( L \). Suppose the circumcircle \( c_1 \) of triangle \( BDC \) meets \( AC \) at point \( T \) and the circumcircle \( c_2 \) of triangle \( BEC \) meets \( AB \) at point \( S \). Prove that the lines \( ST, BC, AL \) are concurrent.
solution:
We will prove first that the circle $c_{1}$ is tangent to $A B$ at the point $B$. In order to prove this, we have to prove that $\measuredangle B D C=\measuredangle A B C$. Indeed, since $B D \| A C$, we have that $\measuredangle D B C=\measuredangle A C B$. Additionally, $\angle B C D=\measuredangle B A C$ (by chord and tangent), which means that the triangles $A B C, B D C$ have two equal angles and so the third ones are also equal. It follows that $\angle B D C=\measuredangle A B C$, so $c_{1}$ is tangent to $A B$ at the point $B$.

Similarly, the circle $c_{2}$ is tangent to $A C$ at the point $C$.
As a consequence, $\measuredangle A B T=\measuredangle A C B$ (by chord and tangent) and also $\measuredangle B S C=\measuredangle A C B$.
By the above, we have that $\measuredangle A B T=\measuredangle B S C$, so the lines $B T, S C$ are parallel.
Now, let $S T$ intersect $B C$ at the point $K$. It suffice to prove that $K$ belongs to $A L$. From the trapezoid $B T C S$ we get that

$$
\frac{B K}{K C}=\frac{B T}{S C}
$$
and from the similar triangles $A B T, A S C$, we have that
$$
\frac{B T}{S C}=\frac{A B}{A S}
$$

By (1), (2) we get that

$$
\frac{B K}{K C}=\frac{A B}{A S}
$$

From the power of point theorem, we have that

$$
A C^{2}=A B \cdot A S \Rightarrow A S=\frac{A C^{2}}{A B}
$$

Going back into (3), it gives that

$$
\frac{B K}{K C}=\frac{A B^{2}}{A C^{2}}
$$

From the last one, it follows that $K$ belongs to the symmedian of the triangle $A B C$.
Finally, recall that the well known fact that since $L B$ and $L C$ are tangents, it follows that $A L$ is the symmedian of the triangle $A B C$, so $K$ belongs to $A L$, as needed.

problem: The acute-angled triangle \(ABC\) with circumcenter \(O\) is given. The midpoints of the sides \(BC\), \(CA\), and \(AB\) are \(D\), \(E\), and \(F\) respectively. An arbitrary point \(M\) on the side \(BC\), different from \(D\), is chosen. The straight lines \(AM\) and \(EF\) intersect at the point \(N\), and the straight line \(ON\) cuts again the circumscribed circle of the triangle \(ODM\) at the point \(P\). Prove that the reflection of the point \(M\) with respect to the midpoint of the segment \(DP\) belongs to the nine-point circle of the triangle \(ABC\).
solution:
The straight lines $D O, E O$ and $F O$ are the perpendicular bisectors of the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ respectively. It follows that $[O M]$ is the diameter of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $O D M$ and $M P \perp O N$. The point $O$ is the ortocenter of the triangle $D E F$ (see the picture)
Let $O_{1}$ be the circumcenter of the triangle $D E F$ and $H$ be the diametrically opposite point of $D$. The circumscribed circle of the triangle $D E F$ is the nine points circle of the triangle $A B C$. It follows that $E H \perp D E, F H \perp F D$ and $E D\|A F, D F\| A E$. So, the point $H$ is the ortocenter of the triangle $A E F$.

Let $A D \cap E F=\{I\}$ and $R$ is the reflection of the point N with respect to the point $I$, i.e. $R \in(E F), N I=R I$. The point $I$ is the simmetry center of the parallelogram $A E D F$. It follows that the point $I$ is the midpoint of the segment $[O H]$ and the quadrilaterals $A E D F$, $A N D R, H N O R$ are all parallelograms.

Let $Q$ be the reflection of the point $M$ with respect to the midpoint of the segment $D P$. It follows that the quadrilaterals $P Q D M$ and $M N R D$ are the parallelograms, which imply that the quadrilateral $P Q R N$ is a parallelogram. So, $N O\|H R, N P\| R Q$, which imply that the points $H, R$ and $Q$ are collinear. We obtain that $m(\angle D Q H)=90^{\circ}$, i.e. the point $Q$ belongs on the nine points circle of the triangle $A B C$.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute-angled triangle with orthocenter \( H \), centroid \( G \), and circumcircle \( \omega \). Let \( D \) and \( M \) be the intersections of lines \( AH \) and \( AG \) with side \( BC \), respectively. Rays \( MH \) and \( DG \) intersect \( \omega \) again at \( P \) and \( Q \), respectively. Prove that \( PD \) and \( QM \) intersect on \( \omega \).
solution:
Note that it is enough to prove that $\angle D P A+\angle M Q A=180^{\circ}$.
Without loss of generality assume that $A B<A C$. Let the reflection of $H$ in point $M$ be $H^{\prime}$. Since $B H C H^{\prime}$ is a paralelogram we get

$$
\measuredangle B H^{\prime} C=\angle B H C=180^{\circ}-\measuredangle B A C
$$
which means $H^{\prime}$ lies on $\omega$. Also we get
$$
\angle A B H^{\prime}=\angle A B C+\angle C B H^{\prime}=\angle A B C+\angle B C H=90^{\circ}
$$

since $C H \perp A B$. This mean $A H^{\prime}$ is the diameter of $\omega$. This means $\measuredangle M P A=\angle H^{\prime} P A=90^{\circ}$. Since $\angle M P A=\angle M D A=90^{\circ}$ we get that $M, D, P, A$ are concyclic.

This gives us $\angle D P A+\angle A M D=180^{\circ}$. So now it is enough to prove that $\measuredangle A M B=\angle M Q A$.
Taking the homothety with center $G$ and factor $-2$ (the homothety taking the $9$ point circle to the circumcircle of $A B C$ ), we get that $Q$ and $A$ are images of $D$ and $M$ respectively.

This means $A Q \| D M$ giving $A Q \| B C$. Since $A Q \| B C$ and $A, B, C, Q$ are concyclic this means $A B C Q$ is an iscoseles trapezoid.
This means $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $A Q$. This gives us $M A=M Q$. Since $A Q \| B C$ this gives us $\angle A Q M=\angle Q A M=\angle A M B$ which concludes our problem.
