problem: Two circles \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{2}\), of equal radius intersect at different points \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\). Consider a circle \(\omega\) externally tangent to \(\omega_{1}\) at \(T_{1}\) and internally tangent to \(\omega_{2}\) at point \(T_{2}\). Prove that lines \(X_{1} T_{1}\) and \(X_{2} T_{2}\) intersect at a point lying on \(\omega\).
solution:
Let  

• \(O_{1},O_{2}\) be the centres of the equal circles \(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\) (common radius \(R\));  
• \(O\) be the centre of the third circle \(\omega\) (radius \(r<R\));  
• \(T_{1},T_{2}\) be the tangency points described in the statement;  
• \(X_{1},X_{2}\) be the intersection points of \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{2}\).

Because the tangency points lie on the lines of centres, the three points  
\(O_{1},O_{2},O\) are collinear; call their common line the \(x\)-axis and put its
mid-point at the origin of a Cartesian system.

Step 1 – placing the three centres.  
Write \(O_{1}=(-d,0),\;O_{2}=(d,0),\;O=(c,0)\;(d>0)\).
External tangency to \(\omega_{1}\) and internal tangency to \(\omega_{2}\) give

\[
\begin{aligned}
OO_{1}&=R+r \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c+d = R+r,\\
OO_{2}&=R-r \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c-d = R-r .
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding and subtracting the two equalities we get  

\[
c=R,\qquad d=r .
\]

Hence  

\[
O_{1}=(-r,0),\quad O_{2}=(r,0),\quad O=(R,0). \tag{1}
\]

Step 2 – the intersection points of \(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\).  
Since the circles have the same radius, their radical axis is the
perpendicular bisector of \(O_{1}O_{2}\), i.e. the \(y\)-axis.
Thus

\[
X_{1}=(0,h),\quad X_{2}=(0,-h),\qquad 
h=\sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}\ (>0). \tag{2}
\]

Step 3 – the tangency points.  
Because tangency occurs on the \(x\)-axis (line of centres):

• for the external tangency \(O_{1}T_{1}=R\) on the segment \(O_{1}O\) of length
\(R+r\); hence  

\[
T_{1}=(-r+R,0)=(R-r,0); \tag{3}
\]

• for the internal tangency \(O_{2}T_{2}=R\) on the ray \(O_{2}O\) beyond \(O\);
therefore  

\[
T_{2}=(r+R,0)=(R+r,0). \tag{4}
\]

Step 4 – the two lines whose intersection we need.

Line \(X_{1}T_{1}\): it passes through \((0,h)\) and \((R-r,0)\);  
its equation is  

\[
y-h=-\frac{h}{R-r}\,x
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y=h\!\left(1-\frac{x}{R-r}\right). \tag{5}
\]

Line \(X_{2}T_{2}\): it passes through \((0,-h)\) and \((R+r,0)\);  
its equation is  

\[
y+h=\frac{h}{R+r}\,x
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y=\frac{h}{R+r}\,x-h. \tag{6}
\]

Step 5 – their intersection \(P\).

Solve (5) and (6):

\[
h\!\left(1-\frac{x}{R-r}\right)=\frac{h}{R+r}\,x-h
\Longrightarrow
2=\frac{x}{R+r}+\frac{x}{R-r}
\Longrightarrow
x=\frac{R^{2}-r^{2}}{R}.
\]

Substituting this \(x\) into (5) gives

\[
y=-\frac{rh}{R}=-\frac{r\sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}}{R}.
\]

Thus  

\[
P=\Bigl(\dfrac{R^{2}-r^{2}}{R},\;-\dfrac{r\sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}}{R}\Bigr). \tag{7}
\]

Step 6 – checking that \(P\) lies on \(\omega\).

The equation of \(\omega\) is \((x-R)^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\).
Using (7):

\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-R)^{2}+y^{2}
&=\left(\frac{R^{2}-r^{2}}{R}-R\right)^{2}
   +\left(-\frac{r\sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}}{R}\right)^{2} \\
&=\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{R}\right)^{2}
   +\frac{r^{2}(R^{2}-r^{2})}{R^{2}}
 =\frac{r^{4}+r^{2}R^{2}-r^{4}}{R^{2}}
 =r^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence \(P\) satisfies the equation of \(\omega\); in other words

\[
P \in \omega .
\]

Step 7 – conclusion.

By construction \(P\) lies on both lines \(X_{1}T_{1}\) and \(X_{2}T_{2}\),
and step 6 proves that \(P\) is a point of the circle \(\omega\).
Therefore

lines \(X_{1}T_{1}\) and \(X_{2}T_{2}\) meet at a point situated on \(\omega\),

which is exactly what had to be shown.
author: llm

problem: Two circles \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{2}\), of equal radius intersect at different points \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\). Consider a circle \(\omega\) externally tangent to \(\omega_{1}\) at \(T_{1}\) and internally tangent to \(\omega_{2}\) at point \(T_{2}\). Prove that lines \(X_{1} T_{1}\) and \(X_{2} T_{2}\) intersect at a point lying on \(\omega\).
solution:
We are given two circles \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) of equal radius \(r\) intersecting at distinct points \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), and a circle \(\omega\) externally tangent to \(\omega_1\) at \(T_1\) and internally tangent to \(\omega_2\) at \(T_2\). We need to prove that the lines \(X_1 T_1\) and \(X_2 T_2\) intersect at a point on \(\omega\).

Since the radii of \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) are equal, and the result is invariant under scaling, we can assume, without loss of generality, that the common radius is 1. This simplifies the calculations, and the general case follows by similarity.

Set up a coordinate system with \(X_1\) at the origin \((0,0)\) and \(X_2\) at \((2d,0)\) for some \(d > 0\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(X_1 X_2\), so \(M\) is at \((d,0)\). Since \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) have equal radius and pass through both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), their centers lie on the perpendicular bisector of \(X_1 X_2\), which is the line \(x = d\). Let the center of \(\omega_1\) be \(O_1\) at \((d, h)\) and the center of \(\omega_2\) be \(O_2\) at \((d, -h)\) for some \(h \neq 0\) (since the circles are distinct and intersect at two points). The distance from \(O_1\) to \(X_1\) is 1, so:
\[
\sqrt{(d - 0)^2 + (h - 0)^2} = 1 \implies d^2 + h^2 = 1.
\]
Similarly, for \(O_2\), \(d^2 + (-h)^2 = 1\) gives the same equation.

Let the center of \(\omega\) be \(O\) at \((p, q)\) with radius \(R\). Since \(\omega\) is externally tangent to \(\omega_1\) at \(T_1\), the distance \(OO_1 = R + 1\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{(p - d)^2 + (q - h)^2} = R + 1.
\]
Squaring both sides:
\[
(p - d)^2 + (q - h)^2 = (R + 1)^2. \quad (1)
\]
Since \(\omega\) is internally tangent to \(\omega_2\) at \(T_2\) (with \(\omega\) inside \(\omega_2\)), the distance \(OO_2 = |1 - R|\). Given that \(\omega\) is internally tangent and inside \(\omega_2\), we have \(R < 1\), so \(OO_2 = 1 - R\). Thus:
\[
\sqrt{(p - d)^2 + (q - (-h))^2} = \sqrt{(p - d)^2 + (q + h)^2} = 1 - R.
\]
Squaring both sides:
\[
(p - d)^2 + (q + h)^2 = (1 - R)^2. \quad (2)
\]
Subtract equation (2) from equation (1):
\[
[(p - d)^2 + (q - h)^2] - [(p - d)^2 + (q + h)^2] = (R + 1)^2 - (1 - R)^2.
\]
Simplify the left side:
\[
(q - h)^2 - (q + h)^2 = (q^2 - 2qh + h^2) - (q^2 + 2qh + h^2) = -4qh.
\]
Simplify the right side:
\[
(R + 1)^2 - (1 - R)^2 = (R^2 + 2R + 1) - (1 - 2R + R^2) = R^2 + 2R + 1 - 1 + 2R - R^2 = 4R.
\]
Thus:
\[
-4qh = 4R \implies qh = -R. \quad (3)
\]
From equation (2) and using \(d^2 + h^2 = 1\):
\[
(p - d)^2 + (q + h)^2 = (1 - R)^2.
\]
Expand and substitute \(q + h\):
\[
(p - d)^2 + q^2 + 2qh + h^2 = 1 - 2R + R^2.
\]
From equation (3), \(2qh = -2R\), and since \(d^2 + h^2 = 1\), we have:
\[
(p - d)^2 + q^2 + h^2 - 2R = 1 - 2R + R^2.
\]
Simplify:
\[
(p - d)^2 + q^2 + h^2 = 1 + R^2.
\]
Substitute \(d^2 + h^2 = 1\):
\[
(p - d)^2 + q^2 + h^2 = d^2 + h^2 + R^2 \implies (p - d)^2 + q^2 = d^2 + R^2. \quad (4)
\]

Now, find the coordinates of \(T_1\). Since \(\omega\) and \(\omega_1\) are externally tangent at \(T_1\), the points \(O\), \(T_1\), and \(O_1\) are collinear, with \(T_1\) between \(O\) and \(O_1\). The vector from \(O\) to \(O_1\) is \((d - p, h - q)\), and the distance \(OO_1 = R + 1\). The point \(T_1\) is at distance \(R\) from \(O\) along this vector:
\[
T_1 = O + \frac{R}{R + 1} (O_1 - O) = (p, q) + \frac{R}{R + 1} (d - p, h - q).
\]
Let \(k = \frac{R}{R + 1}\), so:
\[
T_1 = \left( p + k(d - p), q + k(h - q) \right) = \left( kd + (1 - k)p, kh + (1 - k)q \right).
\]
The line \(X_1 T_1\) passes through \(X_1 = (0,0)\) and \(T_1\), so parametric equations for a point on this line are:
\[
(x, y) = t \left( kd + (1 - k)p, kh + (1 - k)q \right) \quad \text{for some} \quad t \in \mathbb{R}.
\]

Similarly, find the coordinates of \(T_2\). Since \(\omega\) and \(\omega_2\) are internally tangent at \(T_2\), the points \(O_2\), \(O\), and \(T_2\) are collinear, with \(O\) between \(O_2\) and \(T_2\). The vector from \(O_2\) to \(O\) is \((p - d, q - (-h)) = (p - d, q + h)\), and the distance \(O_2 O = 1 - R\). The point \(T_2\) is at distance 1 from \(O_2\) along this vector:
\[
T_2 = O_2 + \frac{1}{1 - R} (O - O_2) \cdot (1 - R) \cdot \frac{1}{|O - O_2|} \cdot |O - O_2|, \quad \text{but} \quad |O - O_2| = 1 - R, \quad \text{so unit vector is} \quad \frac{(p - d, q + h)}{1 - R}.
\]
Thus:
\[
T_2 = (d, -h) + 1 \cdot \frac{(p - d, q + h)}{1 - R} = \left( d + \frac{p - d}{1 - R}, -h + \frac{q + h}{1 - R} \right).
\]
Simplify:
\[
T_2 = \left( \frac{d(1 - R) + p - d}{1 - R}, \frac{-h(1 - R) + q + h}{1 - R} \right) = \left( \frac{p - dR}{1 - R}, \frac{q + hR}{1 - R} \right).
\]
The line \(X_2 T_2\) passes through \(X_2 = (2d, 0)\) and \(T_2\), so parametric equations for a point on this line are:
\[
(x, y) = (2d, 0) + s \left( \frac{p - dR}{1 - R} - 2d, \frac{q + hR}{1 - R} - 0 \right) \quad \text{for some} \quad s \in \mathbb{R}.
\]
The vector part is:
\[
\left( \frac{p - dR - 2d(1 - R)}{1 - R}, \frac{q + hR}{1 - R} \right) = \left( \frac{p - 2d + dR}{1 - R}, \frac{q + hR}{1 - R} \right).
\]

The intersection point \(P\) of lines \(X_1 T_1\) and \(X_2 T_2\) satisfies both parametric equations. Using the \(y\)-coordinate from both lines:
From \(X_1 T_1\):
\[
y = t \left( kh + (1 - k)q \right) = t \left( \frac{R}{R + 1} h + \frac{1}{R + 1} q \right) = t \frac{q + R h}{R + 1}.
\]
From \(X_2 T_2\):
\[
y = s \frac{q + hR}{1 - R}.
\]
Set equal:
\[
t \frac{q + R h}{R + 1} = s \frac{q + hR}{1 - R}.
\]
Since \(q + R h \neq 0\) (as \(h \neq 0\) and \(R > 0\)), divide both sides:
\[
\frac{t}{R + 1} = \frac{s}{1 - R} \implies s = t \frac{1 - R}{R + 1}.
\]
Now use the \(x\)-coordinate. From \(X_1 T_1\):
\[
x = t \left( kd + (1 - k)p \right) = t \left( \frac{R}{R + 1} d + \frac{1}{R + 1} p \right) = t \frac{p + R d}{R + 1}.
\]
From \(X_2 T_2\):
\[
x = 2d + s \frac{p - 2d + dR}{1 - R}.
\]
Substitute \(s = t \frac{1 - R}{R + 1}\):
\[
x = 2d + \left( t \frac{1 - R}{R + 1} \right) \frac{p - 2d + dR}{1 - R} = 2d + t \frac{p - 2d + dR}{R + 1}.
\]
Set the \(x\)-coordinates equal:
\[
t \frac{p + R d}{R + 1} = 2d + t \frac{p - 2d + dR}{R + 1}.
\]
Multiply both sides by \(R + 1\):
\[
t (p + R d) = 2d (R + 1) + t (p - 2d + dR).
\]
Rearrange:
\[
t (p + R d) - t (p - 2d + dR) = 2d (R + 1).
\]
Simplify:
\[
t (p + R d - p + 2d - dR) = 2d (R + 1) \implies t (2d) = 2d (R + 1).
\]
Divide by \(2d\) (since \(d > 0\)):
\[
t = R + 1.
\]
Then \(s = (R + 1) \frac{1 - R}{R + 1} = 1 - R\).

Now find the coordinates of \(P\) using the line \(X_1 T_1\):
\[
P = t \left( kd + (1 - k)p, kh + (1 - k)q \right) = (R + 1) \left( \frac{p + R d}{R + 1}, \frac{q + R h}{R + 1} \right) = (p + R d, q + R h).
\]
To show \(P\) is on \(\omega\), compute the distance from \(O = (p, q)\) to \(P = (p + R d, q + R h)\):
\[
|O P| = \sqrt{ ( (p + R d) - p )^2 + ( (q + R h) - q )^2 } = \sqrt{ (R d)^2 + (R h)^2 } = R \sqrt{d^2 + h^2}.
\]
But \(d^2 + h^2 = 1\), so:
\[
|O P| = R \sqrt{1} = R.
\]
Thus, \(P\) lies on \(\omega\) since the distance to the center equals the radius.

Therefore, the lines \(X_1 T_1\) and \(X_2 T_2\) intersect at \(P\), which is on \(\omega\).
author: llm

problem: Two circles \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{2}\), of equal radius intersect at different points \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\). Consider a circle \(\omega\) externally tangent to \(\omega_{1}\) at \(T_{1}\) and internally tangent to \(\omega_{2}\) at point \(T_{2}\). Prove that lines \(X_{1} T_{1}\) and \(X_{2} T_{2}\) intersect at a point lying on \(\omega\).
solution:
Let \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) be two circles of equal radius, denoted by \(R\). Let their centers be \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) respectively. These circles intersect at two distinct points \(X_1\) and \(X_2\).
Let \(\omega\) be a third circle with center \(O\) and radius \(r\).
\(\omega\) is externally tangent to \(\omega_1\) at \(T_1\). This means that \(O_1, T_1, O\) are collinear, with \(T_1\) between \(O_1\) and \(O\). The distance between their centers is \(O_1O = R+r\).
\(\omega\) is internally tangent to \(\omega_2\) at \(T_2\). This means that \(O_2, O, T_2\) are collinear, with \(O\) between \(O_2\) and \(T_2\). The distance between their centers is \(O_2O = R-r\). This implies \(R>r\), because if \(R=r\), then \(O_2O=0\), so \(O=O_2\), meaning \(\omega=\omega_2\). In this case, \(\omega_2\) would be externally tangent to \(\omega_1\) at \(T_1\), so \(O_1O_2=R+R=2R\). Then \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) would intersect at a single point \(T_1\), which contradicts \(X_1 \ne X_2\). Thus \(R>r\).

Let \(P_L\) be the intersection point of lines \(X_1T_1\) and \(X_2T_2\). We want to show that \(P_L\) lies on \(\omega\).

We use the concept of homothety.
1.  Let \(h_1\) be the homothety centered at \(T_1\) that maps circle \(\omega\) to circle \(\omega_1\).
    Since \(T_1\) is the point of external tangency, \(O_1, T_1, O\) are collinear in that order.
    The point \(T_1\) separates \(O_1\) and \(O\).
    So, \(\vec{T_1O_1}\) and \(\vec{T_1O}\) are in opposite directions. The ratio of homothety is \(k_1 = -R/r\).
    Let \(h_1^{-1}\) be the inverse homothety, mapping \(\omega_1\) to \(\omega\). It is centered at \(T_1\) with ratio \(k_1' = -r/R\).

2.  Let \(h_2\) be the homothety centered at \(T_2\) that maps circle \(\omega\) to circle \(\omega_2\).
    Since \(T_2\) is the point of internal tangency, \(O_2, O, T_2\) are collinear in that order.
    The point \(O\) is between \(O_2\) and \(T_2\).
    So, \(\vec{T_2O_2}\) and \(\vec{T_2O}\) are in the same direction. The ratio of homothety is \(k_2 = R/r\).
    Let \(h_2^{-1}\) be the inverse homothety, mapping \(\omega_2\) to \(\omega\). It is centered at \(T_2\) with ratio \(k_2' = r/R\).

Let \(P_1 = h_1^{-1}(X_1)\). Since \(X_1 \in \omega_1\), \(P_1 \in \omega\). By definition of homothety, \(T_1, X_1, P_1\) are collinear.
Let \(P_2 = h_2^{-1}(X_2)\). Since \(X_2 \in \omega_2\), \(P_2 \in \omega\). By definition of homothety, \(T_2, X_2, P_2\) are collinear.
The problem asks us to prove that the intersection point \(P_L\) of lines \(X_1T_1\) and \(X_2T_2\) lies on \(\omega\).
If we can show that \(P_1=P_2\), then this common point \(P \equiv P_1 \equiv P_2\) lies on \(\omega\). This point \(P\) also lies on line \(X_1T_1\) (since \(T_1,X_1,P_1\) are collinear) and on line \(X_2T_2\) (since \(T_2,X_2,P_2\) are collinear). Thus, \(P\) must be the intersection point \(P_L\). Proving \(P_1=P_2\) is therefore equivalent to solving the problem.

Consider the composite transformation \(H = h_2 \circ h_1^{-1}\). This transformation maps \(\omega_1\) to \(\omega_2\) (since \(h_1^{-1}: \omega_1 \to \omega\) and \(h_2: \omega \to \omega_2\)).
The ratio of \(H\) is \(k = k_1' \cdot k_2 = (-r/R) \cdot (R/r) = -1\).
So \(H\) is a homothety of ratio \(-1\), which means it is a central symmetry. Let \(C\) be the center of this symmetry.
The center \(C\) of the composite homothety \(H\) lies on the line connecting the centers of \(h_1^{-1}\) and \(h_2\), i.e., \(C\) lies on the line \(T_1T_2\).
Since \(H\) maps \(\omega_1\) to \(\omega_2\), it must map the center \(O_1\) of \(\omega_1\) to the center \(O_2\) of \(\omega_2\).
Because \(H\) is a central symmetry with center \(C\), \(C\) must be the midpoint of the segment \(O_1O_2\). Let this midpoint be \(K\). So \(C=K\).
Thus, the midpoint \(K\) of \(O_1O_2\) lies on the line \(T_1T_2\). (This is also a consequence of Monge's Theorem on the collinearity of centers of homothety for three circles \(\omega, \omega_1, \omega_2\). The centers are \(T_1\) (for \(\omega, \omega_1\)), \(T_2\) (for \(\omega, \omega_2\)), and \(K\) (for \(\omega_1, \omega_2\), since radii are equal and ratio is -1)).

Now we need to show that \(H(X_1)=X_2\).
Since \(H\) is a central symmetry with center \(K\) (the midpoint of \(O_1O_2\)), \(H(X_1)=X_2\) means that \(K\) is the midpoint of the segment \(X_1X_2\).
Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(X_1X_2\). We need to show that \(K=M\).
The points \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are the intersection points of \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\).
Therefore, \(O_1X_1 = R\) and \(O_2X_1 = R\). Also, \(O_1X_2 = R\) and \(O_2X_2 = R\).
Consider the quadrilateral \(O_1X_1O_2X_2\). Its four sides are \(O_1X_1\), \(X_1O_2\), \(O_2X_2\), and \(X_2O_1\). All these lengths are equal to \(R\).
So, \(O_1X_1O_2X_2\) is a rhombus.
The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other. These diagonals are \(O_1O_2\) and \(X_1X_2\).
The midpoint of \(O_1O_2\) is \(K\). The midpoint of \(X_1X_2\) is \(M\).
Since the diagonals bisect each other, \(K=M\).
So the center of symmetry \(C=K\) is indeed the midpoint \(M\) of \(X_1X_2\).
This implies that \(H(X_1)=X_2\), because \(X_1, M, X_2\) are collinear and \(M\) is the midpoint of \(X_1X_2\).

We have \(H(X_1)=X_2\), which means \(h_2(h_1^{-1}(X_1)) = X_2\).
Recalling the definitions of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\):
\(P_1 = h_1^{-1}(X_1)\).
So, \(h_2(P_1) = X_2\).
But we also know that \(P_2 = h_2^{-1}(X_2)\). This means \(h_2(P_2) = X_2\).
Since \(h_2\) is a homothety (and thus a bijection), if \(h_2(P_1)=X_2\) and \(h_2(P_2)=X_2\), then we must have \(P_1=P_2\).
Let \(P=P_1=P_2\).
This point \(P\) lies on \(\omega\) (since \(P_1, P_2 \in \omega\)).
This point \(P\) lies on the line \(X_1T_1\) (since \(T_1, X_1, P_1\) are collinear).
This point \(P\) lies on the line \(X_2T_2\) (since \(T_2, X_2, P_2\) are collinear).
Therefore, \(P\) is the intersection point of lines \(X_1T_1\) and \(X_2T_2\), and \(P\) lies on the circle \(\omega\).

This completes the proof. Let's briefly check for degenerate cases.
If \(X_1=T_1\), then \(P_1=h_1^{-1}(T_1)=T_1\) (as \(T_1\) is the center of \(h_1^{-1}\)). So \(P=T_1\). The claim \(P_1=P_2\) means \(T_1=P_2=h_2^{-1}(X_2)\), which implies \(h_2(T_1)=X_2\). This means points \(T_2, T_1, X_2\) are collinear and \(T_2X_2/T_2T_1 = R/r\).
The argument \(H(X_1)=X_2\) becomes \(H(T_1)=X_2\). This is \(h_2(h_1^{-1}(T_1)) = X_2\), which is \(h_2(T_1)=X_2\). This is consistent.
In this case, the line \(X_1T_1\) is \(T_1T_1\). If \(P_L\) is the intersection of lines, this line must be taken as the common tangent to \(\omega\) and \(\omega_1\) at \(T_1\). The point \(P=T_1\) lies on this tangent. The line \(X_2T_2\) must pass through \(T_1\). This is fulfilled by \(T_1, T_2, X_2\) being collinear.

The problem stated \(X_1 \ne X_2\), which ensures \(O_1X_1O_2X_2\) is a rhombus and not a degenerate figure, and that \(R \ne r\).

Final check of the logic:
1.  Definition of homotheties \(h_1, h_2\) and their inverses. Ratios \(k_1 = -R/r\), \(k_2 = R/r\).
2.  Definition of points \(P_1 = h_1^{-1}(X_1)\) and \(P_2 = h_2^{-1}(X_2)\). \(P_1, P_2 \in \omega\).
3.  Goal is to show \(P_1=P_2\). This point is the intersection \(P_L\).
4.  Composite homothety \(H = h_2 \circ h_1^{-1}\) maps \(\omega_1 \to \omega_2\), ratio \(-1\), center \(C\).
5.  \(C\) is on \(T_1T_2\). \(C\) is midpoint of \(O_1O_2\), call it \(K\). So \(C=K\).
6.  Quadrilateral \(O_1X_1O_2X_2\) is a rhombus since all sides are \(R\).
7.  Midpoint of \(O_1O_2\) (\(K\)) is midpoint of \(X_1X_2\) (\(M\)). So \(K=M\).
8.  So center of \(H\) is \(M\). Since ratio is \(-1\), \(H(X_1)\) is symmetric to \(X_1\) wrt \(M\). This is \(X_2\). So \(H(X_1)=X_2\).
9.  \(h_2(h_1^{-1}(X_1)) = X_2 \implies h_2(P_1)=X_2\). Since \(P_2=h_2^{-1}(X_2)\), then \(h_2(P_2)=X_2\).
10. Since \(h_2\) is a bijection, \(P_1=P_2\).
The proof stands.
author: llm

problem: Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^{4} \) has a divisor in the range \( n^{2}+1, n^{2}+2, \ldots, n^{2}+2n \). Prove that there are infinitely many elements of \( S \) of each of the forms \( 7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6 \) and no elements of \( S \) of the form \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \), where \( m \) is an integer.
solution:
Start from the implication

$$
n^{2}+k\left|n^{4} \Longleftrightarrow n^{2}+k\right| k^{2}
$$

Since $1 \leq k \leq 2 n$, in fact the quotient $\frac{k^{2}}{n^{2}+k}$ can only take values from $1$ to $3$. In other words, $S$ is the set of integers $n$ for which at least one equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
n^{2}+k & =k^{2} \\
2\left(n^{2}+k\right) & =k^{2} \\
3\left(n^{2}+k\right) & =k^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

has at least one solution $1 \leq k \leq 2 n$.
The first equation has no solutions with $k \geq 1$ since we can put $(k-1)^{2}<n^{2}<k^{2}$. The other two are Pell equations, and one can check that $n^{2} \equiv 2(\bmod 7)$ has no solutions at all for $k(\bmod 7)$ in either case. The assertion about infinitely many solutions then follows by using the Pell recursion, and taking modulo $7$.
author: human

problem: Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^{4} \) has a divisor in the range \( n^{2}+1, n^{2}+2, \ldots, n^{2}+2n \). Prove that there are infinitely many elements of \( S \) of each of the forms \( 7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6 \) and no elements of \( S \) of the form \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \), where \( m \) is an integer.
solution:
Let 
\[
S=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}:\exists\,d\text{ with }n^2<d\le n^2+2n\text{ and }d\mid n^4\}.
\]
We shall show (i) no $n\equiv3,4\pmod7$ lie in $S$, and (ii) $S$ contains infinitely many $n$ in each of the residue‐classes $0,1,2,5,6\pmod7$.

1.  Reduction to two quadratic Diophantine equations.  
Suppose $n\in S$.  Then there is an integer $d$ satisfying
\[
n^2<d\le n^2+2n,
\qquad
d\mid n^4.
\]
Write 
\[
d=n^2+t,
\qquad
1\le t\le2n.
\]
Since $d\mid n^4$, there is an integer $q$ with
\[
n^4=q\,(n^2+t).
\]
On the other hand polynomial‐dividing $n^4$ by $n^2+t$ gives
\[
n^4=(n^2+t)\,(n^2-t)+t^2,
\]
so $n^2+t\mid t^2$.  Hence there is an integer $k\ge1$ with
\[
t^2=k\,(n^2+t).
\]
Rewriting,
\[
t^2 - k\,t - k\,n^2=0.
\]
Because $1\le t\le2n$ we have
\[
k \;=\;\frac{t^2}{n^2+t}
\;<\;\frac{4n^2}{n^2+1}
\;<\;4,
\]
so $k\in\{1,2,3\}$.  We treat each case:

Case $k=1$.  Then
\[
t^2 - t - n^2=0,
\]
whose discriminant is $\Delta=1+4n^2$.  But for every positive integer $n$,
\[
(2n)^2=4n^2<4n^2+1<4n^2+4n+1=(2n+1)^2,
\]
so $4n^2+1$ is \emph{not} a perfect square.  Hence the quadratic has no integral solution $t$, and therefore $k=1$ is impossible.

Case $k=2$.  Then
\[
t^2 -2t -2n^2=0,
\]
so the discriminant
\[
\Delta \;=\;4 +8n^2 \;=\;4\,(1+2n^2)
\]
must be a perfect square.  Write
\[
4+8n^2 =a^2,
\]
so $a$ is even, say $a=2b$.  Then
\[
4b^2 =4+8n^2
\;\implies\;
b^2 -2n^2 =1.
\]
Thus $(b,n)$ is a solution to the Pell equation
\[
x^2 -2y^2=1.
\tag{P$_2$}
\]
It is classical (for example by the continued‐fraction expansion of $\sqrt2$) that $(P_2)$ has infinitely many positive solutions $(b,y)=(b_k,n_k)$, $k=1,2,3,\dots\,$, with 
\[
b_k+ n_k\sqrt2 \;=\;(3+2\sqrt2)^k.
\]
For each such solution we recover
\[
t \;=\;\frac{2 + a}{2} \;=\;\frac{2+2b}{2} \;=\;1+b,
\]
which indeed satisfies
\[
1\le t\le 1+b = t
\quad\text{and}\quad
t\;\le\;1 + (\sqrt2\,n)\;<\;1+2n
\quad(\text{since }\sqrt2<2).
\]
Hence each Pell solution gives a legitimate divisor
\[
d \;=\;n^2 + t
\;=\;n^2 + (1+b)
\]
of $n^4$, and so each $n=n_k$ lies in $S$.  Thus the Pell‐family $(P_2)$ yields infinitely many elements of $S$.  

Case $k=3$.  Then
\[
t^2 -3t -3n^2=0,
\]
so the discriminant
\[
\Delta \;=\;9 +12n^2
\]
must be a perfect square, say $\Delta=a^2$.  Since $9\mid9+12n^2$, $3\mid a$, so write $a=3b$.  Then
\[
9b^2 =9+12n^2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
b^2 - \tfrac{4}{3}\,n^2 =1.
\]
In particular $3\mid n^2$ so $3\mid n$; write $n=3y$.  Then
\[
b^2 -12y^2=1,
\]
i.e.\ $(b,y)$ satisfies the Pell equation
\[
x^2 -12y^2=1.
\tag{P$_{12}$}
\]
Again by the standard theory of Pell’s equation, $(P_{12})$ has infinitely many positive solutions $(b_\ell,y_\ell)$, $\ell=1,2,3,\dots\,$, each with $b_\ell$ odd (since the minimal nontrivial solution is $x=7,y=2$).  From
\[
a=3b,\qquad k=3
\]
we recover
\[
t \;=\;\frac{3 + a}{2}
\;=\;\frac{3+3b}{2}
\;=\;\frac{3\,(1+b)}{2},
\]
which is integral because $b$ is odd, and one checks easily (from $b/y\approx\sqrt{12}<4$) that indeed $1\le t\le2n=6y$.  Hence each $n=3y_\ell$ yields a divisor
\[
d=n^2 + t
\]
of $n^4$, and so each such $n$ lies in $S$.  Thus the Pell‐family $(P_{12})$ also produces infinitely many elements of $S$.

Conclusion of Step 1.  Every $n\in S$ arises from one of the two Pell families above (with $k=2$ or $k=3$), and each Pell family is infinite.  No other $k$ is possible.  

2.  Excluding $n\equiv3,4\pmod7$.  
Suppose to the contrary that some $n\equiv3\pmod7$ or $n\equiv4\pmod7$ lay in $S$.  Then it must come from either the $k=2$ equation
\[
t^2 -2t -2n^2=0
\]
or the $k=3$ equation
\[
t^2 -3t -3n^2=0.
\]
Work modulo $7$ in each case:

(a) If $k=2$, then
\[
t^2 -2t -2n^2\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
But for $n\equiv3$ or $4\pmod7$ we have $n^2\equiv9\equiv2\pmod7$ or $16\equiv2\pmod7$.  Hence
\[
t^2 -2t -2n^2\equiv t^2 -2t -4\equiv0\pmod7,
\]
i.e.\ 
\[
t^2 -2t -4\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
Completing the square,
\[
(t-1)^2 \equiv5\pmod7.
\]
But $5$ is \emph{not} a quadratic residue modulo $7$ (the residues are $0,1,2,4$), so this congruence has no solution $t$.  Thus no $n\equiv3,4\pmod7$ can arise from $k=2$.

(b) If $k=3$, then
\[
t^2 -3t -3n^2\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
Again for $n^2\equiv2\pmod7$, this reads
\[
t^2 -3t -6\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
One checks exhaustively $t\equiv0,1,\dots,6\pmod7$ and finds no solution.  Hence no $n\equiv3,4\pmod7$ can arise from $k=3$ either.

Therefore no integer $n\equiv3$ or $4\pmod7$ lies in $S$.  

3.  Infinitely many elements in the other five residue‐classes.  
Finally we observe:

– The Pell family $(P_2)\colon b^2 -2n^2=1$ produces the sequence of $n$’s
\[
2,\,12,\,70,\,408,\,\dots
\]
whose residues mod $7$ are
\[
2,\,5,\,0,\,2,\dots
\]
in a $3$‐cycle $(2,5,0)$.  Hence there are infinitely many $n\in S$ in each of the classes $2,5,0\pmod7$.

– The Pell family $(P_{12})\colon b^2 -12y^2=1$ with $n=3y$ produces
\[
n=6,\,84,\,1170,\dots
\]
whose residues mod $7$ are
\[
6,\,0,\,1,\dots
\]
in a $3$‐cycle $(6,0,1)$.  Hence there are infinitely many $n\in S$ in each of the classes $6,0,1\pmod7$.

Taking the union of these two infinite families we obtain infinitely many $n\in S$ in each of the five residue‐classes
\[
0,1,2,5,6\pmod7,
\]
and we have already shown no elements of $S$ can lie in the two forbidden classes $3,4\pmod7$.  This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem: Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^{4} \) has a divisor in the range \( n^{2}+1, n^{2}+2, \ldots, n^{2}+2n \). Prove that there are infinitely many elements of \( S \) of each of the forms \( 7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6 \) and no elements of \( S \) of the form \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \), where \( m \) is an integer.
solution:
Throughout the proof  

• all letters denote integers,  
• we put \(n>1\) (the assertion for \(n=1\) is false and irrelevant),  
• for an integer \(x\) we write \(\overline x\) for its residue modulo \(7\;(0\le \overline x\le 6)\).

1.  A convenient reformulation  

Let  

\[
d\mid n^{4},\qquad n^{2}<d\le n^{2}+2n .
\]

Write \(d=n^{2}+r\;(1\le r\le 2n)\).
Because \((n^{2}+r)-(n^{2})=r\), we have  

\[
n^{2}\equiv -r\pmod{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n^{4}\equiv r^{2}\pmod{d}.
\]

Since \(d\mid n^{4}\), we must have \(d\mid r^{2}\), i.e.

\[
r^{2}=q\,(n^{2}+r)\tag{1}
\]

for some positive integer \(q\).

(a)  \(q\) is small.  
Because \(n\ge 2\),

\[
r\le 2n<n^{2}<n^{2}+r\le n^{2}+2n<(2n)^{2}=4n^{2},
\]

so from (1)

\[
q=\frac{r^{2}}{\,n^{2}+r\,}<\frac{4n^{2}}{n^{2}}=4,\qquad q\ge 2.
\]

Hence always  

\[
q\in\{2,3\}.\tag{2}
\]

(b)  \(q\neq 1\).  
Indeed \(q=1\) would give \(r^{2}=n^{2}+r\).  
But \(n^{2}<n^{2}+r<(n+1)^{2}\) (because \(r\le 2n\)), so \(n^{2}+r\) lies strictly between two consecutive squares and cannot itself be a square.

Thus an integer \(n>1\) lies in the set \(S\) if and only if there are
\(r\;(n<r\le 2n)\) and \(q\in\{2,3\}\) which satisfy (1).

The two values of \(q\) lead to two Pell equations; they yield two infinite families of solutions and, at the same time, exclude the residues \(\overline 3\) and \(\overline 4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The family \(q=2\)

With \(q=2\) equation (1) becomes  

\[
r^{2}=2\bigl(n^{2}+r\bigr)\Longrightarrow (r-1)^{2}-2n^{2}=1. \tag{3}
\]

Put \(x=r-1,\;y=n\).  
Then \(x^{2}-2y^{2}=1\), the classical Pell equation.  
All its positive solutions are

\[
(x_{k},y_{k}),\qquad
x_{k}+y_{k}\sqrt 2=(3+2\sqrt 2)^{\,k}\quad (k=1,2,3,\dots).
\]

Returning to \(r,n\) we obtain

\[
r_{k}=x_{k}+1,\qquad n_{k}=y_{k}\qquad(k\ge 1). \tag{4}
\]

(a)  The divisor really lies in the required interval.  
Assume contrary that \(r_{k}>2n_{k}\).  
Then (3) would give \(r_{k}^{2}\ge (2n_{k}+1)^{2}=4n_{k}^{2}+4n_{k}+1\) while the right-hand side of (3) equals \(2n_{k}^{2}+2r_{k}\le 2n_{k}^{2}+4n_{k}\), a contradiction.  
Hence indeed \(r_{k}\le 2n_{k}\).

Therefore \(d_{k}=n_{k}^{2}+r_{k}\) is a divisor of \(n_{k}^{4}\) situated between
\(n_{k}^{2}\) and \(n_{k}^{2}+2n_{k}\); thus every \(n_{k}\) belongs to \(S\).

(b)  The residues modulo \(7\).
Reducing the fundamental solution \(3+2\sqrt2\) modulo \(7\) gives  

\[
3+2\sqrt2\equiv 3+2\cdot3=3+6\equiv2\pmod7\ (\text{in }\,\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]/7).
\]

Because \(2^{3}\equiv1\pmod7\), the sequence \(\bigl(\overline{y_{k}}\bigr)_{k\ge1}\)
is periodic of length \(3\):
\[
\overline{n_{k}}=\overline{y_{k}}=2,5,0,2,5,0,\dots.
\]
Hence members of the first Pell family furnish infinitely many elements
of \(S\) whose residues are \(\overline0,\overline2,\overline5\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The family \(q=3\)

Put \(q=3\) in (1):

\[
r^{2}=3(n^{2}+r).\tag{5}
\]

Because \(3\mid r^{2}\), necessarily \(3\mid r\); write \(r=3d\;(d>0)\).  
Equation (5) becomes

\[
3d^{2}=n^{2}+3d\Longrightarrow n^{2}=3d(d-1).\tag{6}
\]

Again \(3\mid n\); put \(n=3y\;(y>0)\).  
Then (6) is \(3y^{2}=d(d-1)\).  
Multiply by \(4\) and rewrite:

\[
(2d-1)^{2}-12y^{2}=1.\tag{7}
\]

Set \(X=2d-1,\;Y=y\); we are led to the Pell equation \(X^{2}-12Y^{2}=1\).
Its positive solutions are

\[
(X_{k},Y_{k}),\qquad
X_{k}+Y_{k}\sqrt{12}=(7+2\sqrt{12})^{\,k}\quad(k=1,2,3,\dots).
\]

Returning to \(r,n\):

\[
d_{k}=\frac{X_{k}+1}{2},\quad r_{k}=3d_{k},\quad n_{k}=3Y_{k}\quad(k\ge 1).\tag{8}
\]

Exactly the same estimate as in 2 (a) shows \(r_{k}\le 2n_{k}\);
hence \(d_{k}=n_{k}^{2}+r_{k}\) is again an admissible divisor of \(n_{k}^{4}\) and every \(n_{k}\) is in \(S\).

(b)  Residues modulo \(7\).
Modulo \(7\) one has \(7+2\sqrt{12}\equiv 0+2\cdot4 =1\pmod 7\),
so the sequence \(\overline{Y_{k}}\) is periodic of length \(3\):

\[
\overline{n_{k}}=\overline{3Y_{k}}=6,0,1,6,0,1,\dots .
\]

Hence the second Pell family supplies infinitely many elements
of \(S\) whose residues are  \(\overline0,\overline1,\overline6\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Non-existence of residues \(\overline3,\overline4\)

Assume \(n\in S\) and \(\overline{n}\in\{3,4\}\).
As before there are \(r\;(n<r\le 2n)\) and \(q\in\{2,3\}\) satisfying (1).

Reduce (1) modulo \(7\).
Since \(\overline{n}^{\,2}=2\),

\[
\overline{r}^{\,2}\equiv q\,(\,\overline{r}+2\,)\pmod7.\tag{9}
\]

Squares modulo \(7\) are \(0,1,2,4\).
A short inspection of the seven possible values of \(\overline r\) gives:

•  if \(q=2\) the congruence \(s^{2}\equiv2(s+2)\pmod7\) has no solution,  

•  if \(q=3\) the congruence \(s^{2}\equiv3(s+2)\pmod7\) has no solution.

Consequently (9) is impossible; hence no such \(n\) exists.  
Therefore \(S\) contains no numbers congruent to \(3\) or \(4\) modulo \(7\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Collecting the results

•  The Pell family (3) gives infinitely many elements of \(S\) whose
residues are \(0,2,5\) mod \(7\).

•  The Pell family (7) gives infinitely many elements of \(S\) whose
residues are \(0,1,6\) mod \(7\).

Combining them we obtain infinitely many members of \(S\) in every
congruence class \(\overline0,\overline1,\overline2,\overline5,\overline6\),
and by §4 there are no members with residues \(\overline3,\overline4\).

That is exactly what had to be proved.
author: llm

problem: Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^{4} \) has a divisor in the range \( n^{2}+1, n^{2}+2, \ldots, n^{2}+2n \). Prove that there are infinitely many elements of \( S \) of each of the forms \( 7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6 \) and no elements of \( S \) of the form \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \), where \( m \) is an integer.
solution:
Let $S$ be the set of positive integers $n$ such that $n^4$ has a divisor $d$ with $n^2+1 \le d \le n^2+2n$.

Step 1: Characterize the condition for $n \in S$.
Let $d$ be a divisor of $n^4$ such that $n^2+1 \le d \le n^2+2n$.
We can write $d = n^2+x$ for some integer $x$.
The condition $n^2+1 \le d \le n^2+2n$ translates to $1 \le x \le 2n$.
Since $d | n^4$, we have $n^2+x | n^4$.
As $n^2+x | (n^2+x)(n^2-x) = n^4-x^2$, it must be that $n^2+x | n^4 - (n^4-x^2) = x^2$.
So, $n \in S$ if and only if there exists an integer $x$ such that $1 \le x \le 2n$ and $n^2+x$ divides $x^2$.
Since $n^2+x > 0$ and $x^2 \ge 0$, if $x^2=0$ then $x=0$, which is not in $1 \le x \le 2n$. So $x^2 > 0$.
Thus $n^2+x \le x^2$.
This implies $n^2 \le x^2-x = x(x-1)$.
If $x \le n$, then $x(x-1) \le n(n-1) = n^2-n$.
So $n^2 \le n^2-n$, which implies $n \le 0$.
However, $n$ is a positive integer. So we must have $x > n$.
Thus, the condition for $n \in S$ is that there exists an integer $x$ such that $n < x \le 2n$ and $n^2+x$ divides $x^2$.

Step 2: Determine the possible values for $q = x^2/(n^2+x)$.
Let $x^2 = q(n^2+x)$ for some integer $q$. Since $x^2 > 0$ and $n^2+x > 0$, $q$ must be a positive integer, so $q \ge 1$.
Since $x \le 2n$, $x^2 \le (2n)^2 = 4n^2$.
So $q(n^2+x) \le 4n^2$.
Also, $n^2+x > n^2$. So $q n^2 < q(n^2+x) \le 4n^2$.
This implies $q n^2 < 4n^2$, so $q < 4$.
Thus, $q$ can only be $1, 2,$ or $3$.

Step 3: Analyze $q=1$.
If $q=1$, then $x^2 = n^2+x$, which means $x^2-x-n^2=0$.
Solving for $x$ using the quadratic formula: $x = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+4n^2}}{2}$.
Since $x>0$, we must have $x = \frac{1+\sqrt{1+4n^2}}{2}$.
For $x$ to be an integer, $1+4n^2$ must be a perfect square, say $k^2$.
So $k^2 - (2n)^2 = 1$, which means $(k-2n)(k+2n)=1$.
Since $n$ is a positive integer, $2n>0$. $k+2n$ must be an integer.
Thus $k-2n=1$ and $k+2n=1$. This implies $4n=0$, so $n=0$.
But $n$ must be a positive integer. So $n=0$ is not allowed.
Alternatively, for $n>0$, $(2n)^2 < 1+4n^2 < (2n+1)^2 = 4n^2+4n+1$ as long as $1 < 4n+1$, which is true for $n \ge 1$.
So $1+4n^2$ is a perfect square if and only if it is $(2n)^2$, which means $1=0$, impossible or $4n+1 \le 1$, meaning $n=0$.
Thus, $1+4n^2$ is not a perfect square for $n>0$.
So $q=1$ yields no solutions for $n \in S$.

Step 4: Analyze $q=2$.
If $q=2$, then $x^2 = 2(n^2+x)$, so $x^2-2x-2n^2=0$.
Solving for $x$: $x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4-4(1)(-2n^2)}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{1+2n^2}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{1+2n^2}$.
Since $x>0$, we must have $x = 1+\sqrt{1+2n^2}$.
For $x$ to be an integer, $1+2n^2$ must be a perfect square, say $y^2$.
So we have the Pell equation $y^2-2n^2=1$.
The solutions $(y_k, n_k)$ for $k \ge 1$ are given by $y_k+n_k\sqrt{2} = (y_1+n_1\sqrt{2})^k$, where $(y_1,n_1)=(3,2)$ is the fundamental solution.
The values $n_k$ are $n_1=2, n_2=12, n_3=70, \ldots$. In general, $n_{k+2}=6n_{k+1}-n_k$ with $n_0=0, n_1=2$.
For these values of $n$, we have $x = 1+y_k$.
We must check the condition $n_k < x_k \le 2n_k$, i.e., $n_k < 1+y_k \le 2n_k$.
The first inequality $n_k-1 < y_k = \sqrt{1+2n_k^2}$.
If $n_k=1$, it is $0 < \sqrt{3}$ which is true (but $n_k=1$ is not a solution to $y^2-2n^2=1$). The smallest solution is $n_1=2$.
If $n_k \ge 1$, $n_k-1 \ge 0$, so we can square both sides: $(n_k-1)^2 < 1+2n_k^2 \implies n_k^2-2n_k+1 < 1+2n_k^2 \implies 0 < n_k^2+2n_k$. This is true for all positive $n_k$.
The second inequality $1+y_k \le 2n_k$, so $y_k \le 2n_k-1$.
For $y_k = \sqrt{1+2n_k^2}$ to be well-defined, $2n_k-1 \ge 0$, so $n_k \ge 1/2$. All $n_k$ satisfy this.
Squaring both sides (if $2n_k-1 \ge 0$): $1+2n_k^2 \le (2n_k-1)^2 = 4n_k^2-4n_k+1$.
This simplifies to $0 \le 2n_k^2-4n_k = 2n_k(n_k-2)$.
This inequality holds if $n_k=0$ (not a positive integer solution) or $n_k \ge 2$.
All solutions $n_k$ generated by $(3+2\sqrt{2})^k$ for $k \ge 1$ are $n_1=2, n_2=12, n_3=70, \ldots$. All these are $\ge 2$.
Thus, all $n_k$ for $k \ge 1$ are in $S$. This gives an infinite number of elements in $S$.

We examine the values of $n_k \pmod 7$:
$n_1=2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$.
$n_2=12 \equiv 5 \pmod 7$.
$n_3=70 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$.
$n_4=6n_3-n_2 = 6(70)-12 = 408 = 58 \cdot 7 + 2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$.
$n_5=6n_4-n_3 = 6(408)-70 \equiv 6(2)-0 \equiv 12 \equiv 5 \pmod 7$.
$n_6=6n_5-n_4 \equiv 6(5)-2 = 30-2=28 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$.
The sequence $n_k \pmod 7$ is periodic: $(2,5,0,2,5,0,\ldots)$ with period 3.
These solutions provide infinitely many elements of $S$ of the forms $7m, 7m+2, 7m+5$.

Step 5: Analyze $q=3$.
If $q=3$, then $x^2 = 3(n^2+x)$, so $x^2-3x-3n^2=0$.
Solving for $x$: $x = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{9-4(1)(-3n^2)}}{2} = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{9+12n^2}}{2}$.
Since $x>0$, we must have $x = \frac{3+\sqrt{9+12n^2}}{2}$.
For $x$ to be an integer, $9+12n^2$ must be a perfect square, say $k^2$.
So $k^2 = 9+12n^2 = 3(3+4n^2)$. This means $k^2$ must be a multiple of 3, so $k$ must be a multiple of 3. Let $k=3j$.
Then $(3j)^2 = 3(3+4n^2) \implies 9j^2 = 3(3+4n^2) \implies 3j^2 = 3+4n^2 \implies 3j^2-4n^2=3$.
Let $N=2n$. Then $3j^2-N^2=3$.
Since $N^2 = 3j^2-3 = 3(j^2-1)$, $N^2$ must be a multiple of 3, so $N$ must be a multiple of 3. Let $N=3N'$.
Then $3j^2-(3N')^2=3 \implies 3j^2-9(N')^2=3 \implies j^2-3(N')^2=1$.
This is a Pell equation. The fundamental solution is $(j_1, N'_1)=(2,1)$.
Solutions $(j_s, N'_s)$ are given by $j_s+N'_s\sqrt{3}=(2+\sqrt{3})^s$ for $s \ge 1$.
We have $n=N/2 = 3N'/2$. For $n$ to be an integer, $N'$ must be even.
The sequence $N'_s$ is $N'_1=1, N'_2=4, N'_3=15, N'_4=56, \ldots$. In general $N'_{s+2}=4N'_{s+1}-N'_s$ with $N'_0=0, N'_1=1$.
$N'_s$ is even if $s$ is an even integer. Let $s=2t$ for $t \ge 1$.
Let $n_t^* = 3N'_{2t}/2$. The first few values are $N'_2=4 \implies n_1^*=3(4)/2=6$. $N'_4=56 \implies n_2^*=3(56)/2=84$.
$N'_0=0 \implies n_0^*=0$, which is not a positive integer.
The recurrence relation for $N'_{2t}$ is $N'_{2(t+1)} = (j_2+N'_2\sqrt{3})(j_{2t}+N'_{2t}\sqrt{3})$. No, this is wrong.
The sequence $M_t = N'_{2t}$ satisfies $M_{t+1}= (A_2) M_t - M_{t-1}$. No, this is wrong.
$(j_{2(t+1)}+N'_{2(t+1)}\sqrt{3}) = (j_{2t}+N'_{2t}\sqrt{3})(j_2+N'_2\sqrt{3})^1 = (j_{2t}+N'_{2t}\sqrt{3})(7+4\sqrt{3})$.
So $N'_{2(t+1)} = 7N'_{2t} + 4j_{2t}$. Also $j_{2(t+1)} = 7j_{2t} + 12N'_{2t}$.
The sequence $M_t=N'_{2t}$ satisfies $M_{t+2}=14M_{t+1}-M_t$ with $M_0=N'_0=0, M_1=N'_2=4$.
So $n_t^*$ sequence $n_0^*=0, n_1^*=6, n_2^*=14(6)-0=84, n_3^*=14(84)-6=1176-6=1170, \ldots$.
For these values $n=n_t^*$, we have $x = (3+k)/2 = (3+3j_{2t})/2$.
We must check the condition $n_t^* < x \le 2n_t^*$. This is $3N'_{2t}/2 < (3+3j_{2t})/2 \le 2(3N'_{2t}/2)$.
$N'_{2t} < 1+j_{2t} \le 2N'_{2t}$. (Using $j_{2t} = \sqrt{1+3(N'_{2t})^2}$).
The first inequality $N'_{2t}-1 < j_{2t}$. Since $N'_{2t} \ge N'_2=4$, $N'_{2t}-1>0$.
$(N'_{2t}-1)^2 < 1+3(N'_{2t})^2 \implies (N'_{2t})^2-2N'_{2t}+1 < 1+3(N'_{2t})^2 \implies 0 < 2(N'_{2t})^2+2N'_{2t}$. This is true for $N'_{2t}>0$.
The second inequality $1+j_{2t} \le 2N'_{2t}$, so $j_{2t} \le 2N'_{2t}-1$.
Since $N'_{2t} \ge 4$, $2N'_{2t}-1 > 0$. Squaring both sides: $1+3(N'_{2t})^2 \le (2N'_{2t}-1)^2 = 4(N'_{2t})^2-4N'_{2t}+1$.
This simplifies to $0 \le (N'_{2t})^2-4N'_{2t} = N'_{2t}(N'_{2t}-4)$.
This inequality holds for $N'_{2t} \ge 4$. The smallest value is $N'_2=4$, for which it holds ($0 \le 0$).
Thus, all $n_t^* = 3N'_{2t}/2$ for $t \ge 1$ are in $S$. This gives another infinite number of elements in $S$.

We examine the values of $n_t^* \pmod 7$ for $t \ge 1$:
$n_1^*=6 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$.
$n_2^*=84 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$.
$n_3^*=1170$. $1170 = 14 \cdot 84 - 6 \equiv -6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$.
$n_4^*=14n_3^*-n_2^* \equiv -n_2^* \equiv 0 \pmod 7$.
$n_5^*=14n_4^*-n_3^* \equiv -n_3^* \equiv -1 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$.
The sequence $n_t^* \pmod 7$ for $t \ge 1$ is periodic: $(6,0,1,0,6,0,1,\ldots)$ with period 4.
These solutions provide infinitely many elements of $S$ of the forms $7m, 7m+1, 7m+6$.

Step 6: Combine results and conclude.
The analysis in Steps 1-2 shows that any $n \in S$ must arise from $q=2$ or $q=3$ type solutions.
The $n$ values from $q=2$ have residues modulo 7 in the set $\{0,2,5\}$.
The $n$ values from $q=3$ have residues modulo 7 in the set $\{0,1,6\}$.
Therefore, any $n \in S$ must have a residue modulo 7 in the set $\{0,1,2,5,6\}$.
This means there are no elements of $S$ of the form $7m+3$ or $7m+4$.

Furthermore, we have shown that there are infinite series of solutions for each of these types:
1.  $n_k \pmod 7$ sequence is $(2,5,0,2,5,0,\ldots)$.
    -   $n_{3j+1} \equiv 2 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 0$ gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m+2$. (e.g., $n_1=2, n_4=408$)
    -   $n_{3j+2} \equiv 5 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 0$ gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m+5$. (e.g., $n_2=12, n_5=2378$)
    -   $n_{3j} \equiv 0 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 1$ gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m$. (e.g., $n_3=70, n_6=13860$)
2.  $n_t^* \pmod 7$ sequence (for $t \ge 1$) is $(6,0,1,0,6,0,1,\ldots)$.
    -   $n_{2j}^* \equiv 0 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 1$ gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m$. (e.g., $n_2^*=84, n_4^*=14(1170)-84 = 16296$). This is a distinct sequence from $n_{3j}$ in general.
    -   $n_{4j-3}^* \equiv 6 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 1$ (i.e., $t=1,5,9,\ldots$) gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m+6$. (e.g., $n_1^*=6, n_5^*=14(16296)-1170 = 228144-1170 = 226974$).
    -   $n_{4j-1}^* \equiv 1 \pmod 7$ for $j \ge 1$ (i.e., $t=3,7,11,\ldots$) gives infinitely many $n \in S$ of the form $7m+1$. (e.g., $n_3^*=1170$).

Thus, there are infinitely many elements of $S$ of each of the forms $7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6$.
And there are no elements of $S$ of the form $7m+3$ or $7m+4$.
Small values check:
$n=1$: $1 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$. $1 \notin S$. $1+2(1)^2=3$ not square. $3j^2-4(1)^2=3 \implies 3j^2=7$ no int. $n=1$ is not among the solutions from Pell equations. This is consistent.
$n=2$: $2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$. $2 \in S$ (from $q=2$, $n_1=2$).
$n=3$: $3 \equiv 3 \pmod 7$. $3 \notin S$. ($1+2(3)^2=19$ not square, $3j^2-4(3)^2=3 \implies 3j^2=39$ no int). Consistent.
$n=4$: $4 \equiv 4 \pmod 7$. $4 \notin S$. ($1+2(4)^2=33$ not square, $3j^2-4(4)^2=3 \implies 3j^2=67$ no int). Consistent.
$n=5$: $5 \equiv 5 \pmod 7$. $5 \notin S$. ($1+2(5)^2=51$ not square, $3j^2-4(5)^2=3 \implies 3j^2=103$ no int). Consistent. $n_2=12 \equiv 5 \pmod 7$ is the first solution of this form.
$n=6$: $6 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$. $6 \in S$ (from $q=3$, $n_1^*=6$).

problem: Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^{4} \) has a divisor in the range \( n^{2}+1, n^{2}+2, \ldots, n^{2}+2n \). Prove that there are infinitely many elements of \( S \) of each of the forms \( 7m, 7m+1, 7m+2, 7m+5, 7m+6 \) and no elements of \( S \) of the form \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \), where \( m \) is an integer.
solution:
We define \( S \) as the set of all positive integers \( n \) such that \( n^4 \) has a divisor in the range \( [n^2 + 1, n^2 + 2n] \). We will characterize the elements of \( S \) and analyze their residues modulo 7.

### Step 1: Characterization of \( S \)
The condition for \( n \) to be in \( S \) is that there exists an integer \( d \) with \( n^2 + 1 \leq d \leq n^2 + 2n \) and \( d \mid n^4 \). Set \( d = n^2 + k \) where \( k \) is an integer and \( 1 \leq k \leq 2n \). Since \( d \mid n^4 \), we have \( n^4 \equiv 0 \pmod{d} \). Substituting \( d = n^2 + k \), it follows that \( n^2 \equiv -k \pmod{d} \), and squaring both sides gives \( n^4 \equiv (-k)^2 = k^2 \pmod{d} \). Thus, \( k^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{d} \), meaning \( d \mid k^2 \). Therefore, \( n^2 + k \mid k^2 \).

This implies that \( \frac{k^2}{n^2 + k} \) is an integer, denoted by \( q \). So \( k^2 = q(n^2 + k) \) for some integer \( q \). Rearranging gives:
\[
k^2 - qk - qn^2 = 0.
\]
This is a quadratic in \( k \), and for \( k \) to be an integer, the discriminant \( D = q^2 + 4qn^2 = q(q + 4n^2) \) must be a perfect square. Since \( 1 \leq k \leq 2n \), we have:
\[
q = \frac{k^2}{n^2 + k} \leq \frac{(2n)^2}{n^2} = 4,
\]
and because \( n^2 + k > n^2 \) for \( n \geq 1 \), it follows that \( q < 4 \). As \( q \) is a positive integer (since \( k \geq 1 \) and \( n \geq 1 \) imply \( q > 0 \)), we have \( q \leq 3 \). For \( n = 1 \), the range is \( d \in [2, 3] \), but \( n^4 = 1 \) has no divisors in this range, so \( 1 \notin S \). Thus, for \( n \geq 2 \), \( q \) can be 1, 2, or 3.

- **Case \( q = 1 \):** Then \( k^2 = 1 \cdot (n^2 + k) \), so \( k^2 - k - n^2 = 0 \). The discriminant is \( 1 + 4n^2 \), which must be a perfect square, say \( m^2 \). Thus, \( m^2 - 4n^2 = 1 \), or \( (m - 2n)(m + 2n) = 1 \). For \( n \geq 1 \), the only integer solutions are \( m - 2n = 1 \) and \( m + 2n = 1 \), but this implies \( 4n = 0 \), so no solutions for \( n \geq 1 \).

- **Case \( q = 2 \):** Then \( k^2 = 2(n^2 + k) \), so \( k^2 - 2k - 2n^2 = 0 \). The discriminant is \( 4 + 8n^2 = 4(1 + 2n^2) \), which must be a perfect square. Thus, \( 1 + 2n^2 \) must be a perfect square, say \( m^2 \), so \( m^2 - 2n^2 = 1 \). This is a Pell equation with fundamental solution \( (m, n) = (3, 2) \). The solutions are generated by the recurrence:
  \[
  m_j + n_j \sqrt{2} = (3 + 2\sqrt{2})^j \quad \text{for} \quad j \geq 1,
  \]
  but only for even \( j \) do we have \( m_j^2 - 2n_j^2 = 1 \) (since \( (1 + \sqrt{2})^{2j} \) gives solutions). The sequence for \( n_j \) satisfies \( n_1 = 2 \), \( n_2 \( = 12 \), and \( n_j = 6n_{j-1} - n_{j-2} \) for \( j \geq 3 \). For each such \( n_j \), solving for \( k \) gives \( k = 1 + m_j \), and \( 1 \leq k \leq 2n_j \) holds for \( j \geq 1 \). Thus, these \( n_j \) are in \( S \).

- **Case \( q = 3 \):** Then \( k^2 = 3(n^2 + k) \), so \( k^2 - 3k - 3n^2 = 0 \). The discriminant is \( 9 + 12n^2 = 3(3 + 4n^2) \), which must be a perfect square. Thus, \( 3(3 + 4n^2) = s^2 \) for some integer \( s \). Since 3 is prime, \( s \) must be divisible by 3, so set \( s = 3u \). Then \( 9u^2 = 3(3 + 4n^2) \), so \( 3u^2 = 3 + 4n^2 \), or \( 4n^2 - 3u^2 = -3 \). Modulo 3, \( n^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{3} \), so \( n \) must be divisible by 3. Set \( n = 3v \), then:
  \[
  4(9v^2) - 3u^2 = -3 \implies 36v^2 - 3u^2 = -3 \implies u^2 - 12v^2 = 1.
  \]
  This is another Pell equation with fundamental solution \( (u, v) = (7, 2) \). The solutions are generated by \( u_j + v_j \sqrt{12} = (7 + 2\sqrt{12})^j \) for \( j \geq 1 \), and \( n_j = 3v_j \). The sequence satisfies \( n_1 = 6 \), \( n_2 = 84 \), and \( n_j = 14n_{j-1} - n_{j-2} \) for \( j \geq 3 \). For each such \( n_j \), solving for \( k \) gives \( k = \frac{3(1 + u_j)}{2} \), which is an integer since \( u_j \) is odd, and \( 1 \leq k \leq 2n_j \) holds for \( j \geq 1 \). Thus, these \( n_j \) are in \( S \).

The sequences \( (a_j) \) for \( q = 2 \) and \( (b_j) \) for \( q = 3 \) are disjoint and cover all elements of \( S \), as \( q = 1 \) yields no solutions and other \( q \) are impossible.

### Step 2: Residues Modulo 7
We analyze the residues modulo 7 for the sequences \( (a_j) \) and \( (b_j) \).

- **Sequence \( (a_j) \):** Defined by \( a_1 = 2 \), \( a_2 = 12 \), \( a_j = 6a_{j-1} - a_{j-2} \) for \( j \geq 3 \).
  - Compute residues modulo 7:
    \[
    \begin{align*}
    a_1 &\equiv 2 \pmod{7}, \\
    a_2 &\equiv 12 \equiv 5 \pmod{7}, \\
    a_3 &= 6 \cdot 12 - 2 = 70 \equiv 0 \pmod{7}, \\
    a_4 &= 6 \cdot 70 - 12 = 408 \equiv 408 - 58 \cdot 7 = 408 - 406 = 2 \pmod{7}, \\
    a_5 &= 6 \cdot 408 - 70 = 2378 \equiv 2378 - 339 \cdot 7 = 2378 - 2373 = 5 \pmod{7}, \\
    a_6 &= 6 \cdot 2378 - 408 = 13860 \equiv 0 \pmod{7} \quad (\text{since} \ 13860 \div 7 = 1980), \\
    a_7 &= 6 \cdot 13860 - 2378 = 80782 \equiv 80782 - 11540 \cdot 7 = 80782 - 80780 = 2 \pmod{7}, \\
    &\vdots
    \end{align*}
    \]
    The sequence repeats every 3 terms: \( 2, 5, 0, 2, 5, 0, \ldots \). Thus, residues are only 0, 2, 5 modulo 7, and each appears infinitely often (e.g., residue 0 for \( j \equiv 0 \pmod{3} \), residue 2 for \( j \equiv 1 \pmod{3} \), residue 5 for \( j \equiv 2 \pmod{3} \)).

- **Sequence \( (b_j) \):** Defined by \( b_1 = 6 \), \( b_2 = 84 \), \( b_j = 14b_{j-1} - b_{j-2} \) for \( j \geq 3 \). Since \( 14 \equiv 0 \pmod{7} \), the recurrence modulo 7 is \( b_j \equiv -b_{j-2} \pmod{7} \).
  - Compute residues modulo 7:
    \[
    \begin{align*}
    b_1 &\equiv 6 \pmod{7}, \\
    b_2 &\equiv 84 \equiv 0 \pmod{7}, \\
    b_3 &= 14 \cdot 84 - 6 = 1170 \equiv 1170 - 167 \cdot 7 = 1170 - 1169 = 1 \pmod{7}, \\
    b_4 &= 14 \cdot 1170 - 84 = 16296 \equiv 0 \pmod{7} \quad (\text{since} \ 16296 \div 7 = 2328), \\
    b_5 &= 14 \cdot 16296 - 1170 = 226974 \equiv -b_3 \equiv -1 \equiv 6 \pmod{7}, \\
    b_6 &= 14 \cdot 226974 - 16296 = 3161700 \equiv -b_4 \equiv 0 \pmod{7}, \\
    b_7 &= 14 \cdot 3161700 - 226974 = 43983126 \equiv -b_5 \equiv -6 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}, \\
    &\vdots
    \end{align*}
    \]
    The sequence is 6, 0, 1, 0, 6, 0, 1, 0, 6, \ldots modulo 7. Thus, residues are only 0, 1, 6 modulo 7, and each appears infinitely often (e.g., residue 0 for all even \( j \), residue 1 for \( j \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), residue 6 for \( j \equiv 1 \pmod{4} \)).

Since \( S \) is the union of \( (a_j) \) and \( (b_j) \), the residues modulo 7 in \( S \) are 0, 1, 2, 5, 6. Residues 3 and 4 never occur. Each residue in \( \{0, 1, 2, 5, 6\} \) appears infinitely often in \( S \):
- Residue 0: in both sequences (e.g., \( a_j \) for \( j \equiv 0 \pmod{3} \), \( b_j \) for even \( j \)).
- Residue 1: in \( (b_j) \) (e.g., \( b_j \) for \( j \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \)).
- Residue 2: in \( (a_j) \) (e.g., \( a_j \) for \( j \equiv 1 \pmod{3} \)).
- Residue 5: in \( (a_j) \) (e.g., \( a_j \) for \( j \equiv 2 \pmod{3} \)).
- Residue 6: in \( (b_j) \) (e.g., \( b_j \) for \( j \equiv 1 \pmod{4} \)).

### Step 3: Conclusion
The forms \( 7m \), \( 7m+1 \), \( 7m+2 \), \( 7m+5 \), \( 7m+6 \) correspond to residues 0, 1, 2, 5, 6 modulo 7, respectively, and each has infinitely many elements in \( S \). The forms \( 7m+3 \) and \( 7m+4 \) correspond to residues 3 and 4, which never occur in \( S \).

Thus,

problem:
Let \( n \geq 1 \) be an integer and let \( t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{n} \) be positive integers. In a group of \( t_{n}+1 \) people, some games of chess are played. Two people can play each other at most once. Prove that it is possible for the following two conditions to hold at the same time:
(i) The number of games played by each person is one of \( t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots, t_{n} \).
(ii) For every \( i \) with \( 1 \leq i \leq n \), there is someone who has played exactly \( t_{i} \) games of chess.
solution:
Phrased in graph theory, the problem asks to produce a simple graph $G$ on $t_{n}+1$ vertices such that all degrees are in the set $\left\{t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right\}$ and each degree appears at least once.

We proceed by induction on $n$. If $n=1$, take a clique on $t_{1}+1$ vertices. For $n=2$, take a clique on $t_{1}$ vertices and an empty graph on $t_{2}+1-t_{1}$ vertices, and join them all together. For the inductive step:

- Take an example for the $(n-2)$ tuple $\left(t_{2}-t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n-1}-t_{1}\right)$, which has $t_{n-1}-t_{1}+1$ vertices.
- Then add in $t_{n}-t_{n-1}$ isolated vertices.
- Finally add in $t_{1}$ universal vertices.

Remark. The universal vertices are "forced", so the only parameter is the number of universal vertices to add in.

problem:
An \(n\)-tuple \((a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n})\) of positive integers is expensive if

\[
(a_{1}+a_{2})(a_{2}+a_{3}) \ldots (a_{n-1}+a_{n})(a_{n}+a_{1})=2^{2k-1}
\]

for some positive integer \(k\).

(a) Find all integers \(n \geq 2\) for which there exists an expensive \(n\)-tuple.

(b) Prove that each odd integer \(m \geq 1\) appears in an expensive \(n\)-tuple for some \(n \geq 2\).
solution:
For part (a), the answer is odd $n$, with construction given by setting $a_{1}=\cdots=a_{n}=1$. We show by induction that even $n$ all fail, with $n=2$ being plain.

Construct a regular $n$-gon whose vertices are labeled $a_{i}$ and edges are labeled with $a_{i}+a_{j}$.

Then we observe that it's impossible for an edge to exceed both of its neighbors, since if $a+b=2^{e}$ then $\min (a+1, b+1)>2^{e-1}$. Consequently we can take two adjacent edges $a+b=b+c$ with the same label; hence $a=c$. Then delete $b, c$ and induct down.

For part (b), for odd integers $m$, let $f(m)$ denote $2^{k}-m$ where $2^{k}$ is the smallest power of two exceeding $m$. Note $f(m) \leq m$ with equality if and only if $m=1$. So repeatedly apply $f$ until we wrap around; this gives twice a square of a power of two. Example when $m=13$ :

Remark. By applying the process of (a) in reverse, one essentially finds an inductive characterization of all expensive $n$-tuples.

problem:
An \(n\)-tuple \((a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n})\) of positive integers is expensive if

\[
(a_{1}+a_{2})(a_{2}+a_{3}) \ldots (a_{n-1}+a_{n})(a_{n}+a_{1})=2^{2k-1}
\]

for some positive integer \(k\).

(a) Find all integers \(n \geq 2\) for which there exists an expensive \(n\)-tuple.

(b) Prove that each odd integer \(m \geq 1\) appears in an expensive \(n\)-tuple for some \(n \geq 2\).
solution:
For every positive integer \(n\) let

\[
P(a_{1},a_{2},\dots ,a_{n})=(a_{1}+a_{2})(a_{2}+a_{3})\cdots(a_{n-1}+a_{n})(a_{n}+a_{1})
      =2^{\,2k-1}\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0})
\]

If \(P(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})\) equals such an odd power of \(2\) we shall call  
\((a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})\) an {\it expensive \(n\)-tuple}.  
Throughout the proof the indices of the \(a_{i}\) are understood cyclically
(\(a_{n+1}=a_{1}\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Part (a) For which \(n\) do expensive \(n\)-tuples exist?
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A preliminary observation.  
Because the product \(P(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})\) is a power of \(2\),
every factor \(a_{i}+a_{i+1}\) is itself a power of \(2\); otherwise the
product would contain a prime different from \(2\).
So for suitable integers \(e_{1},\dots ,e_{n}\ge 1\)

\[
a_{i}+a_{i+1}=2^{e_{i}}\qquad(1\le i\le n).
\tag{1}
\]

Necessity: \(n\) must be odd.  
Assume, to obtain a contradiction, that \(n\) is even, say \(n=2r\).
Form the alternating sum of the equations (1):

\[
S=(a_{1}+a_{2})-(a_{2}+a_{3})+\dots +(a_{2r-1}+a_{2r})-(a_{2r}+a_{1})
  =0
\]
(the terms in the middle cancel pairwise).
Using (1) we also have  

\[
S=2^{e_{1}}-2^{e_{2}}+\dots +2^{e_{2r-1}}-2^{e_{2r}}=0.
\tag{2}
\]

Write the right–hand side of (2) in binary.
Because every summand is a single power of two,
each power \(2^{j}\;(j\ge 1)\) appears with coefficient

\[
c_{j}= \#\{i\;\text{odd}\mid e_{i}=j\}-\#\{i\;\text{even}\mid e_{i}=j\}.
\]

Equality (2) implies \(c_{j}=0\) for every \(j\); otherwise the binary
representation of \(S\) would contain a non–zero digit.
Hence every exponent \(j\) occurs equally often in odd and in even
positions, so in particular an {\em even} number of times.
Consequently the total exponent

\[
e_{1}+e_{2}+\dots +e_{n}
\]
is even, contradicting the requirement  
\(e_{1}+e_{2}+\dots +e_{n}=2k-1\) (odd).
Therefore no expensive \(n\)-tuple exists when \(n\) is even.

Sufficiency: all odd \(n\ge 3\) work.  
For any odd \(n\) choose

\[
a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots =a_{n}=1.
\]

Then every sum \(a_{i}+a_{i+1}=2=2^{1}\) and

\[
P(1,1,\dots ,1)=2^{\,n}.
\]

Because \(n\) is odd, the exponent \(n\) has the form \(2k-1\);
hence \((1,1,\dots ,1)\) is expensive.
So an expensive \(n\)-tuple exists iff \(n\) is odd, \(n\ge 3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Part (b) Every odd integer \(m\ge 1\) appears somewhere in an expensive
tuple.
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The case \(m=1\).  
The triple \((1,1,1)\) is expensive (see above), so \(1\) occurs.

From now on fix an odd integer \(m\ge 3\).
We shall construct an expensive \(n\)-tuple that contains \(m\).

Step 1. Descending to \(1\).  
Define a sequence

\[
b_{0}=m,\qquad
b_{i+1}=2^{\lceil\log_{2}b_{i}\rceil}-b_{i}\qquad(i\ge 0)
\tag{3}
\]

and stop as soon as \(b_{t}=1\).
Because \(b_{i}<2^{\lceil\log_{2}b_{i}\rceil}\le 2b_{i}\) we have
\(0<b_{i+1}<b_{i}\); hence \(b_{0}>b_{1}>\dots >b_{t}=1\) and the
process ends after finitely many steps.

For every \(i<t\) equation (3) gives

\[
b_{i}+b_{i+1}=2^{\lceil\log_{2}b_{i}\rceil},
\tag{4}
\]
a power of two.

Step 2. Building the cycle.  
Put  

\[
n=2t+1\quad(\text{odd})\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(a_{1},a_{2},\dots ,a_{n})=
\bigl(b_{0},\,b_{1},\,\dots ,\,b_{t-1},\,1,\,1,\,b_{t-1},\,\dots ,\,b_{1}\bigr).
\]

The number \(m=b_{0}=a_{1}\) is indeed one component of the \(n\)-tuple.
Check that consecutive sums are powers of two:

• For \(1\le i<t\) we have \(a_{i}+a_{i+1}=b_{i-1}+b_{i}\), a power of
two by (4).

• \(a_{t}+a_{t+1}=b_{t-1}+1\) is a power of two (again by (4) with
\(i=t-1\)).

• \(a_{t+1}+a_{t+2}=1+1=2\).

• Because the sequence is palindromic, every remaining sum
\(a_{j}+a_{j+1}\;(j>t+1)\) coincides with an already considered one, so
it is a power of two as well.

Hence all the factors in \(P(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})\) are powers of two.

Step 3. The total exponent is odd.  
Denote by \(E_{1},\dots ,E_{n}\) the exponents of these factors.
All factors except the central one \(a_{t+1}+a_{t+2}=2\;(=2^{1})\)
occur twice (once on each side of the centre), so

\[
E_{1}+E_{2}+\dots +E_{n}=1+2\bigl(\text{an integer}\bigr)\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\]

Therefore \(P(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})=2^{\,2k-1}\) for some
\(k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\),
and the constructed tuple is expensive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
a) An expensive \(n\)-tuple exists exactly for the odd integers
\(n\ge 3\).

b) For every odd \(m\ge 1\) the construction above produces an odd
\(n\;(=2t+1)\) and an expensive \(n\)-tuple that contains \(m\).
Thus every odd positive integer indeed appears in some expensive
\(n\)-tuple.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute-angled triangle in which no two sides have the same length. The reflections of the centroid \( G \) and the circumcenter \( O \) of \( \triangle ABC \) in its sides \( BC, CA, AB \) are denoted by \( G_1, G_2, G_3 \) and \( O_1, O_2, O_3 \), respectively. Show that the circumcircles of triangles \( G_1G_2C, G_1G_3B, G_2G_3A, O_1O_2C, O_1O_3B, O_2O_3A \) and \( ABC \) have a common point.
solution:
Here is an approach with complex numbers. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point. Let $P_{B}$ and $P_{C}$ be the reflections of $P$ across $A B$ and $A C$ and let $Q_{B}$ and $Q_{C}$ be the second intersections of lines $A P_{B}$ and $A P_{C}$ with the circumcircle. Then we will compute the intersection of $\left(A P_{B} P_{C}\right)$ and $\left(A Q_{B} Q_{C}\right) \equiv(A B C)$.

We have $p_{B}=a+c-a c \bar{p}, p_{C}=a+b-a b \bar{p}$. To compute $q_{B}$ note that

$$
\begin{aligned}
a+q_{B} & =p_{B}+a q_{B} \overline{p_{B}} \\
& =a+c-a c \bar{p}+a q_{B}(1 / a+1 / c-p / a c) \\
\Longrightarrow a c \bar{p}-c & =(a / c-p / c) q_{B} \\
\Longrightarrow q_{B} & =c^{2} \frac{a \bar{p}-1}{a-p} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly $q_{C}=b^{2} \frac{a \bar{p}-1}{a-p}$. Then, the desired intersection is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{p_{B} q_{C}-p_{C} q_{B}}{p_{B}-p_{C}+q_{C}-q_{B}} & =\frac{\left(\frac{a \bar{p}-1}{a-p}\right)\left(b^{2}(a+c-a c \bar{p})-c^{2}(a+b-a b \bar{p})\right)}{(b-c)(a \bar{p}-1)+\left(b^{2}-c^{2}\right) \cdot \frac{a \bar{p}-1}{a-p}} \\
& =\frac{b^{2}(a+c-a c \bar{p})-c^{2}(a+b-a b \bar{p})}{(b-c)(a-p)+\left(b+c\right)} \\
& =\frac{(b-c)(a(b+c)+b c)-(b-c) a b c \bar{p}}{(a-p)+(b+c)} \\
& =\frac{a b+b c+c a-a b c \bar{p}}{a+b+c-p}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is in any case symmetric in $a, b, c$. Moreover taking $p=\frac{1}{3}(a+b+c)$ and $p=0$ give the same numbers (and indeed any $p$ on the Euler line).

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute-angled triangle in which no two sides have the same length. The reflections of the centroid \( G \) and the circumcenter \( O \) of \( \triangle ABC \) in its sides \( BC, CA, AB \) are denoted by \( G_1, G_2, G_3 \) and \( O_1, O_2, O_3 \), respectively. Show that the circumcircles of triangles \( G_1G_2C, G_1G_3B, G_2G_3A, O_1O_2C, O_1O_3B, O_2O_3A \) and \( ABC \) have a common point.
solution:
Let △ABC be acute and non-isosceles.  
Denote by  

 H the orthocentre,   ℓ = GO the Euler line,  

and by  

 G₁ ,G₂ ,G₃  (resp. O₁ ,O₂ ,O₃)  

the reflections of G (resp. O) in the sides BC , CA , AB.

We prove that the seven circles

 (ABC), (G₁G₂C), (G₁G₃B), (G₂G₃A),  
 (O₁O₂C), (O₁O₃B), (O₂O₃A)

have a common point.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The anti-Steiner point P of the Euler line
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For every line through the orthocentre the reflections in the three
sides of a triangle are known to be concurrent on the circumcircle;  
the point of concurrence is called the anti-Steiner point of the
line.  (This is a classical fact, see e.g. the article ‘Steiner line’
on Wikipedia.)

Because ℓ = GO passes through H, its three reflections

 ℓ₁  =  G₁O₁  (reflection in BC),  
 ℓ₂  =  G₂O₂  (reflection in CA),  
 ℓ₃  =  G₃O₃  (reflection in AB)

meet at a point P on the circumcircle (ABC).  We shall work with this
point P.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A general cyclicity lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma.  
Let X be any point on the Euler line ℓ.  Let  

 X₁ , X₂  

be the reflections of X in BC and CA respectively.  
Then the four points P, X₁, X₂ and C are concyclic.

Proof.  
All angles are directed and taken modulo 180°.

Because X₁ lies on ℓ₁ = PX₁, ℓ₁ is the reflection of ℓ in BC,
hence

 ∠(PX₁ , BC) = ∠(BC , ℓ).  (1)

Since X₁C is the reflection of XC in BC we also have

 ∠(BC , X₁C) = ∠(XC , BC).  (2)

Adding (1) and (2) gives  

 ∠PX₁C = ∠(BC , ℓ)+∠(XC , BC) = ∠(XC , ℓ).  (3)

In exactly the same way, reflecting in CA we find  

 ∠PX₂C = ∠(XC , ℓ).  (4)

Equations (3) and (4) furnish  

 ∠PX₁C = ∠PX₂C,

so the quadrilateral PX₁X₂C is cyclic. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Application of the lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(i)  Take X = G.  
     Then X₁ = G₁ and X₂ = G₂, and the lemma says that P, G₁, G₂, C
     are concyclic.  Rotating the rôle of the sides we also obtain

 P ∈ (G₁G₃B) and P ∈ (G₂G₃A).

(ii)  Take X = O.  
      Now X₁ = O₁ and X₂ = O₂, so P, O₁, O₂, C are concyclic, and
      similarly

 P ∈ (O₁O₃B) and P ∈ (O₂O₃A).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Point P lies on

 (ABC) (by construction),  
 (G₁G₂C), (G₁G₃B), (G₂G₃A) (from part (i)),  
 (O₁O₂C), (O₁O₃B), (O₂O₃A) (from part (ii)).

Hence the seven circles mentioned in the statement all pass through
the same point P, the anti-Steiner point of the Euler line GO with
respect to △ABC.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( CA = CB \) and \( \angle ACB = 120^\circ \), and let \( M \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( P \) be a variable point on the circumcircle of \( \triangle ABC \), and let \( Q \) be the point on the segment \( CP \) such that \( QP = 2QC \). It is given that the line through \( P \) and perpendicular to \( AB \) intersects the line \( MQ \) at a unique point \( N \). Prove that there exists a fixed circle such that \( N \) lies on this circle for all possible positions of \( P \).
solution:
Since $\vec{N}=3 \vec{Q}-2 \vec{M}$, it suffices to show $Q$ moves on a fixed circle. That fixed circle is the image of $(C A B)$ under a homothety at $C$ with ratio $1 / 3$, so we are done.

Remark. Note that points $A$ and $B$ are superfluous, and the choice of constant $2$ or the definition of $M$ is also arbitrary (only the fact that $\overline{C M} \| \overline{P N}$ matters). Moreover, the condition $\angle A C B=120^{\circ}$ is never used either.

As a result, I did not find this problem very inspiring.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( CA = CB \) and \( \angle ACB = 120^\circ \), and let \( M \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( P \) be a variable point on the circumcircle of \( \triangle ABC \), and let \( Q \) be the point on the segment \( CP \) such that \( QP = 2QC \). It is given that the line through \( P \) and perpendicular to \( AB \) intersects the line \( MQ \) at a unique point \( N \). Prove that there exists a fixed circle such that \( N \) lies on this circle for all possible positions of \( P \).
solution:
Let C be the origin of a vector plane and denote by small bold letters the position-vectors of the corresponding capital letters :

 c = 0 , m = $\vec{CM}$ , p = $\vec{CP}$ , q = $\vec{CQ}$ , n = $\vec{CN}$ ,
 o = $\vec{CO}$ ( O is the circum-centre of ΔABC ).

Step 1  Basic geometric facts

1.  Because CA = CB, the median CM is also the perpendicular bisector of AB; hence CM ⟂ AB.  
    Consequently the line through P that is perpendicular to AB is parallel to CM, i.e.  

                              PN ∥ CM .                                        (1)

2.  Q divides CP internally in the ratio CQ : QP = 1 : 2, whence

                              q = p/3 .                                        (2)

Step 2  Two descriptions of N

•  Since N lies on MQ there is a real number λ such that

                              n = q + λ (m – q).                              (3)

•  By (1) the vector n – p is parallel to m, so for some real μ

                              n = p + μ m.                                     (4)

Step 3  Solving for λ and μ

Insert (2) into (3):

  n = (1 – λ) p/3 + λ m.                                                      (5)

Comparing (4) and (5) we express n simultaneously with the independent vectors p and m:

  p + μ m = (1 – λ) p/3 + λ m.

Because p and m are not collinear (M is not on CP for any admissible P), the coefficients of p
and m must coincide:

  1 = (1 – λ)/3  and  μ = λ.

The first equality gives λ = –2 and therefore μ = –2 as well.
Substituting μ in (4) we obtain the simple relation

                              n = p – 2 m.                                    (6)

Step 4  Relating m to the circum-centre O

Let the common length CA = CB be a.  
With ∠ACB = 120°,

 AB² = a² + a² – 2a² cos120° = 3a² ⇒ AB = a√3.

The length of the median CM is

 CM² = (2CA² + 2CB² – AB²)/4 = (2a² + 2a² – 3a²)/4 = a²/4,
 so    CM = a/2.                                                            (7)

By the sine rule the circum-radius is

 R = CA / (2 sin∠CBA) = a / (2 sin 30°) = a, hence CO = R = a.               (8)

O lies on CM (CM is the perpendicular bisector of AB), and (7)–(8) give

                              CO = 2·CM, so o = 2 m.                          (9)

Step 5  Translating the circumcircle

Substituting (9) into (6):

                              n = p – o.                                      (10)

For every point P on the circumcircle we have |p – o| = R (its radius).  
Equation (10) therefore implies

                              |n| = |p – o| = R.                              (11)

In words: N is obtained from P by the fixed translation by vector –o, hence N
runs on the translate of the circumcircle by –o, i.e. on the circle

  centre C  (because o = $\vec{CO}$)
  radius R  (the circum-radius of ΔABC).

This circle is completely independent of the choice of P, so every admissible point N
lies on the fixed circle with centre C and radius R.

Therefore there exists a fixed circle (the circle with centre C and radius equal to the
circum-radius of ΔABC) that contains the point N for every position of P on the
circumcircle of ΔABC, as was to be proved.
