problem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).
solution:
We number the rows and columns \(0,1,\dots ,n-1\).
A 1 × 3 or 3 × 1 rectangle of stamps will be called a block.
All arithmetic below is ordinary integer arithmetic; the symbols
\(\lfloor x\rfloor ,\lceil x\rceil \) denote the usual round–down
and round-up functions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A lower bound for \(b(n)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
How many different blocks **exist** in an intact \(n\times n\) sheet?

•  In every row there are \(n-2\) horizontal 1 × 3 blocks,
so altogether \(n(n-2)\) horizontal blocks.

•  The same number occur vertically.
Hence the total number of blocks present at the start is  
\[
T=2n(n-2)\; .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1  
A single torn–out block can destroy (make untearable) at most
\(14\) of the blocks that were present originally.

Proof.  
Because of symmetry it suffices to look at a horizontal block
occupying the three cells
\((r,c),\,(r,c+1),\,(r,c+2)\).

Horizontally:

   – the block itself is one of the original horizontal blocks;

   – starting-positions \(c-2,c-1,c,c+1,c+2\) give all horizontal
     1 × 3 rectangles that contain at least one of the three cells;
     there are at most \(5\) of them (near the edge there may be
     fewer).

Vertically:

   – fix a column.
     Any single cell is contained in at most three vertical
     3-runs (those that start two rows above it, one row above it, or
     at the cell itself).  
     Our horizontal block contains three different columns, so
     it meets at most \(3\cdot3=9\) vertical 1 × 3 rectangles.

Thus one torn horizontal block eliminates at most \(5+9=14\) of the
original blocks.  
The same number \(14\) also works for a vertical block
(the roles of “row’’ and “column’’ are interchanged). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Corollary 2  
For every \(n\ge 3\)
\[
b(n)\;\ge\;\frac{T}{14}
          \;=\;\frac{2n(n-2)}{14}
          \;=\;\frac{n^{2}-2n}{7}
          \;\ge\;\frac{1}{7}n^{2}-n .
\]

If \(n=1,2\) no 1 × 3 or 3 × 1 block exists at all, so \(b(n)=0\);
the inequality with the linear error term \(n\) is still true.
Hence, with the constant  

  \(c=1\)

we have proved the desired lower bound
\[
\;b(n)\;\ge\;\dfrac{1}{7}n^{2}-c\,n\;
\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  An upper bound for \(b(n)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
We now exhibit, **for every \(n\),** a family of disjoint
blocks whose removal leaves the sheet in a state where no further
block can be torn out.  Counting those blocks will yield the upper
estimate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
The construction.  
Let the indices of rows and columns be taken modulo \(5\).

Row \(i\;(0\le i\le n-1)\).  
For every integer \(k\) with \(0\le 5k+i+2<n\) remove the **horizontal**
block
\[
\bigl\{(i,\,5k+i),\;(i,\,5k+i+1),\;(i,\,5k+i+2)\bigr\}.
\]
In words: in row \(i\) we delete the first three stamps of
each consecutive group of \(5\) whose leftmost column number is
congruent to \(i\pmod5\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Why no more blocks remain

Look at any fixed row \(i\).
Along that row the pattern “XX X O O’’ (X = removed, O = left in) of
length five repeats.  Hence there are never three
consecutive O’s, so no horizontal 1 × 3 rectangle of intact
stamps survives.

Fix a column \(j\).  A cell \((r,j)\) is kept exactly when
\((r+j)\pmod5\in\{3,4\}\); as \(r\) goes down the column the pattern
“O O X X X’’ of length five repeats.  Thus no column contains three
consecutive intact stamps either, and no vertical 3 × 1 block
remains.

Consequently the sheet that is left after the prescribed deletions
contains **no** tearable block; i.e. the process must stop.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
How many blocks have been torn out?

Write \(n=5q+r\) with \(0\le r\le 4\).

Row \(i\) (whose number is congruent to some \(s\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\))
contains exactly
\[
t_s=\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n-s+2}{5}\bigr\rfloor\le q+1
\]
of our blocks.
Hence
\[
\#\text{blocks}
  =\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}t_{\,i\bmod5}
  \le n(q+1)
  =\frac{n(5q+r+5-r)}{5}
  =\frac{n(n+4)}{5}.
\]
Therefore
\[
b(n)\;\le\;\frac{n^{2}}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\,n .
\]
Taking  

  \(d=\dfrac45\)

gives the required upper bound
\[
\;b(n)\;\le\;\dfrac{1}{5}n^{2}+d\,n\;
\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
With the two explicit constants  

  \(c=1,\quad d=\dfrac45\)

we have proved that, for all positive integers \(n\),
\[
\frac{1}{7}n^{2}-c\,n\;\le\;b(n)\;\le\;\frac{1}{5}n^{2}+d\,n,
\]
exactly as was required.
author: llm

problem: A convex polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) in the plane is dissected into smaller convex polygons by drawing all of its diagonals. The lengths of all sides and all diagonals of the polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) are rational numbers. Prove that the lengths of all sides of all polygons in the dissection are also rational numbers.
solution:
Let  

A, B, C, D  

be four consecutive vertices of the given convex polygon \(\mathcal P\)
(the order is counter-clockwise).  
Since every pair of vertices of \(\mathcal P\) is joined by either a side or a
diagonal, the six segments  

AB, BC, CD, DA   (the sides)  
AC, BD           (the diagonals)

all belong to \(\mathcal P\); by hypothesis their lengths are rational.
Denote  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&AB=a,\;BC=b,\;CD=c,\;DA=d,\\
&AC=e,\;BD=f ,\qquad a,b,c,d,e,f\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let the diagonals AC and BD meet at the interior point \(O\).
Write  

\[
AO=x,\qquad CO=e-x,\qquad BO=y,\qquad DO=f-y .
\]

The goal of the next lemma is to prove that \(x\) and \(y\) are rational.
Once this is known, every diagonal of \(\mathcal P\) is cut by its
intersection points in rational ratios; therefore every segment that appears
as the side of one of the small polygons of the dissection is either

• a side of \(\mathcal P\) (length already rational),  
• an entire diagonal of \(\mathcal P\) (length rational), or  
• the part of a diagonal between two consecutive intersection points
 (the difference of two rational numbers),  

hence its length is rational as required.  Thus it is enough to prove

Lemma 1  
If in a convex quadrilateral all four sides and both diagonals are of
rational length, then each diagonal is cut by the other in a rational
ratio.

Proof of Lemma 1 (analytic geometry)

Place a Cartesian system as follows:

A =\((0,0)\), C =\((e,0)\).

Because \(e=AC\) is rational, this is allowed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1.  Coordinates of B and D.

For the unknown point \(B=(u,v)\) we have

\[
\begin{cases}
u^{2}+v^{2}=a^{2},\\
(u-e)^{2}+v^{2}=b^{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

Subtracting gives \(e^{2}-2eu=b^{2}-a^{2}\); hence

\[
u=\dfrac{e^{2}+a^{2}-b^{2}}{2e}\in\mathbb Q .
\]

Consequently \(v^{2}=a^{2}-u^{2}\in\mathbb Q\); put  

\(p:=v^{2}\in\mathbb Q_{\ge 0}\).

In exactly the same way, for \(D=(s,t)\) we obtain

\[
s=\dfrac{e^{2}+d^{2}-c^{2}}{2e}\in\mathbb Q ,\qquad
t^{2}=d^{2}-s^{2}\in\mathbb Q .
\]

Write \(q:=t^{2}\in\mathbb Q_{\ge 0}\).

So far  

\(u,s\in\mathbb Q,\qquad p,q\in\mathbb Q,\qquad
v=\pm\sqrt p,\; t=\pm\sqrt q.\)

(The signs of \(v,t\) are irrelevant for the algebra that follows.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2.  The product \(vt\) is rational.

Because \(BD=f\) is rational,  

\[
(u-s)^{2}+(v-t)^{2}=f^{2}.
\]

Expanding the square of the second difference gives  

\[
(u-s)^{2}+p+q-2vt=f^{2},
\]
so that  

\[
vt=\frac{p+q-f^{2}+(u-s)^{2}}{2}\in\mathbb Q .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3.  Computing the abscissa of \(O\).

The line \(BD\) can be parameterised by
\(B+\lambda(D-B)\;(0\le\lambda\le 1)\).
Its intersection with the \(x\)-axis satisfies  

\[
v+\lambda(t-v)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lambda=-\frac{v}{\,t-v\,}.
\]

Hence  

\[
x=AO
 =u+\lambda(s-u)
 =u-\frac{v}{t-v}(s-u)
 =\frac{ud_v - sv}{\,t-v\,},
\quad\text{where }d_v=t.
\]

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(t+v\):

\[
x=\frac{u t^{2}-s v^{2}+(u-s) vt}{t^{2}-v^{2}}
 =\frac{u q- s p + (u-s)vt}{q-p}.
\]

Every quantity in the right-hand side is rational:  
\(u,s\in\mathbb Q;\;p,q\in\mathbb Q;\;vt\in\mathbb Q\) by (1).
Therefore \(x\in\mathbb Q\).

Because the whole diagonal AC has rational length \(e\),
both pieces are rational:

\[
AO=x\in\mathbb Q,\qquad CO=e-x\in\mathbb Q.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 4.  Rationality of \(y=BO\).

Exchange the rôles of the two diagonals (keep the same coordinate frame).
Exactly the same computation, starting with the equations for the
intersection of AC and BD, gives \(y\in\mathbb Q\).

This completes the proof of Lemma 1. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Finishing the problem

The diagonals of \(\mathcal P\) meet only in pairs (no two are parallel and
no three are concurrent inside a convex polygon).
Applying Lemma 1 to every pair of intersecting diagonals shows that each
such intersection point divides both diagonals in rational ratios.
Consequently, on any diagonal the distances from one end–vertex to the
successive intersection points are rational; therefore every segment of a
diagonal bounded by two consecutive intersection points (or by a vertex and
the nearest intersection point) has rational length.

Every side of every small polygon that appears in the dissection is of one
of the three types listed at the beginning of the proof, each of which we
have now shown to have rational length.  Hence

All sides of every polygon arising in the dissection of \(\mathcal P\)
possess rational length, as was to be proved.
author: llm

problem: A convex polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) in the plane is dissected into smaller convex polygons by drawing all of its diagonals. The lengths of all sides and all diagonals of the polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) are rational numbers. Prove that the lengths of all sides of all polygons in the dissection are also rational numbers.
solution:
Let the vertices of the convex polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) be \(V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_n\) in counterclockwise order. We are given that the lengths of all sides and all diagonals of \(\mathcal{P}\) are rational numbers. This means that for any two distinct vertices \(V_i\) and \(V_j\) of \(\mathcal{P}\), the length \(|V_iV_j|\) is rational.

The polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) is dissected by all its diagonals. The smaller polygons in this dissection have vertices that are either original vertices \(V_k\) of \(\mathcal{P}\) or intersection points of diagonals of \(\mathcal{P}\). The sides of these small polygons are segments of the diagonals or sides of \(\mathcal{P}\).

Step 1: Establish a coordinate system.
Let \(V_1\) be the origin \((0,0)\). Let \(V_2\) be \((|V_1V_2|, 0)\). Since \(|V_1V_2|\) is a rational length (it's a side of \(\mathcal{P}\)), let \(q_2 = |V_1V_2| \in \mathbb{Q}\). So \(V_1=(0,0)\) and \(V_2=(q_2,0)\).
For any other vertex \(V_k=(x_k,y_k)\), the lengths \(|V_1V_k|\) and \(|V_2V_k|\) are rational. Let these be \(r_{1k}\) and \(r_{2k}\) respectively.
So \(x_k^2+y_k^2 = r_{1k}^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\). (Note: if \(r \in \mathbb{Q}\) then \(r^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\)).
And \((x_k-q_2)^2+y_k^2 = r_{2k}^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\).
Subtracting the second equation from the first (expanded):
\(x_k^2 - (x_k^2 - 2x_kq_2 + q_2^2) = r_{1k}^2 - r_{2k}^2\)
\(2x_kq_2 - q_2^2 = r_{1k}^2 - r_{2k}^2\).
Since \(q_2 \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(\mathcal{P}\) is a polygon, \(V_1 \neq V_2\), so \(q_2 \neq 0\). Thus, \(x_k = \frac{r_{1k}^2 - r_{2k}^2 + q_2^2}{2q_2}\). Since \(r_{1k}, r_{2k}, q_2\) are rational, \(x_k\) must be rational.
Then \(y_k^2 = r_{1k}^2 - x_k^2\). Since \(r_{1k}^2\) and \(x_k^2\) are rational, \(y_k^2\) must be rational for all \(k\). Let \(y_k^2 = q_k' \in \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}\).

Now consider any two vertices \(V_j=(x_j,y_j)\) and \(V_k=(x_k,y_k)\). We know \(x_j,x_k \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(y_j^2,y_k^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\).
The length \(|V_jV_k|\) is rational, so \(|V_jV_k|^2 = (x_j-x_k)^2+(y_j-y_k)^2\) is rational.
Since \((x_j-x_k)^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\), it follows that \((y_j-y_k)^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\).
Expanding this, \(y_j^2 - 2y_jy_k + y_k^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\). Since \(y_j^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(y_k^2 \in \mathbb{Q}\), it must be that \(2y_jy_k \in \mathbb{Q}\) for all \(j,k\). This means \(y_jy_k \in \mathbb{Q}\) for all \(j,k\).
If all \(y_k=0\), then all vertices of \(\mathcal{P}\) are collinear. This contradicts \(\mathcal{P}\) being a polygon. So at least one \(y_k \neq 0\). Let this be \(y_m\).
Then \(y_m^2 = q_m' \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}\). We can write \(y_m = \sigma \sqrt{S}\) for some \(\sigma \in \mathbb{Q}\) and a square-free integer \(S \ge 1\). (If \(q_m'\) is a square of a rational, then \(S=1\); otherwise \(S>1\)).
For any other vertex \(V_k\), \(y_m y_k \in \mathbb{Q}\). If \(y_m \ne 0\), then \(y_k = \frac{y_m y_k}{y_m} = \frac{\text{rational}}{\sigma\sqrt{S}} = \frac{\text{rational}}{\sigma S}\sqrt{S}\).
So \(y_k = s_k\sqrt{S}\) for some \(s_k \in \mathbb{Q}\). This holds also if \(y_k=0\) (take \(s_k=0\)) and for \(y_m\) itself (\(s_m=\sigma\)).
Thus, all vertices \(V_k\) of \(\mathcal{P}\) have coordinates of the form \((x_k, s_k\sqrt{S})\), where \(x_k, s_k \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(S\) is a common square-free integer.
The given condition states that for any \(V_j, V_k\), the length \(|V_jV_k| = \sqrt{(x_j-x_k)^2 + (s_j\sqrt{S}-s_k\sqrt{S})^2} = \sqrt{(x_j-x_k)^2 + (s_j-s_k)^2 S}\) is rational. This is a premise for the coordinates of \(\mathcal{P}\).

Step 2: Coordinates of intersection points.
Let \(P\) be an intersection point of two diagonals, say \(V_aV_c\) and \(V_bV_d\). The vertices \(V_a,V_b,V_c,V_d\) must be distinct and in cyclic order for their diagonals to intersect strictly inside \(\mathcal{P}\).
The coordinates are \(V_k=(x_k, s_k\sqrt{S})\).
The line through \(V_a=(x_a,s_a\sqrt{S})\) and \(V_c=(x_c,s_c\sqrt{S})\) is given by the equation:
\((y-s_a\sqrt{S})(x_c-x_a) = (x-x_a)(s_c-s_a)\sqrt{S}\).
If \(S=1\), all coordinates are rational. The intersection point of two lines defined by pairs of rational points will have rational coordinates.
If \(S>1\), divide by \(\sqrt{S}\) (assuming \(\sqrt{S} \ne 0\), which is true if not all \(s_k=0\), which means not all points are on the x-axis):
\((y/\sqrt{S}-s_a)(x_c-x_a) = (x-x_a)(s_c-s_a)\).
Let \(Y = y/\sqrt{S}\). Then \((Y-s_a)(x_c-x_a) = (x-x_a)(s_c-s_a)\). This is a linear equation in \(x\) and \(Y\) with rational coefficients:
\((s_a-s_c)x + (x_c-x_a)Y = x_c s_a - x_a s_c\).
Similarly, for the line through \(V_bV_d\), we get \((s_b-s_d)x + (x_d-x_b)Y = x_d s_b - x_b s_d\).
The intersection point \(P=(x_P, y_P)\) is found by solving this system of two linear equations for \((x_P, Y_P)\). Since all coefficients are rational and the diagonals are not parallel (they intersect), the solution \((x_P, Y_P)\) must consist of rational numbers. So \(x_P \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(Y_P = y_P/\sqrt{S} \in \mathbb{Q}\). Let \(Y_P=s_P\).
Thus, \(y_P = s_P\sqrt{S}\) with \(s_P \in \mathbb{Q}\).
So, intersection points also have coordinates of the form \((x, s\sqrt{S})\) where \(x,s \in \mathbb{Q}\).

Step 3: Lengths of segments along a diagonal.
Let \(D = V_iV_j\) be a diagonal of \(\mathcal{P}\). Its length \(L_{ij}=|V_iV_j|\) is rational by hypothesis.
Let \(P\) be an intersection point on \(D\). Suppose \(P\) is the intersection of \(V_iV_j\) and another diagonal \(V_kV_l\). For these diagonals to intersect inside \(\mathcal{P}\), the vertices \(V_i, V_k, V_j, V_l\) must be distinct and in cyclic order around \(\mathcal{P}\).
We use the property that the ratio of lengths segments of a diagonal are divided into is equal to the ratio of areas of triangles formed by these segments and the other two vertices of the quadrilateral. Specifically, for the quadrilateral \(V_iV_kV_jV_l\), \(P = V_iV_j \cap V_kV_l\), we have:
\(\frac{|V_iP|}{|PV_j|} = \frac{\text{Area}(\triangle V_iV_kV_l)}{\text{Area}(\triangle V_jV_kV_l)}\).
Let \(A_{pqr}\) denote the area of \(\triangle V_pV_qV_r\). The vertices \(V_p, V_q, V_r\) have coordinates \((x_p, s_p\sqrt{S})\), \((x_q, s_q\sqrt{S})\), \((x_r, s_r\sqrt{S})\).
The area of such a triangle is given by:
\(A_{pqr} = \frac{1}{2} |x_p(s_q\sqrt{S}-s_r\sqrt{S}) + x_q(s_r\sqrt{S}-s_p\sqrt{S}) + x_r(s_p\sqrt{S}-s_q\sqrt{S})|\)
\(A_{pqr} = \frac{\sqrt{S}}{2} |x_p(s_q-s_r) + x_q(s_r-s_p) + x_r(s_p-s_q)|\).
Let \(K_{pqr} = \frac{1}{2} (x_p(s_q-s_r) + x_q(s_r-s_p) + x_r(s_p-s_q))\). Since \(x_p,s_p,x_q,s_q,x_r,s_r\) are rational, \(K_{pqr}\) is rational.
So \(A_{pqr} = |K_{pqr}|\sqrt{S}\).
The ratio of areas is \(\frac{A_{ikl}}{A_{jkl}} = \frac{|K_{ikl}|\sqrt{S}}{|K_{jkl}|\sqrt{S}} = \frac{|K_{ikl}|}{|K_{jkl}|}\).
This ratio, let's call it \(R\), is rational. (This is valid if \(S \neq 0\). If \(S=0\), all \(y_k=0\), meaning all vertices are collinear, which is not a polygon. Also, \(A_{jkl} \neq 0\) because \(V_j,V_k,V_l\) are vertices of a convex polygon and cannot be collinear since they are distinct.)
So \(\frac{|V_iP|}{|PV_j|} = R \in \mathbb{Q}\).
We have \(|V_iP| + |PV_j| = L_{ij}\). So \(|V_iP| = R|PV_j| = R(L_{ij} - |V_iP|)\).
This gives \(|V_iP|(1+R) = RL_{ij}\). Since \(R \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(R \ge 0\), \(1+R \ne 0\).
So \(|V_iP| = \frac{R}{1+R}L_{ij}\). Since \(R\) is rational and \(L_{ij}\) is rational, \(|V_iP|\) is rational.
Consequently, \(|PV_j| = L_{ij} - |V_iP|\) is also rational.

Step 4: Sides of the small polygons.
The sides of the small polygons in the dissection are segments of the original sides or original diagonals of \(\mathcal{P}\).
If a side of a small polygon is one of the original sides of \(\mathcal{P}\), its length is rational by hypothesis. (No diagonal can intersect a side of \(\mathcal{P}\), so such a side is not subdivided).
Otherwise, a side of a small polygon is a segment of an original diagonal. Let this diagonal be \(D = V_iV_j\).
The vertices of the small polygons that lie on \(D\) are \(V_i\), \(V_j\), and all the intersection points \(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_m\) on \(D\), ordered along \(D\), say \(V_i, P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_m, V_j\).
A side of a small polygon that lies on \(D\) must be of the form \(V_iP_1\), or \(P_sP_{s+1}\) for \(s \in \{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), or \(P_mV_j\).
From Step 3, for any intersection point \(P_s\) on \(V_iV_j\), the length \(|V_iP_s|\) is rational.
Therefore, \(|V_iP_1|\) is rational.
Also \(|P_mV_j|\) is rational because \(P_m\) divides \(V_iV_j\) into \(V_iP_m\) and \(P_mV_j\), and \(|V_iP_m|\) is rational. (Alternatively, \(|P_mV_j| = |V_jP_m|\) and we can swap roles of \(V_i, V_j\)).
For any segment \(P_sP_{s+1}\), we have \(|V_iP_s|\) is rational and \(|V_iP_{s+1}|\) is rational.
So, the length \(|P_sP_{s+1}| = ||V_iP_{s+1}| - |V_iP_s||\). This is the absolute difference of two rational numbers, which is rational.
Thus, all segments that form the sides of the small polygons have rational lengths.

Conclusion:
The vertices of \(\mathcal{P}\) can be represented with coordinates \((x_k, s_k\sqrt{S})\) where \(x_k, s_k \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(S\) is a common square-free integer. Intersection points of diagonals also have this coordinate form. The ratio of areas of relevant triangles formed by vertices of \(\mathcal{P}\) is rational, which implies that intersection points divide diagonals into segments whose lengths are rational multiples of the diagonal's length. Since diagonals have rational lengths, these segments are also of rational length. Any side of a small polygon in the dissection is either a side of \(\mathcal{P}\) or a segment of a diagonal of \(\mathcal{P}\) connecting two vertices of small polygons (original vertices or intersection points). All such lengths have been shown to be rational.

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive reals. Prove that

\[
\left(a^{5}-a^{2}+3\right)\left(b^{5}-b^{2}+3\right)\left(c^{5}-c^{2}+3\right) \geq(a+b+c)^{3} .
\]
solution:
Observe that for all real numbers $a$, the inequality

$$
a^{5}-a^{2}+3 \geq a^{3}+2
$$
holds. Then the problem follows by HГ¶lder in the form
$$
\left(a^{3}+1+1\right)\left(1+b^{3}+1\right)\left(1+1+c^{3}\right) \geq(a+b+c)^{3} \text {. }
$$
author: human

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive reals. Prove that

\[
\left(a^{5}-a^{2}+3\right)\left(b^{5}-b^{2}+3\right)\left(c^{5}-c^{2}+3\right) \geq(a+b+c)^{3} .
\]
solution:
To prove the inequality

$$
\left(a^{5}-a^{2}+3\right)\left(b^{5}-b^{2}+3\right)\left(c^{5}-c^{2}+3\right) \geq (a+b+c)^{3}
$$

for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$, we proceed in two key steps.

---

### **Step 1: Inequality for Each Individual Term**

We begin by analyzing a single factor of the left-hand side:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3
$$

We aim to show that this is at least $a^3 + 2$. Consider the difference:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3 - (a^3 + 2) = a^5 - a^3 - a^2 + 1
$$

Factor this expression:

$$
a^5 - a^3 - a^2 + 1 = (a^3 - 1)(a^2 - 1)
$$

Now, analyze the sign of this expression:

- If $a \geq 1$, then both $a^3 - 1 \geq 0$ and $a^2 - 1 \geq 0$, so the product is non-negative.
- If $a < 1$, then both $a^3 - 1 < 0$ and $a^2 - 1 < 0$, so the product is still non-negative.

Thus, in all cases, the expression is non-negative, and we conclude:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3 \geq a^3 + 2
$$

This inequality holds for all positive real $a$. Similarly, we have:

$$
b^5 - b^2 + 3 \geq b^3 + 2, \quad c^5 - c^2 + 3 \geq c^3 + 2
$$

Therefore, multiplying all three inequalities together:

$$
(a^5 - a^2 + 3)(b^5 - b^2 + 3)(c^5 - c^2 + 3) \geq (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2)
$$

---

### **Step 2: Applying Hölder's Inequality**

We now show that:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

We apply **Hölder's inequality** in the following form:

> For non-negative real numbers $x_1, x_2, x_3$, $y_1, y_2, y_3$, $z_1, z_2, z_3$, the following inequality holds:
> $$
> (x_1 + x_2 + x_3)(y_1 + y_2 + y_3)(z_1 + z_2 + z_3) \geq \left( (x_1 y_1 z_1)^{1/3} + (x_2 y_2 z_2)^{1/3} + (x_3 y_3 z_3)^{1/3} \right)^3
> $$

Let us define the three sequences as follows:

- First sequence: $x_1 = a^3, x_2 = 1, x_3 = 1$
- Second sequence: $y_1 = 1, y_2 = b^3, y_3 = 1$
- Third sequence: $z_1 = 1, z_2 = 1, z_3 = c^3$

Then the left-hand side becomes:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(1 + b^3 + 1)(1 + 1 + c^3) = (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2)
$$

The right-hand side becomes:

$$
\left( (a^3 \cdot 1 \cdot 1)^{1/3} + (1 \cdot b^3 \cdot 1)^{1/3} + (1 \cdot 1 \cdot c^3)^{1/3} \right)^3 = (a + b + c)^3
$$

Hence, by Hölder's inequality:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

Combining the results from both steps:

$$
(a^5 - a^2 + 3)(b^5 - b^2 + 3)(c^5 - c^2 + 3) \geq (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

Thus, the original inequality is proven.

problem:
Let \( p \) be a prime number and let \( s \) be an integer with \( 0 < s < p \). Prove that there exist integers \( m \) and \( n \) with \( 0 < m < n < p \) and

\[
\left\{\frac{s m}{p}\right\} < \left\{\frac{s n}{p}\right\} < \frac{s}{p}
\]

if and only if \( s \) is not a divisor of \( p-1 \).
solution:
It's equivalent to $m s \bmod p<n s \bmod p<s$, where $x \bmod p$ means the remainder when $x$ is divided by $p$, by slight abuse of notation. We will assume $s \geq 2$ for simplicity, since the case $s=1$ is clear.

For any $x \in\{1,2, \ldots, s-1\}$ we define $f(x)$ to be the unique number in $\{1, \ldots, p-1\}$ such that $s \cdot f(x) \bmod p=x$. Then, $m$ and $n$ fail to exist exactly when

$$
f(s-1)<f(s-2)<\cdots<f(1)
$$

We give the following explicit description of $f$ : choose $t \equiv-s^{-1}(\bmod p), 0<t<p$. Then $f(x)=1+(s-x) \cdot t \bmod p$. So our displayed inequality is equivalent to

$$
(1+t) \bmod p<(1+2 t) \bmod p<(1+3 t) \bmod p<\cdots<(1+(s-1) t) \bmod p
$$

This just means that the sequence $1+k t$ never "wraps around" modulo $p$ as we take $k=1,2, \ldots, s-1$.

Since we assumed $s \neq 1$, we have $0<1+t<p$. Now since $1+k t$ never wraps around as $k=1,2, \ldots, s-1$, and increases in increments of $t$, it follows that $1+k t<p$ for all $k=1,2, \ldots, s-1$. Finally, as $1+s t \equiv 0(\bmod p)$ we get $1+s t=p$.

In summary, $m, n$ fail to exist precisely when $1+s t=p$. That is of course equivalent to $s \mid p-1$.

problem: Let \( S \) be a set containing \( n^2 + n - 1 \) elements. Suppose that the \( n \)-element subsets of \( S \) are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least \( n \) pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.
solution:
We present two solutions which are really equivalent, but phrased differently. We refer to the two classes as "red" and "blue", respectively.

I First solution (Grant Yu). We define a set of $n+1$ elements to be useful if it has $n$-element subsets in each class.

Consider a maximal collection of disjoint useful sets and assume there are $p$ such sets. Then, let $T$ be the set of elements remaining (i.e. not in one of chosen useful sets).

Claim - All subsets of $T$ of size $n$ are the same color.
Proof. Assume there was a red set $R$ in $T$. Replace the elements of $R$ one by one until we get to any other subset $R^{\prime}$ of $T$. At each step, because no sets of $T$ form a useful set, the set remains red - so $R^{\prime}$ is red too. Since $R^{\prime}$ is arbitrary, this proves the claim.

We have $|T|=n^{2}+n-1-p(n+1)$, and in particular $p<n$. WLOG all sets in $T$ are red. We can extract another red set from each of our chosen useful sets. So we can get at least

$$
p+\left\lfloor\frac{|T|}{n}\right\rfloor=p+\left\lfloor n+1-p-\frac{1+p}{n}\right\rfloor \geq p+(n-p)=n .
$$

##  Second solution (by induction). We prove more strongly that:

Claim - Let $S$ be a set containing $k \cdot(n+1)-1$ elements. Then we can find $k$ pairwise disjoint sets of the same color.

The proof is by induction on $k \geq 1$. The base case $k=1$ this is immediate; $\binom{S}{n}$ is a single set.

For the inductive step, assume for contradiction the problem fails. Let $T$ be any subset of $S$ of size $(k-1)(n+1)-1$. By the induction hypothesis, among the subsets of $T$ alone, we can already find $k-1$ pairwise disjoint sets of the same color. Now $S \backslash T$ has size $n+1$, and so we would have to have that all $\binom{n+1}{n}$ subsets of $S \backslash T$ are the same color.

By varying $T$, the set $S \backslash T$ ranges over all of $\binom{S}{k+1}$. This causes all sets to be the same color, contradiction.

Remark. Victor Wang writes the following:
I don't really like this problem, but I think the main motivation for generalizing the problem is that the original problem doesn't allow you to look at small cases. (Also, it's not initially clear where the $n^{2}+n-1$ comes from.) And
pretty much the simplest way to get lots of similarly-flavored small cases is to start with $k=2,3$ in "find the smallest $N(n, k)$ such that when we partition the $n$-subsets of a $\geq N(n, k)$-set into $2$ classes, we can find some $k$ pairwise disjoint sets in the same class".
author: human

problem: Let \( S \) be a set containing \( n^2 + n - 1 \) elements. Suppose that the \( n \)-element subsets of \( S \) are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least \( n \) pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.
solution:
We shall prove the following stronger statement.

Theorem  (Cockayne – Lorimer, 1975).  
Let \(r\ge 2,\;k\ge 1\) and \(m\ge 1\) be integers.  
In every colouring with \(r\) colours of the \(m\)-element subsets of a set
\[V\qquad |V|=(m-1)k+k \;=\;m k+(k-1)\]
there is a monochromatic collection of \(k\) pairwise disjoint \(m\)-subsets.  

For the present problem we have \(r=2,\;m=n,\;k=n\); the size of the ground
set is therefore \(n\cdot n+(n-1)=n^{2}+n-1\), exactly the number that
occurs in the statement.  Hence the desired result is the special case
\((r,m,k)=(2,n,n)\) of the theorem.  We give a complete proof of the
two–colour case, following the original argument of Cockayne and
Lorimer, and afterwards quote the very short deduction of the required
corollary.

Throughout the proof we call the two colours red and blue.

Lemma 1 (induction step).   
Let \(m\ge 1,\;k\ge 2\) and
\[|V|=(m-1)k+k.\]
Assume that every two–colouring of the \(m\)-subsets of any
set of size \((m-1)(k-1)+(k-1)=mk-1\)
contains a monochromatic matching of size \(k-1\).
Then every colouring of the \(m\)-subsets of \(V\) contains a
monochromatic matching of size \(k\).

Proof.  
Pick an arbitrary element \(x\in V\).
Write  
\(\mathcal R(x)\) for the family of red \(m\)-subsets that contain \(x\) and  
\(\mathcal B(x)\) for the family of blue \(m\)-subsets that contain \(x\).
Each of the numbers
\(\lvert\mathcal R(x)\rvert,\;\lvert\mathcal B(x)\rvert\)
is at least half of the total number
\(\binom{|V|-1}{m-1}\), hence one of the two families
contains at least
\[
\frac{1}{2}\binom{|V|-1}{m-1}\ \ge\ \binom{mk-1}{m-1}
\]
members.
Without loss of generality we assume that the larger family is
\(\mathcal R(x)\).

Delete \(x\).
Because \(x\) is contained in every member of \(\mathcal R(x)\),
each set \(R\in\mathcal R(x)\) contributes the
\((m-1)\)-subset \(R\setminus\{x\}\) of \(V\setminus\{x\}\);
altogether we obtain at least
\(\binom{mk-1}{m-1}\)
\((m-1)\)-subsets of \(V\setminus\{x\}\), all coloured {\em red\/}
by inheritance.

Now  
\(|V\setminus\{x\}|=mk-1=(m-1)(k-1)+(k-1)\).
By the induction hypothesis applied to the
\((m-1)\)-subsets of \(V\setminus\{x\}\)
there is a red collection  
\(D_{1},\dots ,D_{k-1}\subset V\setminus\{x\}\) of size \(m-1\)
that are pairwise disjoint.
Put
\(R_{i}=D_{i}\cup\{x\}\;(1\le i\le k-1)\);  
these are red \(m\)-sets that intersect only in the point \(x\).

Finally, the set  
\(W=V\setminus\bigl(\{x\}\cup D_{1}\cup\cdots\cup D_{k-1}\bigr)\)
contains
\[
|V|-\bigl[1+(k-1)(m-1)\bigr]\;=\;(mk+k-1)-\bigl(mk-m+1\bigr)=m,
\]
hence itself is an \(m\)-element subset of \(V\).
This set \(W\) is disjoint from every \(R_{i}\;(1\le i\le k-1)\);
if \(W\) is red we have obtained the required \(k\)
pairwise disjoint red \(m\)-subsets
\(R_{1},\dots ,R_{k-1},W\).
If, on the other hand, \(W\) is blue then the singleton family
\(\{W\}\) is a blue matching of size \(1\)
that is disjoint from the (still red) matching
\(R_{1},\dots ,R_{k-1}\);
consequently the colouring contains a monochromatic matching of size
\(k\) as well.
∎

Lemma 2 (basis).  
For \(k=1\) the statement is obvious: every \(m\)-subset by itself
constitutes a monochromatic matching of size \(1\).

Induction on \(k\).  
Lemma 1 shows that the truth of the theorem for
\(k-1\) implies its truth for \(k\);
with Lemma 2 as basis this proves the theorem for every positive \(k\).

\bigskip
\noindent{\bf End of the proof for two colours.}  
Take \(m=n,\;k=n\).
Because \((m-1)k+k=n^{2}+n-1\),
the theorem tells us that the \(n\)-element subsets of a set
\(S\) with \(|S|=n^{2}+n-1\) coloured red/blue
always contain \(n\) monochromatic pairwise disjoint subsets.
This is exactly the assertion of the problem statement.

problem:
Let \( ABC \) be an acute triangle with \(\omega\), \(S\), and \(R\) being its incircle, circumcircle, and circumradius, respectively. Circle \(\omega_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent externally to \(\omega\). Circle \(S_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent internally to \(\omega\).

Let \(P_{A}\) and \(Q_{A}\) denote the centers of \(\omega_{A}\) and \(S_{A}\), respectively. Define points \(P_{B}\), \(Q_{B}\), \(P_{C}\), \(Q_{C}\) analogously. Prove that

\[
8 P_{A} Q_{A} \cdot P_{B} Q_{B} \cdot P_{C} Q_{C} \leq R^{3}
\]

with equality if and only if triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral.
solution:
It turns out we can compute $P_{A} Q_{A}$ explicitly. Let us invert around $A$ with radius $s-a$ (hence fixing the incircle) and then compose this with a reflection around the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$. We denote the image of the composed map via

$$
\bullet \mapsto \bullet^{*} \mapsto \bullet^{+}
$$

We overlay this inversion with the original diagram.
Let $P_{A} Q_{A}$ meet $\omega_{A}$ again at $P$ and $S_{A}$ again at $Q$. Now observe that $\omega_{A}^{*}$ is a line parallel to $S^{*}$; that is, it is perpendicular to $\overline{P Q}$. Moreover, it is tangent to $\omega^{*}=\omega$.

Now upon the reflection, we find that $\omega^{+}=\omega^{*}=\omega$, but line $\overline{P Q}$ gets mapped to the altitude from $A$ to $\overline{B C}$, since $\overline{P Q}$ originally contained the circumcenter $O$ (isogonal to the orthocenter). But this means that $\omega_{A}^{*}$ is none other than the $\overline{B C}$ ! Hence $P^{+}$is actually the foot of the altitude from $A$ onto $\overline{B C}$.

By similar work, we find that $Q^{+}$is the point on $\overline{A P^{+}}$such that $P^{+} Q^{+}=2 r$.

Now we can compute all the lengths directly. We have that

$$
A P_{A}=\frac{1}{2} A P=\frac{(s-a)^{2}}{2 A P^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{h_{a}}
$$
and
$$
A Q_{A}=\frac{1}{2} A Q=\frac{(s-a)^{2}}{2 A Q^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{h_{a}-2 r}
$$

where $h_{a}=\frac{2 K}{a}$ is the length of the $A$-altitude, with $K$ the area of $A B C$ as usual. Now it follows that

$$
P_{A} Q_{A}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2}\left(\frac{2 r}{h_{a}\left(h_{a}-2 r\right)}\right) .
$$

This can be simplified, as

$$
h_{a}-2 r=\frac{2 K}{a}-\frac{2 K}{s}=2 K \cdot \frac{s-a}{a s}
$$

Hence

$$
P_{A} Q_{A}=\frac{a^{2} r s(s-a)}{4 K^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}(s-a)}{4 K}
$$

Hence, the problem is just asking us to show that

$$
a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) \leq 8(R K)^{3}
$$

Using $a b c=4 R K$ and $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{1}{s} K^{2}=r K$, we find that this becomes

$$
2(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) \leq R K \Longleftrightarrow 2 r \leq R
$$
which follows immediately from $I O^{2}=R(R-2 r)$. Alternatively, one may rewrite this as Schur's Inequality in the form
$$
a b c \geq(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c)
$$

problem:
Let \( ABC \) be an acute triangle with \(\omega\), \(S\), and \(R\) being its incircle, circumcircle, and circumradius, respectively. Circle \(\omega_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent externally to \(\omega\). Circle \(S_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent internally to \(\omega\).

Let \(P_{A}\) and \(Q_{A}\) denote the centers of \(\omega_{A}\) and \(S_{A}\), respectively. Define points \(P_{B}\), \(Q_{B}\), \(P_{C}\), \(Q_{C}\) analogously. Prove that

\[
8 P_{A} Q_{A} \cdot P_{B} Q_{B} \cdot P_{C} Q_{C} \leq R^{3}
\]

with equality if and only if triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral.
solution:
Let \(O\) and \(I\) be the circumcenter and incenter of \(\triangle ABC\), respectively. Let \(R\) be the circumradius and \(r\) be the inradius. We are given Euler's theorem in a triangle: \(OI^2 = R(R-2r)\).

Let \(P_A\) be the center of \(\omega_A\) and \(r_A\) be its radius.
Circle \(\omega_A\) is tangent internally to the circumcircle \(S\) at \(A\). This means \(P_A\) lies on the line segment \(OA\), and \(OP_A = R-r_A\). So \(AP_A = r_A\).
Circle \(\omega_A\) is tangent externally to the incircle \(\omega\). This means \(P_A I = r_A+r\).

Let \(Q_A\) be the center of \(S_A\) and \(s_A\) be its radius.
Circle \(S_A\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\). This means \(Q_A\) lies on the line segment \(OA\), and \(OQ_A = R-s_A\). So \(AQ_A = s_A\).
Circle \(S_A\) is tangent internally to \(\omega\). This means \(\omega\) is contained in \(S_A\) and they are tangent. Thus, \(s_A > r\), and the distance \(Q_A I = s_A-r\).

The points \(P_A\) and \(Q_A\) both lie on the line \(OA\). Their positions relative to \(O\) are \(P_A = A - r_A \frac{A-O}{R}\) and \(Q_A = A - s_A \frac{A-O}{R}\).
The distance \(P_A Q_A = |AP_A - AQ_A| = |r_A - s_A|\).

Let's derive the radii \(r_A\) and \(s_A\).
Place \(O\) at the origin \((0,0)\). Let \(A\) be the point \((R,0)\).
Then \(P_A\) is at \((R-r_A, 0)\) and \(Q_A\) is at \((R-s_A, 0)\).
Let \(I=(x_I, y_I)\). Then \(OI^2 = x_I^2+y_I^2\). The projection of \(OI\) onto \(OA\) is \(x_I\). Note that \(x_I = OI \cos(\angle AOI)\).
In \(\triangle AOI\), by the Law of Cosines, \(AI^2 = OA^2+OI^2-2OA \cdot OI \cos(\angle AOI) = R^2+OI^2-2R x_I\).
So \(x_I = \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R}\).

For \(P_A\): In \(\triangle OIP_A\), \(P_A\) is on \(OA\).
\(P_A I^2 = ( (R-r_A)-x_I )^2 + y_I^2 = (R-r_A)^2 - 2(R-r_A)x_I + x_I^2+y_I^2 = (R-r_A)^2 - 2(R-r_A)x_I + OI^2\).
Since \(P_A I = r_A+r\), we have \((r_A+r)^2 = (R-r_A)^2+OI^2-2(R-r_A)x_I\).
\(r_A^2+2rr_A+r^2 = R^2-2Rr_A+r_A^2+OI^2-2Rx_I+2r_Ax_I\).
\(2rr_A+2Rr_A-2r_Ax_I = R^2+OI^2-r^2-2Rx_I\).
\(2r_A(R+r-x_I) = R^2+OI^2-r^2-2Rx_I\).
The right side is \(R^2+OI^2-r^2-2R\left(\frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R}\right) = R^2+OI^2-r^2-(R^2+OI^2-AI^2) = AI^2-r^2\).
So \(2r_A(R+r-x_I) = AI^2-r^2\).
The term \(R+r-x_I = R+r - \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R} = \frac{2R^2+2Rr-R^2-OI^2+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2+2Rr-OI^2+AI^2}{2R}\).
Using Euler's Theorem \(OI^2=R(R-2r)\):
\(R+r-x_I = \frac{R^2+2Rr-R(R-2r)+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2+2Rr-R^2+2Rr+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{4Rr+AI^2}{2R}\).
So \(2r_A \frac{AI^2+4Rr}{2R} = AI^2-r^2\).
\(r_A = \frac{R(AI^2-r^2)}{AI^2+4Rr}\).
We know \(AI = r/\sin(A/2)\). So \(AI^2=r^2/\sin^2(A/2)\).
\(AI^2-r^2 = r^2/\sin^2(A/2) - r^2 = r^2 \frac{1-\sin^2(A/2)}{\sin^2(A/2)} = r^2 \frac{\cos^2(A/2)}{\sin^2(A/2)} = r^2\cot^2(A/2)\).
So \(r_A = \frac{R r^2\cot^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)+4Rr} = \frac{R r^2\cos^2(A/2)/\sin^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)+4Rr} = \frac{Rr^2\cos^2(A/2)}{r^2+4Rr\sin^2(A/2)}\).
\(r_A = \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\).

For \(Q_A\): In \(\triangle OIQ_A\), \(Q_A\) is on \(OA\).
\(Q_A I^2 = (R-s_A)^2 - 2(R-s_A)x_I + OI^2\).
Since \(Q_A I = s_A-r\), we have \((s_A-r)^2 = (R-s_A)^2+OI^2-2(R-s_A)x_I\).
This equation is obtained from the one for \(r_A\) by replacing \(r\) with \(-r\) and \(r_A\) with \(s_A\).
So \(2s_A(R-r-x_I) = AI^2-r^2\).
The term \(R-r-x_I = R-r - \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R} = \frac{2R^2-2Rr-R^2-OI^2+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2-2Rr-OI^2+AI^2}{2R}\).
Using \(OI^2=R(R-2r)\):
\(R-r-x_I = \frac{R^2-2Rr-R(R-2r)+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2-2Rr-R^2+2Rr+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{AI^2}{2R}\).
So \(2s_A \frac{AI^2}{2R} = AI^2-r^2\).
\(s_A = \frac{R(AI^2-r^2)}{AI^2} = \frac{R r^2\cot^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)} = \frac{R r^2\cos^2(A/2)/\sin^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)} = R\cos^2(A/2)\).
This is a known formula for such a circle. For \(S_A\) to contain \(\omega\) and be tangent internally, we need \(s_A > r\).
\(R\cos^2(A/2)>r \Leftrightarrow R(1+\cos A)/2 > r\). This inequality is known to hold for all non-degenerate triangles (equality for degenerate \(A=180^\circ, B=C=0\) if we have \(\cos((B-C)/2)=1\), \(1-\sin(A/2)=0\)). More precisely, \(2\sin(A/2)\cos((B-C)/2) \le 1+\sin^2(A/2)\) is equivalent to \((1-\sin(A/2))^2 + (\cos((B-C)/2)- \sin(A/2))^2 \ge 0\) if \(B=C\). It is \(2\sin(A/2) \le 1+\sin^2(A/2)\) which is \((1-\sin(A/2))^2 \ge 0\). The strict inequality \(s_A>r\) holds for non-degenerate triangles.

Now we calculate \(P_A Q_A = |r_A-s_A|\).
Since \(r+4R\sin^2(A/2) > r\), and \(\cos^2(A/2)>0\), it means \(r_A = \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)} < \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r} = R\cos^2(A/2) = s_A\).
So \(P_A Q_A = s_A-r_A\).
\(P_A Q_A = R\cos^2(A/2) - \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)} = R\cos^2(A/2) \left(1 - \frac{r}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\right)\).
\(P_A Q_A = R\cos^2(A/2) \left(\frac{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)-r}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\right) = R\cos^2(A/2) \frac{4R\sin^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\).
The denominator is \(D_A = r+4R\sin^2(A/2)\). Using \(r=4R\prod \sin(A/2)\):
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + 4R\sin^2(A/2)\)
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \sin(A/2))\).
Since \(A/2+B/2+C/2 = \pi/2\), \(\sin(A/2) = \sin(\pi/2-(B/2+C/2)) = \cos((B+C)/2)\).
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \cos(B/2+C/2))\).
Using \(\cos(X+Y) = \cos X \cos Y - \sin X \sin Y\):
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \cos(B/2)\cos(C/2) - \sin(B/2)\sin(C/2))\).
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)\).
Substituting this into the expression for \(P_A Q_A\):
\(P_A Q_A = \frac{R\cos^2(A/2) \cdot 4R\sin^2(A/2)}{4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)} = \frac{R^2 \cdot 4\sin^2(A/2)\cos^2(A/2)}{4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)}\).
\(P_A Q_A = \frac{R \sin(A/2)\cos^2(A/2)}{\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)}\).
This formula is for \(P_A Q_A\). We need to compute the product \(P_A Q_A \cdot P_B Q_B \cdot P_C Q_C\).
Let \(c_A=\cos(A/2), s_A=\sin(A/2)\), etc.
The product is
\[ \left(\frac{R s_A c_A^2}{c_B c_C}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{R s_B c_B^2}{c_A c_C}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{R s_C c_C^2}{c_A c_B}\right) \]
\[ = R^3 \frac{s_A c_A^2 s_B c_B^2 s_C c_C^2}{c_B c_C c_A c_C c_A c_B} = R^3 \frac{s_A s_B s_C c_A^2 c_B^2 c_C^2}{(c_A c_B c_C)^2} \]
\[ = R^3 s_A s_B s_C = R^3 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2). \]
The inequality to prove is \(8 P_A Q_A \cdot P_B Q_B \cdot P_C Q_C \leq R^3\).
Substituting the expression for the product:
\(8 R^3 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) \leq R^3\).
Since \(R>0\), we can divide by \(R^3\):
\(8 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) \leq 1\).
This is a well-known inequality in a triangle. It can be proven using Jensen's inequality on \(f(x)=\ln(\sin(x/2))\), or by using \(r = 4R\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2)\).
The inequality becomes \(8 \frac{r}{4R} \leq 1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{2r}{R} \leq 1 \Leftrightarrow R \geq 2r\).
This is Euler's inequality for triangles, which is true for all non-degenerate triangles.
Equality holds if and only if \(R=2r\), which is true if and only if \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral.
If \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral, then \(A=B=C=60^\circ\), so \(A/2=B/2=C/2=30^\circ\).
\(\sin(30^\circ)=1/2\). So \(8 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) = 8(1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 8(1/8) = 1\).
Thus, equality holds if and only if \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral.

The problem states that \(\triangle ABC\) is an acute triangle. The derivations of radii \(r_A, s_A\) and the identity \(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)\) hold for any triangle. Euler's inequality \(R \geq 2r\) also holds for any triangle. The acuteness condition might be to ensure some geometric configurations or avoid \(P_A Q_A=0\) (which is not an issue for non-degenerate triangles from the formula). The derived value \(P_A Q_A = R \sin(A/2)\cos^2(A/2) / (\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2))\) is always positive for a non-degenerate triangle.

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
In other words, if we let

$$
P(x)=x(x+1)+1
$$
then we would like there to be infinitely many primes dividing some $P(t)$ for some integer $t$.

In fact, this result is true in much greater generality. We first state:

## Theorem $1.1$ (Schur's theorem)

If $P(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is nonconstant and $P(0)=1$, then there are infinitely many primes which divide $P(t)$ for some integer $t$.

Proof. If $P(0)=0$, this is clear. So assume $P(0)=c \neq 0$.  
Let $S$ be any finite set of prime numbers. Consider then the value

$$
P\left(k \prod_{p \in S} p\right)
$$
for some integer $k$. It is $1(\bmod p)$ for each prime $p$, and if $k$ is large enough it should not be equal to $1$ (because $P$ is not constant). Therefore, it has a prime divisor not in $S$.

Remark. In fact the result holds without the assumption $P(0) \neq 1$. The proof requires only small modifications, and a good exercise would be to write down a similar proof that works first for $P(0)=20$, and then for any $P(0) \neq 0$. (The $P(0)=0$ case is vacuous, since then $P(x)$ is divisible by $x$.)

To finish the proof, let $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}$ be primes and $x_{i}$ be integers such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\left(x_{1}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{1}\right) \\
P\left(x_{2}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{2}\right) \\
\vdots & \\
P\left(x_{n}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

as promised by Schur's theorem. Then, by Chinese remainder theorem, we can find $x$ such that $x \equiv x_{i}\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for each $i$, whence $P(x)$ has at least $n$ prime factor.
author: human

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
To prove that for each positive integer \(n\), there exist pairwise relatively prime integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\), all strictly greater than 1, such that \(k_0 k_1 \cdots k_n - 1\) is the product of two consecutive integers, proceed as follows.

The goal is to find integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\) such that their product equals \(m^2 + m + 1\) for some integer \(m\), because then the product minus one is \(m(m+1)\), which is the product of two consecutive integers \(m\) and \(m+1\).

Choose \(n+1\) distinct prime numbers \(q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_n\) such that for each \(q_i\), the equation \(x^2 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\) has a solution. This condition holds for \(q_i = 3\) or \(q_i \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\). Since there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo 3 by Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions, and including the prime 3, such a set of \(n+1\) primes exists for any \(n\).

For each prime \(q_i\), let \(a_i\) be a solution to \(x^2 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\). (Note that there may be one or two solutions modulo \(q_i\), and any choice is valid.) Since the \(q_i\) are distinct primes, the Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees the existence of an integer \(m\) such that
\[
m \equiv a_i \pmod{q_i} \quad \text{for each} \quad i = 0, 1, \ldots, n.
\]

For this \(m\), \(m^2 + m + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\) for each \(i\), so each \(q_i\) divides \(m^2 + m + 1\). Let \(P = m^2 + m + 1\). Then \(P\) is divisible by each \(q_i\), and thus by their product \(Q = \prod_{i=0}^n q_i\). Write the prime factorization of \(P\) as
\[
P = \prod_{i=0}^n q_i^{e_i} \cdot S,
\]
where \(e_i \geq 1\) for each \(i\) (since each \(q_i\) divides \(P\)) and \(S\) is an integer coprime to all \(q_i\) (possibly \(S = 1\)).

Define the integers \(k_i\) as follows:
- For \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\), set \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\).
- For \(i = n\), set \(k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\).

First, verify that each \(k_i > 1\). Since \(q_i \geq 3 > 1\) (as the primes are at least 3, given that primes congruent to 1 modulo 3 or 3 itself are considered), and \(e_i \geq 1\), it follows that \(k_i = q_i^{e_i} \geq q_i \geq 3 > 1\) for \(i = 0, \ldots, n-1\). For \(k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\), since \(q_n^{e_n} \geq q_n \geq 3 > 1\) and \(S \geq 1\), it follows that \(k_n \geq 3 > 1\).

Next, the product of the \(k_i\) is
\[
\prod_{i=0}^n k_i = \left( \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} q_i^{e_i} \right) \cdot (q_n^{e_n} \cdot S) = \left( \prod_{i=0}^n q_i^{e_i} \right) \cdot S = P.
\]
Thus, \(P - 1 = m^2 + m + 1 - 1 = m(m+1)\), which is the product of two consecutive integers.

Now, prove that the \(k_i\) are pairwise relatively prime, meaning \(\gcd(k_i, k_j) = 1\) for all \(i \neq j\) with \(0 \leq i, j \leq n\).

- If both \(i\) and \(j\) are in \(\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}\) and \(i \neq j\), then \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\) and \(k_j = q_j^{e_j}\). Since \(q_i\) and \(q_j\) are distinct primes, \(\gcd(k_i, k_j) = 1\).
- If \(i < n\) and \(j = n\), then \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\) and \(k_j = k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\). Here, \(q_i\) and \(q_n\) are distinct primes, so they share no common factors. Additionally, \(S\) is coprime to all \(q_i\) by definition, so \(S\) shares no common prime factors with \(q_i\). Thus, \(\gcd(k_i, k_n) = 1\).

Since these cases cover all pairs of distinct indices, the \(k_i\) are pairwise relatively prime.

Therefore, for each positive integer \(n\), the constructed integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\) are pairwise relatively prime, all greater than 1, and their product minus one is the product of two consecutive integers.
author: llm

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
Fix a positive integer \(n\).  We will produce \(n+1\) integers
\[
k_0,k_1,\dots,k_{n}
\]
all \(>1\) and pairwise coprime, and an integer \(m\), such that
\[
k_0k_1\cdots k_{n}\;-\;1 \;=\;m(m+1).
\]

1.  Choose \(n\) distinct primes
\[
p_0,p_1,\dots,p_{n-1}
\]
all congruent to \(1\pmod3\).  (There are infinitely many such primes, by Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.)

2.  For each \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), consider the quadratic congruence
\[
x^2 + x + 1 \;\equiv\;0\pmod{p_i}.
\]
Its discriminant is
\[
\Delta \;=\;1^2 -4\cdot1\cdot1 \;=\;-3,
\]
and since \(\bigl(\tfrac{-3}{p_i}\bigr)=1\) whenever \(p_i\equiv1\pmod3\), this congruence has two solutions modulo \(p_i\).  Pick one solution and call it \(s_i\).  Thus
\[
s_i^2 + s_i + 1 \;\equiv\;0\pmod{p_i}.
\]

3.  By the Chinese remainder theorem, there is an integer \(s\) such that
\[
s\;\equiv\;s_i\pmod{p_i}
\quad(i=0,1,\dots,n-1).
\]
Let
\[
P \;=\;p_0\,p_1\cdots p_{n-1}.
\]
Then for each \(i\),
\[
s^2+s+1 \;\equiv\;s_i^2+s_i+1\equiv0\pmod{p_i},
\]
so \(P\) divides \(s^2+s+1\).  In particular
\[
s^2+s+1 \;=\;P\cdot K
\]
for some integer \(K\).

4.  We now replace \(s\) by a large integer of the same residue class: choose
\[
m \;=\;s + tP
\]
with \(t\) so large that
\[
m\ge P.
\]
Then
\[
m^2 + m + 1 \;=\;(s+tP)^2 + (s+tP) +1
             \;=\;s^2+s+1 \;+\;P\cdot(\dots)
             \;=\;P\cdot K'
\]
for some integer \(K'>0\).  Moreover \(m^2+m+1>P^2\) (since \(m\ge P\)), so \(K'\ge P>1\).

5.  Finally set
\[
k_i = p_i\quad(i=0,1,\dots,n-1),
\qquad
k_{n} = K'.
\]
Then each \(k_i>1\), and for \(0\le i<j\le n-1\),
\[
\gcd(k_i,k_j)=\gcd(p_i,p_j)=1
\]
since the \(p_i\) are distinct.  Also for \(0\le i\le n-1\),
\[
\gcd(k_i,k_n)
=\gcd\bigl(p_i,\;K'\bigr)
=1,
\]
because \(p_i\) divides \(m^2+m+1\) exactly once but was already “used up’’ in the factor \(P\), so it cannot divide the co-factor \(K'\).  Hence all the \(k_i\) are pairwise coprime.

6.  On the other hand
\[
k_0k_1\cdots k_n
\;=\;
(p_0p_1\cdots p_{n-1})\;K'
\;=\;
P\;K'
\;=\;
m^2 + m + 1,
\]
and therefore
\[
k_0k_1\cdots k_n \;-\;1
\;=\;
m^2+m
\;=\;
m(m+1),
\]
the product of two consecutive integers.  This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
Let n ≥ 1 be given.  
We shall construct integers  

  k0 , k1 , … , kn  (> 1 and pairwise coprime)

and an integer m such that

  k0 k1 … kn  – 1  =  m(m+1).

The construction uses only three classical facts.

(A)  There are infinitely many primes in every arithmetic progression 3t+1  
  (Dirichlet).

(B)  For an odd prime p the congruence x²+x+1 ≡ 0 (mod p) is solvable  
  iff p ≡ 1 (mod 3).  
  Indeed, 4x²+4x+4 ≡ 0 ⇔ (2x+1)² ≡ –3;  
  by quadratic reciprocity (-3/p)=1 exactly when p≡1 (mod 3).

(C)  The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Choosing suitable primes
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Pick n distinct primes

  p1 , p2 , … , pn  all of them ≡ 1 (mod 3).

(Existence is guaranteed by (A).)  
Adjoin the prime 3 and set

  P := 3·p1 p2 … pn .

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Building an integer m with many prescribed divisors
--------------------------------------------------------------------
•  For the prime 3 one checks directly that r3 = 1 satisfies  
  r3² + r3 + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 3).

•  By (B) every pi (i ≥ 1) admits a root ri of x²+x+1 ≡ 0 (mod pi).

Now apply the CRT to the system

  m ≡ r3  (mod 3),                             (1)  
  m ≡ ri  (mod pi) (i = 1,…,n).                (2)

Because the moduli 3, p1,…,pn are pairwise coprime, there exists an
integer m satisfying all congruences simultaneously.

Put

  R := m² + m + 1.                              (3)

Equations (1)–(2) imply

  3 | R  and  pi | R  for each i,

so R possesses at least n+1 distinct prime divisors, namely
3, p1,…,pn.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Splitting R into n+1 pairwise coprime factors
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For i = 1,…,n let

  ei := v_{pi}(R) (the exponent of pi in the factorisation of R)  
  ki := pi^{ei}   (>1).

Remove these prime–power factors from R and put

  k0 := R / (k1 k2 … kn).                      (4)

Because every occurrence of pi has been placed entirely inside ki,
the integer k0 is divisible by 3 but by none of the pi, hence

  gcd(k0, ki) = 1 = gcd(ki, kj) (i ≠ j).

Thus k0 , … , kn are pairwise relatively prime and all exceed 1
(k0 ≥ 3, each ki ≥ pi ≥ 7).

Moreover, by (4)

  k0 k1 … kn = R = m² + m + 1.                (5)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Finishing the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Subtract 1 from (5):

  k0 k1 … kn – 1 = m² + m = m(m+1),

the product of the consecutive integers m and m+1.

Therefore, for every positive integer n we have produced
n+1 pairwise coprime integers k0 , … , kn > 1 whose product minus 1
is a product of two consecutive integers, as required.

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
We want to prove that for each positive integer $n$, there exist pairwise relatively prime integers $k_0, \ldots, k_n$, all strictly greater than 1, such that $k_0 k_1 \ldots k_n - 1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.

Let the product be $P = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_n$. We require $P-1 = m(m+1)$ for some integer $m$. This means $P = m^2+m+1$.

We construct the integers $k_i$ using a sequence $m_i$.
Let $m_0$ be an integer. We will set $m_0=1$.
For $i \ge 0$, define $m_{i+1} = (m_i+1)^2$.
Since $m_0=1$, we have $m_1 = (1+1)^2=4$, $m_2=(4+1)^2=25$, and so on. In general, $m_i \ge 1$ for all $i \ge 0$.

Now, define a sequence $X_i$ associated with $m_i$:
For $i \ge 0$, let $X_i = m_i^2+m_i+1$.
Since $m_i \ge 1$, $X_i = m_i(m_i+1)+1 \ge 1(2)+1=3$.

We define the integers $k_0, \ldots, k_n$ as follows:
Let $k_0 = X_0 = m_0^2+m_0+1$.
For $1 \le i \le n$, let $k_i = \frac{X_i}{X_{i-1}}$.

We need to show that $k_i$ defined this way are integers and satisfy the given conditions.

1.  **Show that $k_i$ are integers for $i \ge 1$.**
    We need to show that $X_{i-1}$ divides $X_i$ for $i \ge 1$.
    The recurrence $m_i = (m_{i-1}+1)^2$ can be rewritten using $X_{i-1}$:
    $m_i = m_{i-1}^2+2m_{i-1}+1 = (m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1) + m_{i-1} = X_{i-1}+m_{i-1}$.
    So $m_i \equiv m_{i-1} \pmod{X_{i-1}}$.
    Then $X_i = m_i^2+m_i+1 \equiv m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1 \pmod{X_{i-1}}$.
    Since $X_{i-1} = m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1$, we have $X_i \equiv X_{i-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{X_{i-1}}$.
    Thus, $X_{i-1}$ divides $X_i$, so $k_i = X_i/X_{i-1}$ is an integer for $i \ge 1$.

    Let's find an explicit expression for $k_i$ for $i \ge 1$:
    $k_i = \frac{X_i}{X_{i-1}} = \frac{(X_{i-1}+m_{i-1})^2 + (X_{i-1}+m_{i-1}) + 1}{X_{i-1}}$
    $k_i = \frac{X_{i-1}^2 + 2X_{i-1}m_{i-1} + m_{i-1}^2 + X_{i-1} + m_{i-1} + 1}{X_{i-1}}$
    $k_i = X_{i-1} + 2m_{i-1} + 1 + \frac{m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1}{X_{i-1}}$
    $k_i = X_{i-1} + 2m_{i-1} + 1 + \frac{X_{i-1}}{X_{i-1}} = X_{i-1} + 2m_{i-1} + 2$.
    Substituting $X_{i-1} = m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1$:
    $k_i = (m_{i-1}^2+m_{i-1}+1) + 2m_{i-1} + 2 = m_{i-1}^2+3m_{i-1}+3$.

2.  **Show that $k_i > 1$ for all $i=0, \ldots, n$.**
    We choose $m_0=1$.
    Then $k_0 = m_0^2+m_0+1 = 1^2+1+1=3$. So $k_0>1$.
    For $i \ge 1$, $m_{i-1} \ge m_0 = 1$.
    Then $k_i = m_{i-1}^2+3m_{i-1}+3 \ge 1^2+3(1)+3 = 7$. So $k_i>1$ for $i \ge 1$.
    All $k_i$ are strictly greater than 1.

3.  **Show that $k_0, \ldots, k_n$ are pairwise relatively prime.**
    Let $P_j = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_j$.
    From the definition of $k_i$, we have:
    $P_0 = k_0 = X_0$.
    $P_1 = k_0 k_1 = X_0 (X_1/X_0) = X_1$.
    In general, $P_j = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_j = X_0 \frac{X_1}{X_0} \frac{X_2}{X_1} \ldots \frac{X_j}{X_{j-1}} = X_j$.
    So $P_j = X_j = m_j^2+m_j+1$.

    We need to show $\gcd(k_j, k_l)=1$ for $j \ne l$. Assume $j < l$.
    $k_l = X_l/X_{l-1} = m_{l-1}^2+3m_{l-1}+3$.
    $X_{l-1} = P_{l-1} = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_{l-1}$.
    Since $j \le l-1$, $k_j$ is a factor of $X_{l-1}$.
    Let $d = \gcd(k_j, k_l)$.
    Since $d|k_j$ and $k_j|X_{l-1}$, it follows that $d|X_{l-1}$.
    Also, $d|k_l$ by definition of $d$.
    So $d$ is a common divisor of $X_{l-1}$ and $k_l$.
    Let's evaluate $\gcd(X_{l-1}, k_l)$:
    $X_{l-1} = m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1$.
    $k_l = m_{l-1}^2+3m_{l-1}+3$.
    Let $A = m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1$ and $B = m_{l-1}^2+3m_{l-1}+3$.
    $\gcd(A,B) = \gcd(A, B-A)$.
    $B-A = (m_{l-1}^2+3m_{l-1}+3) - (m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1) = 2m_{l-1}+2$.
    So $\gcd(X_{l-1}, k_l) = \gcd(m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1, 2m_{l-1}+2)$.
    Let $g = \gcd(m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1, 2(m_{l-1}+1))$.
    $g$ must divide any linear combination of these.
    $2(m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1) - m_{l-1}(2(m_{l-1}+1)) = (2m_{l-1}^2+2m_{l-1}+2) - (2m_{l-1}^2+2m_{l-1}) = 2$.
    So $g$ must divide 2. Thus $g=1$ or $g=2$.
    However, $X_{l-1} = m_{l-1}^2+m_{l-1}+1 = m_{l-1}(m_{l-1}+1)+1$. Since $m_{l-1}(m_{l-1}+1)$ is always an even number, $X_{l-1}$ is always odd.
    Since $X_{l-1}$ is odd, its divisor $g$ must also be odd. Therefore, $g=1$.
    So $\gcd(X_{l-1}, k_l)=1$.
    Since $d$ is a common divisor of $X_{l-1}$ and $k_l$, $d$ must divide $g=1$. So $d=1$.
    This proves that $k_j$ and $k_l$ are relatively prime for $j < l$.
    Hence, the integers $k_0, \ldots, k_n$ are pairwise relatively prime.

4.  **Show that $k_0 k_1 \ldots k_n - 1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.**
    The product is $P = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_n$.
    As shown in step 3, $P = X_n$.
    So $P = m_n^2+m_n+1$.
    Then $P-1 = (m_n^2+m_n+1)-1 = m_n^2+m_n = m_n(m_n+1)$.
    This is the product of the two consecutive integers $m_n$ and $m_n+1$.
    Since $m_0=1$ and $m_i=(m_{i-1}+1)^2$, $m_n$ is a positive integer for $n \ge 0$. Specifically $m_n \ge 1$. (Actually $m_n \ge 4$ for $n \ge 1$).

All conditions have been satisfied. The construction provides the required set of integers.

To illustrate for $n=2$:
$m_0=1$.
$k_0 = m_0^2+m_0+1 = 1^2+1+1 = 3$.
$m_1 = (m_0+1)^2 = (1+1)^2 = 4$.
$k_1 = m_0^2+3m_0+3 = 1^2+3(1)+3 = 7$. (Alternatively $X_0=3$, $X_1=4^2+4+1=21$, so $k_1=X_1/X_0=21/3=7$)
$m_2 = (m_1+1)^2 = (4+1)^2 = 25$.
$k_2 = m_1^2+3m_1+3 = 4^2+3(4)+3 = 16+12+3 = 31$. (Alternatively $X_1=21$, $X_2=25^2+25+1=651$, so $k_2=X_2/X_1=651/21=31$)
The integers are $k_0=3, k_1=7, k_2=31$.
They are all greater than 1.
They are pairwise relatively prime: $\gcd(3,7)=1, \gcd(3,31)=1, \gcd(7,31)=1$.
Their product is $k_0 k_1 k_2 = 3 \times 7 \times 31 = 651$.
$k_0 k_1 k_2 - 1 = 651-1 = 650$.
This should be $m_2(m_2+1)$. $m_2=25$, so $m_2(m_2+1) = 25 \times (25+1) = 25 \times 26 = 650$.
The statement holds for $n=2$.

The proof is complete.

Final summary of the construction:
Given a positive integer $n$:
1.  Define a sequence $m_0, m_1, \ldots, m_n$ by $m_0=1$ and $m_{i+1}=(m_i+1)^2$ for $0 \le i < n$.
2.  Define the set of integers $\{k_0, k_1, \ldots, k_n\}$ by $k_0=m_0^2+m_0+1$ and $k_i=m_{i-1}^2+3m_{i-1}+3$ for $1 \le i \le n$.
3.  These $n+1$ integers $k_0, \ldots, k_n$ are pairwise relatively prime, all strictly greater than 1.
4.  Their product $P = k_0 k_1 \ldots k_n$ equals $m_n^2+m_n+1$.
5.  Therefore, $P-1 = m_n(m_n+1)$, which is the product of two consecutive integers.

problem: At a certain mathematical conference, every pair of mathematicians are either friends or strangers. At mealtime, every participant eats in one of two large dining rooms. Each mathematician insists upon eating in a room which contains an even number of his or her friends. Prove that the number of ways that the mathematicians may be split between the two rooms is a power of two (i.e., is of the form \(2^{k}\) for some positive integer \(k\)).
solution:
Take the obvious graph interpretation where we are trying to 2-color a graph. Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of the graph over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, except the diagonal of $A \operatorname{has} \operatorname{deg} v(\bmod 2)$ instead of zero. Then let $\vec{d}$ be the main diagonal. Splittings then correspond to $A \vec{v}=\vec{d}$. It's then immediate that the number of ways is either zero or a power of two, since if it is nonempty it is a coset of $\operatorname{ker} A$.

Thus we only need to show that:

```
Claim - At least one coloring exists.
```

Proof. If not, consider a minimal counterexample G. Clearly there is at least one odd vertex $v$. Consider the graph with vertex set $G-v$, where all pairs of neighbors of $v$ have their edges complemented. By minimality, we have a good coloring here. One can check that this extends to a good coloring on $G$ by simply coloring $v$ with the color matching an even number of its neighbors. This breaks minimality of $G$, and hence all graphs $G$ have a coloring.

It's also possible to use linear algebra. We prove the following lemma:

## Lemma (grobber)

Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space, $T: V \rightarrow V$ and $w \in V$. Then $w$ is in the image of $T$ if and only if there are no $\xi \in V^{\vee}$ for which $\xi(w) \neq 0$ and yet $\xi \circ T=0$.

Proof. Clearly if $T(v)=w$, then no $\xi$ exists. Conversely, assume $w$ is not in the image of $T$. Then the image of $T$ is linearly independent from $w$. Take a basis $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ for the image of $T$, add $w$, and then extend it to a basis for all of $V$. Then have $\xi$ kill all $e_{i}$ but not $w$.

## Corollary

In a symmetric matrix $A \bmod 2$, there exists a vector $v$ such that $A v$ is a copy of the diagonal of $A$.

Proof. Let $\xi$ be such that $\xi \circ T=0$. Look at $\xi$ as a column vector $w^{\top}$, and let $d$ be the diagonal. Then

$$
0=w^{\top} \cdot T \cdot w=\xi(d)
$$
because this extracts the sum of coefficients submatrix of $T$, and all the symmetric entries cancel off. Thus no $\xi$ as in the previous lemma exists.

This corollary gives the desired proof.

problem: At a certain mathematical conference, every pair of mathematicians are either friends or strangers. At mealtime, every participant eats in one of two large dining rooms. Each mathematician insists upon eating in a room which contains an even number of his or her friends. Prove that the number of ways that the mathematicians may be split between the two rooms is a power of two (i.e., is of the form \(2^{k}\) for some positive integer \(k\)).
solution:
Let  

• \(V=\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\) be the set of mathematicians,  
• \(G=(V,E)\) the (simple, undirected) “friendship graph’’ in which \(\{i,j\}\in E\) iff \(i\) and \(j\) are friends,  
• \(\deg (i)\;(i\in V)\) the degree of vertex \(i\) in \(G\) (the number of friends of \(i\)).  

We write all equalities in the field  

\[
\mathbb F_{2}:=\{0,1\}\qquad(\text{addition = subtraction = “parity’’}).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Translating an arrangement into algebra
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Number the two dining rooms \(0\) and \(1\).  
For an arrangement put  

\[
x_i=\begin{cases}
0 & \text{ if mathematician } i \text{ eats in room }0,\\
1 & \text{ if mathematician } i \text{ eats in room }1.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus every seating plan corresponds to a vector  

\[
x=(x_1,\dots ,x_n)\in \mathbb F_2^{\,n}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The parity condition as a linear (affine) equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For a fixed vertex \(i\) let us compute (mod 2) the number of friends of \(i\) who
sit in the *same* room as \(i\).

For each friend \(j\) of \(i\) the indicator  
\[
\bigl[x_i=x_j\bigr]\equiv 1-(x_i+x_j)\ (\bmod 2)
            =1+x_i+x_j\ (\bmod 2)
\]  
equals \(1\) when \(x_i=x_j\) and \(0\) otherwise.
Adding over all friends of \(i\) we obtain the parity wanted:

\[
0=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}(1+x_i+x_j)
  =\deg(i)+\deg(i)\,x_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}x_j\pmod 2.
\]

Rearranging gives the *linear* (in \(x\)) equation  

\[
\;\deg(i)\,x_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}x_j=\deg(i)\;\tag{1}
\]
for every vertex \(i\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Matrix form
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let  

• \(A=(a_{ij})\) be the adjacency matrix of \(G\) over \(\mathbb F_2\)
  \((a_{ij}=1\) if \(\{i,j\}\in E\), else \(0)$,  
• \(D=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\deg(1),\dots ,\deg(n)\bigr)\) (taken mod 2),  
• \(b=(\deg(1),\dots ,\deg(n))^{\!T}\) (also mod 2).

With these notations the whole system (1) is

\[
(A+D)\,x=b. \tag{2}
\]

Put \(M:=A+D\); \(M\) is an \(n\times n\) symmetric matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The set of legal arrangements
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Equation (2) is an *affine* system.  
If it is solvable, the set of all solutions is a *coset*
of the kernel of \(M\):

\[
\mathcal S=\{x_0+u\mid u\in\ker M\},
\]
where \(x_0\) is any particular solution.  
Hence  

\[
|\mathcal S|=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if (2) has no solution},\\[2mm]
|\ker M| = 2^{\,\dim\ker M} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]

Equation (3) shows that the desired number of arrangements
is either \(0\) or a power of two.
It remains to prove that (2) *always* has at least one solution;
then the exponent in (3) will automatically be positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Showing that (2) is always solvable
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because \(M\) is symmetric, its row space equals its column space.
Consequently (2) is solvable precisely when the constant vector \(b\)
is orthogonal to every vector in \(\ker M\).
We prove this orthogonality directly.

Let \(s=(s_1,\dots ,s_n)\in\ker M\) and put  
\(S=\{i\in V\mid s_i=1\}\).  
The equality \(M\,s=0\) gives, for each vertex \(i\),

\[
\deg(i)\,s_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}s_j=0. \tag{4}
\]

(a)  If \(i\notin S\;(s_i=0)\), (4) says that \(i\) has an *even*
number of neighbours inside \(S\).

(b)  If \(i\in S\;(s_i=1)\), (4) becomes  
\[
\deg(i)=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}s_j
\]
so that \(\deg(i)\) equals, mod 2,
the number of neighbours of \(i\) that *also* lie in \(S\).

Add the equalities in (b) over all vertices in \(S\):
the left side is  
\[
\sum_{i\in S}\deg(i)=s^{T}b .
\]
On the right, every edge with *both* ends in \(S\)
is counted twice (hence contributes \(0\) mod 2),
whereas every edge with *exactly one* end in \(S\)
is counted once.
Therefore  

\[
s^{T}b \equiv |E(S,V\setminus S)| \pmod 2. \tag{5}
\]

But from (a) each vertex outside \(S\) is incident with an *even*
number of such “crossing’’ edges; summing over all outside vertices
shows that \(|E(S,V\setminus S)|\) itself is even.
Hence the right side of (5) equals \(0\), and we have

\[
s^{T}b=0 \qquad\text{for every }s\in\ker M. \tag{6}
\]

So \(b\) is orthogonal to the kernel; equivalently, \(b\) lies in
the row (column) space of \(M\).  
Thus system (2) possesses at least one solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Finishing the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because (2) is solvable, (3) gives

\[
|\mathcal S|=2^{\,\dim\ker M}.
\]

Finally, notice that the all-ones vector \(\mathbf 1=(1,1,\dots ,1)^{T}\)
satisfies \(M\mathbf 1=0\) (each row of \(M\) sums to
\(\deg(i)+\deg(i)=0\) mod 2), so \(\mathbf 1\neq 0\) lies in \(\ker M\).
Hence \(\dim\ker M\ge 1\) and

\[
|\mathcal S| = 2^{\,k}\quad\text{for some positive integer }k.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The number of ways in which the conference participants can be divided
between the two dining rooms so that *every* mathematician finds an
even number of friends in his or her room is always a (positive)
power of two.

problem: At a certain mathematical conference, every pair of mathematicians are either friends or strangers. At mealtime, every participant eats in one of two large dining rooms. Each mathematician insists upon eating in a room which contains an even number of his or her friends. Prove that the number of ways that the mathematicians may be split between the two rooms is a power of two (i.e., is of the form \(2^{k}\) for some positive integer \(k\)).
solution:
Let $n$ be the number of mathematicians. Let $V = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ be the set of mathematicians.
Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of the friendship graph, where $A_{ij}=1$ if $i$ and $j$ are friends, and $A_{ij}=0$ otherwise. Since friendship is mutual, $A$ is a symmetric matrix ($A_{ij} = A_{ji}$). We assume $A_{ii}=0$ for all $i$ (a mathematician is not their own friend).

Let $x_i$ be a variable associated with mathematician $i$, such that $x_i=0$ if $i$ is in room $R_1$ and $x_i=1$ if $i$ is in room $R_2$. A split of mathematicians is a vector $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \{0,1\}^n$.

For each mathematician $i$, let $F_i$ be the set of friends of $i$. The number of friends of $i$ is $d_i = |F_i|$.
The condition for mathematician $i$ is that the number of their friends in the room they are in must be even.
Let $S_1 = \{j \in V \mid x_j=0\}$ be the set of mathematicians in $R_1$.
Let $S_2 = \{j \in V \mid x_j=1\}$ be the set of mathematicians in $R_2$.

If mathematician $i$ is in $R_1$ (i.e., $x_i=0$), the number of their friends in $R_1$ is $\sum_{j \in F_i, x_j=0} 1$. This must be even.
In $\mathbb{F}_2$ (the field with two elements $\{0,1\}$), this condition is $\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(1-x_j) = 0$.
Since $1-x_j \equiv 1+x_j \pmod 2$, this is $\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(1+x_j) = 0$.
Expanding this, we get $\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} + \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j = 0$.
Let $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}$ be the total number of friends of mathematician $i$ (the degree of vertex $i$ in the friendship graph). The elements $d_i$ are considered modulo 2.
Let $(Ax)_i = \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j$. The condition becomes $d_i + (Ax)_i = 0$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$.

If mathematician $i$ is in $R_2$ (i.e., $x_i=1$), the number of their friends in $R_2$ is $\sum_{j \in F_i, x_j=1} 1$. This must be even.
In $\mathbb{F}_2$, this condition is $\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j = 0$. So $(Ax)_i = 0$.

We can combine these two conditions for each $i \in V$. The condition for mathematician $i$ is:
$(1-x_i)(d_i + (Ax)_i) + x_i((Ax)_i) = 0$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$.
This equation holds if $x_i=0$ and $d_i + (Ax)_i=0$, or if $x_i=1$ and $(Ax)_i=0$.
Expanding the equation:
$d_i + (Ax)_i - x_i d_i - x_i (Ax)_i + x_i (Ax)_i = 0$
$d_i + (Ax)_i - x_i d_i = 0$
Since we are in $\mathbb{F}_2$, $-1 \equiv 1$. So, $d_i + (Ax)_i + x_i d_i = 0$.

This is a system of $n$ linear equations over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Let $s$ be the column vector $(d_1, \dots, d_n)^T$. Let $D$ be the diagonal matrix where $D_{ii} = d_i$ (all $d_i$ are taken modulo 2). The $i$-th equation is $(Ax)_i + D_{ii}x_i + d_i = 0$.
So the system can be written in matrix form as $Ax + Dx + s = 0$, or $(A+D)x = s$.
Let $M = A+D$. Then the system is $Mx=s$.
The matrix $M$ has entries $M_{ij} = A_{ij}$ for $i \ne j$, and $M_{ii} = A_{ii} + D_{ii} = 0 + d_i = d_i$. (Remember $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} \pmod 2$).

The number of solutions to a linear system $Mx=s$ is either 0 (if $s$ is not in the column space of $M$) or $2^{n-\text{rank}(M)}$ (if $s$ is in the column space of $M$). We need to show that this number is a power of $2$, specifically $2^k$ for some positive integer $k$.

First, let's handle the $n=0$ case. If there are no mathematicians, there is 1 way to assign them (everyone to $R_1$, or $S_1=\emptyset, S_2=\emptyset$). The condition for every mathematician is vacuously satisfied. So there is $1=2^0$ way. The problem specifies $k$ must be a positive integer, so $k=0$ is not allowed. Thus, we must have $n > 0$. From now on, assume $n \ge 1$.

The matrix $M$ is symmetric. This is because $A$ is symmetric ($A_{ij}=A_{ji}$) and $D$ is a diagonal matrix, so $M^T = (A+D)^T = A^T+D^T = A+D = M$.

Consider the sum of entries in any row $i$ of $M$. This is $\sum_{j=1}^n M_{ij}$.
$\sum_{j=1}^n M_{ij} = M_{ii} + \sum_{j \ne i} M_{ij}$.
By definition, $M_{ii} = d_i = \sum_{l=1}^n A_{il} \pmod 2$. Since $A_{ii}=0$, $d_i = \sum_{l \ne i} A_{il} \pmod 2$.
Also, for $j \ne i$, $M_{ij}=A_{ij}$.
So the sum of entries in row $i$ is $d_i + \sum_{j \ne i} A_{ij} = d_i + d_i = 2d_i \equiv 0 \pmod 2$.
Let $\mathbf{1}$ be the column vector of all ones, $\mathbf{1} = (1, \dots, 1)^T$. Then $M\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$ (the zero vector).
Since $n \ge 1$, $\mathbf{1} \ne \mathbf{0}$. Thus, $\mathbf{1}$ is a non-zero vector in the null space of $M$ (denoted $\ker(M)$).
This implies that $M$ is singular, so $\text{rank}(M) \le n-1$.
The dimension of the null space is $n-\text{rank}(M) \ge n-(n-1) = 1$.
So, if the system $Mx=s$ is consistent, the number of solutions will be $2^{n-\text{rank}(M)}$ where $n-\text{rank}(M) \ge 1$. This ensures $k$ is a positive integer.

Now we need to show that the system $Mx=s$ is consistent.
A linear system $Mx=s$ is consistent if and only if $s$ is in the image (or column space) of $M$. This is true if and only if $s$ is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of $M^T$ (by the Fredholm alternative).
Since $M$ is symmetric, $M^T=M$. So $Mx=s$ is consistent if and only if $y^T s = 0$ for all $y \in \ker(M)$.
Let $y \in \ker(M)$. This means $My=0$. We want to show $y^T s = 0$.
The components of $s$ are $d_i$, and $M_{ii}=d_i$. So $y^T s = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i d_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i M_{ii}$.
Let's consider the quadratic form $y^T M y$.
Since $My=0$, we have $y^T M y = y^T \mathbf{0} = 0$.
Let's expand $y^T M y$:
$y^T M y = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n y_i M_{ij} y_j$.
This can be written as $\sum_{i=1}^n y_i M_{ii} y_i + \sum_{i \ne j} y_i M_{ij} y_j$.
Since $y_i \in \{0,1\}$, $y_i^2 = y_i$. So the first term is $\sum_{i=1}^n y_i M_{ii}$.
The second term is $\sum_{i < j} (y_i M_{ij} y_j + y_j M_{ji} y_i)$.
Since $M$ is symmetric, $M_{ij}=M_{ji}$. So this becomes $\sum_{i < j} (y_i M_{ij} y_j + y_j M_{ij} y_i)$.
In $\mathbb{F}_2$, $a+a = 2a = 0$. So $y_i M_{ij} y_j + y_j M_{ij} y_i = (M_{ij}+M_{ij})y_i y_j = 0 \cdot M_{ij} y_i y_j = 0$.
Thus, for any $y \in \{0,1\}^n$ and symmetric $M$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, $y^T M y = \sum_{i=1}^n M_{ii} y_i$.
So we have $y^T s = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i d_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i M_{ii} = y^T M y$.
Since $y \in \ker(M)$, $My=0$, which implies $y^T M y = 0$.
Therefore, $y^T s = 0$ for all $y \in \ker(M)$.
This shows that the system $Mx=s$ is consistent.

The number of solutions is $2^{n-\text{rank}(M)}$.
Let $k = n-\text{rank}(M)$.
As shown earlier, if $n \ge 1$, then $M\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}$ implies $\mathbf{1} \in \ker(M)$, so $\text{rank}(M) \le n-1$.
Thus $k = n-\text{rank}(M) \ge 1$.
So the number of ways the mathematicians may be split between the two rooms is $2^k$ for some positive integer $k$, provided $n \ge 1$.
If $n=0$, the number of ways is $1=2^0$. The problem's condition that $k$ is a positive integer implies $n \ge 1$. Conferences usually have attendees. For $n=1$, $A=[0]$, $d_1=0$, so $D=[0]$, $s=[0]$. $M=[0]$. $Mx=s$ is $0x_1=0$. Solutions are $x_1=0$ and $x_1=1$. Number of ways is $2$. Here $k=1-\mathrm{rank}([0]) = 1-0=1$, which is a positive integer.

Conclusion: The set of valid assignments of mathematicians to rooms is the set of solutions to the linear system $(A+D)x=s$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$. This system is consistent, and its solution space is an affine subspace. The number of solutions is $2^k$ where $k = n-\text{rank}(A+D)$. Given $n \ge 1$, $k \ge 1$. Thus, the number of ways is a power of two, $2^k$, for some positive integer $k$.
