problem:
For each real number \( x \), define \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) to be the greatest integer less than or equal to \( x \).

Let \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\). Prove that

\[
\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}, \text{ for } n=0,1,2, \ldots
\]
solution:
Define the conjugate number
\[
\beta \;=\; 2 - \sqrt{3}.
\]
Then \(\alpha=2+\sqrt3\) and \(\beta\) are exactly the two (real) roots of the quadratic equation
\[
x^2 \;-\;4x\;+\;1\;=\;0.
\]
Indeed, one checks
\[
(2+\sqrt3)^2 \;-\;4(2+\sqrt3)\;+\;1 \;=\;4+4\sqrt3+3 \;-\;8-4\sqrt3\;+\;1\;=\;0,
\]
and similarly for \(2-\sqrt3\).  From Vieta’s relations it follows that
\[
\alpha+\beta \;=\;4,
\qquad
\alpha\beta \;=\;1.
\]
In particular,
\[
\alpha>1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\beta \;=\;\frac1\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
0<\beta<1.
\]

Next, for each integer \(n\ge0\) set
\[
S_n \;=\;\alpha^n+\beta^n.
\]
We claim that \(S_n\in\Bbb Z\) for all \(n\).  We prove this by induction on \(n\).

Base cases:
\[
S_0 \;=\;\alpha^0+\beta^0 \;=\;1+1\;=\;2\in\Bbb Z,
\qquad
S_1 \;=\;\alpha+\beta \;=\;4\in\Bbb Z.
\]

Inductive step:  suppose \(S_n\) and \(S_{n+1}\) are integers.  Since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) each satisfy
\[
x^2 \;=\;4x-1,
\]
we have
\[
\alpha^{n+2}
\;=\;
4\alpha^{n+1}
\;-\;
\alpha^n,
\qquad
\beta^{n+2}
\;=\;
4\beta^{n+1}
\;-\;
\beta^n.
\]
Adding these two identities gives the recurrence
\[
S_{n+2}
\;=\;
\alpha^{n+2}+\beta^{n+2}
\;=\;
4(\alpha^{n+1}+\beta^{n+1})
\;-\;
(\alpha^n+\beta^n)
\;=\;
4S_{n+1}-S_n.
\]
Since \(S_n\) and \(S_{n+1}\) are integers by the inductive hypothesis, it follows that \(S_{n+2}\) is also an integer.  This completes the induction and proves \(S_n\in\Bbb Z\) for all \(n\ge0\).

---

Because \(S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n\), we can solve for \(\alpha^n\):
\[
\alpha^n
\;=\;
S_n \;-\;\beta^n.
\]
Since \(0<\beta<1\), we have for \(n\ge1\) the strict inequalities
\[
0<\beta^n<1,
\]
and for \(n=0\) the value \(\beta^0=1\).  Hence:

– If \(n\ge1\), then
\[
S_n-1 \;<\;S_n-\beta^n\;<\;S_n,
\]
that is
\[
S_n-1 \;<\;\alpha^n\;<\;S_n.
\]
– If \(n=0\), then
\[
\alpha^0 \;=\;1
\;=\;
S_0-\beta^0
\;=\;
2-1,
\]
so
\[
S_0-1 \;=\;1 \;\le\;\alpha^0\;\le\;2=S_0.
\]
In either case we obtain
\[
S_n-1\;\le\;\alpha^n\;<\;S_n,
\]
and since \(S_n\) is an integer this implies
\[
\lfloor \alpha^n\rfloor \;=\;S_n-1.
\]

Finally, the fractional part of \(\alpha^n\) is
\[
\alpha^n-\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor
\;=\;
\alpha^n-(S_n-1)
\;=\;
\bigl(S_n-\beta^n\bigr)\;-\;(S_n-1)
\;=\;
1-\beta^n.
\]
But \(\beta=1/\alpha\), so \(\beta^n=\alpha^{-n}\).  Therefore
\[
\alpha^n-\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor
\;=\;
1-\alpha^{-n},
\]
as required.
author: llm

problem:
For each real number \( x \), define \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) to be the greatest integer less than or equal to \( x \).

Let \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\). Prove that

\[
\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}, \text{ for } n=0,1,2, \ldots
\]
solution:
Throughout the proof we write  
\[ \alpha = 2+\sqrt 3,\qquad  
   \beta  = 2-\sqrt 3 .\]

1.  β is the reciprocal of α.  
    Indeed
    \[
       \alpha\beta \;=\;(2+\sqrt 3)(2-\sqrt 3)=4-3=1,
    \]
    hence \(\beta=\alpha^{-1}\).

2.  The numbers \(\alpha^n+\beta^n\;(n\ge 0)\) are integers.

    a)  The quadratic polynomial
        \[
           p(x)=x^{2}-4x+1
        \]
        has the two distinct roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), because
        \[
           \alpha^{2}=4\alpha-1,\qquad
           \beta ^{2}=4\beta -1 .
        \]

    b)  For every integer \(n\ge 0\) we obtain from the above relation
        \[
           \alpha^{\,n+2}=4\alpha^{\,n+1}-\alpha^{\,n},\qquad
           \beta^{\,n+2}=4\beta^{\,n+1}-\beta^{\,n}.
        \]

    c)  Define \(S_n=\alpha^{\,n}+\beta^{\,n}\).  Adding the two identities in
        part b) gives the linear recurrence
        \[
           S_{n+2}=4S_{n+1}-S_{n}\qquad(n\ge 0),
        \]
        with initial values
        \[
           S_0=\alpha^{0}+\beta^{0}=1+1=2,\qquad
           S_1=\alpha+\beta=4 .
        \]
        Because the right–hand side of the recurrence uses only integer
        coefficients, an easy induction shows
        \[
           S_n\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for every }n\ge 0 .
        \]

3.  The integer that lies immediately below \(\alpha^{\,n}\).

    Write \(S_n=\alpha^{\,n}+\beta^{\,n}\) as above.  
    Since \(\beta=\alpha^{-1}\) (step 1), we have
    \[
       S_n-1=\alpha^{\,n}+\alpha^{-n}-1 .
    \]
    We compare this number with \(\alpha^{\,n}\).

    •  Because \(\alpha>1\), we have \(0<\alpha^{-n}\le 1\) (the equality
       occurs only when \(n=0\)).  Hence
       \[
          S_n-1=\alpha^{\,n}+(\alpha^{-n}-1)\le\alpha^{\,n}.
       \]

    •  At the same time \(\alpha^{-n}>0\), so \(S_n=\alpha^{\,n}+\alpha^{-n} >
       \alpha^{\,n}\).

    Therefore the two real numbers \(\alpha^{\,n}\) and \(S_n-1\) differ by
    \[
       \alpha^{\,n}-(S_n-1)=1-\alpha^{-n}\in(0,1],
    \]
    i.e. the distance is smaller than \(1\).
    Since \(S_n-1\) itself is an integer (because \(S_n\) is an integer by
    step 2), there cannot be any other integer strictly between
    \(S_n-1\) and \(\alpha^{\,n}\).  Consequently
    \[
       \bigl\lfloor\alpha^{\,n}\bigr\rfloor = S_n-1
       =\alpha^{\,n}+\alpha^{-n}-1 .
    \]

4.  The fractional part of \(\alpha^{\,n}\).

    Finally,
    \[
       \alpha^{\,n}-\bigl\lfloor\alpha^{\,n}\bigr\rfloor
       =\alpha^{\,n}-(\alpha^{\,n}+\alpha^{-n}-1)
       =1-\alpha^{-n}.
    \]

5.  Verification for \(n=0\).

    For completeness, let \(n=0\).  Then \(\alpha^{0}=1\),
    \(\lfloor\alpha^{0}\rfloor=1\) and \(\alpha^{-0}=1\); hence
    \[
       \alpha^{0}-\lfloor\alpha^{0}\rfloor=1-1=0=1-\alpha^{-0},
    \]
    so the equality also holds when \(n=0\).

Thus for every integer \(n\ge 0\) we have proved
\[
   \;\alpha^{\,n}-\lfloor\alpha^{\,n}\rfloor
          =1-\alpha^{-n}\;
\]
as required.

problem:
For each real number \( x \), define \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) to be the greatest integer less than or equal to \( x \).

Let \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\). Prove that

\[
\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}, \text{ for } n=0,1,2, \ldots
\]
solution:
Let the given equation be
\[ \alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n} \quad (*) \]
where \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\) and \(n=0,1,2,\ldots\).

The term \(\alpha^n - \lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor\) is the definition of the fractional part of \(\alpha^n\), often denoted by \(\{\alpha^n\}\). So the equation can be rewritten as \(\{\alpha^n\} = 1-\alpha^{-n}\).

To prove this statement, we need to show two things:
1. The quantity \(\alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1\) is an integer.
2. The quantity \(1-\alpha^{-n}\) is in the interval \([0,1)\).

If these two conditions are met, then we can write \(\alpha^n\) as
\[ \alpha^n = (\alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1) + (1 - \alpha^{-n}) \]
Let \(I_n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1\) and \(f_n = 1 - \alpha^{-n}\). If \(I_n\) is an integer and \(0 \le f_n < 1\), then by the definition of the floor function, \(I_n = \lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor\).
Then, \(\alpha^n - \lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor = \alpha^n - I_n = \alpha^n - (\alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1) = 1 - \alpha^{-n}\), which is the identity we want to prove.

Let's prove these two conditions.

Step 1: Show that \(\alpha^n + \alpha^{-n}\) is an integer for all \(n \ge 0\).
Let \(\beta = \alpha^{-1}\). We can calculate \(\beta\):
\[ \beta = \frac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2^2 - (\sqrt{3})^2} = \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{4-3} = 2-\sqrt{3} \]
Let \(S_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n}\). We want to show that \(S_n\) is an integer for all \(n \ge 0\).
We can use a linear recurrence relation for \(S_n\).
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are related by their sum and product:
Sum: \(\alpha+\beta = (2+\sqrt{3}) + (2-\sqrt{3}) = 4\).
Product: \(\alpha\beta = (2+\sqrt{3})(2-\sqrt{3}) = 1\) (as shown by \(\beta = \alpha^{-1}\)).
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - (\text{sum of roots})x + (\text{product of roots}) = 0\), which is \(x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0\).
Since \(\alpha\) is a root, \(\alpha^2 - 4\alpha + 1 = 0\), which implies \(\alpha^2 = 4\alpha - 1\).
Multiplying by \(\alpha^{k}\) for \(k \ge 0\), we get \(\alpha^{k+2} = 4\alpha^{k+1} - \alpha^k\). Let \(n=k+2\), so this is \(\alpha^n = 4\alpha^{n-1} - \alpha^{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\).
Similarly for \(\beta\): \(\beta^n = 4\beta^{n-1} - \beta^{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\).
Adding these two equations:
\[ \alpha^n + \beta^n = 4(\alpha^{n-1} + \beta^{n-1}) - (\alpha^{n-2} + \beta^{n-2}) \]
So, \(S_n = 4S_{n-1} - S_{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\).

Now we establish the base cases for the recurrence:
For \(n=0\): \(S_0 = \alpha^0 + \beta^0 = 1+1=2\). This is an integer.
For \(n=1\): \(S_1 = \alpha^1 + \beta^1 = (2+\sqrt{3}) + (2-\sqrt{3}) = 4\). This is an integer.

Now we use induction to show \(S_n\) is an integer for all \(n \ge 0\).
Base cases: \(S_0=2\) and \(S_1=4\) are integers.
Inductive hypothesis: Assume that for some integer \(k \ge 1\), \(S_j\) is an integer for all \(0 \le j \le k\).
Inductive step: We want to show \(S_{k+1}\) is an integer. Using the recurrence relation for \(n=k+1 \ge 2\):
\(S_{k+1} = 4S_k - S_{k-1}\).
By the inductive hypothesis, \(S_k\) and \(S_{k-1}\) are integers.
Since \(4\) is an integer, \(4S_k\) is an integer. The difference of two integers \(4S_k - S_{k-1}\) is also an integer.
Thus, \(S_{k+1}\) is an integer.
By the principle of strong induction, \(S_n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n}\) is an integer for all \(n \ge 0\).

Since \(S_n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n}\) is an integer, it follows that \(I_n = S_n - 1 = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1\) is also an integer for all \(n \ge 0\). This fulfills the first condition.

Step 2: Show that \(f_n = 1-\alpha^{-n}\) is in the interval \([0,1)\) for all \(n \ge 0\).
We examine two cases for \(n\):
Case 1: \(n=0\).
\(f_0 = 1 - \alpha^{-0} = 1 - 1/ \alpha^0 = 1 - 1/1 = 1-1=0\).
So \(f_0 = 0\). The condition \(0 \le f_0 < 1\) becomes \(0 \le 0 < 1\), which is true.

Case 2: \(n \ge 1\).
\(\alpha = 2+\sqrt{3}\). Since \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\), \(\alpha \approx 3.732\).
Clearly, \(\alpha > 1\).
Therefore, \(\alpha^n > 1\) for \(n \ge 1\).
This implies that \(0 < \frac{1}{\alpha^n} < 1\), so \(0 < \alpha^{-n} < 1\).
Multiplying the inequality by \(-1\) reverses the inequality signs: \(-1 < -\alpha^{-n} < 0\).
Adding \(1\) to all parts of the inequality:
\(1-1 < 1-\alpha^{-n} < 1+0\)
\(0 < 1-\alpha^{-n} < 1\).
So, for \(n \ge 1\), \(0 < f_n < 1\).

Combining both cases (\(n=0\) and \(n \ge 1\)), we have \(0 \le f_n < 1\) for all \(n \ge 0\). This fulfills the second condition.

Step 3: Conclusion.
We have shown that \(I_n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1\) is an integer for all \(n \ge 0\), and that \(f_n = 1-\alpha^{-n}\) satisfies \(0 \le f_n < 1\) for all \(n \ge 0\).
We can write \(\alpha^n\) as \(\alpha^n = I_n + f_n\).
By the definition of the floor function, if a number \(x\) can be written as \(x = k+g\) where \(k\) is an integer and \(0 \le g < 1\), then \(\lfloor x \rfloor = k\) and \(\{x\} = g\).
In our case, \(x=\alpha^n\), \(k=I_n\), and \(g=f_n\).
So, \(\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor = I_n = \alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1\).
The expression we want to prove is \(\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}\).
Substituting the expression for \(\lfloor\alpha^n\rfloor\):
\[ \alpha^n - (\alpha^n + \alpha^{-n} - 1) = \alpha^n - \alpha^n - \alpha^{-n} + 1 = 1 - \alpha^{-n} \]
This confirms the identity \(\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}\).

The proof is complete.

Final check for \(n=0\):
\(\alpha^0 - \lfloor\alpha^0\rfloor = 1 - \lfloor 1 \rfloor = 1-1=0\).
\(1 - \alpha^{-0} = 1 - 1 = 0\).
The identity holds for \(n=0\).
Our proof considered \(n=0\) within the general framework correctly. For \(n=0\), \(S_0 = \alpha^0+\alpha^{-0} = 1+1=2\), which is an integer. \(I_0 = S_0-1 = 1\).
\(f_0 = 1-\alpha^{-0} = 1-1=0\). The condition \(0 \le f_0 < 1\) holds.
So \(\lfloor\alpha^0\rfloor = \lfloor 1 \rfloor = I_0 = 1\), which is correct.
And \(\alpha^0-\lfloor\alpha^0\rfloor = f_0 = 0\). This matches \(1-\alpha^{-0}=0\).
author: llm

problem:
For each real number \( x \), define \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) to be the greatest integer less than or equal to \( x \).

Let \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\). Prove that

\[
\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}, \text{ for } n=0,1,2, \ldots
\]
solution:
To prove the identity

$$
\alpha^{n} - \left\lfloor \alpha^{n} \right\rfloor = 1 - \alpha^{-n}, \quad \text{for } n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
$$

where $ \alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3} $, we proceed through a structured and detailed analysis of the properties of $ \alpha $ and its conjugate.

---

### Step 1: Define the Conjugate and Verify Inverse

Let $ \alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3} $, and define $ \beta = 2 - \sqrt{3} $, the conjugate of $ \alpha $. We compute:

$$
\alpha \beta = (2 + \sqrt{3})(2 - \sqrt{3}) = 4 - 3 = 1
$$

Thus, $ \beta = \alpha^{-1} $.

---

### Step 2: Characteristic Equation

We verify that $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ are roots of the quadratic equation:

$$
x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0
$$

Substituting $ \alpha $:

$$
\alpha^2 - 4\alpha + 1 = (2 + \sqrt{3})^2 - 4(2 + \sqrt{3}) + 1 = (7 + 4\sqrt{3}) - (8 + 4\sqrt{3}) + 1 = 0
$$

Similarly for $ \beta $, the same computation shows:

$$
\beta^2 - 4\beta + 1 = 0
$$

Thus, $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ are roots of this quadratic.

---

### Step 3: Define a Sequence and Establish Recurrence

Define the sequence $ s_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n $. Since $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ satisfy the quadratic $ x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0 $, the sequence $ s_n $ satisfies the recurrence:

$$
s_{n+2} = 4s_{n+1} - s_n
$$

with initial conditions:

$$
s_0 = \alpha^0 + \beta^0 = 1 + 1 = 2 \\
s_1 = \alpha^1 + \beta^1 = (2 + \sqrt{3}) + (2 - \sqrt{3}) = 4
$$

We now prove by **strong induction** that $ s_n \in \mathbb{Z} $ for all $ n \geq 0 $.

- **Base cases:** $ s_0 = 2 $, $ s_1 = 4 $ are integers.
- **Inductive step:** Assume $ s_k $ and $ s_{k-1} $ are integers for all $ k \leq n $. Then:

$$
s_{n+1} = 4s_n - s_{n-1}
$$

Since $ s_n $ and $ s_{n-1} $ are integers by the inductive hypothesis, and the recurrence uses only integer coefficients, $ s_{n+1} $ is also an integer.

Hence, by induction, $ s_n \in \mathbb{Z} $ for all $ n \geq 0 $.

---

### Step 4: Analyze the Structure of $ \alpha^n $

We now express $ \alpha^n $ in terms of $ s_n $ and $ \beta^n $:

$$
\alpha^n = s_n - \beta^n
$$

Since $ 0 < \beta < 1 $, it follows that $ 0 < \beta^n < 1 $ for all $ n \geq 1 $. Therefore:

$$
s_n - 1 < \alpha^n < s_n
$$

This implies that the floor of $ \alpha^n $ is $ s_n - 1 $:

$$
\left\lfloor \alpha^n \right\rfloor = s_n - 1
$$

---

### Step 5: Compute the Fractional Part

Using the identity:

$$
\text{frac}(\alpha^n) = \alpha^n - \left\lfloor \alpha^n \right\rfloor
$$

we substitute the expressions:

$$
\alpha^n - \left\lfloor \alpha^n \right\rfloor = (s_n - \beta^n) - (s_n - 1) = 1 - \beta^n
$$

Recall that $ \beta = \alpha^{-1} $, so $ \beta^n = \alpha^{-n} $. Therefore:

$$
\text{frac}(\alpha^n) = 1 - \alpha^{-n}
$$

---

### Step 6: Verify the Base Case $ n = 0 $

For $ n = 0 $, we have:

$$
\alpha^0 = 1, \quad \left\lfloor \alpha^0 \right\rfloor = 1, \quad \text{frac}(\alpha^0) = 0
$$

The formula gives:

$$
1 - \alpha^{-0} = 1 - 1 = 0
$$

So the identity holds for $ n = 0 $.

---

### Final Conclusion

We have shown that for all $ n \geq 0 $:

- $ \alpha^n + \beta^n = s_n \in \mathbb{Z} $
- $ \beta^n = \alpha^{-n} \in (0,1) $
- $ \left\lfloor \alpha^n \right\rfloor = s_n - 1 $
- $ \text{frac}(\alpha^n) = \alpha^n - \left\lfloor \alpha^n \right\rfloor = 1 - \alpha^{-n} $

Thus, the identity is proven.
author: llm

problem:
For each real number \( x \), define \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) to be the greatest integer less than or equal to \( x \).

Let \(\alpha=2+\sqrt{3}\). Prove that

\[
\alpha^{n}-\left\lfloor\alpha^{n}\right\rfloor=1-\alpha^{-n}, \text{ for } n=0,1,2, \ldots
\]
solution:
We proceed as follows.

Define \(\beta = 2 - \sqrt{3}\). Note that \(\alpha \beta = (2 + \sqrt{3})(2 - \sqrt{3}) = 4 - 3 = 1\), so \(\beta = \alpha^{-1}\) and \(\beta^n = \alpha^{-n}\) for all integers \(n\).

Both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0\), which can be verified by substituting \(\alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3}\):
\[
(2 + \sqrt{3})^2 - 4(2 + \sqrt{3}) + 1 = 4 + 4\sqrt{3} + 3 - 8 - 4\sqrt{3} + 1 = 7 + 4\sqrt{3} - 8 - 4\sqrt{3} + 1 = 0.
\]
A similar calculation holds for \(\beta\).

Define the sequence \(u_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n\). This sequence satisfies the recurrence relation \(u_n = 4u_{n-1} - u_{n-2}\) for \(n \geq 2\), with initial conditions \(u_0 = \alpha^0 + \beta^0 = 1 + 1 = 2\) and \(u_1 = \alpha + \beta = (2 + \sqrt{3}) + (2 - \sqrt{3}) = 4\). Both initial values are integers, and the recurrence relation preserves integers, so \(u_n\) is an integer for all \(n \geq 0\).

Now, express \(\alpha^n\) in terms of \(u_n\) and \(\beta^n\):
\[
\alpha^n = u_n - \beta^n.
\]
Since \(\beta = 2 - \sqrt{3} \approx 0.2679 < 1\), it follows that \(0 < \beta^n \leq 1\) for all \(n \geq 0\), with equality to 1 only when \(n = 0\). Thus,
\[
u_n - 1 \leq \alpha^n < u_n
\]
for all \(n \geq 0\), because \(\beta^n > 0\) implies \(\alpha^n < u_n\), and \(\beta^n \leq 1\) implies \(\alpha^n \geq u_n - 1\).

Since \(u_n\) and \(u_n - 1\) are consecutive integers, the floor function \(\lfloor \alpha^n \rfloor\) is the greatest integer less than or equal to \(\alpha^n\). Given that \(u_n - 1 \leq \alpha^n < u_n\), it follows that \(\lfloor \alpha^n \rfloor = u_n - 1\) for all \(n \geq 0\).

Now, compute the fractional part:
\[
\alpha^n - \lfloor \alpha^n \rfloor = \alpha^n - (u_n - 1) = \alpha^n - u_n + 1.
\]
Substitute \(\alpha^n = u_n - \beta^n\):
\[
\alpha^n - u_n + 1 = (u_n - \beta^n) - u_n + 1 = -\beta^n + 1 = 1 - \beta^n.
\]
Since \(\beta^n = \alpha^{-n}\), we have:
\[
\alpha^n - \lfloor \alpha^n \rfloor = 1 - \alpha^{-n}.
\]
This equality holds for all non-negative integers \(n\), as required.

problem:
4. Eight players, Ann, Bob, Con, Dot, Eve, Fay, Guy and Hal compete in a chess tournament. No pair plays together more than once and there is no group of five people in which each one plays against all of the other four.
(a) Write down an arrangement for a tournament of $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
(b) Show that it is impossible to have a tournament of more than $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
solution:
We translate the situation into the language of graph theory.  
Put a vertex for every player and join two vertices by an edge when the corresponding pair of players meet.  
The two requirements of the question are therefore:

1. The graph is simple (no multiple edges, no loops).  
2. It contains no complete sub-graph on five vertices, i.e. it is $K_{5}$–free.

For eight vertices the complete graph $K_{8}$ has  
$\binom 82 = 28$ edges, so a tournament of $m$ games corresponds to a $K_{5}$-free graph on eight vertices with $m$ edges.

Part (a)   A $24$-game tournament without a $K_{5}$  

Partition the eight players into four pairs

Group 1 : Ann, Bob  
Group 2 : Con, Dot  
Group 3 : Eve, Fay  
Group 4 : Guy, Hal  

Let every player meet everyone who is **not in the same group**, and let the two members of each group **not** meet.  
The 24 games are listed once only:

Ann–Con Ann–Dot Ann–Eve Ann–Fay Ann–Guy Ann–Hal  
Bob–Con Bob–Dot Bob–Eve Bob–Fay Bob–Guy Bob–Hal  
Con–Eve Con–Fay Con–Guy Con–Hal  
Dot–Eve Dot–Fay Dot–Guy Dot–Hal  
Eve–Guy Eve–Hal  
Fay–Guy Fay–Hal  

Number of games.  
The four parts are of size $2,2,2,2$.  
Between any two different parts there are $2\times2 = 4$ games; there are $\binom 42 = 6$ pairs of parts, so

$\;6\times4 = 24$ games.

Why there is no $K_{5}$.  
Take any five players.  By the pigeon-hole principle two of them must come from the same group, and those two never meet.  
Hence the five players cannot form a complete sub-graph.  
Therefore the arrangement above satisfies both requirements.

(What we have constructed is the balanced Turán graph $T_{4}(8)$.)

Part (b)   $24$ games are the most possible  

Assume, for contradiction, that a tournament with **more than** 24 games exists;  
so there are at least $25$ games.  
Consequently at most $28-25=3$ pairs of players do **not** meet.  
Call these missing games the *non-edges*; the sub-graph they form is a graph $H$ on eight vertices with at most three edges.

Covering the non-edges.  
For every edge of $H$ choose one of its two end-vertices and collect these chosen vertices in a set $X$.  
Because $H$ has at most three edges we have $|X|\le 3$.

Let $Y=\;V\setminus X$.  
Since $|V|=8$, we have $|Y|\ge 8-3 =5$.

No non-edge lies wholly inside $Y$.  
Indeed, if $uv$ were a missing game with $u,v\in Y$, that edge would not be incident with any vertex of $X$, contradicting the way $X$ was chosen.  
Therefore every pair of vertices in $Y$ **does** meet; i.e. $Y$ spans a complete graph $K_{|Y|}$, and $|Y|\ge5$ gives a $K_{5}$.

But the problem statement forbids a group of five players each of whom meets all the other four, so we have obtained a contradiction.  
Hence a $K_{5}$-free graph on eight vertices can have **at most 24 edges**.

Since part (a) shows that 24 edges are attainable, 24 is the maximum possible.

Therefore

(a) the schedule displayed above realises 24 games and meets the conditions;  
(b) any schedule with more than 24 games would necessarily contain a forbidden
set of five mutually-playing players, so 24 is the greatest possible number of games.

problem:
4. Eight players, Ann, Bob, Con, Dot, Eve, Fay, Guy and Hal compete in a chess tournament. No pair plays together more than once and there is no group of five people in which each one plays against all of the other four.
(a) Write down an arrangement for a tournament of $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
(b) Show that it is impossible to have a tournament of more than $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
solution:
Below we represent the tournament by a simple graph \(G\) on the vertex set 
\(\{A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H\}\) (standing for Ann, Bob, Con, Dot, Eve, Fay, Guy, Hal),  
where an edge between two vertices means those two players have met.  Since no pair meets more than once we have at most one edge per pair, and the condition “no five of them form a complete sub‐tournament” is exactly “\(G\) has no \(K_5\) subgraph.”  Since there are \(\binom8{2}=28\) possible pairs, letting \(e(G)\) denote the number of edges (games played) we have
\[
0\le e(G)\le28,
\]
and we must arrange \(G\) so that it is \(K_5\)–free.

(a)  An explicit arrangement with \(24\) games is obtained by partitioning the eight players into four disjoint pairs and then playing every game between players in different pairs, but no games within a pair.  For instance, let the pairs be
\[
\{A,B\},\;\{C,D\},\;\{E,F\},\;\{G,H\}.
\]
We then draw every edge between vertices in different pairs, and draw no edge inside a pair.  Since there are
\[
\binom8{2}=28
\]
total possible edges, and we omit exactly the \(4\) edges
\[
AB,\;CD,\;EF,\;GH,
\]
this produces
\[
28-4=24
\]
edges.  Clearly no five vertices can induce a \(K_5\), because each of our omitted edges lies inside one of the four “pairs,” and any set of five vertices must contain at least one of those pairs and hence misses that edge.

Thus we have exhibited a \(K_5\)–free graph on \(8\) vertices with \(24\) edges.

(b)  We now show that \emph{no} \(K_5\)–free graph on \(8\) vertices can have more than \(24\) edges.  Equivalently, if \(G\) is \(K_5\)–free on \(8\) vertices then
\[
e(G)\;\le\;24.
\]
There are at most \(28\) edges total, so it suffices to show that any such \(G\) must \emph{miss} at least \(4\) edges.  Write
\[
m \;=\;\text{number of non–edges of }G
\;=\;\;28 \;-\;e(G).
\]
We will prove \(m\ge4\), whence \(e(G)\le28-4=24\).

Observe that forbidding a \(K_5\) means that \emph{every} set of \(5\) vertices must fail to be complete, i.e.\ must contain at least one non‐edge of \(G\).  There are
\[
\binom85 \;=\;56
\]
different \(5\)–element subsets of our \(8\) vertices.  On the other hand, each non‐edge \(xy\) of \(G\) lies in exactly
\[
\binom{6}{3}=20
\]
of those \(5\)–sets (namely, any choice of the other three vertices from the remaining six).  Thus if \(\mathcal N\) is the family of all non‐edges, the union of the families
\[
\bigl\{\;
\text{5‐sets containing }e
\;\bigr\}_{\,e\in\mathcal N}
\]
must cover all \(56\) five‐sets, because each five‐set must contain at least one non‐edge.

A simple inclusion–exclusion (or just the pigeon‐hole principle) now shows that \(\lvert\mathcal N\rvert=m\) cannot be less than \(4\).  Indeed:

– If \(m=1\), one non‐edge covers only \(20\) of the \(56\) five‐sets.  
– If \(m=2\), two non‐edges cover at most 
  \[
     2\cdot20 \;-\; \bigl|\text{5‐sets containing both non‐edges}\bigr|
     \;=\;40 \;-\; \text{(at least \(4\))}
     \;<\;56.
  \]
  (Here any two distinct edges—even if vertex–disjoint—lie together in exactly \(\binom{4}{1}=4\) of the five‐sets.)

– If \(m=3\), similarly the maximum possible coverage is
  \[
     3\cdot20
     \;-\;3\cdot4  \quad(\text{pairwise overlaps})
     \;=\;60-12
     \;=\;48
     \;<\;56.
  \]
  Hence three non‐edges cannot cover all \(56\) five‐sets.

Therefore one needs at least \(m\ge4\) non‐edges to destroy every potential \(K_5\).  Consequently
\[
e(G)\;=\;28-m
\;\le\;28-4
\;=\;24.
\]
This completes the proof that no \(K_5\)–free tournament on \(8\) players can have more than \(24\) games.

Remark.  One sees that the extremal case \(m=4\) arises exactly when the four non‐edges form a perfect matching (so that their “coverage” of five‐sets overlaps as little as possible).  That matching describes the same complete \(4\)–partite graph with parts of size \(2\) each that we gave in part (a).  This is exactly the \(T(8,4)\)–Turán graph, whose edge‐count is
\[
\bigl(1-\tfrac1{4}\bigr)\frac{8^2}{2}
\;=\;\frac{3}{4}\times32
\;=\;24.
\]
author: llm

problem:
4. Eight players, Ann, Bob, Con, Dot, Eve, Fay, Guy and Hal compete in a chess tournament. No pair plays together more than once and there is no group of five people in which each one plays against all of the other four.
(a) Write down an arrangement for a tournament of $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
(b) Show that it is impossible to have a tournament of more than $24$ games satisfying these conditions.
solution:
For part (a), an arrangement with 24 games is given by dividing the players into four pairs: \(\{ 	ext{Ann}, 	ext{Bob} \}\), \(\{ 	ext{Con}, 	ext{Dot} \}\), \(\{ 	ext{Eve}, 	ext{Fay} \}\), and \(\{ 	ext{Guy}, 	ext{Hal} \}\). The games consist of all possible pairs except these four pairs. Since there are \( inom{8}{2} = 28\) possible pairs and 4 pairs are excluded, there are \(28 - 4 = 24\) games. No pair plays more than once by construction, and there is no group of five players where each plays all others because the graph is 4-partite, which contains no clique of size 5.

For part (b), it must be shown that a tournament with more than 24 games is impossible under the given conditions. Suppose there are 25 games. In graph theory terms, the graph has 8 vertices (players) and 25 edges (games). The total number of possible edges is \( inom{8}{2} = 28\), so the complement graph has \(28 - 25 = 3\) edges. The independence number of a graph is the size of the largest independent set. For any graph with \(n\) vertices and matching number \(
u\) (the size of the largest matching), the independence number \(\alpha \geq n - 
u\). Here, \(n = 8\) and the maximum matching size \(
u \leq 3\), so \(\alpha \geq 8 - 3 = 5\). Thus, the complement graph has an independent set of size at least 5. An independent set in the complement graph corresponds to a clique in the original graph, so there is a clique of size at least 5 in the game graph. This means there is a group of five players where each plays all others, violating the condition. Therefore, it is impossible to have more than 24 games without such a group.
