problem: Determine, with proof, the smallest positive multiple of \(99\) all of whose digits are either \(1\) or \(2\).
solution:
Let a positive integer   
\(N=\overline{d_{1}d_{2}\ldots d_{n}}\;(d_i\in\{1,2\})\)   
be a multiple of \(99=9\cdot 11\).
Put  

• \(S   = d_{1}+d_{2}+\dots +d_{n}\)   (ordinary digit–sum),  

• \(T   = (d_{1}+d_{3}+d_{5}+\dots )-(d_{2}+d_{4}+d_{6}+\dots )\)  
  (alternating digit–sum).

Divisibility rules give

(1) \(9\mid N\iff 9\mid S\),

(2) \(11\mid N\iff 11\mid T\).

Throughout the proof write  

\(n=2k\) (even) or \(n=2k+1\) (odd) and let  

c  = number of 2’s in the odd positions,  
d  = number of 2’s in the even positions.

(The remaining digits are 1’s.)

---------------------------------------------------
1.  A lower bound for the number of digits
---------------------------------------------------
Because every digit is 1 or 2,

\(S \le 2n.\)

If \(n\le 4\) then \(S\le 8<9\), so \(9\nmid S\).  
Hence \(n\ge 5\).

---------------------------------------------------
2.  A bound for the alternating sum when \(n\le 9\)
---------------------------------------------------
For \(n\le 9\) we have at most five odd positions, so

\(|T|\le 2\cdot 5=10<11.\)

Consequently, whenever \(n\le 9\) one must have \(T=0\).  
We now show that \(T=0\) cannot occur together with \(9\mid S\) for any
\(5\le n\le 9\).

---------------------------------------------------
3.  No solution with \(5\le n\le 9\)
---------------------------------------------------

––––– 3.1  Even number of digits  (\(n=2k,\,k=3,4\) i.e. \(n=6,8\))

Here \(k\) odd positions and \(k\) even positions give  

\(T=0\Longrightarrow c=d.\)

The digit–sum is  

\(S=n+c+d=n+2c.\)

Because \(n\le 8\), the interval \([n,2n]\) lies inside \([6,16]\);
the only multiple of \(9\) in this interval is \(9\).
Thus \(S=9\), i.e. \(n+2c=9\).

For \(n=6\): \(2c=3\) – impossible.  
For \(n=8\): \(2c=1\) – impossible.

Hence no such number exists when \(n=6\) or \(8\).

––––– 3.2  Odd number of digits  (\(n=2k+1,\,k=2,3,4\) i.e. \(n=5,7,9\))

There are \(k+1\) odd and \(k\) even positions; therefore

\(T=(k+1+c)-(k+d)=1+(c-d)=0\Longrightarrow d=c+1.\)

Hence the number of 2’s equals  

\(a=c+d=2c+1,\)

and  

\(S=n+a=(2k+1)+(2c+1)=2(k+c+1).\)

Again, for \(n\le 9\) the only possible multiples of \(9\) are \(9\) or (for
\(n=9\)) \(18\).

•  \(n=5\): \(S=9 \Longrightarrow 2(k+c+1)=9\Longrightarrow 2c=3\)
  – impossible.

•  \(n=7\): \(S=9 \Longrightarrow 2c=1\)
  – impossible.

•  \(n=9\): \(S\) could be \(9\) or \(18\).

   – If \(S=9\): \(2c=-1\) – impossible.  
   – If \(S=18\): every digit must be 2, giving
     \(T=10-8=2\neq 0\).

Thus no admissible number exists for \(n=5,7,9\).

Combining 3.1 and 3.2, no number with at most nine digits is a
multiple of \(99\).  Therefore

\(n\ge 10.\)

---------------------------------------------------
4.  The structure when \(n=10\)
---------------------------------------------------
Now let \(n=10\;(k=5)\).

Because \(n\ge 10\) and all digits are at most \(2\), the
first two possible digit–sums that are multiples of \(9\) are \(18,27\).
But \(S\le 2n=20\), so necessarily \(S=18\).

Hence the number of 2’s is  

\(a=S-n=18-10=8,\)

and the number of 1’s is \(2\).

With \(T=0\) we must have \(c=d\).  Because there are five odd and five
even positions,

\(c=d=4.\)

Therefore

• four of the five odd places contain 2’s, one contains 1,  
• four of the five even places contain 2’s, one contains 1.

---------------------------------------------------
5.  The smallest ten–digit candidate
---------------------------------------------------
To obtain the smallest possible value we put the digit \(1\) into the
earliest places:

odd position 1 and even position 2.

All remaining positions receive the digit \(2\).
That gives

\(N_0=1122222222.\)

Check of the divisibility conditions:

• Digit–sum \(1+1+8\cdot 2=18\) is a multiple of \(9\).

• Odd–place sum \(1+2+2+2+2=9\),

  even–place sum \(1+2+2+2+2=9\);

  their difference is \(0\), a multiple of \(11\).

Thus \(99\mid N_0\).

---------------------------------------------------
6.  Minimality of \(N_0\)
---------------------------------------------------
Any ten–digit multiple of \(99\) with digits \(1,2\) must, as shown
above, contain exactly one \(1\) in odd position and one in even
position, all other digits being \(2\).

•  The first digit cannot be \(2\) (otherwise the odd–positions would
   contain no \(1\)), hence it is \(1\).

•  If the second digit were \(2\) we would already exceed \(N_0\)
   (whose second digit is \(1\)).  Therefore the second digit is
   also \(1\) and the remaining eight digits are \(2\), i.e. the
   number is exactly \(N_0\).

Consequently \(N_0\) is not only a multiple of \(99\) but the
smallest possible one whose digits are all \(1\) or \(2\).

---------------------------------------------------
7.  Answer
---------------------------------------------------
The smallest positive multiple of \(99\) whose decimal digits are
all \(1\) or \(2\) is

\[
1122222222.
\]
author: llm

problem: Determine, with proof, the smallest positive multiple of \(99\) all of whose digits are either \(1\) or \(2\).
solution:
Let \(N\) be a positive integer whose decimal digits are all in \(\{1,2\}\) and suppose \(N\) is divisible by \(99\).  Since 
\[
99=9\times 11,
\]
it follows that \(N\) is divisible by both \(9\) and \(11\).  We recall the standard tests:

(i) A positive integer is divisible by \(9\) if and only if the sum of its decimal digits is divisible by \(9\).

(ii) A positive integer is divisible by \(11\) if and only if the alternating sum of its decimal digits (sum of the digits in odd positions minus sum of the digits in even positions) is divisible by \(11\).

Write \(k\) for the total number of digits of \(N\), and write \(y\) for the number of digits equal to \(2\).  Then the number of digits equal to \(1\) is \(k-y\), so the sum of all digits of \(N\) is
\[
s \;=\;(k-y)\cdot1 \;+\;y\cdot2 \;=\;k + y.
\]
By divisibility by \(9\) we must have
\[
k + y \;\equiv\;0\pmod9.
\tag{1}
\]
Also clearly \(0\le y\le k\).

We first show that no solution exists with \(k\le9\).  Then we exhibit a solution for \(k=10\).

1.  No solution for \(k\le9\).

(a) If \(k\le4\), then \(s=k+y\le k+k=2k\le8\), so \(s\) cannot be a multiple of \(9\).  Hence \(k\ge5\).

(b) For \(5\le k\le8\), from \((1)\) we must have \(k+y=9\) (since \(5\le k+y\le2k\le16\) and the only multiple of \(9\) in that range is \(9\)).  Hence
\[
y \;=\;9-k,
\quad
0\;\le\;9-k\;\le\;k
\quad(\text{which holds for }5\le k\le8).
\]
Let 
\[
m \;=\;\bigl\lceil\tfrac{k}{2}\bigr\rceil
\]
be the number of odd positions among the \(k\) digits.  Write \(a\) for the number of those odd positions in which the digit is \(2\).  Then
\[
0\;\le\;a\;\le\;m,
\]
and the sum of the digits in odd positions is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{odd}}d_i
\;=\;
(m-a)\cdot1 \;+\;a\cdot2
\;=\;
m + a.
\]
Since the total digit‐sum is \(9\), the sum of the digits in the even positions is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{even}}d_i
\;=\;
9 \;-\;(m + a).
\]
Therefore the alternating sum is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{odd}}d_i
\;-\;
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{even}}d_i
\;=\;
(m + a)\;-\;(9 - (m + a))
\;=\;
2(m + a)\;-\;9.
\]
We now check each \(k\in\{5,6,7,8\}\):

– If \(k=5\), then \(m=3\) and \(y=9-5=4\), so \(0\le a\le3\).  Thus
\[
2(m+a)-9 =2(3+a)-9 =2a-3 \,\in\{-3,-1,1,3\},
\]
none of which is divisible by \(11\).  Hence no solution for \(k=5\).

– If \(k=6\), then \(m=3\) and \(y=9-6=3\), so again \(0\le a\le3\) and
\[
2(m+a)-9 =2a-3 \in\{-3,-1,1,3\},
\]
no multiple of \(11\).  No solution for \(k=6\).

– If \(k=7\), then \(m=4\) and \(y=9-7=2\), so \(0\le a\le2\) and
\[
2(m+a)-9 =2(4+a)-9 =2a-1 \in\{-1,1,3\},
\]
none divisible by \(11\).  No solution for \(k=7\).

– If \(k=8\), then \(m=4\) and \(y=9-8=1\), so \(0\le a\le1\) and
\[
2(m+a)-9 =2a-1 \in\{-1,1\},
\]
none divisible by \(11\).  No solution for \(k=8\).

(c) Finally, if \(k=9\), then \(k+y\) must be \(9\) or \(18\).  
– If \(k+y=9\) then \(y=0\) and \(N=111111111\); its alternating sum is \(5-4=1\not\equiv0\pmod{11}\).  
– If \(k+y=18\) then \(y=9\) and \(N=222222222\); its alternating sum is \(10-8=2\not\equiv0\pmod{11}\).  
Thus no solution for \(k=9\).

We conclude that any solution must have \(k\ge10\).

2.  Existence of a solution for \(k=10\).

Take \(k=10\).  Then \((1)\) forces
\[
k + y =18,
\quad
\text{so }y=8.
\]
There are \(5\) odd positions and \(5\) even positions.  Let \(a\) be the number of those odd positions carrying the digit \(2\), and \(b\) the number of even positions carrying the digit \(2\).  Then
\[
a+b \;=\;y \;=\;8,
\qquad
0\le a\le5,\quad0\le b\le5.
\]
The sum of the digits in odd positions is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{odd}}d_i
\;=\;
(5-a)\cdot1 + a\cdot2
\;=\;
5 + a,
\]
and hence the sum in the even positions is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{even}}d_i
\;=\;
18 \;-\;(5 + a)
\;=\;
13 - a.
\]
Therefore the alternating sum is
\[
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{odd}}d_i
\;-\;
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{even}}d_i
\;=\;
(5 + a)\;-\;(13 - a)
\;=\;
2a - 8.
\]
Divisibility by \(11\) requires
\[
2a - 8 \;\equiv\;0\pmod{11}.
\]
Checking \(a=0,1,2,3,4,5\) gives
\[
2a-8\;\in\;\{-8,-6,-4,-2,0,2\},
\]
so the only multiple of \(11\) is \(0\), which forces
\[
a=4,
\quad
b=8-4=4.
\]
Hence among the \(5\) odd positions exactly \(4\) are digit \(2\) (and \(1\) is digit \(1\)), and among the \(5\) even positions exactly \(4\) are digit \(2\) (and \(1\) is digit \(1\)).  To make \(N\) as small as possible in the usual decimal order, we place the single odd‐position 1 in position \(1\) and the single even‐position 1 in position \(2\), and all other positions are filled with \(2\).  Thus the smallest candidate is
\[
N \;=\;1122222222.
\]
Finally we verify
\[
\sum_{\text{digits}} 
=1+1+8\cdot2=18\equiv0\pmod9,
\qquad
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{odd}}d_i
-
\sum_{i\ \mathrm{even}}d_i
=(1+2+2+2+2)-(1+2+2+2+2)=0\equiv0\pmod{11}.
\]
Therefore \(1122222222\) is divisible by both \(9\) and \(11\), hence by \(99\), and by the above analysis no smaller positive integer with digits in \(\{1,2\}\) can be a multiple of \(99\).  This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem:
A line segment \( B_{0} B_{n} \) is divided into \( n \) equal parts at points \( B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n-1} \) and \( A \) is a point such that \( \angle B_{0} A B_{n} \) is a right angle. Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
\]
solution:
Let \(A\) be a point in the plane. Let \(B_0\) and \(B_n\) be two distinct points such that \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\).
Let \(l_0 = |A B_0|\) and \(l_n = |A B_n|\) be the lengths of the segments \(A B_0\) and \(A B_n\), respectively. Since \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\), triangle \(B_0 A B_n\) is a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse \(B_0 B_n\). By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the segment \(B_0 B_n\) is given by:
\[ |B_0 B_n|^2 = |A B_0|^2 + |A B_n|^2 = l_0^2 + l_n^2 \]
The points \(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_{n-1}\) divide the line segment \(B_0 B_n\) into \(n\) equal parts. This means that the points \(B_0, B_1, \ldots, B_n\) are collinear.
For any \(k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}\), the point \(B_k\) is such that the distance from \(B_0\) to \(B_k\) along the segment \(B_0 B_n\) is \(k\) times the length of one part. The length of each part is \(\frac{|B_0 B_n|}{n}\).
So, \(|B_0 B_k| = k \cdot \frac{|B_0 B_n|}{n}\).
Squaring this expression, we get:
\[ |B_0 B_k|^2 = \left(k \frac{|B_0 B_n|}{n}\right)^2 = \frac{k^2}{n^2} |B_0 B_n|^2 \]
Substituting \(|B_0 B_n|^2 = l_0^2 + l_n^2\), we have:
\[ |B_0 B_k|^2 = \frac{k^2 (l_0^2 + l_n^2)}{n^2} \]
We want to calculate the sum on the right-hand side (RHS) of the given equation:
\[ \text{RHS} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} |B_0 B_k|^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{k^2 (l_0^2 + l_n^2)}{n^2} \]
We can factor out the constant terms \( (l_0^2 + l_n^2)/n^2 \):
\[ \text{RHS} = \frac{l_0^2 + l_n^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 \]
The sum of the first \(n\) squares is a well-known formula: \( \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \).
Since \(0^2 = 0\), the sum \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = 0^2 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \).
Substituting this into the expression for the RHS:
\[ \text{RHS} = \frac{l_0^2 + l_n^2}{n^2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = \frac{(l_0^2 + l_n^2)(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n} \]

Now, we calculate the left-hand side (LHS) of the given equation: \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2 \).
Let \(A\) be the origin \((0,0)\) in a Cartesian coordinate system. Since \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\), we can align \(B_0\) with the y-axis and \(B_n\) with the x-axis.
So, the coordinates of \(B_0\) are \((0, l_0)\) and the coordinates of \(B_n\) are \((l_n, 0)\). (We can assume \(l_0, l_n > 0\) as \(A \neq B_0\) and \(A \neq B_n\) for the angle to be well-defined. The case where \(l_0=0\) or \(l_n=0\) can be handled as a degenerate case, but the resulting formulas still hold).
The point \(B_k\) divides the segment \(B_0 B_n\) in the ratio \(k : (n-k)\). That is, \(\vec{AB_k} = \frac{n-k}{n}\vec{AB_0} + \frac{k}{n}\vec{AB_n}\).
The coordinates of \(B_k\) are given by the section formula:
\[ B_k = \left( (1-\frac{k}{n}) \cdot 0 + \frac{k}{n} \cdot l_n, (1-\frac{k}{n}) \cdot l_0 + \frac{k}{n} \cdot 0 \right) = \left( \frac{k l_n}{n}, \frac{(n-k)l_0}{n} \right) \]
The square of the distance from \(A=(0,0)\) to \(B_k\) is:
\[ |A B_k|^2 = \left(\frac{k l_n}{n}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{(n-k)l_0}{n}\right)^2 = \frac{k^2 l_n^2}{n^2} + \frac{(n-k)^2 l_0^2}{n^2} \]
Now we sum these quantities for \(k=0, \ldots, n\):
\[ \text{LHS} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( \frac{k^2 l_n^2}{n^2} + \frac{(n-k)^2 l_0^2}{n^2} \right) \]
We can split the sum into two parts:
\[ \text{LHS} = \frac{l_n^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 + \frac{l_0^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n-k)^2 \]
Let's analyze the second sum \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n-k)^2 \).
When \(k=0\), the term is \((n-0)^2 = n^2\).
When \(k=1\), the term is \((n-1)^2\).
...
When \(k=n\), the term is \((n-n)^2 = 0^2\).
So, \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n-k)^2 = n^2 + (n-1)^2 + \ldots + 1^2 + 0^2 \).
This is equivalent to \( \sum_{j=0}^{n} j^2 \), where \(j = n-k\). As \(k\) goes from \(0\) to \(n\), \(j\) goes from \(n\) to \(0\).
Thus, \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} (n-k)^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{n} j^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \).
Substituting this back into the expression for LHS:
\[ \text{LHS} = \frac{l_n^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 + \frac{l_0^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 \]
\[ \text{LHS} = \left(\frac{l_n^2+l_0^2}{n^2}\right) \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 \]
Using the sum of squares formula \( \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \):
\[ \text{LHS} = \frac{l_n^2+l_0^2}{n^2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = \frac{(l_0^2+l_n^2)(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n} \]
Comparing the expressions for LHS and RHS:
\[ \text{LHS} = \frac{(l_0^2+l_n^2)(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n} \]
\[ \text{RHS} = \frac{(l_0^2+l_n^2)(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n} \]
Both sides are equal. This completes the proof.

To be more explicit about the vector approach for \(|A B_k|^2\):
Let \(A\) be the origin. Let \(\mathbf{b}_k\) be the position vector of \(B_k\). So \(|\vec{AB_k}|^2 = |\mathbf{b}_k|^2\).
We have \(l_0 = |\mathbf{b}_0|\) and \(l_n = |\mathbf{b}_n|\).
The condition \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\) means \(\mathbf{b}_0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_n = 0\).
The point \(B_k\) is given by \(\mathbf{b}_k = (1-\frac{k}{n})\mathbf{b}_0 + \frac{k}{n}\mathbf{b}_n\).
Then \(|\mathbf{b}_k|^2 = \left((1-\frac{k}{n})\mathbf{b}_0 + \frac{k}{n}\mathbf{b}_n\right) \cdot \left((1-\frac{k}{n})\mathbf{b}_0 + \frac{k}{n}\mathbf{b}_n\right)\)
\(|\mathbf{b}_k|^2 = (1-\frac{k}{n})^2 |\mathbf{b}_0|^2 + (\frac{k}{n})^2 |\mathbf{b}_n|^2 + 2 (1-\frac{k}{n})\frac{k}{n} (\mathbf{b}_0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_n)\).
Since \(\mathbf{b}_0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_n = 0\), this simplifies to:
\(|\mathbf{b}_k|^2 = (1-\frac{k}{n})^2 |\mathbf{b}_0|^2 + (\frac{k}{n})^2 |\mathbf{b}_n|^2 = \frac{(n-k)^2}{n^2} l_0^2 + \frac{k^2}{n^2} l_n^2\).
This is the same expression as obtained using coordinate geometry \(\left( |A B_k|^2 = \frac{k^2 l_n^2}{n^2} + \frac{(n-k)^2 l_0^2}{n^2} \right)\), and leads to the same result for the LHS.
author: llm

problem:
A line segment \( B_{0} B_{n} \) is divided into \( n \) equal parts at points \( B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n-1} \) and \( A \) is a point such that \( \angle B_{0} A B_{n} \) is a right angle. Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
\]
solution:
To prove the identity:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
$$

we begin by analyzing the geometric configuration and translating it into a coordinate-based algebraic framework.

---

### **Step 1: Coordinate Setup**

Let us place the segment $ B_0B_n $ on the x-axis for simplicity. Define the coordinates of the points as follows:

- $ B_0 = (0, 0) $
- $ B_n = (n, 0) $
- $ B_k = (k, 0) $ for $ k = 0, 1, \dots, n $

This setup ensures that the segment $ B_0B_n $ is divided into $ n $ equal parts, each of length 1.

Let point $ A $ have coordinates $ (x, y) $, and suppose that $ \angle B_0AB_n $ is a right angle. This implies that triangle $ B_0AB_n $ is a right triangle with the right angle at $ A $.

---

### **Step 2: Use of the Right Angle Condition**

Since $ \angle B_0AB_n = 90^\circ $, the vectors $ \vec{AB_0} $ and $ \vec{AB_n} $ are perpendicular. Using vector dot product:

$$
\vec{AB_0} = (0 - x, 0 - y) = (-x, -y)
$$
$$
\vec{AB_n} = (n - x, 0 - y) = (n - x, -y)
$$

Their dot product is:

$$
(-x)(n - x) + (-y)(-y) = -nx + x^2 + y^2 = 0
$$

Thus, we obtain the condition:

$$
x^2 - nx + y^2 = 0 \tag{1}
$$

This is the key geometric constraint that point $ A $ must satisfy.

---

### **Step 3: Compute the Left-Hand Side (LHS)**

We compute the sum $ \sum_{k=0}^{n} |AB_k|^2 $, where $ |AB_k|^2 $ is the square of the distance from $ A = (x, y) $ to $ B_k = (k, 0) $:

$$
|AB_k|^2 = (k - x)^2 + y^2
$$

So the sum becomes:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left[(k - x)^2 + y^2\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (k^2 - 2kx + x^2 + y^2)
$$

Break this into separate sums:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 - 2x \sum_{k=0}^{n} k + (x^2 + y^2) \sum_{k=0}^{n} 1
$$

Use standard summation formulas:

- $ \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} $
- $ \sum_{k=0}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} $
- $ \sum_{k=0}^{n} 1 = n + 1 $

Substitute these into the expression:

$$
\text{LHS} = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - 2x \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (x^2 + y^2)(n + 1)
$$

Simplify:

$$
\text{LHS} = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - x n(n+1) + (x^2 + y^2)(n + 1)
$$

---

### **Step 4: Compute the Right-Hand Side (RHS)**

Now compute $ \sum_{k=0}^{n} |B_0B_k|^2 $. Since $ B_0 = (0, 0) $ and $ B_k = (k, 0) $, we have:

$$
|B_0B_k|^2 = k^2
$$

So the sum is:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}
$$

---

### **Step 5: Compare LHS and RHS**

We now subtract the RHS from the LHS:

$$
\text{LHS} - \text{RHS} = -x n(n+1) + (x^2 + y^2)(n + 1)
$$

Factor out $ n + 1 $:

$$
(n + 1)(-x n + x^2 + y^2)
$$

From equation (1), we know that $ x^2 - nx + y^2 = 0 $, so the expression becomes:

$$
(n + 1)(0) = 0
$$

Thus, $ \text{LHS} = \text{RHS} $, and the identity is proven.

---

### **Conclusion**

By placing the points on a coordinate system, using the geometric condition of a right angle to derive a constraint on the coordinates of point $ A $, and computing both sides of the identity using standard summation formulas, we have shown that:

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
$$

This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem:
A line segment \( B_{0} B_{n} \) is divided into \( n \) equal parts at points \( B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n-1} \) and \( A \) is a point such that \( \angle B_{0} A B_{n} \) is a right angle. Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
\]
solution:
We work in the Euclidean plane using vectors and the dot‐product.  Label the points so that \(B_{0}\) is the origin \(O\), and let
\[
\mathbf u \;=\;\overrightarrow{B_{0}B_{1}}.
\]
Since the points \(B_{0},B_{1},\dots,B_{n}\) divide the segment \(B_{0}B_{n}\) into \(n\) equal parts, we have
\[
B_{k}\;=\;k\,\mathbf u,\quad k=0,1,\dots,n,
\]
and in particular
\[
B_{n}=n\,\mathbf u.
\]
Let \(\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{O A}\) be the position vector of \(A\).  The condition that \(\angle B_{0}A B_{n}\) is a right angle is equivalent to the perpendicularity of the vectors \(\overrightarrow{AB_{0}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AB_{n}}\).  In vector form,
\[
\overrightarrow{AB_{0}}\;\cdot\;\overrightarrow{AB_{n}}
\;=\;{\bf0}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\,O - A\bigr)\,\cdot\bigl(B_{n}-A\bigr)=0.
\]
Since \(O-A=-\mathbf a\) and \(B_{n}-A=n\,\mathbf u-\mathbf a\), this gives
\[
(-\mathbf a)\cdot\bigl(n\,\mathbf u-\mathbf a\bigr)\;=\;0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
-\;n\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)\;+\;\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a\;=\;0,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;=\;
n\;(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u).
\tag{1}
\]

We must show
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|A B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
\;=\;
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|B_{0}B_{k}\bigr|^{2}.
\]
Observe first that
\[
\bigl|AB_{k}\bigr|^{2}
\;=\;
\bigl|\mathbf a - k\,\mathbf u\bigr|^{2}
\;=\;
(\mathbf a - k\,\mathbf u)\,\cdot(\mathbf a - k\,\mathbf u)
\;=\;
\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;-\;2k\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)
\;+\;k^{2}\,(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u).
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|AB_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\Bigl[
\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;-\;2k\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)
\;+\;k^{2}\,(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u)
\Bigr].
\]
We split this sum term‐by‐term.  Since there are \((n+1)\) values of \(k\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
=
(n+1)\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a,
\]
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}2k\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)
=
2(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)\sum_{k=0}^{n}k
=
2(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)\;\frac{n(n+1)}2
=
n(n+1)\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u),
\]
and
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u)
=
(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u)\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|AB_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
(n+1)\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;-\;n(n+1)\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)
\;+\;(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u)\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

On the other hand, since \(B_{k}=k\,\mathbf u\),
\[
\bigl|B_{0}B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
|k\,\mathbf u|^{2}
=
k^{2}\,(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u),
\]
so
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|B_{0}B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u)\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}.
\tag{3}
\]

Subtracting \((3)\) from \((2)\) gives
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|AB_{k}\bigr|^{2}
\;-\;
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|B_{0}B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
(n+1)\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;-\;
n(n+1)\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u).
\]
Factor out \((n+1)\):
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|AB_{k}\bigr|^{2}
\;-\;
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|B_{0}B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
(n+1)\Bigl[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a
\;-\;n\,(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)\Bigr].
\]
But by the perpendicularity condition \((1)\), \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a-n(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf u)=0\).  Hence the right‐hand side vanishes, and we conclude
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|A B_{k}\bigr|^{2}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl|B_{0} B_{k}\bigr|^{2},
\]
as required.
author: llm

problem:
A line segment \( B_{0} B_{n} \) is divided into \( n \) equal parts at points \( B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n-1} \) and \( A \) is a point such that \( \angle B_{0} A B_{n} \) is a right angle. Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
\]
solution:
Step 1.  A convenient coordinate system.  
Because only ratios of lengths matter, we may place the figure in a Cartesian plane in such a way that  
B₀ is the origin O=(0,0) and Bₙ lies on the positive x–axis.  
Choose the scale so that the distance between two consecutive division points equals 1; then

 B₀=(0,0), Bₙ=(n,0), and B_k=(k,0) for k=0,1,…,n.

Let the unknown point A have coordinates A=(x,y).

Step 2.  The right–angle condition.  
The vectors  

 \(\overrightarrow{AB_0}=(-x,-y)\) and \(\overrightarrow{AB_n}= (\,n-x,\,-y)\)

are perpendicular, so their dot product is zero:

\[
(-x)(\,n-x) + (-y)(-y)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x\,(n-x)=y^{2}. \tag{1}
\]

Step 3.  The required sum on the left–hand side.  
For every k,

\[
|AB_k|^{2}=(x-k)^{2}+y^{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|AB_k|^{2}
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl[(x-k)^{2}+y^{2}\bigr] \\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(x-k)^{2} + (n+1)y^{2}. \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

Expand the first sum:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{n}(x-k)^{2}
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\bigl(k^{2}-2kx+x^{2}\bigr) \\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}-2x\sum_{k=0}^{n}k +(n+1)x^{2}. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

The well–known formulas 

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2},
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}
\]

give

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}(x-k)^{2}
      =\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - x\,n(n+1) + (n+1)x^{2}. \tag{4}
\]

Insert (4) into (2):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|AB_k|^{2}
      =\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}
        - x\,n(n+1)
        + (n+1)(x^{2}+y^{2}). \tag{5}
\]

Factor \(n+1\):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|AB_k|^{2}
      =\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}
        +(n+1)\bigl(x^{2}+y^{2}-nx\bigr). \tag{6}
\]

Step 4.  Using the right–angle condition.  
Because of (1),

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=x^{2}+x(n-x)=nx,
\]

so the bracket in (6) vanishes:

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}-nx=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|AB_k|^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}. \tag{7}
\]

Step 5.  The sum on the right–hand side.  
For every k,  \(|B_0B_k|=k\); hence

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|B_0B_k|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^{2}
                         =\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}. \tag{8}
\]

Step 6.  Equality of the two sums.  
Comparing (7) and (8) we obtain

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}|AB_k|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}|B_0B_k|^{2}.
\]

Step 7.  Removing the special scaling.  
If the original segment \(B_0B_n\) has any length L (not necessarily n), every distance used above is multiplied by the common factor \(L/n\).  Both sums are then multiplied by the same factor \((L/n)^2\), so the equality remains true.

Thus, for every right–angled configuration described in the statement,

\[
\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\! |AB_{k}|^{2}
       =\sum_{k=0}^{n}\! |B_{0}B_{k}|^{2}.
\]
author: llm

problem:
A line segment \( B_{0} B_{n} \) is divided into \( n \) equal parts at points \( B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n-1} \) and \( A \) is a point such that \( \angle B_{0} A B_{n} \) is a right angle. Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left|B_{0} B_{k}\right|^{2}
\]
solution:
To prove that for a line segment \(B_0 B_n\) divided into \(n\) equal parts at points \(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_{n-1}\) and a point \(A\) such that \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\), the equality

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{n} |B_0 B_k|^2
\]

holds, we use coordinate geometry.

Place point \(A\) at the origin \((0, 0)\) in the coordinate plane. Since \(\angle B_0 A B_n = 90^\circ\), the vectors \(\overrightarrow{A B_0}\) and \(\overrightarrow{A B_n}\) are perpendicular, so their dot product is zero. Let the coordinates of \(B_0\) be \((x_0, y_0)\) and \(B_n\) be \((x_n, y_n)\). Then,

\[
x_0 x_n + y_0 y_n = 0.
\]

The points \(B_k\) for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, n\) divide the segment \(B_0 B_n\) into \(n\) equal parts. The position vector of \(B_k\) is given by

\[
\overrightarrow{A B_k} = \overrightarrow{A B_0} + \frac{k}{n} (\overrightarrow{A B_n} - \overrightarrow{A B_0}).
\]

Thus, the coordinates of \(B_k\) are

\[
\left( x_0 + \frac{k}{n} (x_n - x_0), \, y_0 + \frac{k}{n} (y_n - y_0) \right).
\]

Define \(dx = x_n - x_0\) and \(dy = y_n - y_0\). Then the squared distance \(|A B_k|^2\) is

\[
|A B_k|^2 = \left( x_0 + \frac{k}{n} dx \right)^2 + \left( y_0 + \frac{k}{n} dy \right)^2.
\]

The sum \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2\) is

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left[ \left( x_0 + \frac{k}{n} dx \right)^2 + \left( y_0 + \frac{k}{n} dy \right)^2 \right] = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( x_0 + \frac{k}{n} dx \right)^2 + \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( y_0 + \frac{k}{n} dy \right)^2.
\]

Consider the sum \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} (a + b k)^2\) for constants \(a\) and \(b\):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} (a + b k)^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (a^2 + 2 a b k + b^2 k^2) = (n+1) a^2 + 2 a b \sum_{k=0}^{n} k + b^2 \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2.
\]

The sums are

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} (a + b k)^2 = (n+1) a^2 + 2 a b \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + b^2 \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = (n+1) a^2 + a b n (n+1) + b^2 \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}.
\]

For the \(x\)-part, set \(a = x_0\) and \(b = \frac{dx}{n}\):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( x_0 + \frac{k}{n} dx \right)^2 = (n+1) x_0^2 + x_0 \cdot \frac{dx}{n} \cdot n (n+1) + \left( \frac{dx}{n} \right)^2 \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = (n+1) \left( x_0^2 + x_0 dx + \frac{dx^2 (2n+1)}{6 n} \right).
\]

Similarly, for the \(y\)-part, set \(a = y_0\) and \(b = \frac{dy}{n}\):

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( y_0 + \frac{k}{n} dy \right)^2 = (n+1) \left( y_0^2 + y_0 dy + \frac{dy^2 (2n+1)}{6 n} \right).
\]

Adding these together,

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2 = (n+1) \left[ x_0^2 + x_0 dx + \frac{dx^2 (2n+1)}{6 n} + y_0^2 + y_0 dy + \frac{dy^2 (2n+1)}{6 n} \right] = (n+1) \left[ (x_0^2 + y_0^2) + (x_0 dx + y_0 dy) + \frac{2n+1}{6 n} (dx^2 + dy^2) \right].
\]

From the perpendicularity condition, \(x_0 x_n + y_0 y_n = 0\), and substituting \(x_n = x_0 + dx\), \(y_n = y_0 + dy\),

\[
x_0 (x_0 + dx) + y_0 (y_0 + dy) = x_0^2 + x_0 dx + y_0^2 + y_0 dy = 0.
\]

Thus, \(x_0^2 + y_0^2 + x_0 dx + y_0 dy = 0\), so

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2 = (n+1) \left[ 0 + \frac{2n+1}{6 n} (dx^2 + dy^2) \right] = (n+1) \frac{2n+1}{6 n} (dx^2 + dy^2).
\]

Now, \(dx^2 + dy^2 = (x_n - x_0)^2 + (y_n - y_0)^2 = |B_n - B_0|^2\), the squared distance between \(B_0\) and \(B_n\).

For the right-hand side, \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} |B_0 B_k|^2\), note that \(|B_0 B_k| = \frac{k}{n} |B_0 B_n|\) since the points are equally spaced. Thus,

\[
|B_0 B_k|^2 = \left( \frac{k}{n} \right)^2 |B_0 B_n|^2 = \left( \frac{k}{n} \right)^2 (dx^2 + dy^2).
\]

Summing over \(k\),

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n} |B_0 B_k|^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( \frac{k}{n} \right)^2 (dx^2 + dy^2) = \frac{dx^2 + dy^2}{n^2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} k^2 = \frac{dx^2 + dy^2}{n^2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = (dx^2 + dy^2) \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6 n}.
\]

This matches the expression for \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} |A B_k|^2\). Therefore, the equality holds.

problem: Mary and Pat play the following number game. Mary picks an initial integer greater than 2017. She then multiplies this number by \(2017\) and adds \(2\) to the result. Pat will add \(2019\) to this new number and it will again be Mary's turn. Both players will continue to take alternating turns. Mary will always multiply the current number by \(2017\) and add \(2\) to the result when it is her turn. Pat will always add \(2019\) to the current number when it is his turn. Pat wins if one of the numbers obtained is divisible by \(2018\). Mary wants to prevent Pat from winning the game. Determine, with proof, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose in order to achieve this.
solution:
Let  

a₀  (> 2017)  be the integer chosen by Mary, and for every non–negative integer n let aₙ be the number that is on the board after the n-th move of the game (Mary makes moves 1,3,5,… , Pat makes moves 2,4,6,…).

The rules give the following recursions  

(Mary’s move)     a_{2k+1}=2017·a_{2k}+2,  
(Pat’s  move)     a_{2k+2}=a_{2k+1}+2019.                                       (1)

Pat wins as soon as some aₙ is divisible by 2018.  
Consequently only the remainders of the aₙ modulo 2018 matter.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The game modulo 2018
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Write rₙ for the remainder of aₙ upon division by 2018, i.e. rₙ≡aₙ (mod 2018) and 0≤rₙ≤2017.

Because  
2017≡−1 (mod 2018) and 2019≡ 1 (mod 2018),

relations (1) become

(Mary)     r_{2k+1}≡−r_{2k}+2   (mod 2018),  
(Pat)      r_{2k+2}≡ r_{2k+1}+1  (mod 2018).                                   (2)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  One full round (Mary followed by Pat)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let C be the combined operation “Mary then Pat’’ acting on a remainder x:

C(x) ≡ ( (−x+2) + 1 ) ≡ −x+3    (mod 2018).                                  (3)

Applying C twice gives

C(C(x)) ≡ −(−x+3)+3 ≡ x   (mod 2018).                                        (4)

Thus C has order 2 modulo 2018, i.e. two complete rounds (four single moves) bring the remainder back to its initial value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The four remainders that can ever occur
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Starting from the initial remainder r₀, the successive remainders are

r₀,                                      (initial position)
r₁ = −r₀+2,  
r₂ = −r₀+3,  
r₃ =  r₀−1,  
r₄ = r₀  (=r₀ again, by (4)), and the pattern now repeats.                   (5)

Hence the only remainders that can ever appear are

  r₀, 2−r₀, 3−r₀, r₀−1      (all taken modulo 2018).                     (6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  When does Pat win?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Pat wins iff one of the four numbers in (6) is 0 modulo 2018.  
This happens precisely when

r₀ ≡ 0, or r₀ ≡ 1, or r₀ ≡ 2, or r₀ ≡ 3  (mod 2018).                     (7)

Indeed
• r₀≡0    trivially makes a₀ a multiple of 2018;  
• r₀≡1    gives r₃ = r₀−1 ≡0;  
• r₀≡2    gives r₁ = 2−r₀ ≡0;  
• r₀≡3    gives r₂ = 3−r₀ ≡0.

Conversely, if r₀ is not in {0,1,2,3}, then none of the four numbers in (6) is 0, so the sequence of remainders never reaches 0 and Pat can never win.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  The smallest safe starting integer
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Mary needs a₀>2017 with remainder r₀∉{0,1,2,3}.

List the first integers larger than 2017 and their remainders:

2018 ≡0, 2019 ≡1, 2020 ≡2, 2021 ≡3, 2022 ≡4.

The first remainder outside {0,1,2,3} is 4, attained by the integer 2022.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Verification
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Start with a₀ = 2022 (r₀=4):

• After Mary a₁ = 2017·2022+2,   r₁ = −4+2 = 2016 ≠0;  
• After Pat   a₂ = a₁+2019,      r₂ = 2016+1 = 2017 ≠0;  
• After Mary  a₃:                r₃ = 4−1 = 3 ≠0;  
• After Pat   a₄:                r₄ = 4 (back to the start).

Thus the multiples of 2018 never appear, and by Section 4 this will remain true forever.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Pat wins if and only if Mary’s initial number is congruent to 0, 1, 2 or 3 modulo 2018.  
The smallest integer greater than 2017 that avoids those four residues is 2022.

Therefore the least starting integer that allows Mary to prevent Pat from ever winning is

  boxed {\,2022\,}.
author: llm

problem: Mary and Pat play the following number game. Mary picks an initial integer greater than 2017. She then multiplies this number by \(2017\) and adds \(2\) to the result. Pat will add \(2019\) to this new number and it will again be Mary's turn. Both players will continue to take alternating turns. Mary will always multiply the current number by \(2017\) and add \(2\) to the result when it is her turn. Pat will always add \(2019\) to the current number when it is his turn. Pat wins if one of the numbers obtained is divisible by \(2018\). Mary wants to prevent Pat from winning the game. Determine, with proof, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose in order to achieve this.
solution:
Let Mary’s initial integer be \(a_{0}>2017\), and define the sequence of “current numbers” \(\bigl(a_{k}\bigr)_{k\ge0}\) by the rules

1.  On Mary’s turn (when \(k\) is even),  
    \[
       a_{k+1} \;=\; 2017\,a_{k} \;+\;2.
    \]
2.  On Pat’s turn (when \(k\) is odd),  
    \[
       a_{k+1} \;=\; a_{k} \;+\;2019.
    \]

Pat wins as soon as one of the \(a_{k}\) is divisible by \(2018\).  Mary’s goal is to choose \(a_{0}\) so that no \(a_{k}\) ever satisfies
\[
   a_{k}\;\equiv\;0\pmod{2018}.
\]

---

Step 1.  Pass to residues mod 2018.  
Define
\[
   x_{k}\;=\;a_{k}\bmod2018,
\]
so \(0\le x_k\le2017\), and Pat wins exactly if some \(x_k=0\).  We compute the recurrence for \(x_k\).

Since on Mary’s move
\[
   a_{k+1}=2017\,a_{k}+2,
\]
we have
\[
   x_{k+1}
   \;=\;
   2017\,x_{k}+2
   \;\bmod2018.
\]
On Pat’s move
\[
   a_{k+1}=a_{k}+2019,
\]
so
\[
   x_{k+1}
   \;=\;
   x_{k}+2019
   \;\bmod2018
   \;=\;
   x_{k}+1
   \;\bmod2018,
\]
because \(2019\equiv1\pmod{2018}\).

Moreover
\[
   2017\equiv -1\pmod{2018},
\]
so the two rules become, for all \(n\ge0\),
\[
   x_{2n+1}\;\equiv\;2017\,x_{2n}+2\;\equiv\;-x_{2n}+2,
   \quad
   x_{2n+2}\;\equiv\;x_{2n+1}+1.
\]
In particular, starting from \(x_{0}\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
   x_{1}&\equiv -\,x_{0}+2,\\
   x_{2}&\equiv x_{1}+1\;\equiv\;(-\,x_{0}+2)+1
                  \;=\;-\,x_{0}+3,\\
   x_{3}&\equiv -\,x_{2}+2
           \;=\;-\,(-\,x_{0}+3)+2
           \;=\;x_{0}-3+2
           \;=\;x_{0}-1,\\
   x_{4}&\equiv x_{3}+1
           \;=\;(x_{0}-1)+1
           \;=\;x_{0}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the sequence of residues mod 2018 is periodic of period 4, and its four distinct values are
\[
   x_{0},\quad
   -\,x_{0}+2,\quad
   -\,x_{0}+3,\quad
   x_{0}-1,
\]
repeating in that order.  

---

Step 2.  Preventing \(x_{k}=0\).  
For Pat never to see a multiple of 2018, none of these four residues may be \(\equiv0\pmod{2018}\).  Thus we require simultaneously
\[
\begin{aligned}
   &x_{0}\not\equiv0,\\
   &-\,x_{0}+2\not\equiv0
     \;\Longrightarrow\;
     x_{0}\not\equiv2,\\
   &-\,x_{0}+3\not\equiv0
     \;\Longrightarrow\;
     x_{0}\not\equiv3,\\
   &x_{0}-1\not\equiv0
     \;\Longrightarrow\;
     x_{0}\not\equiv1,
\end{aligned}
\]
all taken mod 2018.  In other words,
\[
   x_{0}\;\bmod2018
   \;\notin\;
   \{0,1,2,3\}.
\]

---

Step 3.  Choosing the smallest \(a_{0}>2017\).  
Since \(a_{0}>2017\), its residue \(x_{0}=a_{0}\bmod2018\) cannot itself represent a number \(\ge2018\).  Thus \(x_{0}\) lies in \(\{0,1,\dots,2017\}\).  To satisfy \(x_{0}\notin\{0,1,2,3\}\), we need
\[
   x_{0}\in\{4,5,\dots,2017\}.
\]
The smallest integer \(a_{0}>2017\) with residue \(x_{0}=4\) is
\[
   a_{0}=2018\cdot1 +4 = 2022.
\]
For that choice one checks immediately that
\[
   x_{0}=4,\;
   x_{1}=(-4+2)\bmod2018=2016,\;
   x_{2}=2017,\;
   x_{3}=3,
\]
and then \(x_{4}=4\) again, and so on; none of these is \(0\).  Hence Pat never wins.

We conclude that the minimal initial integer Mary can choose is
\[
   2022.
\]
author: llm

problem: Mary and Pat play the following number game. Mary picks an initial integer greater than 2017. She then multiplies this number by \(2017\) and adds \(2\) to the result. Pat will add \(2019\) to this new number and it will again be Mary's turn. Both players will continue to take alternating turns. Mary will always multiply the current number by \(2017\) and add \(2\) to the result when it is her turn. Pat will always add \(2019\) to the current number when it is his turn. Pat wins if one of the numbers obtained is divisible by \(2018\). Mary wants to prevent Pat from winning the game. Determine, with proof, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose in order to achieve this.
solution:
The game proceeds with Mary multiplying the current number by 2017 and adding 2, and Pat adding 2019, with alternating turns starting with Mary's move on the initial number \(N\).

Consider the sequence of numbers obtained after each move, modulo 2018. The winning condition for Pat is that any number in this sequence is congruent to 0 modulo 2018. The operations modulo 2018 simplify as follows:  
- Mary's move: \(x \to 2017x + 2 \equiv -x + 2 \pmod{2018}\) (since \(2017 \equiv -1 \pmod{2018}\)),  
- Pat's move: \(x \to x + 2019 \equiv x + 1 \pmod{2018}\) (since \(2019 \equiv 1 \pmod{2018}\)).  

Let \(S_1\) be the first number after Mary's move on \(N\), so \(S_1 = 2017N + 2 \equiv -N + 2 \pmod{2018}\). The subsequent numbers are:  
- \(S_2 = S_1 + 1 \equiv (-N + 2) + 1 = -N + 3 \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(S_3 = -S_2 + 2 \equiv -(-N + 3) + 2 = N - 1 \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(S_4 = S_3 + 1 \equiv (N - 1) + 1 = N \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(S_5 = -S_4 + 2 \equiv -N + 2 \pmod{2018}\), which is equal to \(S_1\).  

Thus, the sequence modulo 2018 is periodic with period 4, and the values are congruent to \(-N + 2\), \(-N + 3\), \(N - 1\), and \(N\) modulo 2018, repeating indefinitely.

For Pat not to win, none of these values should be congruent to 0 modulo 2018:  
- \(N \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(N - 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N \not\equiv 1 \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(-N + 2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N \not\equiv 2 \pmod{2018}\),  
- \(-N + 3 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N \not\equiv 3 \pmod{2018}\).  

Therefore, \(N\) must not be congruent to 0, 1, 2, or 3 modulo 2018. Since \(N > 2017\), the smallest integer \(N \geq 2018\). Checking the residues modulo 2018:  
- \(2018 \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}\), forbidden,  
- \(2019 \equiv 1 \pmod{2018}\), forbidden,  
- \(2020 \equiv 2 \pmod{2018}\), forbidden,  
- \(2021 \equiv 3 \pmod{2018}\), forbidden,  
- \(2022 \equiv 4 \pmod{2018}\), not forbidden.  

For \(N = 2022\), the sequence modulo 2018 is:  
- \(S_1 \equiv -4 + 2 = -2 \equiv 2016 \pmod{2018}\), not 0,  
- \(S_2 \equiv -4 + 3 = -1 \equiv 2017 \pmod{2018}\), not 0,  
- \(S_3 \equiv 4 - 1 = 3 \pmod{2018}\), not 0,  
- \(S_4 \equiv 4 \pmod{2018}\), not 0,  
and the cycle repeats with no value congruent to 0. Since 2022 is the smallest integer greater than 2017 not congruent to 0, 1, 2, or 3 modulo 2018, it is the smallest initial integer Mary can choose to prevent Pat from winning.
author: llm

problem: Mary and Pat play the following number game. Mary picks an initial integer greater than 2017. She then multiplies this number by \(2017\) and adds \(2\) to the result. Pat will add \(2019\) to this new number and it will again be Mary's turn. Both players will continue to take alternating turns. Mary will always multiply the current number by \(2017\) and add \(2\) to the result when it is her turn. Pat will always add \(2019\) to the current number when it is his turn. Pat wins if one of the numbers obtained is divisible by \(2018\). Mary wants to prevent Pat from winning the game. Determine, with proof, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose in order to achieve this.
solution:
We analyze the sequence of operations and their behavior modulo 2018.

---

### **Understanding the Game Mechanics**

Mary and Pat take turns applying the following operations:

- **Mary's move**: Multiply the current number by 2017 and add 2.
- **Pat's move**: Add 2019 to the current number.

Pat wins if **any** of the numbers obtained during the game is divisible by 2018. Mary wants to **prevent** this from happening.

Let’s denote the initial number chosen by Mary as $ N $. The sequence of numbers generated is:

- $ M_1 = N \cdot 2017 + 2 $
- $ P_1 = M_1 + 2019 $
- $ M_2 = P_1 \cdot 2017 + 2 $
- $ P_2 = M_2 + 2019 $
- and so on...

We are interested in whether **any** of these numbers is divisible by 2018. That is, whether any of $ M_1, P_1, M_2, P_2, \ldots $ is congruent to 0 modulo 2018.

---

### **Modulo 2018 Simplifications**

We can simplify the operations modulo 2018:

- $ 2017 \equiv -1 \mod 2018 $
- $ 2019 \equiv 1 \mod 2018 $

Thus, the operations become:

- **Mary's move**: $ x \mapsto -x + 2 \mod 2018 $
- **Pat's move**: $ x \mapsto x + 1 \mod 2018 $

Starting from $ N \mod 2018 $, the sequence of residues modulo 2018 is:

- $ M_1 \equiv -N + 2 \mod 2018 $
- $ P_1 \equiv -N + 3 \mod 2018 $
- $ M_2 \equiv N - 1 \mod 2018 $
- $ P_2 \equiv N \mod 2018 $

Then the cycle repeats: $ M_3 \equiv -N + 2 \mod 2018 $, and so on.

Thus, the sequence of residues modulo 2018 is **periodic with period 4**, and the four residues that are checked for divisibility by 2018 are:

1. $ -N + 2 $
2. $ -N + 3 $
3. $ N - 1 $
4. $ N $

We require **none** of these to be congruent to 0 modulo 2018.

---

### **Conditions for Mary to Win**

We must ensure that:

- $ -N + 2 \not\equiv 0 \mod 2018 \Rightarrow N \not\equiv 2 \mod 2018 $
- $ -N + 3 \not\equiv 0 \mod 2018 \Rightarrow N \not\equiv 3 \mod 2018 $
- $ N - 1 \not\equiv 0 \mod 2018 \Rightarrow N \not\equiv 1 \mod 2018 $
- $ N \not\equiv 0 \mod 2018 $

So, the forbidden residues for $ N \mod 2018 $ are: $ \{0, 1, 2, 3\} $

Therefore, Mary must choose $ N $ such that $ N \mod 2018 \in \{4, 5, \ldots, 2017\} $

---

### **Finding the Smallest Valid $ N > 2017 $**

We now find the **smallest** integer $ N > 2017 $ such that $ N \mod 2018 \notin \{0, 1, 2, 3\} $

- $ 2018 \equiv 0 \mod 2018 $ → forbidden
- $ 2019 \equiv 1 \mod 2018 $ → forbidden
- $ 2020 \equiv 2 \mod 2018 $ → forbidden
- $ 2021 \equiv 3 \mod 2018 $ → forbidden
- $ 2022 \equiv 4 \mod 2018 $ → **valid**

Thus, the **smallest** such $ N > 2017 $ is $ 2022 $

---

### **Verification**

Let’s verify that $ N = 2022 $ satisfies the conditions:

- $ N \equiv 4 \mod 2018 $
- $ M_1 \equiv -4 + 2 = -2 \equiv 2016 \mod 2018 \ne 0 $
- $ P_1 \equiv 2016 + 1 = 2017 \mod 2018 \ne 0 $
- $ M_2 \equiv 2017 + 2 = 2019 \equiv 1 \mod 2018 \ne 0 $
- $ P_2 \equiv 1 + 1 = 2 \mod 2018 \ne 0 $

The cycle repeats every 4 steps, and none of the residues are 0 modulo 2018. Thus, Pat never wins.

---

### **Conclusion**

The smallest integer $ N > 2017 $ that Mary can choose to prevent Pat from winning is:

$$
2022
$$

problem: Mary and Pat play the following number game. Mary picks an initial integer greater than 2017. She then multiplies this number by \(2017\) and adds \(2\) to the result. Pat will add \(2019\) to this new number and it will again be Mary's turn. Both players will continue to take alternating turns. Mary will always multiply the current number by \(2017\) and add \(2\) to the result when it is her turn. Pat will always add \(2019\) to the current number when it is his turn. Pat wins if one of the numbers obtained is divisible by \(2018\). Mary wants to prevent Pat from winning the game. Determine, with proof, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose in order to achieve this.
solution:
Let $N_0$ be the initial integer Mary picks. According to the problem statement, $N_0 > 2017$.
Let $N_k$ for $k \ge 1$ be the sequence of numbers generated by the game.
Mary's operation is $M(x) = 2017x + 2$.
Pat's operation is $P(x) = x + 2019$.

The sequence of numbers is generated as follows:
1. Mary chooses $N_0$.
2. Mary computes $N_1 = M(N_0) = 2017 N_0 + 2$.
3. Pat computes $N_2 = P(N_1) = N_1 + 2019$.
4. Mary computes $N_3 = M(N_2) = 2017 N_2 + 2$.
5. Pat computes $N_4 = P(N_3) = N_3 + 2019$.
And so on. In general, for $k \ge 0$, Mary computes $N_{2k+1} = M(N_{2k})$ (where $N_0$ is her initial choice), and for $k \ge 1$, Pat computes $N_{2k} = P(N_{2k-1})$.

Pat wins if any of the numbers $N_k$ for $k \ge 1$ is divisible by $2018$. Mary wants to choose $N_0$ such that $N_k \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$ for all $k \ge 1$.

Let's analyze the numbers modulo $2018$. Let $m = 2018$.
The coefficients and constants in the operations are:
$2017 \equiv -1 \pmod{2018}$.
$2 \equiv 2 \pmod{2018}$.
$2019 \equiv 1 \pmod{2018}$.

So, Mary's operation modulo $m$ is $M(x) \equiv -x + 2 \pmod{2018}$.
Pat's operation modulo $m$ is $P(x) \equiv x + 1 \pmod{2018}$.

Let $r_k = N_k \pmod{2018}$ for $k \ge 1$. Let $r_0 = N_0 \pmod{2018}$.
The sequence of residues modulo $2018$ is:
$r_1 = N_1 \pmod{2018} \equiv M(N_0) \pmod{2018} \equiv -N_0 + 2 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_2 = N_2 \pmod{2018} \equiv P(N_1) \pmod{2018} \equiv r_1 + 1 \pmod{2018} \equiv (-N_0 + 2) + 1 \pmod{2018} \equiv -N_0 + 3 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_3 = N_3 \pmod{2018} \equiv M(N_2) \pmod{2018} \equiv -r_2 + 2 \pmod{2018} \equiv -(-N_0 + 3) + 2 \pmod{2018} \equiv N_0 - 3 + 2 \pmod{2018} \equiv N_0 - 1 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_4 = N_4 \pmod{2018} \equiv P(N_3) \pmod{2018} \equiv r_3 + 1 \pmod{2018} \equiv (N_0 - 1) + 1 \pmod{2018} \equiv N_0 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_5 = N_5 \pmod{2018} \equiv M(N_4) \pmod{2018} \equiv -r_4 + 2 \pmod{2018} \equiv -N_0 + 2 \pmod{2018}$.

We observe that $r_5 \equiv r_1$. Since each term $r_k$ depends only on the previous term $r_{k-1}$ (or $N_0$ for $r_1$), the sequence of residues $r_k$ will be periodic.
The sequence of residues is $(r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4, r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4, \dots)$. The period is 4.
Pat wins if any of $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ are congruent to $0 \pmod{2018}$.
Mary wants to choose $N_0$ such that $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ are all non-zero modulo $2018$.
The conditions for Mary to win are:
1. $r_1 = -N_0 + 2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N_0 \not\equiv 2 \pmod{2018}$.
2. $r_2 = -N_0 + 3 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N_0 \not\equiv 3 \pmod{2018}$.
3. $r_3 = N_0 - 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018} \implies N_0 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{2018}$.
4. $r_4 = N_0 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$.

So, Mary must choose $N_0$ such that $N_0 \pmod{2018}$ is not $0, 1, 2,$ or $3$.
Mary must choose $N_0 > 2017$. We are looking for the smallest such integer $N_0$.
Let's test integers $N_0 > 2017$ in increasing order:

Case 1: $N_0 = 2018$.
$N_0 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2018 \pmod{2018} \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$.
This is one of the forbidden residues ($N_0 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$).
If Mary chooses $N_0 = 2018$, then $r_4 \equiv N_0 \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$. Thus $N_4$ will be divisible by $2018$. So Pat wins.
Thus, $N_0 = 2018$ is not a valid choice for Mary.

Case 2: $N_0 = 2019$.
$N_0 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2019 \pmod{2018} \equiv 1 \pmod{2018}$.
This is one of the forbidden residues ($N_0 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{2018}$).
If Mary chooses $N_0 = 2019$, then $r_3 \equiv N_0 - 1 \equiv 1 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$. Thus $N_3$ will be divisible by $2018$. So Pat wins.
Thus, $N_0 = 2019$ is not a valid choice for Mary.

Case 3: $N_0 = 2020$.
$N_0 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2020 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2 \pmod{2018}$.
This is one of the forbidden residues ($N_0 \not\equiv 2 \pmod{2018}$).
If Mary chooses $N_0 = 2020$, then $r_1 \equiv -N_0 + 2 \equiv -2 + 2 \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$. Thus $N_1$ will be divisible by $2018$. So Pat wins.
Thus, $N_0 = 2020$ is not a valid choice for Mary.

Case 4: $N_0 = 2021$.
$N_0 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2021 \pmod{2018} \equiv 3 \pmod{2018}$.
This is one of the forbidden residues ($N_0 \not\equiv 3 \pmod{2018}$).
If Mary chooses $N_0 = 2021$, then $r_2 \equiv -N_0 + 3 \equiv -3 + 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{2018}$. Thus $N_2$ will be divisible by $2018$. So Pat wins.
Thus, $N_0 = 2021$ is not a valid choice for Mary.

Case 5: $N_0 = 2022$.
$N_0 \pmod{2018} \equiv 2022 \pmod{2018} \equiv 4 \pmod{2018}$.
This residue $4$ is not in the set of forbidden residues $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$.
Let's verify the residues $r_k$ for $N_0 = 2022$:
$r_1 \equiv -N_0 + 2 \equiv -4 + 2 \equiv -2 \equiv 2016 \pmod{2018}$. This is not $0 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_2 \equiv -N_0 + 3 \equiv -4 + 3 \equiv -1 \equiv 2017 \pmod{2018}$. This is not $0 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_3 \equiv N_0 - 1 \equiv 4 - 1 \equiv 3 \pmod{2018}$. This is not $0 \pmod{2018}$.
$r_4 \equiv N_0 \equiv 4 \pmod{2018}$. This is not $0 \pmod{2018}$.
Since none of $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ are congruent to $0 \pmod{2018}$, and the sequence of residues $r_k$ is periodic with period 4, none of the numbers $N_k$ (for $k \ge 1$) will be divisible by $2018$.
Thus, if Mary chooses $N_0 = 2022$, Pat will not win.

We have checked the integers greater than $2017$ in increasing order: $2018, 2019, 2020, 2021$. All of these lead to Pat winning. The next integer is $2022$, and we have shown that this choice allows Mary to prevent Pat from winning.
Therefore, the smallest initial integer Mary could choose is $2022$.
author: llm

problem:
Jenny is going to attend a sports camp for 7 days. Each day, she will play exactly one of three sports: hockey, tennis, or camogie. The only restriction is that in any period of 4 consecutive days, she must play all three sports.

Find, with proof, the number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week.
solution:
We are given the constraint that **in any 4 consecutive days**, she must play **all three sports**: hockey (H), tennis (T), and camogie (C). This means that each 4-day window must contain **at least one day of each sport**.

---

### **Understanding the Problem**

We are to count the number of sequences of length 7 over the alphabet {H, T, C}, such that **every 4-day block** (i.e., days 1–4, 2–5, 3–6, and 4–7) contains **all three sports**.

This is a **combinatorics with constraints** problem, and the key is to model the transitions between days while ensuring the constraint is satisfied.

---

### **Modeling the Problem with Recurrence**

We define a **dynamic programming** approach based on the last three days of the schedule. This is because the constraint involves **4-day windows**, and to validate a new window (e.g., days $ k-3 $ to $ k $), we need to know the sports played on the previous three days.

We define three types of states based on the last three days:

- **Aₙ**: Number of sequences of length $ n $ ending with a **Type A** triplet (i.e., all three sports are present).
- **Fₙ**: Number of sequences ending with a **Type B** triplet where the **first element** is the **unique** sport.
- **Sₙ**: Number of sequences ending with a **Type B** triplet where the **unique** sport is in the **second or third** position.

These types are sufficient to capture all valid sequences of length $ n $, as **Type C** (all same sport) is **invalid** due to the 4-day constraint.

---

### **Recurrence Relations**

From the structure of the transitions and the constraints, we derive the following recurrence relations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{n+1} &= A_n + S_n \\
F_{n+1} &= A_n \\
S_{n+1} &= A_n + F_n
\end{aligned}
$$

These relations are derived from analyzing how each state can transition to the next by appending a new sport, while ensuring the 4-day constraint is maintained.

---

### **Initial Conditions (n = 3)**

At day 3, we can compute the initial values:

- **Type A** triplets: All permutations of H, T, C → $ 3! = 6 $
- **Type B** triplets:
  - For each pair of sports (3 pairs), and each of the two sports being the unique one (2 choices), and 3 arrangements (1 with the unique in front, 2 with it in the middle or end), we get:
    - 6 Type F (unique in front)
    - 12 Type S (unique in middle or end)

So:

$$
A_3 = 6,\quad F_3 = 6,\quad S_3 = 12
$$

---

### **Computing the Values Step-by-Step**

Using the recurrence relations and the initial values, we compute the values up to $ n = 7 $:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_4 &= A_3 + S_3 = 6 + 12 = 18 \\
F_4 &= A_3 = 6 \\
S_4 &= A_3 + F_3 = 6 + 6 = 12 \\
\text{Total}_4 &= 18 + 6 + 12 = 36 \\
\\
A_5 &= A_4 + S_4 = 18 + 12 = 30 \\
F_5 &= A_4 = 18 \\
S_5 &= A_4 + F_4 = 18 + 6 = 24 \\
\text{Total}_5 &= 30 + 18 + 24 = 72 \\
\\
A_6 &= A_5 + S_5 = 30 + 24 = 54 \\
F_6 &= A_5 = 30 \\
S_6 &= A_5 + F_5 = 30 + 18 = 48 \\
\text{Total}_6 &= 54 + 30 + 48 = 132 \\
\\
A_7 &= A_6 + S_6 = 54 + 48 = 102 \\
F_7 &= A_6 = 54 \\
S_7 &= A_6 + F_6 = 54 + 30 = 84 \\
\text{Total}_7 &= 102 + 54 + 84 = 240 \\
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

After computing the values step-by-step and verifying the recurrence logic, we find that the total number of valid sports schedules for Jenny's 7-day camp, satisfying the 4-day constraint, is:

$$
240
$$

problem:
Jenny is going to attend a sports camp for 7 days. Each day, she will play exactly one of three sports: hockey, tennis, or camogie. The only restriction is that in any period of 4 consecutive days, she must play all three sports.

Find, with proof, the number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week.
solution:
Let the three sports be denoted by H, T, C. Let $S_i$ be the sport Jenny plays on day $i$. The sequence of sports is $S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4, S_5, S_6, S_7$.
The condition is that for any $k \in \{1,2,3,4\}$, the set of sports $\{S_k, S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}\}$ must be equal to $\{H,T,C\}$. This means that in any four consecutive days, all three sports must be played. Since there are 4 days, exactly one sport must be repeated in such a period.

Let's analyze the relationship between $S_k, S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}$ and $S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}, S_{k+4}$.
Let $A_k = \{S_k, S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}\}$ and $A_{k+1} = \{S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}, S_{k+4}\}$.
We are given $A_k = \{H,T,C\}$ and $A_{k+1} = \{H,T,C\}$.
Let $M_k = \{S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}\}$ be the set of sports played on days $k+1, k+2, k+3$.
Then $A_k = \{S_k\} \cup M_k = \{H,T,C\}$ and $A_{k+1} = M_k \cup \{S_{k+4}\} = \{H,T,C\}$.

We can distinguish two cases for $M_k$:
Case 1: $M_k = \{H,T,C\}$. This means $S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}$ are all distinct, e.g., $(H,T,C)$ in some order.
Since $A_k = \{S_k\} \cup M_k = \{H,T,C\}$ and $M_k$ already contains all three sports, $S_k$ must be one of the sports in $M_k$. That is, $S_k \in \{S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}\}$. This is required because $A_k$ must have one sport repeated. Similarly, $S_{k+4} \in \{S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}\}$.
So, if $S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}$ are distinct, $S_k$ must be one of them, and $S_{k+4}$ must be one of them. There are 3 choices for $S_k$ and 3 choices for $S_{k+4}$.

Case 2: $M_k$ consists of exactly two distinct sports (e.g., $\{H,T\}$). This means $S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}$ are not all distinct, for example $(H,H,T)$, $(H,T,H)$, or $(H,T,T)$.
Since $A_k = \{S_k\} \cup M_k = \{H,T,C\}$, $S_k$ must be the third sport not in $M_k$. For example, if $M_k=\{H,T\}$, then $S_k=C$.
Similarly, since $A_{k+1} = M_k \cup \{S_{k+4}\} = \{H,T,C\}$, $S_{k+4}$ must be the third sport not in $M_k$. So $S_{k+4}=C$.
Thus, if $S_{k+1}, S_{k+2}, S_{k+3}$ use only two distinct sports, then $S_k$ and $S_{k+4}$ must both be the third distinct sport. This implies $S_k = S_{k+4}$.

This pair of rules governs how the sequence can be constructed. We need to determine $S_1, \dots, S_7$.
The above rules relate $S_k$ and $S_{k+4}$ for $k=1,2,3$.
$k=1$: $(S_1,S_5)$ are related based on $(S_2,S_3,S_4)$.
$k=2$: $(S_2,S_6)$ are related based on $(S_3,S_4,S_5)$.
$k=3$: $(S_3,S_7)$ are related based on $(S_4,S_5,S_6)$.

We first choose $S_1, S_2, S_3$. These three sports cannot all be the same. If $S_1=S_2=S_3=X$, then $\{S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4\} = \{X,X,X,S_4\}$. For this set to be $\{H,T,C\}$, $S_4$ would need to be two distinct sports, which is impossible.
So $S_1,S_2,S_3$ must comprise either two or three distinct sports.

Let's denote $X,Y,Z$ as distinct sports from $\{H,T,C\}$.
Part I: $S_1,S_2,S_3$ are distinct (e.g., $(H,T,C)$). There are $3! = 6$ ways to assign $X,Y,Z$ to $S_1,S_2,S_3$.
Let $(S_1,S_2,S_3)=(X,Y,Z)$.
For $A_1 = \{S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4\} = \{X,Y,Z,S_4\}$ to be $\{H,T,C\}$, $S_4$ must be $X, Y,$ or $Z$.
Subcase I.A: $S_4=X$. (e.g., $H,T,C,H$). (1 choice for $S_4$ for fixed $X,Y,Z$).
  The triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(Y,Z,X)$ consists of 3 distinct sports. By Case 1, $S_1=X \in \{Y,Z,X\}$ (consistent) and $S_5 \in \{Y,Z,X\}$ (3 choices for $S_5$).
  1. $S_5=Y$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Y)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Z,X,Y)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_2=Y \in \{Z,X,Y\}$ (consistent) and $S_6 \in \{Z,X,Y\}$ (3 choices for $S_6$).
     a. $S_6=Z$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Y,Z)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(X,Y,Z)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_3=Z \in \{X,Y,Z\}$ (consistent) and $S_7 \in \{X,Y,Z\}$ (3 choices for $S_7$). This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 3 = 18$ schedules. (e.g. $H,T,C,H,T,C, (H/T/C)$)
     b. $S_6=X$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Y,X)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(X,Y,X)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Y\}$. By Case 2, $S_3=Z$ (consistent, $Z$ is the third sport) and $S_7=Z$ (1 choice for $S_7$). This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 6$ schedules. (e.g. $H,T,C,H,T,H,C$)
     c. $S_6=Y$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Y,Y)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(X,Y,Y)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Y\}$. By Case 2, $S_3=Z$ (consistent) and $S_7=Z$ (1 choice for $S_7$). This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 6$ schedules. (e.g. $H,T,C,H,T,T,C$)
     Total for $S_5=Y$: $18+6+6=30$ schedules.
  2. $S_5=Z$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Z)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Z,X,Z)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_2=Y$ (consistent) and $S_6=Y$ (1 choice for $S_6$).
     Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,Z,Y)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(X,Z,Y)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_3=Z \in \{X,Z,Y\}$ (consistent) and $S_7 \in \{X,Z,Y\}$ (3 choices for $S_7$). This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 3 = 18$ schedules.
  3. $S_5=X$. Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,X)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Z,X,X)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_2=Y$ (consistent) and $S_6=Y$ (1 choice for $S_6$).
     Sequence $(X,Y,Z,X,X,Y)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(X,X,Y)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Y\}$. By Case 2, $S_3=Z$ (consistent) and $S_7=Z$ (1 choice for $S_7$). This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 = 6$ schedules.
  Total for Subcase I.A ($S_1,S_2,S_3$ distinct, $S_4=S_1$): $30+18+6 = 54$ schedules.

Subcase I.B: $S_4=Y$. (e.g., $H,T,C,T$).
  Triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(Y,Z,Y)$ uses 2 sports $\{Y,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_1=X$ (consistent) and $S_5=X$ (1 choice for $S_5$).
  Sequence $(X,Y,Z,Y,X)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Z,Y,X)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_2=Y \in \{Z,Y,X\}$ (consistent) and $S_6 \in \{Z,Y,X\}$ (3 choices for $S_6$).
  This situation ($S_3,S_4,S_5$ distinct, $S_2, S_6$ related) is analogous to $S_2,S_3,S_4$ distinct and $S_1,S_5$ related in Subcase I.A. Thus, it also yields $(1 \times (3+1+1)) = 5$ branching factor for $S_6,S_7$.
  So, this gives $6 \times 1 \times (1 \times 1 \times 3 + 1 \times 1 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 \times 1) = 6 \times 5 = 30$ schedules.

Subcase I.C: $S_4=Z$. (e.g., $H,T,C,C$).
  Triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(Y,Z,Z)$ uses 2 sports $\{Y,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_1=X$ (consistent) and $S_5=X$ (1 choice for $S_5$).
  Sequence $(X,Y,Z,Z,X)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Z,Z,X)$ uses 2 sports $\{X,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_2=Y$ (consistent) and $S_6=Y$ (1 choice for $S_6$).
  Sequence $(X,Y,Z,Z,X,Y)$. Triplet $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=(Z,X,Y)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_3=Z \in \{Z,X,Y\}$ (consistent) and $S_7 \in \{Z,X,Y\}$ (3 choices for $S_7$).
  This gives $6 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 3 = 18$ schedules.

Total for Part I ($S_1,S_2,S_3$ distinct): $54 + 30 + 18 = 102$ schedules.

Part II: $S_1,S_2,S_3$ use exactly two distinct sports. There are $3 \times 2 \times 3 = 18$ such initial triplets. (Choose 2 sports $X,Y$: 3 ways. Choose which is repeated: 2 ways. Choose position for non-repeated sport: 3 ways. $3 \times 2 \times 1 \times 3=18$). Or, (Choose X (repeated): 3 ways. Choose Y (non-repeated): 2 ways. Choose position of Y (3 pos): $3 \times 2 \times 3=18$). These are of 3 forms:
  - $X,X,Y$: 6 ways (e.g. $H,H,T$)
  - $X,Y,X$: 6 ways (e.g. $H,T,H$)
  - $X,Y,Y$: 6 ways (e.g. $H,T,T$)
For any of these, say $(S_1,S_2,S_3)=(X,X,Y)$, the set $\{S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4\}=\{X,X,Y,S_4\}$ must be $\{X,Y,Z\}$. Thus $S_4$ must be $Z$ (1 choice).

Subcase II.A: $(S_1,S_2,S_3)=(X,X,Y)$ (6 ways). So $S_4=Z$. (e.g. $H,H,T,C$)
  Triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(X,Y,Z)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_1=X \in \{X,Y,Z\}$ (consistent) and $S_5 \in \{X,Y,Z\}$ (3 choices).
  This structure $(S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4) = (X,X,Y,Z)$ with $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(X,Y,Z)$ distinct makes the determination of $S_5,S_6,S_7$ identical to Subcase I.A by shifting indices. The number of ways from this point is $ (30+18+6)/6 = 9$.
  So this gives $6 \times 1 \times 9 = 54$ schedules.

Subcase II.B: $(S_1,S_2,S_3)=(X,Y,X)$ (6 ways). So $S_4=Z$. (e.g. $H,T,H,C$)
  Triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(Y,X,Z)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_1=X \in \{Y,X,Z\}$ (consistent) and $S_5 \in \{Y,X,Z\}$ (3 choices).
  This is also identical to Subcase I.A from $S_2$ onwards.
  So this gives $6 \times 1 \times 9 = 54$ schedules.

Subcase II.C: $(S_1,S_2,S_3)=(X,Y,Y)$ (6 ways). So $S_4=Z$. (e.g. $H,T,T,C$)
  Triplet $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=(Y,Y,Z)$ uses 2 sports $\{Y,Z\}$. By Case 2, $S_1=X$ (consistent) and $S_5=X$ (1 choice).
  Sequence $(X,Y,Y,Z,X)$. Triplet $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=(Y,Z,X)$ is distinct. By Case 1, $S_2=Y \in \{Y,Z,X\}$ (consistent) and $S_6 \in \{Y,Z,X\}$ (3 choices).
  This is identical to Subcase I.B from $S_2$ onwards (after $(S_1,S_5)$ fixed). The number of ways from this point is $30/6=5$.
  So this gives $6 \times 1 \times 5 = 30$ schedules.

Total for Part II ($S_1,S_2,S_3$ use two sports): $54+54+30 = 138$ schedules.

Total number of possible sports schedules: Sum of Part I and Part II totals.
Total = $102 + 138 = 240$.

Let's verify the branching factors:
Subcase I.A has $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4 = X,Y,Z,X$. $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=Y,Z,X$ (distinct). $S_5$ has 3 choices.
  $S_5=Y \implies (S_3,S_4,S_5)=Z,X,Y$ (distinct). $S_6$ has 3 choices.
    $S_6=Z \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=X,Y,Z$ (distinct). $S_7$ has 3 choices. (3 schedules)
    $S_6=X \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=X,Y,X$ (2 sports). $S_7=Z$. (1 schedule)
    $S_6=Y \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=X,Y,Y$ (2 sports). $S_7=Z$. (1 schedule)
    Total: $3+1+1=5$ schedules starting from $X,Y,Z,X,Y,...$
  $S_5=Z \implies (S_3,S_4,S_5)=Z,X,Z$ (2 sports). $S_6=Y$.
    $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=X,Z,Y$ (distinct). $S_7$ has 3 choices. (3 schedules)
    Total: $1 \times 3 = 3$ schedules starting from $X,Y,Z,X,Z,...$
  $S_5=X \implies (S_3,S_4,S_5)=Z,X,X$ (2 sports). $S_6=Y$.
    $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=X,X,Y$ (2 sports). $S_7=Z$. (1 schedule)
    Total: $1 \times 1 = 1$ schedule starting from $X,Y,Z,X,X,...$
Total ways for fixed $X,Y,Z$ and $S_4=X$: $5+3+1=9$. $6 \times 9 = 54$. This is correct.

Subcase I.B has $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4 = X,Y,Z,Y$. $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=Y,Z,Y$ (2 sports). $S_5=X$.
  $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=Z,Y,X$ (distinct). $S_6$ has 3 choices.
    $S_6=Z \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=Y,X,Z$ (distinct). $S_7$ has 3 choices. (3 schedules)
    $S_6=Y \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=Y,X,Y$ (2 sports). $S_7=Z$. (1 schedule)
    $S_6=X \implies (S_4,S_5,S_6)=Y,X,X$ (2 sports). $S_7=Z$. (1 schedule)
    Total: $3+1+1=5$ schedules starting from $X,Y,Z,Y,X,...$
Total ways for fixed $X,Y,Z$ and $S_4=Y$: $1 \times 5 = 5$. $6 \times 5 = 30$. This is correct.

Subcase I.C has $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4 = X,Y,Z,Z$. $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=Y,Z,Z$ (2 sports). $S_5=X$.
  $(S_3,S_4,S_5)=Z,Z,X$ (2 sports). $S_6=Y$.
    $(S_4,S_5,S_6)=Z,X,Y$ (distinct). $S_7$ has 3 choices. (3 schedules)
Total ways for fixed $X,Y,Z$ and $S_4=Z$: $1 \times 1 \times 3 = 3$. $6 \times 3 = 18$. This is correct.

The calculations for Part I sum to $54+30+18 = 102$.

Subcase II.A has $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4 = X,X,Y,Z$. $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=X,Y,Z$ (distinct). $S_5$ has 3 choices. This is like starting with $S'_1=S_2, S'_2=S_3, S'_3=S_4$ which are distinct, and $S'_4=S_5$. $6 \times 9 = 54$. Correct.

Subcase II.C has $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4 = X,Y,Y,Z$. $(S_2,S_3,S_4)=Y,Y,Z$ (2 sports). $S_5=X$. This is like starting with $S'_1,S'_2,S'_3 = (Y,Y,Z)$ and previous sport $S'_0=X$. This matches Case 2. $S_5=X$ is fixed by Case 2. Branching factor for $S_5,S_6,S_7$ is 5. (Calculated in I.B: $1 \times (3+1+1)=5$).

problem:
Jenny is going to attend a sports camp for 7 days. Each day, she will play exactly one of three sports: hockey, tennis, or camogie. The only restriction is that in any period of 4 consecutive days, she must play all three sports.

Find, with proof, the number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week.
solution:
Let H , T , C denote hockey, tennis, camogie and write a weekly
schedule as a word  
\(s_{1}s_{2}\dots s_{7}\) of length \(7\) over the alphabet  
\(\{H,T,C\}\).

Condition (★) For every \(i=1,2,3,4\) the block
\(s_{i}s_{i+1}s_{i+2}s_{i+3}\) contains the three letters H , T , C.

We must count all words of length \(7\) that satisfy (★).

-------------------------------------------------
1.  A local description
-------------------------------------------------

While we are building the word from left to right, at the moment we want
to choose \(s_{k+1}\) we only have to look at the last three letters
\(s_{k-2}s_{k-1}s_{k}\); the four–letter block that will have to satisfy
(★) is precisely  

\[
s_{k-2}\,s_{k-1}\,s_{k}\,s_{k+1}.
\]

Thus the possibility of extending a partial word depends **only** on the
ordered triple formed by its last three letters.  
Call such an ordered triple a *state*.

-------------------------------------------------
2.  Which states can occur?
-------------------------------------------------

Let a state be written \(abc\).

•  If all three letters coincide ( \(a=b=c\) ) then, no matter what
letter \(d\) is appended, the ensuing block \(abcd\) will contain at
most two different sports, contradicting (★).  
Therefore states of the form HHH, TTT, CCC can never appear once
condition (★) has to be respected.

Hence every state that can actually occur uses either

A. all three different letters, or  
B. exactly two different letters.

Let us inspect these two kinds in more detail.

-------------------------------------------------
3.  A refined classification of states
-------------------------------------------------

Write a state of kind B in the form that shows where the two equal
letters stand.

B\(_1\).  The two equal letters are the last two:  \(YXX\);

B\(_2\).  The equal letters are *not* the last two:
 \(XXY\)   or   \(XYX\).

Counting the concrete states of each type:

•  Kind A (all letters different):  the letters H , T , C can be
arranged in \(3!=6\) ways.

•  Kind B\(_1\):

 Choose the repeated letter \(X\;(=H,T\text{ or }C)\) – 3 choices  
 Choose \(Y\neq X\) – 2 choices.  

That gives \(3\cdot 2=6\) states of type B\(_1\).

•  Kind B\(_2\):

 Pattern \(XXY\): again \(3\cdot 2=6\) states;  
 pattern \(XYX\): again \(3\cdot 2=6\) states.  

So there are \(6+6=12\) states of type B\(_2\).

In total there are \(6+6+12=24\) usable states – exactly the \(3^{3}-3\)
three–letter words that are *not* constant.

-------------------------------------------------
4.  How can one state follow another?
-------------------------------------------------

Suppose the current state is \(abc\) and we append a letter \(d\).
The new state is \(bcd\).  
We list the *only* possibilities consistent with (★).

A →  

 The present state \(abc\) has three different letters  
 \(\,\Longrightarrow\) every choice of \(d\in\{H,T,C\}\) is legal.  

 More precisely, for each state A there is  

 • one choice (namely \(d=a\)) giving a new state of type A,  
 • one choice (\(d=b\)) giving a new state of type B\(_2\) (pattern
\(bcb\)),  
 • one choice (\(d=c\)) giving a new state of type B\(_1\) (pattern
\(bcc\)).

B\(_1\) →  

 The letters occurring are \(X,X,Y\) with \(Y\) at the front.  
 The fourth letter must be the *missing* sport \(Z\), and that choice is
unique.  
 The new state is \(X,X,Z\), a pattern \(XXY\), i.e. of type B\(_2\).

B\(_2\) →  

 Again the fourth letter must be the single missing sport and is
therefore unique.  
 Appending it produces three different letters, so the new state is of
type A.

Summarised:

 A ⟶ ( exactly one A, one B\(_1\), one B\(_2\) )  
 B\(_1\) ⟶ ( exactly one B\(_2\) )  
 B\(_2\) ⟶ ( exactly one A )

Hence, if we let  

\(A_k , B_{1k} , B_{2k}\) be the numbers of length–\(k\) partial
schedules whose last three letters are of the respective kinds, then for
every \(k\ge 3\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{k+1}&=A_k+B_{2k},\\
B_{1,k+1}&=A_k,\\
B_{2,k+1}&=A_k+B_{1k}.
\end{aligned}\tag{1}
\]

-------------------------------------------------
5.  Initial numbers (length 3)
-------------------------------------------------

For \(k=3\) all \(3^{3}=27\) words are possible except the three
constant ones, so

\[
A_3=6 ,\qquad B_{1,3}=6 ,\qquad B_{2,3}=12 .
\]

-------------------------------------------------
6.  Counting up to length 7
-------------------------------------------------

Repeatedly using (1):

•  \(k=4\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_4 &= A_3+B_{2,3}=6+12=18,\\
B_{1,4}&=A_3=6,\\
B_{2,4}&=A_3+B_{1,3}=6+6=12.
\end{aligned}
\]

•  \(k=5\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_5 &=18+12=30,\\
B_{1,5}&=18,\\
B_{2,5}&=18+6=24.
\end{aligned}
\]

•  \(k=6\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_6 &=30+24=54,\\
B_{1,6}&=30,\\
B_{2,6}&=30+18=48.
\end{aligned}
\]

•  \(k=7\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_7 &=54+48=102,\\
B_{1,7}&=54,\\
B_{2,7}&=54+30=84.
\end{aligned}
\]

-------------------------------------------------
7.  The final answer
-------------------------------------------------

Every length-7 schedule satisfying (★) ends in one of the three kinds of
states, so the desired number is

\[
A_7+B_{1,7}+B_{2,7}=102+54+84=240.
\]

-------------------------------------------------
8.  Verification for the first window
-------------------------------------------------

As a check note that for \(k=4\) the formula gave
\(A_4+B_{1,4}+B_{2,4}=36\).  
That is precisely the number of 4-letter words that contain
H , T , C, confirming that our transition rules are correct.

-------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
-------------------------------------------------

There are exactly 240 possible 7-day sports schedules in which every set
of four consecutive days contains each of hockey, tennis and camogie.
author: llm

problem:
Jenny is going to attend a sports camp for 7 days. Each day, she will play exactly one of three sports: hockey, tennis, or camogie. The only restriction is that in any period of 4 consecutive days, she must play all three sports.

Find, with proof, the number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week.
solution:
The number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week is 240. Below is a complete and self-contained proof using dynamic programming to count the valid sequences.

We need to find the number of sequences of length 7 over the set of sports \(\{H, T, C\}\) (hockey, tennis, camogie) such that every substring of 4 consecutive days contains all three sports. To solve this, we use dynamic programming.

Define \(dp[n][a][b][c]\) as the number of valid sequences of length \(n\) that end with the sports \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) in the last three days (i.e., day \(n-2\) is \(a\), day \(n-1\) is \(b\), day \(n\) is \(c\)), and satisfy the condition that every 4-consecutive-day substring within the first \(n\) days contains all three sports.

For \(n = 3\), there are no 4-consecutive-day windows, so all sequences of length 3 are valid. There are \(3^3 = 27\) such sequences, and each corresponds to a specific triple \((a, b, c)\). Thus, \(dp[3][a][b][c] = 1\) for all \(a, b, c \in \{H, T, C\}\).

For \(n \geq 4\), when adding a new day with sport \(w\) to a sequence of length \(n\), the new sequence has length \(n+1\) and ends with \(b, c, w\). The new 4-consecutive-day window that must be checked is from day \(n-2\) to day \(n+1\), which corresponds to sports \(a, b, c, w\). This window must contain all three sports for the sequence to remain valid. The transition is:
\[
dp[n+1][b][c][w] = \sum_{\substack{a \in \{H, T, C\} \\ \{a, b, c, w\} \text{ contains all three sports}}} dp[n][a][b][c]
\]
This ensures that the new window satisfies the condition, and by induction, all previous windows are valid since the sequence up to length \(n\) was valid.

We compute the values step by step up to \(n = 7\).

First, for \(n = 4\):
- For each triple \((a, b, c)\), \(dp[4][b][c][w]\) is computed by summing over \(a\) such that \(\{a, b, c, w\}\) contains all three sports, with \(dp[3][a][b][c] = 1\).
- The values depend on the set \(\{b, c, w\}\):
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 3\), \(dp[4][b][c][w] = 3\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b \neq c\), \(dp[4][b][c][w] = 1\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\), \(dp[4][b][c][w] = 0\) (but this case does not occur since \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\) implies \(w \neq b\), leading to inconsistency with the sum condition).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 1\), \(dp[4][b][c][w] = 0\).
- Summing over all \((b, c, w)\), the total number of valid sequences of length 4 is 36.

For \(n = 5\):
- Using the transition from \(dp[4]\), the values are:
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 3\), \(dp[5][b][c][w] = 5\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b \neq c\), \(dp[5][b][c][w] = 3\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\), \(dp[5][b][c][w] = 1\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 1\), \(dp[5][b][c][w] = 0\).
- Summing over all \((b, c, w)\), the total number is 72.

For \(n = 6\):
- Using the transition from \(dp[5]\), the values are:
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 3\), \(dp[6][b][c][w] = 9\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b \neq c\), \(dp[6][b][c][w] = 5\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\), \(dp[6][b][c][w] = 3\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 1\), \(dp[6][b][c][w] = 0\).
- Summing over all \((b, c, w)\), the total number is 132.

For \(n = 7\):
- Using the transition from \(dp[6]\), the values are:
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 3\), \(dp[7][b][c][w] = 17\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b \neq c\), \(dp[7][b][c][w] = 9\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\), \(dp[7][b][c][w] = 5\).
  - If \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 1\), \(dp[7][b][c][w] = 0\).
- Summing over all \((b, c, w)\):
  - \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 3\): 6 triples, each with value 17, sum \(6 \times 17 = 102\).
  - \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b \neq c\): 12 triples, each with value 9, sum \(12 \times 9 = 108\).
  - \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 2\) and \(b = c\): 6 triples, each with value 5, sum \(6 \times 5 = 30\).
  - \(|\{b, c, w\}| = 1\): 3 triples, each with value 0, sum 0.
- Total sum: \(102 + 108 + 30 = 240\).

Thus, the number of valid sequences of length 7 is 240, which is the number of possible sports schedules for Jenny's week.
