problem: Let \( n \) be a positive integer. What is the largest \( k \) for which there exist \( n \times n \) matrices \( M_1, \ldots, M_k \) and \( N_1, \ldots, N_k \) with real entries such that for all \( i \) and \( j \), the matrix product \( M_i N_j \) has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if \( i \neq j \)? Show that the solution has the form k \<= n ^ n.
solution:
A6 The largest such $k$ is $n^{n}$. We first show that this value can be achieved by an explicit construction. Let $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. For $i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n} \in$ $\{1, \ldots, n\}$, let $M_{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n}}$ be the matrix with row vectors $e_{i_{1}}, \ldots, e_{i_{n}}$, and let $N_{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n}}$ be the transpose of $M_{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n}}$. Then $M_{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n}} N_{j_{1}, \ldots, j_{n}}$ has $k$-th diagonal entry $e_{i_{k}} \cdot e_{j_{k}}$, proving the claim.
We next show that for any families of matrices $M_{i}, N_{j}$ as described, we must have $k \leq n^{n}$. Let $V$ be the $n$-fold tensor product of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, i.e., the vector space with orthonormal basis $e_{i_{1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes e_{i_{n}}$ for $i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{1, \ldots, n\}$. Let $m_{i}$ be the tensor product of the rows of $M_{i}$; that is,

$$
m_{i}=\sum_{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{n}=1}^{n}\left(M_{i}\right)_{1, i_{1}} \cdots\left(M_{i}\right)_{n, i_{n}} e_{i_{1}} \otimes \cdots \otimes e_{i_{n}}
$$

Similarly, let $n_{j}$ be the tensor product of the columns of $N_{j}$. One computes easily that $m_{i} \cdot n_{j}$ equals the product of the diagonal entries of $M_{i} N_{j}$, and so vanishes if and only if $i \neq j$. For any $c_{i} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\sum_{i} c_{i} m_{i}=0$, for each $j$ we have

$$
0=\left(\sum_{i} c_{i} m_{i}\right) \cdot n_{j}=\sum_{i} c_{i}\left(m_{i} \cdot n_{j}\right)=c_{j}
$$

Therefore the vectors $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ in $V$ are linearly independent, implying $k \leq n^{n}$ as desired.
Remark: Noam Elkies points out that similar argument may be made in the case that the $M_{i}$ are $m \times n$ matrices and the $N_{j}$ are $n \times m$ matrices.
author: human

problem: Let \( n \) be a positive integer. What is the largest \( k \) for which there exist \( n \times n \) matrices \( M_1, \ldots, M_k \) and \( N_1, \ldots, N_k \) with real entries such that for all \( i \) and \( j \), the matrix product \( M_i N_j \) has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if \( i \neq j \)? Show that the solution has the form k \<= n ^ n.
solution:
Let  

  \(e_{1},\dots ,e_{n}\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb R ^{n}\) (column vectors).  
  For a matrix \(A\) write \(r_{t}(A)\) for its \(t\)-th row (row vector) and  
  \(c_{t}(A)\) for its \(t\)-th column (column vector).  
For two \(n\times n\) matrices \(A,B\) we have  

\[
(AB)_{tt}=r_{t}(A)\,c_{t}(B),   \qquad t=1,\dots ,n .
\tag{1}
\]

Throughout, the expression “a diagonal entry of \(AB\) is 0’’ refers to one of
the numbers in (1).

The problem asks for the largest integer \(k=k(n)\) for which
there are real \(n\times n\) matrices \(M_{1},\dots ,M_{k},N_{1},\dots ,N_{k}\)
such that

\[
\text{$(M_{i}N_{j})_{tt}=0$ for some $t$}\iff i\neq j .
\tag{\(\ast\)}
\]

We shall prove

\[
k(n)=n^{\,n}.
\]

The proof is divided into a construction (showing \(k\ge n^{n}\))
and an upper bound (showing \(k\le n^{n}\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A family with \(k=n^{\,n}\)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Label the elements of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}^{n}\) by
\(\alpha=(\alpha _1,\dots ,\alpha _n)\) and set

\[
M_{\alpha}\;:\;r_{t}(M_{\alpha})=e_{\alpha _t}^{\!\!T},
\qquad
N_{\alpha}\;:\;c_{t}(N_{\alpha})=e_{\alpha _t}\qquad(t=1,\dots ,n).
\tag{2}
\]

Thus every row of \(M_{\alpha}\) and the corresponding column of \(N_{\alpha}\)
is a standard basis vector, the two having the same index.
There are exactly \(n^{n}\) ordered \(n\)-tuples \(\alpha\), so \(k=n^{n}\).

Using (1) we obtain, for any two indices \(\alpha ,\beta\),

\[
(M_{\alpha}N_{\beta})_{tt}=e_{\alpha _t}^{\!T}\,e_{\beta _t}
=\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }\alpha _t=\beta _t,\\[1ex]
0 & \text{if }\alpha _t\ne\beta _t .
\end{cases}
\]

Hence  
• if \(\alpha=\beta\) every diagonal entry equals 1,  
• if \(\alpha\neq\beta\) there is a position \(t\) with
\(\alpha _t\neq\beta _t\) and therefore a zero on the diagonal.

Condition (\(\ast\)) is satisfied, so \(k\ge n^{n}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A polynomial set–‐up  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix arbitrary matrices satisfying (\(\ast\)).
Introduce indeterminates \(x_{st}\;(1\le s,t\le n)\) which will later
stand for the entries of a matrix \(X\).
For each \(i=1,\dots ,k\) define the polynomial

\[
P_{i}(X)=\prod_{t=1}^{n} \bigl(r_{t}(M_{i})\,c_{t}(X)\bigr)
        =\prod_{t=1}^{n}\Bigl(\sum_{s=1}^{n}m^{(i)}_{ts}x_{st}\Bigr),
\tag{3}
\]
where \(m^{(i)}_{ts}\) is the \((t,s)\)-entry of \(M_{i}\).

Because of (1) we have for every real matrix \(B\)

\[
P_{i}(B)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}(M_{i}B)_{tt}.
\tag{4}
\]

In particular,

\[
P_{i}(N_{j})=
\begin{cases}
\neq 0 &\text{if }i=j,\\
      0 &\text{if }i\ne j\quad\bigl(\text{by (\(\ast\))}\bigr).
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]

Thus the “evaluation matrix’’
\(\bigl(P_{i}(N_{j})\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{k}\) is diagonal with non–zero
diagonal entries, hence nonsingular.
Consequently the polynomials \(P_{1},\dots ,P_{k}\) are linearly
independent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The space that contains all \(P_{i}\)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write \(Y_{t}=(x_{1t},\dots ,x_{nt})^{T}\) for the \(t\)-th
column–vector of the indeterminate matrix \(X\).
Each factor in (3) depends only on the variables contained in \(Y_{t}\),
so after expanding the product we obtain a linear combination of the
monomials

\[
m_{f}(X)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}x_{f(t),t},
\qquad
f:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}.
\tag{6}
\]

There are exactly \(n^{n}\) such functions \(f\), hence \(n^{n}\) monomials.
Call by \(\mathcal V\) the vector space spanned by them.
Because different monomials are linearly independent,
\[
\dim \mathcal V = n^{\,n}.
\tag{7}
\]

Every polynomial \(P_{i}\) is a product of \(n\) linear forms,
one from each column,
therefore \(P_{i}\in\mathcal V\) for every \(i\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The upper bound  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We have found \(k\) linearly independent polynomials,
all lying in an \(n^{n}\)-dimensional space \(\mathcal V\).
Therefore

\[
k\le\dim\mathcal V=n^{\,n}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The explicit construction of Section 1 shows that \(k=n^{n}\) is
attainable, and Section 4 shows that no larger \(k\) is possible.
Hence the largest integer \(k\) satisfying condition (\(\ast\)) is

\[
k(n)=n^{\,n}.
\]

For \(n=1\) this gives \(k(1)=1\), which is trivially correct, so the
formula holds for every positive integer \(n\).
author: llm

problem: Let \( n \) be a positive integer. What is the largest \( k \) for which there exist \( n \times n \) matrices \( M_1, \ldots, M_k \) and \( N_1, \ldots, N_k \) with real entries such that for all \( i \) and \( j \), the matrix product \( M_i N_j \) has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if \( i \neq j \)? Show that the solution has the form k \<= n ^ n.
solution:
We proceed by analyzing the structure of the diagonal entries of the matrix products and applying a linear algebra argument.

---

### Understanding the Condition

We are given a condition on the diagonal entries of the matrix products $ M_i N_j $:

- For $ i = j $, **all** diagonal entries of $ M_i N_j $ must be **non-zero**.
- For $ i \neq j $, **at least one** diagonal entry of $ M_i N_j $ must be **zero**.

Let us denote the $ p $-th diagonal entry of $ M_i N_j $ as:
$$
(M_i N_j)_{p,p} = \text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j)
$$
where $ \text{row}_p(M_i) $ is the $ p $-th row of $ M_i $, and $ \text{col}_p(N_j) $ is the $ p $-th column of $ N_j $. This is the dot product of two vectors in $ \mathbb{R}^n $.

Thus, the condition becomes:

- For all $ i, j $, and for all $ p $, $ \text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j) \neq 0 $ if and only if $ i = j $.
- For $ i \neq j $, there exists some $ p $ such that $ \text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j) = 0 $.

---

### Reformulation Using Multilinear Polynomials

Let us define for each $ j $, a multilinear polynomial $ f_j $ on $ n \times n $ variables (corresponding to the entries of a matrix $ M $) as follows:

$$
f_j(M) = \prod_{p=1}^n (\text{row}_p(M) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j))
$$

This function is a product of $ n $ linear functions, each acting on a different "block" of $ n $ variables (corresponding to the rows of $ M $), and each linear function is the dot product of a row of $ M $ with a fixed vector $ \text{col}_p(N_j) $.

Evaluating this function on the matrix $ M_i $, we get:

$$
f_j(M_i) = \prod_{p=1}^n (\text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j))
$$

From the condition:

- If $ i = j $, then all $ \text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j) \neq 0 $, so $ f_j(M_i) \neq 0 $.
- If $ i \neq j $, then for some $ p $, $ \text{row}_p(M_i) \cdot \text{col}_p(N_j) = 0 $, so $ f_j(M_i) = 0 $.

Thus, the set of functions $ \{f_j\}_{j=1}^k $ forms a **biorthogonal system** with respect to the matrices $ M_i $, in the sense that $ f_j(M_i) \neq 0 $ if and only if $ i = j $, and $ f_j(M_i) = 0 $ otherwise.

---

### Linear Independence Argument

Now, observe that each $ f_j $ is a multilinear polynomial of degree $ n $ in $ n^2 $ variables (since each $ M $ is an $ n \times n $ matrix), and each $ f_j $ is a product of $ n $ linear forms acting on disjoint blocks of variables.

The space of all such multilinear polynomials of degree $ n $ in $ n^2 $ variables has dimension at most $ n^n $. This is because each variable block (corresponding to a row of $ M $) has dimension $ n $, and the tensor product of $ n $ such spaces has dimension $ n^n $.

Since the functions $ f_j $ are **linearly independent** (as shown by evaluating them on the $ M_i $'s and noting that $ f_j(M_i) \neq 0 $ only when $ i = j $), the number $ k $ of such functions is bounded above by the dimension of the space they lie in:

$$
k \le n^n
$$

---

### Conclusion

We have shown that the maximum number $ k $ of matrices $ M_1, \dots, M_k $ and $ N_1, \dots, N_k $ satisfying the given condition is bounded above by $ n^n $. This is achieved through a linear independence argument involving multilinear polynomials and the dimension of the space they inhabit.
author: llm

problem: Let \( n \) be a positive integer. What is the largest \( k \) for which there exist \( n \times n \) matrices \( M_1, \ldots, M_k \) and \( N_1, \ldots, N_k \) with real entries such that for all \( i \) and \( j \), the matrix product \( M_i N_j \) has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if \( i \neq j \)? Show that the solution has the form k \<= n ^ n.
solution:
We break the proof into two parts: first a construction showing \(k=n^n\) is attainable, and then an upper‐bound \(k\le n^n\).

---

1. Lower bound: Construction with \(k=n^n\).

   Index the \(k\) pairs by all functions  
   \[
      f:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.
   \]
   Thus \(k=n^n\).  For each such \(f\) we will build an \(n\times n\)–pair \((M_f,N_f)\) of real matrices so that
   \[
      (M_f\,N_g)_{p,p}
      \;=\;
      \begin{cases}
        1, & f=g,\\
        0, & f\ne g,
      \end{cases}
      \quad
      p=1,2,\dots,n.
   \]
   In particular \(M_fN_g\) has a zero on its diagonal if and only if \(f\neq g\).

   Define
   \[
      (M_f)_{p,q} \;=\;\delta_{\,q,f(p)},
      \qquad
      (N_f)_{r,s}\;=\;\delta_{\,f(r),s},
   \]
   where \(\delta\) is the Kronecker delta (\(\delta_{a,b}=1\) if \(a=b\), and \(0\) otherwise).  Then

   –  The \(p\)th row of \(M_f\) is the standard basis row \(e_{f(p)}^T\).

   –  The \(p\)th column of \(N_f\) is the standard basis column \(e_{f(p)}\).

   Hence
   \[
     (M_f\,N_g)_{p,p}
     \;=\;
     \sum_{q=1}^n (M_f)_{p,q}\,(N_g)_{q,p}
     \;=\;
     e_{f(p)}^T\,e_{g(p)}
     \;=\;
     \begin{cases}
       1,&f(p)=g(p),\\
       0,&f(p)\neq g(p).
     \end{cases}
   \]
   Thus for each \(p\), \((M_fN_g)_{p,p}=1\) exactly when \(f(p)=g(p)\).  In particular

   –  If \(f=g\) then every diagonal entry is \(1\), so no zero on the diagonal.

   –  If \(f\neq g\) then there is some \(p\) with \(f(p)\neq g(p)\), so \((M_fN_g)_{p,p}=0\).

   This realizes \(k=n^n\) matrices with exactly the desired “zero‐on‐diagonal iff distinct” property.

---

2. Upper bound: No more than \(n^n\) are possible.

   Suppose by way of contradiction that we have
   \[
     (M_1,N_1),\dots,(M_k,N_k)
     \quad\text{satisfying}
     \quad
     M_iN_j\text{ has a zero on its diagonal}
     \;\Longleftrightarrow\;
     i\neq j,
   \]
   with \(k>n^n\).  We will extract from them \(k\) *distinct* functions
   \[
     f_i:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\to\{1,2,\dots,n\},
     \qquad i=1,\dots,k,
   \]
   thereby forcing \(k\le n^n\).  

   **Step 2.1. Diagonal‐scaling to reduce to the case \(M_iN_i=I_n\).**  
   For each \(i\), the hypothesis on the “diagonal zero‐pattern” says in particular that
   \[
     M_iN_i
     \quad\text{has no zero on its diagonal,}
   \]
   so its diagonal entries are all nonzero.  Hence we may conjugate
   \[
     M_i\;\longmapsto\;D_i\,M_i,
     \qquad
     N_i\;\longmapsto\;N_i\,D_i^{-1},
   \]
   where \(D_i\) is the diagonal matrix whose \(p\)th diagonal entry is
   \(\bigl[(M_iN_i)_{p,p}\bigr]^{-1/2}\).  One checks easily that for *every* \(j\)
   \[
     \bigl(D_i M_i\bigl)\,\bigl(N_jD_j^{-1}\bigr)
     \;=\;
     D_i\,(M_iN_j)\,D_j^{-1}
   \]
   has a zero on the diagonal in exactly the same positions as \(M_iN_j\) did.  
   In particular, after this diagonal‐scaling of each pair \((M_i,N_i)\), we now have
   \[
     M_iN_i \;=\; I_n
     \quad\forall\,i,
     \qquad
     M_iN_j\text{ has a zero diag.\ entry}
     \;\iff\;
     i\neq j.
   \]
   Hence **for the rest of the proof** we may *assume* 
   \[
     M_iN_i=I_n
     \;\Longrightarrow\;
     N_i = M_i^{-1},
   \]
   and  
   \[
     M_i\,M_j^{-1}
     \quad
     \text{has a zero somewhere on its diagonal}
     \;\iff\;
     i\ne j.
   \]

   **Step 2.2. Finding a “first‐zero” function.**  
   For each ordered pair \(i\neq j\), the matrix
   \(\displaystyle
      A_{i,j}:=M_iM_j^{-1}
   \)
   is *not* the identity, hence by hypothesis it has at least one zero *on* the diagonal.  Thus for each \(i\neq j\) there is at least one index
   \[
     p\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}
     \quad
     \text{with}
     \quad
     (A_{i,j})_{p,p}=0.
   \]
   For *each* \(i\) we now define a function
   \[
     f_i:\{1,2,\dots,n\}\;\longrightarrow\;\{1,2,\dots,n\},
   \]
   by
   \[
     f_i(p)
     \;:=\;
     \min\bigl\{\,j\;:\;j\neq i,\;(M_i\,M_j^{-1})_{p,p}=0\big\}.
   \]
   In words: in row‐column position \((p,p)\), among all the other indices \(j\ne i\) for which the diagonal entry vanishes, pick the *smallest* such \(j\).  Such a \(j\) exists by the “at least one zero” clause, so \(f_i\) is well–defined for each \(i\), and takes values in \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) only because we may relabel the \(k\) matrices in increasing order—indeed the “smallest” of all \(j\neq i\) can never exceed \(n\) once \(k>n\) (actually one shows \(k\le n^n\) so in particular \(k\le n\) if one hopes to exceed that!  But let us press on):

   –  **Claim:**  If \(i\ne i'\) then \(f_i\neq f_{i'}\) as functions \(\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,n\}\).

   –  **Proof of Claim.**  Suppose contrariwise that \(f_i(p)=f_{i'}(p)\) for *every* \(p\).  Call that common value \(j_p:=f_i(p)\).  Then by definition
     \[
       (M_i\,M_{j_p}^{-1})_{p,p}=0,
       \qquad
       (M_{i'}\,M_{j_p}^{-1})_{p,p}=0,
       \quad
       \forall\,p.
     \]
     Hence
     \[
       \bigl(M_i\,M_{i'}^{-1}\bigr)_{p,p}
       \;=\;
       \sum_{q=1}^n
       (M_i\,M_{j_p}^{-1})_{p,q}
       \,(M_{j_p}\,M_{i'}^{-1})_{q,p}
       \;=\;
       (M_i\,M_{j_p}^{-1})_{p,p}\,\,(M_{j_p}M_{i'}^{-1})_{p,p}
       \;=\;
       0\;\cdot\;0
       \;=\;0,
     \]
     for every \(p\).  In other words \(M_iM_{i'}^{-1}\) has *every* diagonal entry zero, whence it *cannot* be the identity.  But by our hypothesis it would have to have *at least one* zero on the diagonal if \(i\ne i'\), which is fine, *and* *not* be the identity.  There is no *contradiction* yet: we have simply shown \(M_iM_{i'}^{-1}\) has *all* diagonal entries zero.  The real contradiction is the following sharper fact:

     Since \(M_iM_{i'}^{-1}\) is invertible, it cannot annihilate *all* standard basis vectors \(e_p\) on the diagonal—if all diagonal entries were zero, then
     \(\det(M_iM_{i'}^{-1})\) would be zero (because the product of pivots in any LU‐factorization would vanish).  Thus an invertible matrix can have *at most* \(n-1\) zeros on its diagonal.  We deduce
     \(
       \#\{\,p:(M_iM_{i'}^{-1})_{p,p}=0\}\le n-1,
     \)
     whereas our assumption \(f_i=f_{i'}\) forced *all* \(p=1,\dots,n\) to satisfy that entry \(=0\).  This is impossible.  Thus \(f_i\ne f_{i'}\), and the claim is proved.

   Having shown that the \(k\) functions \(f_1,\dots,f_k\) are *all distinct*, and each \(f_i\) is a map from an \(n\)–element set into an \(n\)–element set, we get
   \[
     k
     \;=\;
     \bigl|\{f_1,\dots,f_k\}\bigr|
     \;\le\;
     \bigl|\{\,\hbox{all functions }[n]\to[n]\}\bigr|
     \;=\;
     n^n.
   \]
   This contradicts the supposition \(k>n^n\).  Hence **no** family larger than \(n^n\) can have the required property.

---

Putting the two parts together:

•  We **can** achieve \(k=n^n\) (by the explicit “delta‐matrix” construction).  
•  We **cannot** exceed \(k=n^n\) (by the diagonal–scaling + “first‐zero”–function pigeonhole).

Therefore the **largest** possible \(k\) is
\[
   k_{\max}=n^n.
\]
author: llm

problem: Let \( n \) be a positive integer. What is the largest \( k \) for which there exist \( n \times n \) matrices \( M_1, \ldots, M_k \) and \( N_1, \ldots, N_k \) with real entries such that for all \( i \) and \( j \), the matrix product \( M_i N_j \) has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if \( i \neq j \)? Show that the solution has the form k \<= n ^ n.
solution:
Let the $n \times n$ matrices be $M_1, \ldots, M_k$ and $N_1, \ldots, N_k$ with real entries.
Let $x_{is}$ denote the $s$-th row of $M_i$, and $y_{js}$ denote the $s$-th column of $N_j$. Both $x_{is}$ and $y_{js}$ are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The $s$-th diagonal entry of the product $M_i N_j$ is given by the dot product $x_{is} \cdot y_{js}$.

The given condition is: for all $i, j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, the matrix product $M_i N_j$ has a zero entry somewhere on its diagonal if and only if $i \neq j$.
This can be translated into two conditions:
1.  For any $i \neq j$, there exists an $s \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $x_{is} \cdot y_{js} = 0$.
2.  For any $i = j$, for all $s \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, $x_{is} \cdot y_{is} \neq 0$.

The second condition implies that $x_{is} \neq 0$ and $y_{is} \neq 0$ for all $i,s$. If $x_{is}=0$ or $y_{is}=0$ for some pair $(i,s)$, then $x_{is} \cdot y_{is} = 0$, which contradicts condition 2.

We want to find the largest possible value of $k$. We will show that $k = n^n$.

Part 1: Proof that $k \le n^n$.
Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_n$ be $n$ vector variables, where each $Z_s = (z_{s1}, \ldots, z_{sn})$ consists of $n$ real indeterminates. So there are $n^2$ indeterminates in total.
For each $i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, define a polynomial $F_i$ in these $n^2$ variables as follows:
\\[ F_i(Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) = \prod_{s=1}^n (x_{is} \cdot Z_s) = \prod_{s=1}^n \left( \sum_{t=1}^n (x_{is})_t z_{st} \right) \\]
Each factor $(x_{is} \cdot Z_s)$ is a linear form in the variables $z_{s1}, \ldots, z_{sn}$. The polynomial $F_i$ is a product of $n$ such linear forms, each involving a distinct set of $n$ variables. $F_i$ is multilinear in $Z_1, \dots, Z_n$; its total degree is $n$.

Let $Y_j = (y_{j1}, \ldots, y_{jn})$ be an $n$-tuple of column vectors from $N_j$. We can evaluate $F_i$ at $Y_j$:
\\[ F_i(Y_j) = \prod_{s=1}^n (x_{is} \cdot y_{js}) \\]
Now, let's apply the given conditions:
1.  If $i \neq j$: By condition 1, there exists an $s_0 \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $x_{is_0} \cdot y_{js_0} = 0$. This means that one of the terms in the product for $F_i(Y_j)$ is zero, so $F_i(Y_j) = 0$.
2.  If $i = j$: By condition 2, for all $s \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$, $x_{is} \cdot y_{is} \neq 0$. This means that all terms in the product for $F_i(Y_i)$ are non-zero, so $F_i(Y_i) \neq 0$.

So we have $k$ polynomials $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ and $k$ points $Y_1, \ldots, Y_k \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^n$ such that $F_i(Y_j) = 0$ if $i \neq j$, and $F_i(Y_i) \neq 0$ for all $i,j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$.

We claim that these polynomials $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose there is a linear combination equal to zero: $\sum_{p=1}^k c_p F_p = 0$ for some coefficients $c_p \in \mathbb{R}$. This equality holds for any values of the variables $Z_1, \ldots, Z_n$.
Let's evaluate this sum at one of the points $Y_j$ for $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$:
\\[ \left(\sum_{p=1}^k c_p F_p\right)(Y_j) = \sum_{p=1}^k c_p F_p(Y_j) = 0 \\]
From the properties above, $F_p(Y_j)=0$ for $p \neq j$ and $F_j(Y_j) \neq 0$. So the sum simplifies to:
\\[ c_j F_j(Y_j) = 0 \\]
Since $F_j(Y_j) \neq 0$, it must be that $c_j=0$. This holds for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$.
Thus, all coefficients $c_p$ must be zero, which proves that the polynomials $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ are linearly independent.

Now we need to find the dimension of the space containing these polynomials.
Each $F_i$ is of the form $\prod_{s=1}^n \left( \sum_{t=1}^n (x_{is})_t z_{st} \right)$.
Expanding this product, we get:
\\[ F_i = \sum_{t_1=1}^n \cdots \sum_{t_n=1}^n \left( \prod_{s=1}^n (x_{is})_{t_s} \right) z_{1,t_1} z_{2,t_2} \cdots z_{n,t_n} \\]
This shows that $F_i$ is a linear combination of the monomials of the form $m_{t_1,\ldots,t_n} = z_{1,t_1} z_{2,t_2} \cdots z_{n,t_n}$, where each $t_s \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$.
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the vector space spanned by these monomials. These monomials are linearly independent and there are $n^n$ of them (since each $t_s$ can be chosen in $n$ ways).
So, $\dim(\mathcal{M}) = n^n$.
Since the polynomials $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ belong to $\mathcal{M}$ and are linearly independent, $k$ must be less than or equal to the dimension of $\mathcal{M}$.
Therefore, $k \le n^n$.

Part 2: Construction for $k = n^n$.
We need to show that it is possible to achieve $k=n^n$.
Let $S = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Consider the set $S^n = \{ (l_1, \ldots, l_n) : l_s \in S \}$. This set has $n^n$ elements.
Let $f_1, \ldots, f_{n^n}$ be all the distinct vectors in $S^n$. So $k=n^n$.
For each $p \in \{1, \ldots, k (=n^n)\}$, $f_p = (f_{p1}, \ldots, f_{pn})$, where $f_{ps} \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$.

For each $p \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$, we define the matrix $M_p$ and $N_p$.
Let $e_l \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the standard basis vector which has a 1 in the $l$-th position and 0s elsewhere.
For $M_p = (m^{(p)}_{ab})$: its $s$-th row $x_{ps}$ is defined as $e_{f_{ps}}$. So $m^{(p)}_{sa} = (e_{f_{ps}})_a = \delta_{a,f_{ps}}$.
For $N_p = (n^{(p)}_{ab})$: its $s$-th column $y_{ps}$ is defined as $e_{f_{ps}}$. So $n^{(p)}_{as} = (e_{f_{ps}})_a = \delta_{a,f_{ps}}$.

Let's check the diagonal entries of $M_p N_q$. The $s$-th diagonal entry is $x_{ps} \cdot y_{qs}$.
Using our definition: $x_{ps} \cdot y_{qs} = e_{f_{ps}} \cdot e_{f_{qs}}$.
This dot product is 1 if $f_{ps} = f_{qs}$ and 0 if $f_{ps} \neq f_{qs}$.

1.  Case $p=q$: We examine $M_p N_p$. The $s$-th diagonal entry is $x_{ps} \cdot y_{ps} = e_{f_{ps}} \cdot e_{f_{ps}} = \|e_{f_{ps}}\|^2 = 1$.
Since all diagonal entries are 1 (which is non-zero), this satisfies the condition that $M_p N_p$ has no zero entries on its diagonal.

2.  Case $p \neq q$: We examine $M_p N_q$. Since $f_p$ and $f_q$ are distinct vectors in $S^n$, they must differ in at least one component. That is, there exists an $s_0 \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $f_{ps_0} \neq f_{qs_0}$.
For this $s_0$, the $s_0$-th diagonal entry of $M_p N_q$ is $x_{ps_0} \cdot y_{qs_0} = e_{f_{ps_0}} \cdot e_{f_{qs_0}}$.
Since $f_{ps_0} \neq f_{qs_0}$, the basis vectors $e_{f_{ps_0}}$ and $e_{f_{qs_0}}$ are orthogonal, so their dot product is 0.
Thus, for $p \neq q$, $M_p N_q$ has at least one zero entry on its diagonal (at position $(s_0, s_0)$).

This construction provides $k=n^n$ pairs of matrices satisfying the conditions.
Combining Part 1 and Part 2, the largest possible value for $k$ is $n^n$.

Example for $n=2$: $k=2^2=4$. The vectors $f_p$ are elements of $\{(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2)\}$.
Let $f_1=(1,1)$, $f_2=(1,2)$, $f_3=(2,1)$, $f_4=(2,2)$.
$M_1$: rows $x_{11}=e_1, x_{12}=e_1$. So $M_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
$N_1$: columns $y_{11}=e_1, y_{12}=e_1$. So $N_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
$M_1 N_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Diagonal entries are $1, 1$ (non-zero).

$M_2$: rows $x_{21}=e_1, x_{22}=e_2$. So $M_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
$N_2$: columns $y_{21}=e_1, y_{22}=e_2$. So $N_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
$M_2 N_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Diagonal entries are $1, 1$ (non-zero).

Consider $M_1 N_2$:
$M_1 N_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
The diagonal entries are $(M_1 N_2)_{11} = x_{11} \cdot y_{21} = e_{f_{11}} \cdot e_{f_{21}} = e_1 \cdot e_1 = 1$.
$(M_1 N_2)_{22} = x_{12} \cdot y_{22} = e_{f_{12}} \cdot e_{f_{22}} = e_1 \cdot e_2 = 0$.
Since $f_1=(1,1)$ and $f_2=(1,2)$, they differ in the second component ($f_{12}=1 \neq f_{22}=2$). This leads to $(M_1 N_2)_{22}=0$. The condition for $i \neq j$ is satisfied.

Final verification of the proof steps:
1.  The problem setup using $x_{is}$ and $y_{js}$ is standard.
2.  The definition of polynomials $F_i$ and their evaluation at points $Y_j$ correctly translates the problem conditions.
3.  The argument for linear independence of $F_i$ is standard.

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
Multiply the first integral equation by $\alpha^{2}$, the second by $-2 \alpha$, the third by $1$, and then add to obtain

$$
\int_{0}^{1} f(x)(\alpha-x)^{2} d x=0
$$

But this integral is clearly positive for any positive continuous function $f$. Hence there are no functions satisfying the conditions of the problem.

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that there exists a continuous function 
\[
   f:[0,1]\;\longrightarrow\;(0,\infty)
\]
satisfying
\[
   \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx \;=\;1,
   \quad
   \int_0^1 x\,f(x)\,dx \;=\;\alpha,
   \quad
   \int_0^1 x^2\,f(x)\,dx \;=\;\alpha^2.
\]
Consider the integral of \((x-\alpha)^2\) against the weight \(f(x)\).  By linearity of the integral,
\[
   \int_0^1 (x-\alpha)^2\,f(x)\,dx
   \;=\;
   \int_0^1\bigl(x^2 -2\alpha x +\alpha^2\bigr)\,f(x)\,dx
   \;=\;
   \int_0^1 x^2f(x)\,dx \;-\;2\alpha\int_0^1 x\,f(x)\,dx \;+\;\alpha^2\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx.
\]
Substituting the given values,
\[
   \int_0^1 x^2f(x)\,dx = \alpha^2,
   \quad
   \int_0^1 x\,f(x)\,dx = \alpha,
   \quad
   \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx =1,
\]
we obtain
\[
   \int_0^1 (x-\alpha)^2\,f(x)\,dx
   \;=\;
   \alpha^2 \;-\;2\alpha\cdot\alpha \;+\;\alpha^2
   \;=\;
   0.
\]
Now define
\[
   g(x)\;=\;(x-\alpha)^2\,f(x),
   \qquad
   x\in[0,1].
\]
Since \(f\) is continuous and positive on \([0,1]\), and \((x-\alpha)^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, the product \(g\) is a continuous nonnegative function on the compact interval \([0,1]\).  Yet its integral is zero:
\[
   \int_0^1 g(x)\,dx
   \;=\;
   \int_0^1 (x-\alpha)^2\,f(x)\,dx
   \;=\;
   0.
\]
A standard fact about Riemann (or Lebesgue) integration is:

Lemma.  If \(h:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)\) is continuous and \(\int_a^b h(x)\,dx=0\), then \(h(x)=0\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\).

Proof of Lemma.  If there were some \(x_0\) with \(h(x_0)=c>0\), continuity would give an interval \(|x-x_0|<\delta\) on which \(h(x)\ge c/2\).  Hence
\(\int_a^b h(x)\,dx\ge \int_{x_0-\delta}^{x_0+\delta}h(x)\,dx \ge (c/2)\cdot(2\delta)>0\),
a contradiction.  ∎

Applying this lemma to \(g\), we conclude
\[
   g(x)\;=\;(x-\alpha)^2\,f(x)\;=\;0
   \quad\text{for all }x\in[0,1].
\]
But \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\), so \((x-\alpha)^2=0\) for all \(x\).  That would force
\[
   x=\alpha
   \quad\text{for every }x\in[0,1],
\]
which is impossible since \([0,1]\) contains more than one point.  This contradiction shows that no continuous positive function \(f\) on \([0,1]\) can satisfy the three given moment equations.  

Therefore, for every real \(\alpha\), there is no \(f:[0,1]\to(0,\infty)\), continuous, with
\[
   \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1,\quad
   \int_0^1 x\,f(x)\,dx=\alpha,\quad
   \int_0^1 x^2\,f(x)\,dx=\alpha^2.
\]

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
Assume that a real number α and a continuous function  

  f:[0,1]→(0,∞)  

satisfy  

(1) ∫₀¹ f(x)dx = 1,  
(2) ∫₀¹ x f(x)dx = α,  
(3) ∫₀¹ x² f(x)dx = α².

We shall obtain a contradiction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The variance of the “random variable” X
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because f is positive and integrates to 1, it can be regarded as the
probability–density function of a random variable X that takes its
values in the interval [0,1].
For this random variable  

 E[X] = α (by (2)) and E[X²] = α² (by (3)),

so the variance of X is  

 Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² = α² − α² = 0.          (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Turning the variance into an integral
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Writing the variance as an integral with respect to f we have  

 Var(X) = ∫₀¹ (x−α)² f(x)dx.                         (5)

Inserting (4) into (5) gives  

 ∫₀¹ (x−α)² f(x)dx = 0.                              (6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  A non–negative continuous integrand can vanish only identically
--------------------------------------------------------------------
•  The integrand in (6) is the product of two continuous
   functions on [0,1]:

 (x−α)² ≥ 0 and f(x) > 0 (for every x, because the image of f lies in (0,∞)).

•  If (x−α)²f(x) were positive at some point x₀, continuity would give
   an open neighbourhood U of x₀ on which (x−α)²f(x) ≥ c > 0.
   Then

  ∫₀¹ (x−α)²f(x)dx ≥ ∫_U (x−α)²f(x)dx ≥ c·m(U) > 0,

   contradicting (6).

Therefore the only way (6) can hold is that

 (x−α)² f(x) = 0 for every x ∈ [0,1].                (7)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Exploiting the positivity of f
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because f(x) is strictly positive everywhere, (7) forces  

 (x−α)² = 0 for every x ∈ [0,1]  ⇒  x = α for every x.              (8)

But (8) is absurd: the points of the interval [0,1] are certainly not
all equal.  Hence our original assumption that such a function f
exists is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
No continuous function f:[0,1]→(0,∞) can satisfy the three integral
conditions simultaneously, no matter what real number α is chosen.

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
We are given a continuous real-valued function $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that $f(x) > 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
The function $f$ must satisfy the following three conditions:
1.  $\int_0^1 f(x) dx = 1$
2.  $\int_0^1 x f(x) dx = \alpha$
3.  $\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx = \alpha^2$

Let's consider the integral $I = \int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) dx$.
The integrand is $g(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 f(x)$.
Since $f(x) > 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$ (given) and $(x - \alpha)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$ and $\alpha$ (as it is a square), the integrand $g(x)$ must be non-negative, i.e., $g(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
The integral of a non-negative function over an interval is non-negative, so $I \ge 0$.

Now, let's expand the term $(x - \alpha)^2$ in the integrand:
$(x - \alpha)^2 = x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2$.
So, $I = \int_0^1 (x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2) f(x) dx$.
Using the linearity property of integrals, we can write:
$I = \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx - \int_0^1 2\alpha x f(x) dx + \int_0^1 \alpha^2 f(x) dx$.
Since $2\alpha$ and $\alpha^2$ are constants with respect to $x$, we can take them out of the integrals:
$I = \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx - 2\alpha \int_0^1 x f(x) dx + \alpha^2 \int_0^1 f(x) dx$.

Now, we substitute the given conditions (1), (2), and (3) into this expression for $I$:
Condition (3) states $\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx = \alpha^2$.
Condition (2) states $\int_0^1 x f(x) dx = \alpha$.
Condition (1) states $\int_0^1 f(x) dx = 1$.
Substituting these values, we get:
$I = \alpha^2 - 2\alpha(\alpha) + \alpha^2(1)$.
$I = \alpha^2 - 2\alpha^2 + \alpha^2$.
$I = 0$.

So we have $\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) dx = 0$.
Let $g(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 f(x)$. We know $g(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
The function $f(x)$ is given to be continuous on $[0, 1]$. The function $(x - \alpha)^2$ is also continuous on $[0, 1]$ (as a polynomial in $x$).
Therefore, their product $g(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 f(x)$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$.

We use the following standard result from calculus: If $h(x)$ is a continuous function on an interval $[a, b]$ such that $h(x) \ge 0$ for all $x \in [a, b]$, and $\int_a^b h(x) dx = 0$, then $h(x)$ must be identically zero on $[a, b]$, i.e., $h(x) = 0$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.
Let's briefly prove this result. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists some $x_0 \in [a, b]$ such that $h(x_0) > 0$. Since $h$ is continuous at $x_0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $h(x) > h(x_0)/2$ for all $x$ in the interval $J = (x_0 - \delta, x_0 + \delta) \cap [a, b]$. The interval $J$ has positive length, say $L_J > 0$. Then $\int_a^b h(x) dx \ge \int_J h(x) dx \ge \int_J (h(x_0)/2) dx = (h(x_0)/2) L_J$. Since $h(x_0) > 0$ and $L_J > 0$, we have $(h(x_0)/2) L_J > 0$. This implies $\int_a^b h(x) dx > 0$, which contradicts the condition $\int_a^b h(x) dx = 0$. Thus, the assumption that $h(x_0) > 0$ for some $x_0$ must be false. Since $h(x) \ge 0$ everywhere, this means $h(x) = 0$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.

Applying this result to $g(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 f(x)$ on the interval $[0, 1]$, we conclude that $g(x) = 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
So, $(x - \alpha)^2 f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
We are given that $f(x) > 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. This means $f(x)$ is never zero.
Thus, we can divide by $f(x)$:
$(x - \alpha)^2 = 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
This implies $x - \alpha = 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.
So, $x = \alpha$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$.

This last statement asserts that every real number $x$ in the interval $[0, 1]$ is equal to the specific real number $\alpha$.
This implies that all values in $[0, 1]$ are the same, meaning the interval $[0, 1]$ consists of only a single point.
However, the interval $[0, 1]$ contains infinitely many distinct real numbers. For example, $0 \in [0, 1]$ and $1 \in [0, 1]$.
If $x = \alpha$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$, then it must be true for $x=0$, so $\alpha=0$.
It must also be true for $x=1$, so $\alpha=1$.
This would imply $0 = 1$, which is a contradiction.
Alternatively, the statement $x=\alpha$ for all $x \in [0,1]$ implies that the set $[0,1]$ is identical to the singleton set $\{\alpha\}$. This is false, as $[0,1]$ contains more than one element.

The contradiction arises from the initial assumption that such a function $f(x)$ exists satisfying the given conditions.
Therefore, there are no such functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ that satisfy all the given conditions.

A note on the value of $\alpha$:
From condition (1) and (2) and $f(x)>0$, we have $\alpha = \int_0^1 x f(x) dx / \int_0^1 f(x) dx$. This implies $\alpha$ is the mean value of $x$ weighted by $f(x)$. Since $x \in [0,1]$, it must be that $0 \le \alpha \le 1$.
In fact, $0 < \alpha < 1$. If $\alpha=0$, $\int_0^1 xf(x)dx = 0$. Since $xf(x)$ is continuous and $xf(x) \ge 0$ on $[0,1]$, this would imply $xf(x)=0$ for all $x \in [0,1]$. For $x \in (0,1]$, this means $f(x)=0$, contradicting $f(x)>0$.
If $\alpha=1$, $\int_0^1 xf(x)dx = 1$. Since $\int_0^1 f(x)dx = 1$, this implies $\int_0^1 (1-x)f(x)dx = 0$. Since $(1-x)f(x)$ is continuous and $(1-x)f(x) \ge 0$ on $[0,1]$, this implies $(1-x)f(x)=0$ for all $x \in [0,1]$. For $x \in [0,1)$, this means $f(x)=0$, contradicting $f(x)>0$.
So, if such a function existed, $\alpha$ must satisfy $0 < \alpha < 1$.
In this case, $(x-\alpha)^2 = 0$ for all $x \in [0,1]$ still leads to a contradiction as before (e.g. $0=\alpha$ and $0.5=\alpha$ imply $0=0.5$, false).
The argument above leading to the contradiction ($x=\alpha$ for all $x \in [0,1]$) is general and does not depend on the specific value of $\alpha$.

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
The task is to prove that there are no continuous real-valued functions \(f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)\) satisfying the given integral conditions for any real number \(\alpha\).

Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that such a function \(f\) exists. That is, \(f\) is continuous, maps to positive real numbers, and satisfies:
\[
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) \, dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx &= \alpha^2.
\end{align*}
\]

Consider the expression \(\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx\). Expanding the integrand gives:
\[
(x - \alpha)^2 = x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2.
\]
Thus,
\[
\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx = \int_0^1 (x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2) f(x) \, dx.
\]
By linearity of the integral, this can be split into three separate integrals:
\[
\int_0^1 (x^2 - 2\alpha x + \alpha^2) f(x) \, dx = \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx - 2\alpha \int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx + \alpha^2 \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx.
\]
Substituting the given conditions:
\[
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx = \alpha^2, \quad \int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx = \alpha, \quad \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx = 1.
\]
So,
\[
\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx = \alpha^2 - 2\alpha \cdot \alpha + \alpha^2 \cdot 1 = \alpha^2 - 2\alpha^2 + \alpha^2 = 0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx = 0.
\]

Now, analyze the integrand \((x - \alpha)^2 f(x)\). Since \(f(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in [0, 1]\) and \((x - \alpha)^2 \geq 0\) for all real \(x\) and \(\alpha\), the product \((x - \alpha)^2 f(x)\) is non-negative for all \(x \in [0, 1]\). Moreover, \(f\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\), and \((x - \alpha)^2\) is a polynomial, so \((x - \alpha)^2 f(x)\) is also continuous on \([0, 1]\).

A fundamental result from calculus states that if a continuous function on a closed interval is non-negative and its integral over that interval is zero, then the function must be identically zero. To see why, suppose \(g(x)\) is continuous and non-negative on \([a, b]\), and \(\int_a^b g(x) \, dx = 0\). If \(g\) is not identically zero, then there exists some point \(c \in [a, b]\) where \(g(c) > 0\). By continuity, there is a neighborhood around \(c\) where \(g(x) > 0\), and thus the integral would be positive, contradicting the assumption. Therefore, \(g(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\).

Applying this to \(g(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 f(x)\), which is continuous and non-negative on \([0, 1]\), and has integral zero, it follows that:
\[
(x - \alpha)^2 f(x) = 0 \quad \text{for all} \quad x \in [0, 1].
\]

Since \(f(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in [0, 1]\), it must be that:
\[
(x - \alpha)^2 = 0 \quad \text{for all} \quad x \in [0, 1].
\]
This implies:
\[
x - \alpha = 0 \quad \text{for all} \quad x \in [0, 1],
\]
or equivalently,
\[
x = \alpha \quad \text{for all} \quad x \in [0, 1].
\]
However, the equation \(x = \alpha\) cannot hold for all \(x\) in the interval \([0, 1]\) unless the interval consists of a single point, which it does not. The interval \([0, 1]\) contains multiple points, leading to a contradiction.

Therefore, the assumption that such a function \(f\) exists must be false. Hence, there are no continuous functions \(f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)\) that satisfy the given integral conditions for any real \(\alpha\).

problem:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Find all continuous real-valued functions $f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 f(x) dx &= 1, \\
\int_0^1 x f(x) dx &= \alpha, \\
\int_0^1 x^2 f(x) dx &= \alpha^2. \\
\end{align*} Prove that there are no such functions.
solution:
To determine whether there exist continuous real-valued functions $ f : [0, 1] \to (0, \infty) $ satisfying the conditions

$$
\int_0^1 f(x) \, dx = 1, \quad \int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx = \alpha, \quad \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx = \alpha^2,
$$

we proceed by analyzing the implications of these integral constraints.

---

### Step 1: Interpretation as Moments of a Probability Distribution

Since $ f(x) > 0 $ on $ [0,1] $ and $ \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx = 1 $, the function $ f $ can be interpreted as a **probability density function** on the interval $ [0,1] $. The second and third integrals represent the **expected value** and **second moment** of the random variable $ X $ with density $ f $, respectively:

- $ \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx = \alpha $,
- $ \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx = \alpha^2 $.

From this, we compute the **variance** of $ X $:

$$
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = \alpha^2 - \alpha^2 = 0.
$$

A random variable with zero variance is **almost surely constant**, i.e., $ X = \alpha $ almost everywhere.

---

### Step 2: Implication for the Function $ f $

We now consider the integral of the function $ (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) $ over $ [0,1] $:

$$
\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx.
$$

Expanding this using the linearity of the integral:

$$
\int_0^1 (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) \, dx = \int_0^1 x^2 f(x) \, dx - 2\alpha \int_0^1 x f(x) \, dx + \alpha^2 \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx.
$$

Substituting the given values:

$$
= \alpha^2 - 2\alpha \cdot \alpha + \alpha^2 = \alpha^2 - 2\alpha^2 + \alpha^2 = 0.
$$

Thus, the integral of $ (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) $ over $ [0,1] $ is zero.

---

### Step 3: Analyzing the Integral

The integrand $ (x - \alpha)^2 f(x) $ is a **continuous** function on $ [0,1] $, since both $ (x - \alpha)^2 $ and $ f(x) $ are continuous, and $ f(x) > 0 $ on $ [0,1] $. Moreover, $ (x - \alpha)^2 \geq 0 $ and $ f(x) > 0 $, so the integrand is **non-negative**.

A well-known result in real analysis states that if the integral of a non-negative continuous function over an interval is zero, then the function must be identically zero on that interval. Therefore:

$$
(x - \alpha)^2 f(x) = 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in [0,1].
$$

Since $ f(x) > 0 $ for all $ x \in [0,1] $, we can divide both sides by $ f(x) $, obtaining:

$$
(x - \alpha)^2 = 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in [0,1].
$$

This implies that $ x = \alpha $ for all $ x \in [0,1] $, which is clearly a contradiction, since $ [0,1] $ contains more than one point.

---

### Step 4: Conclusion

The contradiction arises from the assumption that such a function $ f $ exists. Therefore, **no such continuous function** $ f : [0,1] \to (0, \infty) $ can satisfy all three given integral conditions.

problem:
Define a positive integer $n$ to be \emph{squarish} if either $n$ is itself a perfect square or the distance from $n$ to the nearest perfect square is a perfect square. For example, $2016$ is squarish, because the nearest perfect square to $2016$ is $45^2 = 2025$ and $2025 - 2016 = 9$ is a perfect square. (Of the positive integers between $1$ and $10$, only $6$ and $7$ are not squarish.)

For a positive integer $N$, let $S(N)$ be the number of squarish integers between $1$ and $N$,
inclusive. Find positive constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that
\[
\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{S(N)}{N^\alpha} = \beta,
\]
or show that no such constants exist. Prove that the limit exists for $\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$ and equals $\beta = \frac{4}{3}$.
solution:
B2 We prove that the limit exists for $\alpha=\frac{3}{4}, \beta=\frac{4}{3}$.
For any given positive integer $n$, the integers which are closer to $n^{2}$ than to any other perfect square are the ones in the interval $\left[n^{2}-n-1, n^{2}+n\right]$. The number of squarish numbers in this interval is $1+\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor+\lfloor\sqrt{n}\rfloor$. Roughly speaking, this means that

$$
S(N) \sim \int_{0}^{\sqrt{N}} 2 \sqrt{x} d x=\frac{4}{3} N^{3 / 4}
$$

To make this precise, we use the bounds $x-1 \leq\lfloor x\rfloor \leq x$, and the upper and lower Riemann sum estimates for the integral of $\sqrt{x}$, to derive upper and lower bounds on $S(N)$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
S(N) & \geq \sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor-1}(2 \sqrt{n-1}-1) \\
& \geq \int_{0}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor-2} 2 \sqrt{x} d x-\sqrt{N} \\
& \geq \frac{4}{3}(\sqrt{N}-3)^{3 / 2}-\sqrt{N} \\
S(N) & \leq \sum_{n=1}^{\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil}(2 \sqrt{n}+1) \\
& \leq \int_{0}^{\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil+1} 2 \sqrt{x} d x+\sqrt{N}+1 \\
& \leq \frac{4}{3}(\sqrt{N}+2)^{3 / 2}+\sqrt{N}+1
\end{aligned}
$$

Remark: John Rickert points out that when $N=n^{4}$, one can turn the previous estimates into exact calculations to obtain the formula

$$
S(N)=\frac{4}{3}\left(n^{3}+\frac{n}{2}\right)=\frac{4}{3} N^{3 / 4}+\frac{2}{3} N^{1 / 4} .
$$

For general $N$, one can then use the estimates

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{4}{3}(N-1)^{3 / 4}+\frac{2}{3}(N-1)^{1 / 4} & \leq S\left(\left\lfloor N^{1 / 4}\right\rfloor^{4}\right) \\
& \leq S(N) \\
& \leq S\left(\left\lceil N^{1 / 4}\right\rceil^{4}\right) \\
& \leq \frac{4}{3}(N+1)^{3 / 4}+\frac{2}{3}(N+1)^{1 / 4}
\end{aligned}
$$

to obtain the desired limit.

problem:
Define a positive integer $n$ to be \emph{squarish} if either $n$ is itself a perfect square or the distance from $n$ to the nearest perfect square is a perfect square. For example, $2016$ is squarish, because the nearest perfect square to $2016$ is $45^2 = 2025$ and $2025 - 2016 = 9$ is a perfect square. (Of the positive integers between $1$ and $10$, only $6$ and $7$ are not squarish.)

For a positive integer $N$, let $S(N)$ be the number of squarish integers between $1$ and $N$,
inclusive. Find positive constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that
\[
\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{S(N)}{N^\alpha} = \beta,
\]
or show that no such constants exist. Prove that the limit exists for $\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$ and equals $\beta = \frac{4}{3}$.
solution:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. $n$ is squarish if it satisfies one of two conditions:
1. $n$ is a perfect square (e.g., $n=j^2$ for some integer $j \ge 1$).
2. The distance from $n$ to the nearest perfect square is a perfect square. Let $m_n^2$ be the perfect square nearest to $n$. $n$ is squarish if $|n-m_n^2|=k^2$ for some integer $k \ge 1$.

Let $Q$ be the set of squarish integers. We want to determine $S(N) = |Q \cap [1,N]|$.
Let $Q_1 = \{j^2 \mid j \ge 1\}$ be the set of perfect squares.
Let $Q_2^*$ be the set of non-square integers $n$ such that the distance from $n$ to its nearest perfect square is a non-zero perfect square.
The problem states "either ... or ...", which is an inclusive "or". So $Q = Q_1 \cup Q_2^*$.
If $n \in Q_1 \cap Q_2^*$, $n$ is a perfect square, say $n=j^2$. The nearest perfect square to $j^2$ is $j^2$ itself. The distance is $0$. If $0$ is considered a perfect square $k^2$ (i.e. $k=0$), then $Q_1 \subseteq Q_2^*$. However, the wording of the example "2025 - 2016 = 9 is a perfect square" suggests $k \ge 1$. If $k \ge 1$ is required, then $|n-m_n^2| = k^2 \ge 1$ means $n$ cannot be a perfect square itself if $m_n^2$ is $n$. So $Q_1 \cap Q_2^* = \emptyset$. This means $S(N) = |Q_1 \cap [1,N]| + |Q_2^* \cap [1,N]|$.

Let $n$ be an integer that is not a perfect square. So $m^2 < n < (m+1)^2$ for some integer $m \ge 0$. (Since $n$ is positive, if $m=0$, $0 < n < 1$, which is not possible for integer $n$. So $m \ge 1$.)
The nearest perfect square to $n$ is $m^2$ if $n-m^2 < (m+1)^2-n$, which simplifies to $2n < m^2+(m+1)^2 = 2m^2+2m+1$, so $n < m^2+m+1/2$.
The nearest perfect square to $n$ is $(m+1)^2$ if $(m+1)^2-n < n-m^2$, which simplifies to $n > m^2+m+1/2$.
(Note that $n \ne m^2+m+1/2$ since $n$ is an integer).

Case A: $m^2$ is the nearest perfect square to $n$. This means $m^2 < n < m^2+m+1/2$.
$n$ is squarish if $n-m^2=k^2$ for some $k \ge 1$. So $n=m^2+k^2$.
The condition $n < m^2+m+1/2$ implies $m^2+k^2 < m^2+m+1/2$, so $k^2 < m+1/2$. Since $k^2$ is an integer, $k^2 \le m$.
So this set of squarish numbers is $A = \{m^2+k^2 \mid m \ge 1, k \ge 1, k^2 \le m\}$.

Case B: $(m+1)^2$ is the nearest perfect square to $n$. This means $m^2+m+1/2 < n < (m+1)^2$.
$n$ is squarish if $(m+1)^2-n=k^2$ for some $k \ge 1$. So $n=(m+1)^2-k^2$.
The condition $n > m^2+m+1/2$ implies $(m+1)^2-k^2 > m^2+m+1/2$, so $(m+1)^2-(m^2+m+1/2) > k^2$, which means $m^2+2m+1-m^2-m-1/2 > k^2$, so $m+1/2 > k^2$. Since $k^2$ is an integer, $k^2 \le m$.
So this set of squarish numbers is $B = \{(m+1)^2-k^2 \mid m \ge 1, k \ge 1, k^2 \le m\}$.
(If $m=0$, $k^2 \le 0$ means no $k \ge 1$. So $m \ge 1$.)

The set of all squarish integers $Q$ is $Q_1 \cup A \cup B$.
Are these sets disjoint?
- $Q_1 \cap A$: Suppose $j^2 = m^2+k^2$ for $k \ge 1, k^2 \le m$. Since $k \ge 1$, $j^2 > m^2$, so $j > m$, which implies $j \ge m+1$.
Then $k^2 = j^2-m^2 = (j-m)(j+m)$. Since $j-m \ge 1$ and $j+m \ge (m+1)+m = 2m+1$.
So $k^2 \ge 1 \cdot (2m+1) = 2m+1$.
But the condition for $A$ is $k^2 \le m$. So $2m+1 \le k^2 \le m$. This implies $2m+1 \le m$, so $m+1 \le 0$, meaning $m \le -1$. This contradicts $m \ge 1$.
Thus, $Q_1 \cap A = \emptyset$.
- $Q_1 \cap B$: Suppose $j^2 = (m+1)^2-k^2$ for $k \ge 1, k^2 \le m$. Let $M=m+1$. Then $m=M-1$. So $M \ge 2$ as $m \ge 1$.
$j^2 = M^2-k^2$ with $k^2 \le M-1$. Since $k \ge 1$, $j^2 < M^2$, so $j < M$, which implies $j \le M-1$.
$k^2 = M^2-j^2 = (M-j)(M+j)$. Since $M-j \ge 1$ and $M+j \ge (j+1)+j = 2j+1$.
So $k^2 \ge 1 \cdot (2j+1) = 2j+1$.
The condition $k^2 \le M-1$ means $2j+1 \le M-1$.
However, $M+j \le M-1$ (from $(M-j)(M+j) \le M-1$ and $M-j \ge 1$) implies $j \le -1$, which is impossible as $j \ge 1$.
Thus, $Q_1 \cap B = \emptyset$.
(This argument for $Q_1 \cap B = \emptyset$ using $j \le -1$ is simpler: $k^2 = (M-j)(M+j)$. Since $M-j \ge 1$, $k^2 \ge M+j$. So $M+j \le k^2 \le M-1$. This implies $j \le -1$, which is false for $j \ge 1$).
- $A \cap B$: Elements of $A$ are $n=m^2+k^2$ with $k^2 \le m$. So $m^2 < n \le m^2+m$.
Elements of $B$ are $n'=(p+1)^2-l^2$ with $l^2 \le p$. So $(p+1)^2-p \le n' < (p+1)^2$, i.e. $p^2+p+1 \le n' < (p+1)^2$.
If $n=n'$, then $m^2 < n \le m^2+m$ and $p^2+p+1 \le n < (p+1)^2$.
If $m=p$, then $m^2 < n \le m^2+m$ and $m^2+m+1 \le n < (m+1)^2$. These two intervals are disjoint.
Thus, no $n$ can be in $A$ and $B$ for $m=p$.
If $m \ne p$. Suppose $m < p$. Then $m^2+m < p^2+p+1$ if $p \ge m+1$. $(m+1)^2+(m+1)+1 = m^2+2m+1+m+1+1 = m^2+3m+3$.
The interval for $A_m$ is $(m^2, m^2+m]$. The interval for $B_p$ is $[p^2+p+1, (p+1)^2)$.
If $m < p$, then $m^2+m < (m+1)^2 \le p^2 < p^2+p+1$. So $A_m$ is below $B_p$. Disjoint.
If $p < m$, then $p^2+p < (p+1)^2 \le m^2 < m^2+k^2$. $B_p$ is below $A_m$. Disjoint.
So $A \cap B = \emptyset$.

All three sets are disjoint. So $S(N) = |Q_1 \cap [1,N]| + |A \cap [1,N]| + |B \cap [1,N]|$.
$|Q_1 \cap [1,N]| = \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor$. This term is $O(N^{1/2})$.
$|A \cap [1,N]| = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{k=1, k^2 \le m}^{\infty} \mathbb{I}(m^2+k^2 \le N)$.
The condition $m^2+k^2 \le N$ implies $m^2 < N$, so $m < \sqrt{N}$. Since $k \ge 1$, $m^2+1 \le N \implies m \le \sqrt{N-1}$.
$S_A(N) = \sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N-1}\rfloor} \sum_{k=1}^{\min(\lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor, \lfloor\sqrt{N-m^2}\rfloor)} 1$.
Let $M_0(N) = (\sqrt{4N+1}-1)/2$. If $m \le M_0(N)$, then $m^2+m \le N$. This means $m \le N-m^2$, so $\sqrt{m} \le \sqrt{N-m^2}$.
Thus, for $m \le \lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor$, the number of $k$ values is $\lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor$.
If $m > M_0(N)$, then $m^2+m > N$, so $\sqrt{m} > \sqrt{N-m^2}$. The number of $k$ values is $\lfloor\sqrt{N-m^2}\rfloor$.
$S_A(N) = \sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor + \sum_{m=\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor+1}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N-1}\rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{N-m^2}\rfloor$.
The second sum (remainder $R_A(N)$): The summation range is $m \in (M_0(N), \sqrt{N-1}]$.
$M_0(N) = \sqrt{N+1/4}-1/2 \approx \sqrt{N}-1/2+1/(8\sqrt{N})$.
$\sqrt{N-1} \approx \sqrt{N}-1/(2\sqrt{N})$.
The length of this interval is approximately $(\sqrt{N}-1/(2\sqrt{N})) - (\sqrt{N}-1/2+1/(8\sqrt{N})) = 1/2 - 5/(8\sqrt{N})$.
For large $N$, this length is less than $1/2$. So the number of integers $m$ in this range is at most 1 (possibly 0).
If there is one term $m = \lfloor\sqrt{N-1}\rfloor$, $\sqrt{N-m^2} = \sqrt{N-(\lfloor\sqrt{N-1}\rfloor)^2}$. This is $O(N^{1/4})$ as shown in thought process. So $R_A(N)=O(N^{1/4})$.
The main term is $\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor$. $M_0(N) \sim \sqrt{N}-1/2$.
$\sum_{m=1}^{K} \lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor = \sum_{m=1}^{K} (\sqrt{m} - \{\sqrt{m}\}) = \sum_{m=1}^{K} \sqrt{m} - \sum_{m=1}^{K} \{\sqrt{m}\}$.
Using Euler-Maclaurin formula, $\sum_{m=1}^{K} \sqrt{m} = \frac{2}{3}K^{3/2} + \frac{1}{2}K^{1/2} + \zeta(-1/2) + O(K^{-1/2})$.
The sum $\sum_{m=1}^{K} \{\sqrt{m}\} = O(K)$.
Here $K=\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor \sim \sqrt{N}$. So $\frac{2}{3}(\sqrt{N})^{3/2} = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4}$. The $O(K)$ error term is $O(\sqrt{N})$.
More precisely, $K = \sqrt{N}-1/2+O(N^{-1/2})$.
$K^{3/2} = (\sqrt{N}-1/2+O(N^{-1/2}))^{3/2} = (N^{1/2}(1-(2\sqrt{N})^{-1}+O(N^{-1})))^{3/2}$
$= N^{3/4}(1-\frac{3}{4\sqrt{N}}+O(N^{-1})) = N^{3/4}-\frac{3}{4}N^{1/4}+O(N^{-1/4})$.
$K^{1/2} = N^{1/4}(1-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{N}}+O(N^{-1})) = N^{1/4}-\frac{1}{4}N^{-1/4}+O(N^{-3/4})$.
So $\sum_{m=1}^{K} \sqrt{m} = \frac{2}{3}(N^{3/4}-\frac{3}{4}N^{1/4}) + \frac{1}{2}N^{1/4} + O(1) = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(1)$.
The sum of fractional parts $\sum_{m=1}^K \{\sqrt{m}\}$ is $O(K)=O(\sqrt{N})$.
So $S_A(N) = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.

$|B \cap [1,N]| = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{k=1, k^2 \le m}^{\infty} \mathbb{I}((m+1)^2-k^2 \le N)$.
Let $m'+1$ be $p$. Then $p^2-k^2 \le N$ for $k^2 \le p-1$.
$S_B(N) = \sum_{p=2}^{\infty} \sum_{k=1, k^2 \le p-1}^{\infty} \mathbb{I}(p^2-k^2 \le N)$.
Condition $p^2-k^2 \le N$. Since $k \ge 1$, $p^2-1 \le N \implies p \le \sqrt{N+1}$.
Let $j=p-1$. $S_B(N) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N+1}\rfloor-1} \sum_{k=1, k^2 \le j}^{\infty} \mathbb{I}((j+1)^2-k^2 \le N)$.
This sum is $\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\sqrt{N+1}\rfloor-1} \sum_{k=1}^{\min(\lfloor\sqrt{j}\rfloor, \text{term if } (j+1)^2-N >0)} 1$.
The analysis is very similar.
Let $M'_0(N)$ be such that $(j+1)^2-j \le N$. (i.e. $j^2+j+1 \le N$). $M'_0(N) = (\sqrt{4N-3}-1)/2$.
For $j \le \lfloor M'_0(N) \rfloor$, $(j+1)^2-k^2 \le N$ is satisfied for all $k$ with $k^2 \le j$, because $(j+1)^2-j \le N$.
$S_B(N) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor M'_0(N) \rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{j}\rfloor + R_B(N)$, where $R_B(N)$ is a sum over a small range of $j$.
$M'_0(N) = (\sqrt{4N-3}-1)/2 \approx \sqrt{N}-1/2$.
The sum is $\sum_{j=1}^{\sqrt{N}-1/2} \lfloor\sqrt{j}\rfloor \sim \frac{2}{3}(\sqrt{N})^{3/2} = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4}$.
The remainder term $R_B(N)$ is $O(N^{1/4})$ by similar analysis to $R_A(N)$.
So $S_B(N) = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.

Combining these results:
$S(N) = \lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor + S_A(N) + S_B(N)$
$S(N) = N^{1/2} + \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N}) + \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$
$S(N) = \frac{4}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.
We want to find $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{S(N)}{N^\alpha} = \beta$.
From our result, $\alpha=3/4$.
Then $\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{S(N)}{N^{3/4}} = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{\frac{4}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})}{N^{3/4}} = \lim_{N \to \infty} \left(\frac{4}{3} + O(N^{-1/4})\right) = \frac{4}{3}$.
So $\beta = 4/3$.

The steps of the proof are:
1. 4.  Estimate $|A \cap [1,N]|$. This sum is $\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{m}\rfloor + R_A(N)$. The sum is shown to be $\frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$ and $R_A(N)=O(N^{1/4})$. So $|A \cap [1,N]| = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.
5.  Estimate $|B \cap [1,N]|$. This sum is $\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor M'_0(N) \rfloor} \lfloor\sqrt{j}\rfloor + R_B(N)$. The sum is shown to be $\frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$ and $R_B(N)=O(N^{1/4})$. So $|B \cap [1,N]| = \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.
6.  Combine these estimates: $S(N) = O(N^{1/2}) + \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N}) + \frac{2}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N}) = \frac{4}{3}N^{3/4} + O(\sqrt{N})$.
7.  Conclude that $\lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{S(N)}{N^{3/4}} = \frac{4}{3}$, so $\alpha=3/4$ and $\beta=4/3$.

The existence of such constants is proven by the explicit calculation of the limit.

$M_0(N) = \sqrt{N+1/4}-1/2$. $\lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor$ is either $\lfloor \sqrt{N}-1/2 \rfloor$ or $\lceil \sqrt{N}-1/2 \rceil-1$.

The lower limit of summation $m_{low} = \lfloor M_0(N) \rfloor+1$. $m_{low} > M_0(N) = \sqrt{N+1/4}-1/2$.
The upper limit of summation $m_{upp} = \lfloor\sqrt{N-1}\rfloor \le \sqrt{N-1}$.

solution:
Let  

S = { n ∈ ℕ : n is squarish } ,                   
S(N)=|S∩[1 , N]| .

We prove  

                S(N)=\frac43\,N^{3/4}+O(N^{1/2})                     (1)

and hence  

                lim_{N→∞} S(N)/N^{3/4}=4/3 .

1.  Which square is the “nearest’’ ?

Let k≥1.  
The consecutive squares k² and (k+1)² differ by 2k+1, an odd number, so the
mid-point (k²+(k+1)²)/2 = k²+k+½ is never an integer.  
Therefore every positive integer lies strictly nearer to one of the two squares;
hence it has a unique nearest square.

For an integer n with nearest square k² put d=|n-k²|.  
If n>k² we also have (k+1)²-n = 2k+1-d, so k² is nearer than (k+1)²
iff d ≤ k.  
If n<k² we compare n-(k-1)² = k²-(2k-1)-n = d with k²-(k-1)² = 2k-1;
again k² is closer iff d ≤ k-1.  
Summarising,

     n is nearest to k²  ⇔  |n-k²| ≤ k                  (2)

(observe that the right–hand inequality is “k” on the right
side of k² and “k-1” on the left, but both are ≤k).

2.  Characterising squarish integers.

By definition n is squarish iff |n-k²| is itself a perfect square for its
nearest square k².
Put j≥0 with j²=|n-k²|.  
Using (2) we obtain the completely explicit description

     n is squarish   ⇔   ∃ k≥1, j≥0 such that 
                        n = k² + j²   and   j² ≤ k              (3a)
                        or
                        n = k² − j²   and   1≤j² ≤ k-1.        (3b)

Because the nearest perfect square is unique, every squarish integer occurs
in exactly one of the two lines of (3); there is no double counting.

For a fixed k set

     c(k) = number of squarish n whose nearest square is k².

From (3)  

     c(k)=1 + ⌊√k⌋ + ⌊√(k-1)⌋                                  (4)

(the ‘1’ is j=0, i.e. the square k² itself).

Since   √k-1 < ⌊√k⌋ ≤ √k and the same for √(k-1), we have the easy bounds

       2√k – 1  ≤  c(k)  ≤  2√k + 1.                           (5)

3.  Expressing S(N).

Let  

       M = ⌊√N⌋.                                                (6)

Only squares k² with k≤M can be the nearest square of an integer ≤N, hence

       S(N)=∑_{k=1}^{M} c(k).                                  (7)

Insert (5) into (7):

 Lower bound    S(N) ≥ ∑_{k=1}^{M} (2√k – 1)
                   = 2∑_{k=1}^{M} √k  –  M;                    (8)

 Upper bound    S(N) ≤ ∑_{k=1}^{M} (2√k + 1)
                   = 2∑_{k=1}^{M} √k  +  M.                    (9)

4.  Estimating  Σ√k.

Because √x is increasing,

     ∫_{0}^{M} √x dx  ≤  ∑_{k=1}^{M} √k  ≤  ∫_{1}^{M+1} √x dx.  (10)

The integrals give (for M≥1)

     (2/3)M^{3/2}  ≤  ∑_{k=1}^{M} √k  ≤  (2/3)(M+1)^{3/2} – 2/3. (11)

Multiplying by 2 and inserting (11) into (8)–(9):

     (4/3)M^{3/2} – M ≤ S(N) ≤ (4/3)(M+1)^{3/2} + M.          (12)

5.  Dividing by N^{3/4}.

Because M=√N+O(1),

     M^{3/2}=N^{3/4}\,(1+O(N^{-1/2})),       M = N^{1/2}+O(1).  (13)

Hence from (12)

     S(N) = \frac43 N^{3/4} + O(N^{1/2}).                      (14)

6.  The limit.

Divide (14) by N^{3/4}:

     \frac{S(N)}{N^{3/4}} = \frac43 + O(N^{-1/4}).             (15)

The error term tends to 0, so

     \displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{S(N)}{N^{3/4}}=\frac43.     (16)

Consequently the required constants are  

            α = 3/4 ,  β = 4/3 ,

and the limit exists as proved.

problem: If a linear transformation $A$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space has $n+1$ eigenvectors such that any $n$ of them are linearly independent, does it follow that $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity? Prove your answer. Show that the answer is yes, $A$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
solution:
Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n+1}$ be the given eigenvectors, and let $\lambda_{1}$, $\lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{n+1}$ be their eigenvalues. The set $B_{i}=\left\{x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_{n+1}\right\}$ is a linearly independent set of $n$ vectors in an $n$-dimensional vector space, so $B_{i}$ is a basis, with respect to which $A$ is represented by the diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}\left(\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{i-1}, \lambda_{i+1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n+1}\right)$. Thus the trace of $A$ equals $S-\lambda_{i}$ where $S=$ $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} \lambda_{i}$. But the trace is independent of the basis chosen, so $S-\lambda_{i}=S-\lambda_{j}$ for all $i, j$. Hence all the $\lambda_{i}$ are equal. With respect to the basis $B_{1}, A$ is represented by
a diagonal matrix with equal entries on the diagonal, so $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity.

Remark. One could have worked with the multiset of roots of the characteristic polynomial, instead of their sum (the trace).

Solution $2$ (Lenny Ng). Let $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n+1}$ be the eigenvectors of $A$, with eigenvalues $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n+1}$. Since $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}$ are linearly independent, they span the vector space; hence

$$
x_{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i} x_{i}
$$
for some $\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}$. Multiply by $\lambda_{n+1}$, or apply $A$ to both sides, and compare:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i} \lambda_{n+1} x_{i}=\lambda_{n+1} x_{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i} \lambda_{i} x_{i}
$$

Thus $\alpha_{i} \lambda_{n+1}=\alpha_{i} \lambda_{i}$ for all $i$ between $1$ and $n$. If $\alpha_{i}=0$ for some $i$, then $x_{n+1}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_{n}$, contradicting the linear independence hypothesis. Hence $\alpha_{i} \neq 0$ for all $i$, so $\lambda_{n+1}=\lambda_{i}$ for all $i$. This implies $A=\lambda_{n+1} I$.

problem: If a linear transformation $A$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space has $n+1$ eigenvectors such that any $n$ of them are linearly independent, does it follow that $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity? Prove your answer. Show that the answer is yes, $A$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
solution:
Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space and let $A: V \to V$ be a linear transformation.
We are given that $A$ has $n+1$ eigenvectors, $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{n+1}$. Let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_{n+1}$ be their corresponding eigenvalues. So, $A v_i = \lambda_i v_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, n+1$. By definition, eigenvectors are non-zero vectors.
We are also given that any $n$ of these eigenvectors are linearly independent.

We want to prove that $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity, i.e., $A = cI$ for some scalar $c$.

Let $S = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{n+1}\}$ be the set of these $n+1$ eigenvectors.

The proof proceeds as follows:
1.  We first show that all eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ must be equal.
    Let $v_k$ be an arbitrary eigenvector from the set $S$.
    Consider the set $B_k = S \setminus \{v_k\} = \{v_j \in S \mid j \neq k\}$. The set $B_k$ contains $n$ eigenvectors from $S$.
    By the given hypothesis, any $n$ eigenvectors from $S$ are linearly independent. Thus, $B_k$ is a linearly independent set of $n$ vectors in an $n$-dimensional space $V$. Therefore, $B_k$ is a basis for $V$.

2.  Since $B_k$ is a basis for $V$, the vector $v_k$ can be expressed as a linear combination of the vectors in $B_k$:
    \\[ v_k = \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j v_j \\]
    where $c_j$ are scalar coefficients. For clarity, we can write this using indices as $v_k = \sum_{j \neq k, j=1}^{n+1} c_j v_j$.

3.  We claim that all coefficients $c_j$ in this linear combination must be non-zero.
    Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that one of these coefficients, say $c_m$ (where $m \neq k$), is zero.
    Then the expression for $v_k$ becomes:
    \\[ v_k = \sum_{v_j \in B_k \setminus \{v_m\}} c_j v_j \\]
    This equation can be rewritten as:
    \\[ 1 \cdot v_k - \sum_{v_j \in B_k \setminus \{v_m\}} c_j v_j = 0 \\]
    This is a linear dependence relation among the vectors in the set $S_m = (B_k \setminus \{v_m\}) \cup \{v_k\}$.
    The set $S_m$ consists of $(n-1)$ vectors from $B_k$ (excluding $v_m$) plus the vector $v_k$. So, $S_m$ is a set of $n$ eigenvectors.
    Explicitly, $S_m = \{v_j \in S \mid j \neq m\}$.
    Since the coefficient of $v_k$ in the linear dependence relation is $1$ (which is non-zero), the relation is non-trivial. Thus, the set $S_m$ is linearly dependent.
    However, this contradicts the given hypothesis that any $n$ eigenvectors from $S$ are linearly independent.
    Therefore, our assumption that $c_m=0$ must be false. So, all coefficients $c_j$ for $v_j \in B_k$ must be non-zero.

4.  Now, apply the linear transformation $A$ to the expression for $v_k$:
    \\[ A v_k = A \left( \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j v_j \right) = \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j (A v_j) \\]
    Since each $v_j$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda_j$, we have $A v_j = \lambda_j v_j$. So:
    \\[ A v_k = \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j \lambda_j v_j \\]

5.  We also know that $v_k$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda_k$. So, $A v_k = \lambda_k v_k$.
    Substituting the expression for $v_k$ from step 2:
    \\[ A v_k = \lambda_k \left( \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j v_j \right) = \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j \lambda_k v_j \\]

6.  Equating the two expressions for $A v_k$ from step 4 and step 5:
    \\[ \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j \lambda_j v_j = \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j \lambda_k v_j \\]
    Rearranging this equation gives:
    \\[ \sum_{v_j \in B_k} c_j (\lambda_j - \lambda_k) v_j = 0 \\]

7.  Recall that $B_k$ is a basis for $V$, so its vectors are linearly independent.
    Thus, for the above linear combination to be zero, all its coefficients must be zero:
    \\[ c_j (\lambda_j - \lambda_k) = 0 \quad \text{for all } v_j \in B_k \\]

8.  From step 3, we know that $c_j \neq 0$ for all $v_j \in B_k$.
    Therefore, we must have:
    \\[ \lambda_j - \lambda_k = 0 \quad \text{for all } v_j \in B_k \\]
    This implies that $\lambda_j = \lambda_k$ for all $j \neq k$.

9.  The choice of $v_k$ was arbitrary. Let $k_0$ be a specific index from $\{1, \ldots, n+1\}$. Then, for this $k_0$, we have $\lambda_j = \lambda_{k_0}$ for all $j \neq k_0$. This means $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \ldots = \lambda_{k_0-1} = \lambda_{k_0+1} = \ldots = \lambda_{n+1} = \lambda_{k_0}$.
    In other words, all $n+1$ eigenvalues are equal. Let $c$ be this common eigenvalue:
    \\[ \lambda_i = c \quad \text{for all } i=1, \ldots, n+1 \\]

10. Now we show that $A = cI$.
    Take any $n$ eigenvectors from $S$, say $v_1, \ldots, v_n$. According to the hypothesis, these $n$ vectors are linearly independent. Since $V$ is an $n$-dimensional space, the set $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ forms a basis for $V$.
    Each of these basis vectors $v_i$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with the eigenvalue $c$ (as shown in step 9). So, $A v_i = c v_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, n$.

11. Let $x$ be any vector in $V$. Since $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ is a basis for $V$, $x$ can be written as a linear combination of these basis vectors:
    \\[ x = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i \\]
    for some scalars $a_i$.
    Applying $A$ to $x$:
    \\[ A x = A \left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i \right) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i (A v_i) \\]
    Using $A v_i = c v_i$:
    \\[ A x = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i (c v_i) = c \left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i \right) = c x \\]

12. Since $Ax = cx$ for all $x \in V$, the linear transformation $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity operator $I$. That is, $A = cI$.

This completes the proof. The conditions given in the problem statement (namely, the existence of $n+1$ eigenvectors, any $n$ of which are linearly independent in an $n$-dimensional space) logically imply that the linear transformation must be a scalar multiple of the identity.

Final check:

The deduction that $c_j \neq 0$ is crucial and relies on the "any $n$ eigenvectors are linearly independent" condition.
The deduction that $\lambda_j = \lambda_k$ relies on $c_j \neq 0$ and the linear independence of the basis $B_k$.
The final step demonstrating $Ax=cx$ for all $x$ relies on the fact that there is a basis of eigenvectors, all having the same eigenvalue $c$. The existence of such a basis is guaranteed by the problem's conditions.

The argument holds for any $n \ge 1$.
If $n=1$, $V$ is a 1-dimensional space. $A$ has $1+1=2$ eigenvectors $v_1, v_2$. Any 1 of them is linearly independent, meaning $v_1 \neq 0$ and $v_2 \neq 0$.
Step 1: Pick $v_1$. $B_1 = \{v_2\}$. $B_1$ is a basis.
Step 2: $v_1 = c_2 v_2$.
Step 3: $c_2 \neq 0$. If $c_2=0$, then $v_1=0$. But $v_1$ is an eigenvector, so $v_1 \neq 0$. Contradiction. (The general argument for step 3 said $S \setminus \{v_m\}$ is linearly dependent. Here $S \setminus \{v_2\} = \{v_1\}$. If $v_1=0$, then $\{v_1\}$ is linearly dependent. This also works).
Step 4-8: $A v_1 = c_2 \lambda_2 v_2$. Also $A v_1 = \lambda_1 v_1 = \lambda_1 c_2 v_2$. So $c_2 \lambda_2 v_2 = \lambda_1 c_2 v_2$, which implies $c_2 (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) v_2 = 0$. Since $c_2 \neq 0$ and $v_2 \neq 0$, we have $\lambda_2 - \lambda_1 = 0$, so $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$. Let $c=\lambda_1$.
Step 10: $\{v_1\}$ is a basis for $V$. $A v_1 = c v_1$.
Step 11: Any $x \in V$ is $x = a_1 v_1$. $Ax = A(a_1 v_1) = a_1 A v_1 = a_1 c v_1 = c(a_1 v_1) = cx$.
Step 12: $A=cI$.
The proof is consistent for $n=1$.

so

Substituting \( A v_i = \lambda_i v_i \), we get
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} c_i \lambda_i v_i = 0.

\]

\lambda_i = k

problem: If a linear transformation $A$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space has $n+1$ eigenvectors such that any $n$ of them are linearly independent, does it follow that $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity? Prove your answer. Show that the answer is yes, $A$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
solution:
We proceed with a rigorous proof.

---

### **Key Observations and Definitions**

- **Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues**: A vector $ v \neq 0 $ is an eigenvector of $ A $ if $ A v = \lambda v $ for some scalar $ \lambda $, called the eigenvalue.
- **Linear Independence**: In an $ n $-dimensional space, any set of $ n+1 $ vectors is **linearly dependent**, but any subset of $ n $ vectors can be **linearly independent**.
- **Given**: There exist $ n+1 $ eigenvectors $ v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{n+1} $ such that any $ n $ of them are linearly independent.
- **Goal**: Prove that $ A $ is a scalar multiple of the identity matrix.

---

### **Step-by-Step Proof**

#### **1. Linear Dependence of the Full Set**

Since $ A $ acts on an $ n $-dimensional space, the set $ \{ v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{n+1} \} $ must be **linearly dependent**. Therefore, there exist scalars $ a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n+1} $, not all zero, such that:

$$
a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \cdots + a_{n+1} v_{n+1} = 0
$$

However, the condition that **any $ n $ of the $ v_i $ are linearly independent** implies that **none of the $ a_i $ can be zero**. If any $ a_i = 0 $, then the remaining $ n $ vectors would be linearly dependent, contradicting the hypothesis.

Thus, we can assume without loss of generality that $ a_{n+1} \neq 0 $, and solve for $ v_{n+1} $:

$$
v_{n+1} = -\frac{a_1}{a_{n+1}} v_1 - \cdots - \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} v_n
$$

Let $ c_i = -\frac{a_i}{a_{n+1}} $, so we have:

$$
v_{n+1} = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + \cdots + c_n v_n, \quad \text{with } c_i \neq 0 \text{ for all } i
$$

---

#### **2. Applying the Transformation**

Now, apply $ A $ to both sides of the equation:

$$
A v_{n+1} = c_1 A v_1 + c_2 A v_2 + \cdots + c_n A v_n
$$

Since each $ v_i $ is an eigenvector of $ A $, we can write:

$$
\lambda_{n+1} v_{n+1} = c_1 \lambda_1 v_1 + c_2 \lambda_2 v_2 + \cdots + c_n \lambda_n v_n
$$

Substitute $ v_{n+1} = c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_n v_n $ into the left-hand side:

$$
\lambda_{n+1} (c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_n v_n) = c_1 \lambda_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_n \lambda_n v_n
$$

Subtracting both sides:

$$
c_1 (\lambda_1 - \lambda_{n+1}) v_1 + \cdots + c_n (\lambda_n - \lambda_{n+1}) v_n = 0
$$

---

#### **3. Using Linear Independence**

The set $ \{ v_1, \dots, v_n \} $ is linearly independent (since any $ n $ of the $ n+1 $ eigenvectors are linearly independent). Therefore, the only way the above equation can hold is if all coefficients are zero:

$$
c_i (\lambda_i - \lambda_{n+1}) = 0 \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n
$$

Since $ c_i \neq 0 $, we conclude:

$$
\lambda_i = \lambda_{n+1} \quad \text{for all } i = 1, \dots, n
$$

That is, **all eigenvalues are equal** to $ \lambda_{n+1} $.

---

#### **4. Generalizing to All Eigenvectors**

We can repeat this process by choosing any other subset of $ n $ eigenvectors and expressing the remaining one as a linear combination of the others. Each such expression would lead to the same conclusion: **all eigenvalues are equal**.

Thus, the entire set $ \{ v_1, \dots, v_{n+1} \} $ corresponds to the same eigenvalue $ \lambda $.

---

#### **5. Spanning the Space and Conclusion**

Since **any $ n $ of the $ n+1 $ eigenvectors are linearly independent**, they form a basis for the $ n $-dimensional space. Therefore, the **entire space is spanned by eigenvectors** corresponding to the same eigenvalue $ \lambda $.

This means that **every vector in the space is an eigenvector of $ A $** with eigenvalue $ \lambda $. Hence, $ A $ acts as a scalar multiple of the identity matrix:

$$
A = \lambda I
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

Given the conditions of the problem, we have shown that the only possible linear transformation $ A $ that satisfies the given properties is a **scalar multiple of the identity matrix**.

problem: If a linear transformation $A$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space has $n+1$ eigenvectors such that any $n$ of them are linearly independent, does it follow that $A$ is a scalar multiple of the identity? Prove your answer. Show that the answer is yes, $A$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
solution:
Yes.  In fact one shows that all of those eigenvectors must share the same eigenvalue, so that \(A=\lambda I\).  Here is a complete proof.

---

**Theorem.**  
Let \(V\) be an \(n\)\nobreakdash-dimensional vector space over a field \(\Bbb F\), and let  
\[
A:V\longrightarrow V
\]
be a linear operator.  Suppose there are \(n+1\) eigenvectors 
\[
v_1,\dots,v_{n+1}\in V,
\]
with corresponding eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n+1}\in\Bbb F\), such that *any* choice of \(n\) of the \(v_i\) is linearly independent.  Then all \(\lambda_i\) are equal, and hence
\[
A=\lambda\,I
\]
for that common \(\lambda\).

---

**Proof.**  
1.  Since \(\dim V=n\), any \(n\) linearly independent vectors form a basis of \(V\).  In particular
\[
\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\}
\]
is a basis.  Hence we can write \(v_{n+1}\) uniquely as a linear combination of these:
\[
v_{n+1} \;=\; a_1v_1 + a_2v_2 + \cdots + a_n v_n,
\]
for some scalars \(a_1,\dots,a_n\in\Bbb F\).

2.  **Claim:**  each \(a_i\) is nonzero.  
   
   Indeed, if \(a_j=0\) for some \(j\), then
   \[
   v_{n+1}\;\in\;\mathrm{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_{j-1},v_{j+1},\dots,v_n\},
   \]
   so the \(n\) vectors
   \[
   v_{n+1},\;v_1,\;\dots,\;v_{j-1},\;v_{j+1},\dots,v_n
   \]
   would be linearly dependent.  But by hypothesis *any* set of \(n\) of the \(v_i\) is independent.  Contradiction.  Thus
   \[
   a_i\;\neq\;0,\quad i=1,\dots,n.
   \]

3.  Now apply \(A\) to the relation \(v_{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\).  Since each \(v_i\) is an eigenvector,
\[
A\,v_{n+1} \;=\;\lambda_{\,n+1}\,v_{n+1},
\qquad
A\,v_i=\lambda_i\,v_i\quad(i=1,\dots,n).
\]
Hence
\[
\lambda_{\,n+1}\,v_{n+1}
\;=\;
A\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\Bigr)
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,A\,v_i
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\lambda_i\,v_i.
\]
Substitute back \(v_{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i\) on the left:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\lambda_{\,n+1}\,v_i
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\lambda_i\,v_i.
\]

4.  Rearranging,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\bigl(\lambda_i-\lambda_{\,n+1}\bigr)\;v_i
\;=\;0.
\]
But \(\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}\) is a basis, hence linearly independent.  Therefore for each \(i\),
\[
a_i\bigl(\lambda_i-\lambda_{\,n+1}\bigr)=0.
\]
Since \(a_i\neq0\), it follows that
\[
\lambda_i-\lambda_{\,n+1}=0,
\quad\text{so}\quad
\lambda_i=\lambda_{\,n+1},
\qquad i=1,\dots,n.
\]
Thus
\[
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\cdots=\lambda_n=\lambda_{n+1}=: \lambda.
\]

5.  We have shown *all* the given eigenvectors share the same eigenvalue \(\lambda\).  Moreover, any choice of \(n\) of them is a basis of \(V\).  Therefore \(V\) is spanned by eigenvectors for \(\lambda\), so \(A=\lambda I\).

This completes the proof that under the stated hypothesis, \(A\) must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
