problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( |AC| \neq |BC| \). Let \( P \) and \( Q \) be the intersection points of the line \( AB \) with the internal and external angle bisectors at \( C \), so that \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \). Prove that if \( M \) is any point on the circle with diameter \( PQ \), then \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \).
solution:
Let  

• \(ABC\) be a non-isosceles triangle \((AC\neq BC)\);  
• \(P\) be the point in which the internal bisector of \(\angle ACB\) meets the straight line \(AB\)  (so \(P\) is between \(A\) and \(B\));  
• \(Q\) be the point in which the external bisector of \(\angle ACB\) meets the same line \(AB\) ( \(Q\) is the “outer” point).

We have to show that for every point \(M\) on the circle with diameter \(PQ\)

\[
\angle AMP=\angle BMP .\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------
1.  The point \(C\) lies on the circle with diameter \(PQ\)

The internal and external bisectors of an angle are perpendicular.  
Hence  

\[
\angle PCQ = 90^{\circ}.
\]

By Thales’s theorem, the vertices \(P,Q,C\) are therefore concyclic, the circle being the one whose diameter is \(PQ\).  
Denote this circle by \(\omega\).

--------------------------------------------------
2.  How \(P\) and \(Q\) divide the side \(AB\)

By the (internal and external) Angle–Bisector Theorems we have  

\[
\frac{AP}{PB}= \frac{AC}{CB},\qquad  
\frac{AQ}{QB}= \frac{AC}{CB}. \tag{2}
\]

Set  

\[
k:=\frac{AC}{CB}\quad (k\ne 1).
\]

Thus \(P\) and \(Q\) divide the line \(AB\) internally and externally in the same positive ratio \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------
3.  The Apollonius circle of \(AB\) for the ratio \(k\)

A classical and well–known result (the “Apollonius circle”; see, e.g., its Wikipedia page) says:

For a fixed segment \(AB\) and for a fixed \(k>0,\,k\ne 1\),  
the locus of points \(X\) that satisfy \(XA/XB = k\) is a circle.  
That circle passes through the two points in which the line \(AB\) is cut internally and externally in the ratio \(k\).

Because of (2) this Apollonius circle passes through \(P\) and \(Q\);  
because \(AC/BC=k\), it passes through \(C\) as well.

But \(\omega\) already contains the three non-collinear points \(P,Q,C\); hence  

\[
\;\omega\text{ is exactly the Apollonius circle of }AB\text{ corresponding to the ratio }k=\dfrac{AC}{CB}\; .
\]

Consequently

\[
\frac{AM}{BM}=k=\frac{AC}{CB}\quad\text{for every }M\in\omega .\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------
4.  The segment \(MP\) bisects \(\angle AMB\)

In the triangle \(AMB\) the point \(P\) lies on the side \(AB\).  
From (2) and (3) we get

\[
\frac{AP}{PB}=k=\frac{AM}{BM}.
\]

By the (internal) Angle–Bisector Theorem applied to triangle \(AMB\), the equality of the two ratios implies that the segment \(MP\) is the internal bisector of the angle \(\angle AMB\); hence

\[
\angle AMP=\angle BMP .
\]

--------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion

The equality (1) holds for every point \(M\) on the circle with diameter \(PQ\) (except, of course, the endpoints \(P,Q\) themselves, where the angle is not defined).

\[
\angle AMP=\angle BMP.
\]

The problem is solved.
author: llm

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( |AC| \neq |BC| \). Let \( P \) and \( Q \) be the intersection points of the line \( AB \) with the internal and external angle bisectors at \( C \), so that \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \). Prove that if \( M \) is any point on the circle with diameter \( PQ \), then \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \).
solution:
Let  
\[
k \;=\;\frac{AC}{BC}\,.
\]  
Since \(CP\) is the internal bisector of \(\angle ACB\) meeting \(AB\) at \(P\), the (internal) Angle-Bisector Theorem gives  
\[
\frac{AP}{PB}\;=\;\frac{AC}{BC}\;=\;k.
\]  
Similarly, since \(CQ\) is the external bisector of \(\angle ACB\) meeting the (extension of) \(AB\) at \(Q\), the external Angle-Bisector Theorem yields  
\[
\frac{AQ}{QB}\;=\;\frac{AC}{BC}\;=\;k.
\]  
Hence \(P\) and \(Q\) are exactly the two points on line \(AB\) (one in the interior of segment \(AB\), the other on its extension) which divide \(AB\) in the ratio \(k\!:\!1\).  

It is a classical fact (the “Apollonius-circle” lemma) that for two fixed points \(A,B\) and a fixed \(k\neq1\), the locus of all points \(M\) satisfying  
\[
\frac{MA}{MB}\;=\;k
\]  
is a circle whose diameter is the segment joining the two points on line \(AB\) that divide \(AB\) in the ratio \(k\!:\!1\).  Since \(AC\neq BC\) we have \(k\neq1\), so the Apollonius locus is a nondegenerate circle, and by the two ratio-equalities above that circle is exactly the circle with diameter \(PQ\).  In particular, for any \(M\) on the circle with diameter \(PQ\),  
\[
\frac{MA}{MB}\;=\;k
\;=\;\frac{AP}{PB}\,. 
\]  

Finally, in \(\triangle ABM\), the point \(P\) lies on side \(AB\) and divides it in the same ratio as the adjacent sides, namely  
\[
\frac{AP}{PB}\;=\;\frac{MA}{MB}.
\]  
By the converse of the Angle-Bisector Theorem, \(MP\) is therefore the bisector of \(\angle AMB\).  Hence  
\[
\angle AMP \;=\;\angle BMP,
\]  
as required.
author: llm

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle with \( |AC| \neq |BC| \). Let \( P \) and \( Q \) be the intersection points of the line \( AB \) with the internal and external angle bisectors at \( C \), so that \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \). Prove that if \( M \) is any point on the circle with diameter \( PQ \), then \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \).
solution:
Let \( C A \) and \( C B \) be sides of the triangle \( \triangle ABC \) with lengths \( |AC|=b \) and \( |BC|=a \). We are given \( b \neq a \). Let \( CP \) be the internal angle bisector of \( \angle C \), and \( CQ \) be the external angle bisector of \( \angle C \), with \( P \) and \( Q \) on the line \( AB \). We are given that \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \).

Step 1: Properties of points P and Q.
By the Angle Bisector Theorem, applied to the internal bisector \( CP \), we have
\[ \frac{|AP|}{|PB|} = \frac{|AC|}{|BC|} = \frac{b}{a} \]
Since \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \), \( P \) divides the segment \( AB \) internally in the ratio \( b:a \).
By the Angle Bisector Theorem, applied to the external bisector \( CQ \), we have
\[ \frac{|AQ|}{|BQ|} = \frac{|AC|}{|BC|} = \frac{b}{a} \]
Since \( b \neq a \), the ratio \( k = b/a \) is not equal to 1.
If \( b>a \), then \( |AQ|>|BQ| \). Since \( Q \) is on line \( AB \), \( B \) must be between \( A \) and \( Q \). So \( Q \) is external to segment \( AB \).
If \( b<a \), then \( |AQ|<|BQ| \). \( A \) must be between \( Q \) and \( B \). So \( Q \) is external to segment \( AB \).
So \( P \) is an internal division point and \( Q \) is an external division point of the segment \( AB \) for the same ratio \( k = b/a \).
The set of points \( (A,B; P,Q) \) forms a harmonic range.

Step 2: The circle with diameter PQ is the Circle of Apollonius.
The internal angle bisector \( CP \) and the external angle bisector \( CQ \) of \( \angle C \) are perpendicular. To see this, let \( \angle ACB = \gamma \). Then \( \angle ACP = \gamma/2 \). Let \( C' \) be a point on \( AC \) such that \( C \) is between \( A \) and \( C' \). The external angle at \( C \) is \( \angle BCC' = \pi - \gamma \). Then \( \angle BCQ = (\pi-\gamma)/2 \). So \( \angle PCQ = \angle PCB + \angle BCQ = \gamma/2 + (\pi-\gamma)/2 = \pi/2 \). (This configuration holds if \( B \) is between \( P \) and \( Q \). Other configurations lead to the same result by taking sums/differences of angles appropriately, or using directed angles).
Since \( \angle PCQ = \pi/2 \), the point \( C \) lies on the circle with diameter \( PQ \).

The locus of points \( X \) such that \( \frac{|XA|}{|XB|} = k \) (where \( k>0, k \neq 1 \)) is known as the Circle of Apollonius. The points \( P \) and \( Q \) as defined above are key points in constructing this circle. Specifically, \( P \) and \( Q \) are the unique points on the line \( AB \) that satisfy this condition for the ratio \( k = b/a \), and the segment \( PQ \) is a diameter of this Apollonius circle.
Let's prove this. Let \( A \) and \( B \) be points on the x-axis, with \( A=(0,0) \) and \( B=(c,0) \) where \( c=|AB|>0 \).
A point \( X=(x,y) \) is on the Apollonius circle if \( |XA|^2 = k^2 |XB|^2 \).
So, \( x^2+y^2 = k^2((x-c)^2+y^2) \).
\( x^2+y^2 = k^2(x^2-2xc+c^2+y^2) \).
Since \( k \neq 1 \), \( k^2-1 \neq 0 \). Rearranging the terms, we get
\( (k^2-1)x^2 - 2k^2cx + k^2c^2 + (k^2-1)y^2 = 0 \).
Dividing by \( (k^2-1) \):
\( x^2 - \frac{2k^2c}{k^2-1}x + \frac{k^2c^2}{k^2-1} + y^2 = 0 \).
This is the equation of a circle. To find its center and radius, we complete the square for \( x \):
\( \left(x - \frac{k^2c}{k^2-1}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{k^2c}{k^2-1}\right)^2 + \frac{k^2c^2}{k^2-1} + y^2 = 0 \).
\( \left(x - \frac{k^2c}{k^2-1}\right)^2 + y^2 = \frac{k^4c^2}{(k^2-1)^2} - \frac{k^2c^2(k^2-1)}{(k^2-1)^2} = \frac{k^4c^2 - k^4c^2 + k^2c^2}{(k^2-1)^2} = \left(\frac{kc}{|k^2-1|}\right)^2 \).
So the center of the Apollonius circle is \( O = \left(\frac{k^2c}{k^2-1}, 0\right) \) and its radius is \( R_{Apollonius} = \left|\frac{kc}{k^2-1}\right| \).

The points \( P \) and \( Q \) lie on the line \( AB \) (the x-axis in our setup).
\( P \) divides \( AB \) internally: \( |AP|/|PB|=k \). Let \( P=(x_P,0) \). Then \( x_P / (c-x_P) = k \) (since \( P \) is between \( A \) and \( B \), \( 0<x_P<c \)). This gives \( x_P = kc-kx_P \), so \( (1+k)x_P = kc \), so \( x_P = \frac{kc}{1+k} \).
\( Q \) divides \( AB \) externally: \( |AQ|/|BQ|=k \). Let \( Q=(x_Q,0) \).
If \( k>1 \) (\( b>a \)), then \( Q \) is such that \( B \) is between \( A \) and \( Q \). So \( x_Q>c \). Then \( x_Q/(x_Q-c)=k \), so \( x_Q = kx_Q-kc \), so \( (k-1)x_Q=kc \), \( x_Q=\frac{kc}{k-1} \).
If \( k<1 \) (\( b<a \)), then \( Q \) is such that \( A \) is between \( Q \) and \( B \). So \( x_Q<0 \). Then \( (-x_Q)/(c-x_Q)=k \), so \( -x_Q = kc-kx_Q \), so \( (k-1)x_Q=kc \), \( x_Q=\frac{kc}{k-1} \). This expression is negative, consistent with \( x_Q<0 \).
The midpoint of the segment \( PQ \) is \( \left( \frac{1}{2}(x_P+x_Q), 0 \right) \).
\( \frac{1}{2}(x_P+x_Q) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{kc}{k+1} + \frac{kc}{k-1}\right) = \frac{kc}{2} \frac{(k-1)+(k+1)}{(k+1)(k-1)} = \frac{kc}{2} \frac{2k}{k^2-1} = \frac{k^2c}{k^2-1} \).
This is the x-coordinate of the center \( O \) of the Apollonius circle.
The radius of the circle with diameter \( PQ \) is \( \frac{1}{2}|x_Q-x_P| \).
\( \frac{1}{2}|x_Q-x_P| = \frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{kc}{k-1} - \frac{kc}{k+1}\right| = \frac{1}{2}|kc|\left|\frac{1}{k-1} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right| = \frac{1}{2}|kc|\left|\frac{(k+1)-(k-1)}{(k-1)(k+1)}\right| = \frac{1}{2}|kc|\left|\frac{2}{k^2-1}\right| = \left|\frac{kc}{k^2-1}\right| \).
This is the radius \( R_{Apollonius} \).
Thus, the circle with diameter \( PQ \) is precisely the Apollonius circle defined by points \( A, B \) and ratio \( k = b/a \).

Step 3: Conclusion using the Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem.
Let \( M \) be any point on the circle with diameter \( PQ \). From Step 2, this means \( M \) is on the Apollonius circle for points \( A, B \) and ratio \( k=b/a \). Therefore, \( M \) satisfies
\[ \frac{|MA|}{|MB|} = k = \frac{b}{a} \]
We also know from Step 1 that \( P \) is a point on \( AB \) such that
\[ \frac{|AP|}{|PB|} = k = \frac{b}{a} \]
So, for any point \( M \) on the circle with diameter \( PQ \), we have
\[ \frac{|MA|}{|MB|} = \frac{|AP|}{|PB|} \]
We need to show that \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \). This means that \( MP \) is the internal angle bisector of \( \angle AMB \).
The angles \( \angle AMP \) and \( \angle BMP \) are well-defined provided \( M \neq P \), \( M \neq A \), and \( M \neq B \).
The points \( A \) and \( B \) cannot lie on the Apollonius circle: if \( A \) were on the circle, then \( |AA|/|AB| = k \), which implies \( 0/|AB| = k \), so \( k=0 \). This means \( b=|AC|=0 \), which is impossible for a triangle. Similarly for \( B \). So \( M \neq A \) and \( M \neq B \).
If \( M=P \), then \( \vec{MP} = \vec{PP} = \vec{0} \), so the angles \( \angle AMP \) and \( \angle BMP \) (which are \( \angle APP \) and \( \angle BPP \)) are not defined in the usual sense as angles in a triangle. We will assume \( M \neq P \).
If \( M=Q \): The line segment \( PQ \) is the diameter of the circle. The points \( A, P, B, Q \) are collinear (possibly in a different order, e.g. \( Q,A,P,B \)). Let's assume \( A, P, B, Q \) lie in that order on the line \( AB \). Then \( \vec{QA} \), \( \vec{QP} \), \( \vec{QB} \) are all vectors along the line \( AB \), pointing from \( Q \) towards \( A, P, B \). So \( \vec{QA} \), \( \vec{QP} \) are collinear and in the same direction, hence \( \angle AQP = 0 \). Similarly, \( \vec{QB} \) and \( \vec{QP} \) are collinear and in the same direction, so \( \angle BQP = 0 \). Thus \( \angle AQP = \angle BQP = 0 \). This holds for any order of \( A,P,B,Q \) as long as \( Q \) is an external point to \( AB \) and \( P \) is internal. For instance, if \( Q,A,P,B \) is the order, \( \vec{QA}, \vec{QP}, \vec{QB} \) all point in the opposite direction, and the angles are still zero. So the statement holds for \( M=Q \).

Now, assume \( M \neq P \) and \( M \) is not on the line \( AB \). Then \( \triangle AMB \) is a non-degenerate triangle. The point \( P \) lies on the side \( AB \) of \( \triangle AMB \).
By the Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, if a point \( P \) on the side \( AB \) of \( \triangle AMB \) satisfies \( \frac{|MA|}{|MB|} = \frac{|AP|}{|PB|} \), then the line segment \( MP \) is the internal angle bisector of \( \angle AMB \).
Therefore, \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \).

The point \( C \) is one such point \( M \). For \( M=C \), \( CP \) is the internal angle bisector of \( \angle ACB \), so \( \angle ACP = \angle BCP \). This is true by the definition of \( P \).

In summary:
1.  \( P \) and \( Q \) are points on line \( AB \) such that \( |AP|/|PB| = |AQ|/|BQ| = |AC|/|BC| = k \). (P divides \( AB \) internally, Q externally). We have \( k \neq 1 \) since \( |AC| \neq |BC| \).
2.  The circle with diameter \( PQ \) is the Apollonius circle for points \( A,B \) and ratio \( k \).
3.  Any point \( M \) on this circle satisfies \( |MA|/|MB|=k \).
4.  Combining \( |MA|/|MB|=k \) and \( |AP|/|PB|=k \), we get \( |MA|/|MB|=|AP|/|PB| \).
5.  If \( M \) is not on line \( AB \), by the Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, \( MP \) is the internal bisector of \( \angle AMB \). So \( \angle AMP = \angle BMP \).
6.  If \( M \) is on line \( AB \), then \( M=Q \) (since we assumed \( M \neq P \)). In this case, \( \angle AQP = \angle BQP = 0 \), so the equality holds.
The condition \( M \neq P \) is necessary for the angles \( \angle AMP, \angle BMP \) to be well-defined in the usual geometric sense, as \( \vec{MP} \) would otherwise be a zero vector.

problem:
A5 Each of the integers from $1$ to $n$ is written on a separate card, and then the cards are combined into a deck and shuffled. Three players, $A, B$, and $C$, take turns in the order $A, B, C, A, \ldots$ choosing one card at random from the deck. (Each card in the deck is equally likely to be chosen.) After a card is chosen, that card and all higher-numbered cards are removed from the deck, and the remaining cards are reshuffled before the next turn. Play continues until one of the three players wins the game by drawing the card numbered $1$.
Show that for each of the three players, there are arbitrarily large values of $n$ for which that player has the highest probability among the three players of winning the game.
solution:
A5 First solution. Let $a_{n}, b_{n}, c_{n}$ be the probabilities that players $A, B, C$, respectively, will win the game. We compute these by induction on $n$, starting with the values

$$
a_{1}=1, \quad b_{1}=0, \quad c_{1}=0
$$

If player $A$ draws card $k$, then the resulting game state is that of a deck of $k-1$ cards with the players taking turns in the order $B, C, A, B, \ldots$ In this state, the probabilities that players $A, B, C$ will win are $c_{k-1}, a_{k-1}, b_{k-1}$ provided that we adopt the convention that

$$
a_{0}=0, \quad b_{0}=0, \quad c_{0}=1
$$

We thus have
$a_{n}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} c_{k-1}, \quad b_{n}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k-1}, \quad c_{n}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} b_{k-1}$.
Put

$$
x_{n}=a_{n}-b_{n}, \quad y_{n}=b_{n}-c_{n}, \quad z_{n}=c_{n}-a_{n}
$$
we then have
\$\$\begin{aligned}

\& x_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1} x_{n}+\frac{1}{n+1} z_{n} 
\& y_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1} y_{n}+\frac{1}{n+1} x_{n}, 
\& z_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1} z_{n}+\frac{1}{n+1} y_{n} .

\end{aligned}\$\$

Note that if $a_{n+1}=b_{n+1}=c_{n+1}=0$, then

$$
x_{n}=-n z_{n}=n^{2} y_{n}=-n^{3} x_{n}=n^{4} z_{n}
$$
and so $x_{n}=z_{n}=0$, or in other words $a_{n}=b_{n}=c_{n}$. By induction on $n$, we deduce that $a_{n}, b_{n}, c_{n}$ cannot all be equal. That is, the quantities $x_{n}, y_{n}, z_{n}$ add up to zero and at most one of them vanishes; consequently, the quantity $r_{n}=\sqrt{x_{n}^{2}+y_{n}^{2}+z_{n}^{2}}$ is always positive and the quantities
$$
x_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{x_{n}}{r_{n}}, \quad y_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{y_{n}}{r_{n}}, \quad z_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{z_{n}}{r_{n}}
$$

form the coordinates of a point $P_{n}$ on a fixed circle $C$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.

Let $P_{n}^{\prime}$ be the point $\left(z_{n}, x_{n}, y_{n}\right)$ obtained from $P_{n}$ by a clockwise rotation of angle $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$. The point $P_{n+1}$ then lies on the ray through the origin passing through the point dividing the chord from $P_{n}$ to $P_{n}^{\prime}$ in the ratio $1: n$. The (clockwise) arc from $P_{n}$ to $P_{n+1}$ therefore has a measure of

$$
\arctan \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 n-1}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 n-1}+O\left(n^{-3}\right)
$$
these measures form a null sequence whose sum diverges. It follows that any arc of $C$ contains infinitely many of the $P_{n}$; taking a suitably short arc around the point $\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$, we deduce that for infinitely many $n, A$ has the highest winning probability, and similarly for $B$ and $C$.
Remark: From the previous analysis, we also deduce that
$$
\frac{r_{n+1}}{r_{n}}=\frac{\sqrt{n^{2}-n+1}}{n+1}=1-\frac{3}{2(n+1)}+O\left(n^{-2}\right)
$$

from which it follows that $r_{n} \sim c n^{-3 / 2}$ for some $c>0$.
Second solution. (by Noam Elkies) In this approach, we instead compute the probability $p_{n}(m)$ that the game ends after exactly $m$ turns (the winner being determined
by the residue of $m \bmod 3)$. We use the convention that $p_{0}(0)=1, p_{0}(m)=0$ for $m>0$. Define the generating function $P_{n}(X)=\sum_{m=0}^{n} p_{n}(m) x^{m}$. We will establish that

$$
P_{n}(X)=\frac{X(X+1) \cdots(X+n-1)}{n!}
$$
(which may be guessed by computing $p_{n}(m)$ for small $n$ by hand). There are several ways to do this; for instance, this follows from the recursion
$$
P_{n}(X)=\frac{1}{n} X P_{n-1}(X)+\frac{(n-1)}{n} P_{n-1}(X) .
$$

(In this recursion, the first term corresponds to conditional probabilities given that the first card drawn is $n$, and the second term corresponds to the remaining cases.)
Let $\omega$ be a primitive cube root of $1$. With notation as in the first solution, we have

$$
P_{n}(\omega)=a_{n}+b_{n} \omega+c_{n} \omega
$$
combining this with the explicit formula for $P_{n}(X)$ and the observation that
$$
\arg (w+n)=\arctan \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 n-1}
$$

recovers the geometric description of $a_{n}, b_{n}, c_{n}$ given in the first solution (as well as the remark following the first solution).
Third solution. For this argument, we use the auxiliary quantities

$$
a_{n}^{\prime}=a_{n}-\frac{1}{3}, \quad b_{n}^{\prime}=b_{n}-\frac{1}{3}, \quad c_{n}^{\prime}=c_{n}-\frac{1}{3}
$$
these satisfy the relations
$$
a_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} c_{k-1}^{\prime}, \quad b_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k-1}^{\prime}, \quad c_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} b_{k-1}^{\prime}
$$

as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{n+1}^{\prime}=a_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& b_{n+1}^{\prime}=b_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(a_{n}^{\prime}-b_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& c_{n+1}^{\prime}=c_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(b_{n}^{\prime}-c_{n}^{\prime}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We now show that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}^{\prime}$ cannot diverge to $+\infty$ (and likewise for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n}^{\prime}$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_{n}^{\prime}$ by similar reasoning). Suppose the contrary; then there exists some $\varepsilon>0$ and some $n_{0}>0$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k}^{\prime} \geq \varepsilon$ for all $n \geq n_{0}$. For $n>n_{0}$, we have $b_{n}^{\prime} \geq \varepsilon$; this in turn implies that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n}^{\prime}$ diverges to $+\infty$. Continuing around the circle, we deduce that for $n$ sufficiently large, all three of $a_{n}^{\prime}, b_{n}^{\prime}, c_{n}^{\prime}$ are positive; but this contradicts the identity
$a_{n}^{\prime}+b_{n}^{\prime}+c_{n}^{\prime}=0$. We thus conclude that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}^{\prime}$ does not diverge to $+\infty$; in particular, $\liminf _{n \rightarrow \infty} a_{n}^{\prime} \leq 0$.
By the same token, we may see that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}^{\prime}$ cannot converge to a positive limit $L$ (and likewise for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n}^{\prime}$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_{n}^{\prime}$ by similar reasoning). Namely, this would imply that $b_{n}^{\prime} \geq L / 2$ for $n$ sufficiently large, contradicting the previous argument.

By similar reasoning, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}^{\prime}$ cannot diverge to $-\infty$ or converge to a negative limit $L$ (and likewise for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n}^{\prime}$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_{n}^{\prime}$ by similar reasoning).
We next establish that there are infinitely many $n$ for which $a_{n}^{\prime}>0$ (and likewise for $b_{n}^{\prime}$ and $c_{n}^{\prime}$ by similar reasoning). Suppose to the contrary that for $n$ sufficiently large, we have $a_{n}^{\prime} \leq 0$. By the previous arguments, the sum $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}^{\prime}$ cannot diverge to $\infty$ or converge to a nonzero limit; it must therefore converge to $0$. In particular, for $n$ sufficiently large, we have $b_{n}^{\prime}=\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{k-1}^{\prime} \geq 0$. Iterating the construction, we see that for $n$ sufficiently large, we must have $c_{n}^{\prime} \leq 0, a_{n}^{\prime} \geq 0$, $b_{n}^{\prime} \leq 0$, and $c_{n}^{\prime} \geq 0$. As a result, for $n$ sufficiently large we must have $a_{n}^{\prime}=b_{n}^{\prime}=c_{n}^{\prime}=0$; but we may rule this out as in the original solution.
By similar reasoning, we may deduce that there are infinitely many $n$ for which $a_{n}^{\prime}<0$ (and likewise for $b_{n}^{\prime}$ and $c_{n}^{\prime}$ by similar reasoning). We now continue using a suggestion of Jon Atkins. Define the values of the sequence $x_{n}$ according to the relative comparison of $a_{n}^{\prime}, b_{n}^{\prime}, c_{n}^{\prime}$ (using the fact that these cannot all be equal):

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
x_{n}=1: & a_{n}^{\prime} \leq b_{n}^{\prime}<c_{n}^{\prime} \\
x_{n}=2: & b_{n}^{\prime} \leq c_{n}^{\prime}<a_{n}^{\prime} \\
x_{n}=3: & c_{n}^{\prime} \leq a_{n}^{\prime}<b_{n}^{\prime} \\
x_{n}=4: & a_{n}^{\prime}<c_{n}^{\prime} \leq b_{n}^{\prime} \\
x_{n}=5: & b_{n}^{\prime}<a_{n}^{\prime} \leq c_{n}^{\prime} \\
x_{n}=6: & c_{n}^{\prime}<b_{n}^{\prime} \leq a_{n}^{\prime} .
\end{array}
$$

We consider these values as states and say that there is a transition from state $i$ to state $j$, and write $i \Rightarrow j$, if for every $n \geq 2$ with $x_{n}=i$ there exists $n^{\prime}>n$ with $x_{n^{\prime}}=j$. (In all cases when we use this notation, it will in fact be the case that the first value of $n^{\prime}>n$ for which $x_{n^{\prime}} \neq i$ satisfes $x_{n^{\prime}}=j$, but this is not logically necessary for our final conclusion.)
Suppose that $x_{n}=1$. By the earlier discussion, we must have $a_{n^{\prime}}^{\prime}>0$ for some $n^{\prime}>n$, and so we cannot have $x_{n^{\prime}}=1$ for all $n^{\prime}>n$. On the other hand, as long as $x_{n}=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_{n+1}^{\prime}-b_{n+1}^{\prime} & =c_{n}^{\prime}-b_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(2 b_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}-c_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& =\frac{n-1}{n+1}\left(c_{n}^{\prime}-b_{n}^{\prime}\right)+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)>0 \\
c_{n+1}^{\prime}-a_{n+1}^{\prime} & =c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(a_{n}^{\prime}+b_{n}^{\prime}-2 c_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& =\frac{n-1}{n+1}\left(c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(b_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)>0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, for $n^{\prime}$ the smallest value for which $x_{n^{\prime}} \neq$ $x_{n}$, we must have $x_{n^{\prime}}=2$. By this and two similar arguments, we deduce that

$$
1 \Rightarrow 5, \quad 2 \Rightarrow 6, \quad 3 \Rightarrow 4
$$

Suppose that $x_{n}=4$. By the earlier discussion, we must have $a_{n^{\prime}}^{\prime}<0$ for some $n^{\prime}>n$, and so we cannot have $x_{n^{\prime}}=4$ for all $n^{\prime}>n$. On the other hand, as long as $x_{n}=4$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+1}^{\prime}-a_{n+1}^{\prime} & =b_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(2 a_{n}^{\prime}-b_{n}^{\prime}-c_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& =\frac{n-1}{n+1}\left(b_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(b_{n}^{\prime}-c_{n}^{\prime}\right)>0 \\
c_{n+1}^{\prime}-a_{n+1}^{\prime} & =c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(a_{n}^{\prime}+b_{n}^{\prime}-2 c_{n}^{\prime}\right) \\
& =\frac{n-1}{n+1}\left(c_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)+\frac{1}{n+1}\left(b_{n}^{\prime}-a_{n}^{\prime}\right)>0
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, for $n^{\prime}$ the smallest value for which $x_{n^{\prime}} \neq$ $x_{n}$, we must have $x_{n^{\prime}}=1$. By this and two similar arguments, we deduce that

$$
4 \Rightarrow 1, \quad 5 \Rightarrow 2, \quad 6 \Rightarrow 3
$$

Combining, we obtain

$$
1 \Rightarrow 5 \Rightarrow 2 \Rightarrow 6 \Rightarrow 3 \Rightarrow 4 \Rightarrow 1
$$
and hence the desired result.

problem: You are given a set of \( n \) blocks, each weighing at least 1; their total weight is \( 2n \). Prove that for every real number \( r \) with \( 0 \leq r \leq 2n-2 \), you can choose a subset of the blocks whose total weight is at least \( r \) but at most \( r+2 \).
solution:
We prove the following more general statement by induction on $n$.
Claim. Suppose that you have $n$ blocks, each of weight at least $1$, and of total weight $s \leqslant 2 n$. Then for every $r$ with $-2 \leqslant r \leqslant s$, you can choose some of the blocks whose total weight is at least $r$ but at most $r+2$.
Proof. The base case $n=1$ is trivial. To prove the inductive step, let $x$ be the largest block weight. Clearly, $x \geqslant s / n$, so $s-x \leqslant \frac{n-1}{n} s \leqslant 2(n-1)$. Hence, if we exclude a block of weight $x$, we can apply the inductive hypothesis to show the claim holds (for this smaller set) for any $-2 \leqslant r \leqslant s-x$. Adding the excluded block to each of those combinations, we see that the claim also holds when $x-2 \leqslant r \leqslant s$. So if $x-2 \leqslant s-x$, then we have covered the whole interval $[-2, s]$. But each block weight is at least $1$, so we have $x-2 \leqslant(s-(n-1))-2=s-(2 n-(n-1)) \leqslant s-(s-(n-1)) \leqslant s-x$, as desired.

Comment. Instead of inducting on sets of blocks with total weight $s \leqslant 2 n$, we could instead prove the result only for $s=2 n$. We would then need to modify the inductive step to scale up the block weights before applying the induction hypothesis.

problem:
Let \((a_{n})_{n \geqslant 1}\) be a sequence of positive real numbers with the property that

\[
(a_{n+1})^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+2} \leqslant a_{n} + a_{n+2}
\]

for all positive integers \(n\). Show that \(a_{2022} \leqslant 1\).
solution:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\subset(0,\infty)\) satisfy  

\[
(a_{n+1})^{2}+a_{n}a_{n+2}\le a_{n}+a_{n+2}\qquad(\ast)
\]
for every integer \(n\ge 1\).
Put  
\[
b_n:=1-a_n\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
Throughout the proof we use repeatedly the equivalent form  

\[
(a_{n+1})^{2}+b_nb_{\,n+2}\le 1\qquad(n\ge 1),
\tag{1}
\]
which is obtained from \((\ast)\) by replacing \(a_{k}=1-b_k\) and expanding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  
If \(a_n>1\) and \(a_{n+1}>1\) then \(a_{n+2}<1\).

Proof.  
Assume \(a_n>1,\ a_{n+1}>1\) and \(a_{n+2}\ge 1\).  
Put \(x=a_n,\;y=a_{n+1},\;z=a_{n+2}\).  
Because \(x>1\), the function
\[
F(t)=y^{2}+xt-(x+t)\qquad(t>0)
\]
is strictly increasing (\(F'(t)=x-1>0\)).
Consequently  
\[
0\ge F(z)\ge F(1)=y^{2}-1>0 ,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus \(a_{n+2}<1\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 2.  
It is impossible that \(a_k\le 1<a_{k+1}\) for some \(k\).

Proof.  
Suppose \(a_k=u\le 1,\ a_{k+1}=v>1\).
Let \(w=a_{k+2}\).  
From \((\ast)\) with \(n=k\) we obtain
\[
v^{2}+uw\le u+w\Longrightarrow (u-1)w\le u-v^{2}.
\tag{2}
\]
Since \(u-1\le 0\) and \(u-v^{2}<0\), division by the negative number
\(u-1\) reverses the inequality:
\[
w\ge\frac{v^{2}-u}{1-u}.
\tag{3}
\]

Using \((\ast)\) with \(n=k+1\) we get
\[
w^{2}+v\,a_{k+3}\le v+a_{k+3}\Longrightarrow
w^{2}\le v,
\tag{4}
\]
hence \(w<\sqrt v\).

Inequalities (3) and (4) together give
\[
\frac{v^{2}-u}{1-u}<\sqrt v.
\tag{5}
\]

Define  
\[
G(u,v):=\bigl(v^{2}-u\bigr)^{2}-v(1-u)^{2}\qquad
\bigl(0\le u<1,\;v>1\bigr).
\]
A short calculation yields  

\[
\frac{\partial G}{\partial u}=2(1-v)(u+v)<0,
\]
so \(G(u,v)\) is decreasing in \(u\).
Thus \(G(u,v)\ge G(1,v)=(v^{2}-1)^{2}>0\).
Inequality \(G(u,v)\ge 0\) is exactly
\[
\frac{v^{2}-u}{1-u}\ge\sqrt v,
\]
which contradicts (5).  Hence the configuration
\(a_k\le 1<a_{k+1}\) is impossible. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Corollary 3.  
Once the sequence drops to (or below) the level \(1\) it never
returns above it:  
if \(a_m\le 1\) for some \(m\), then \(a_{m+r}\le 1\) for every
\(r\ge 0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 4.  
At least one of the three first terms does not exceed \(1\); i.e.  
\[
\min\{a_1,a_2,a_3\}\le 1.
\]

Proof.  
If \(a_1\le 1\) we are done.  
Assume \(a_1>1\).

•  If \(a_2\le 1\) we are done again.

•  If \(a_2>1\) then Lemma 1 (applied with \(n=1\))
forces \(a_3<1\).

Thus in every case some \(a_m\;(m\le 3)\) is \(\le 1\).
∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Completion of the proof.

Let \(m\le 3\) be the first index with \(a_m\le 1\) (Lemma 4).
By Corollary 3 all later terms are also \(\le 1\):
\(a_{m+1},a_{m+2},\dots\le 1\).
Since \(2022\ge m\), we conclude
\[
\,a_{2022}\le 1\,.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Hence every sequence of positive numbers obeying \((\ast)\)
satisfies \(a_{2022}\le 1\), as was to be shown.

problem:
Let \((a_{n})_{n \geqslant 1}\) be a sequence of positive real numbers with the property that

\[
(a_{n+1})^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+2} \leqslant a_{n} + a_{n+2}
\]

for all positive integers \(n\). Show that \(a_{2022} \leqslant 1\).
solution:
Let the given inequality be
\[ (a_{n+1})^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+2} \leqslant a_{n} + a_{n+2} \quad (*). \]
This inequality holds for all positive integers \(n\). The sequence \((a_n)_{n \geqslant 1}\) consists of positive real numbers, so \(a_n > 0\) for all \(n\).
We can rewrite the inequality as:
\[ (a_{n+1})^2 \leqslant a_n + a_{n+2} - a_n a_{n+2}. \]
The right hand side can be factored:
\[ a_n + a_{n+2} - a_n a_{n+2} = 1 - (1 - a_n - a_{n+2} + a_n a_{n+2}) = 1 - (1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2}). \]
So the inequality becomes
\[ (a_{n+1})^2 \leqslant 1 - (1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2}) \quad (**). \]

An alternative way to rewrite the inequality is in terms of \(b_n = a_n-1\). Since \(a_n>0\), \(b_n > -1\).
The original inequality is \((1+b_{n+1})^2 + (1+b_n)(1+b_{n+2}) \le (1+b_n) + (1+b_{n+2})\).
Expanding this, we get \(1+2b_{n+1}+b_{n+1}^2 + 1+b_n+b_{n+2}+b_n b_{n+2} \le 1+b_n+1+b_{n+2}\).
Simplifying, we have \(2b_{n+1}+b_{n+1}^2+b_n b_{n+2} \le 0\).
This can be written as \(b_{n+1}(2+b_{n+1}) + b_n b_{n+2} \le 0 \quad (***)\).
Note that \(2+b_{n+1} = a_{n+1}+1\). Since \(a_{n+1}>0\), \(a_{n+1}+1>1\). So \(2+b_{n+1}>1\).

Let's analyze the consequences of these inequalities.

Step 1: Consequences of \(a_k > 1\) for its neighbours.
Suppose \(a_{n+1} > 1\) for some \(n \ge 1\). Then \((a_{n+1})^2 > 1\).
From \((**)\), we have \(1 < (a_{n+1})^2 \leqslant 1 - (1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2})\).
This implies \(1 < 1 - (1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2})\), which simplifies to \(0 < -(1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2})\), or \((1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2}) < 0\).
This means that \(1-a_n\) and \(1-a_{n+2}\) must have opposite signs.
Therefore, one of \(a_n, a_{n+2}\) must be strictly less than 1, and the other must be strictly greater than 1.
Let's call this (Prop F*): If \(a_{n+1} > 1\), then (\(a_n < 1\) and \(a_{n+2} > 1\)) or (\(a_n > 1\) and \(a_{n+2} < 1\)).
This property holds for \(n \ge 1\), so it applies to \(a_2, a_3, \dots\). That is, if \(a_k > 1\) for \(k \ge 2\), then its neighbours \(a_{k-1}, a_{k+1}\) must be one strictly less than 1 and one strictly greater than 1.

Step 2: Show that two consecutive terms \(a_k, a_{k+1}\) cannot both be greater than 1 for \(k \ge 2\).
Assume for contradiction that \(a_k > 1\) and \(a_{k+1} > 1\) for some \(k \ge 2\).
In terms of \(b_n=a_n-1\), this means \(b_k > 0\) and \(b_{k+1} > 0\).
Applying (Prop F*) to \(a_k > 1\) (since \(k \ge 2\)): Its neighbours \(a_{k-1}\) and \(a_{k+1}\) must be one \(<1\) and one \(>1\). Since \(a_{k+1}>1\) is assumed, it must be that \(a_{k-1} < 1\). So \(b_{k-1} < 0\).
Applying (Prop F*) to \(a_{k+1} > 1\) (since \(k+1 \ge 3 > 2\)): Its neighbours \(a_k\) and \(a_{k+2}\) must be one \(<1\) and one \(>1\). Since \(a_k>1\) is assumed, it must be that \(a_{k+2} < 1\). So \(b_{k+2} < 0\).
So, if \(a_k>1\) and \(a_{k+1}>1\) for \(k \ge 2\), then we must have the pattern \(a_{k-1}<1, a_k>1, a_{k+1}>1, a_{k+2}<1\). In terms of \(b_n\): \(b_{k-1}<0, b_k>0, b_{k+1}>0, b_{k+2}<0\).
Also, we know \(a_n > 0\), so \(b_n > -1\) for all \(n\). Thus \(b_{k-1} \in (-1,0)\) and \(b_{k+2} \in (-1,0)\).

Now we use inequality \((***)\) for two consecutive values of \(n\):
For \(n=k-1\): (using \(b_{k-1}, b_k, b_{k+1}\))
\(b_k(2+b_k) + b_{k-1}b_{k+1} \le 0\).
Since \(b_k>0\) and \(2+b_k>1\), \(b_k(2+b_k)>0\).
Since \(b_{k-1}<0\) and \(b_{k+1}>0\), \(b_{k-1}b_{k+1}<0\).
The inequality can be written as \(b_k(2+b_k) \le -b_{k-1}b_{k+1}\).
Since \(b_{k-1} > -1\), we have \(-b_{k-1} < 1\).
So, \(b_k(2+b_k) \le -b_{k-1}b_{k+1} < (1) \cdot b_{k+1} = b_{k+1}\).
Thus, \(b_k(2+b_k) < b_{k+1}\). (Eq 1)

For \(n=k\): (using \(b_k, b_{k+1}, b_{k+2}\))
\(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1}) + b_k b_{k+2} \le 0\).
Since \(b_{k+1}>0\) and \(2+b_{k+1}>1\), \(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1})>0\).
Since \(b_k>0\) and \(b_{k+2}<0\), \(b_k b_{k+2}<0\).
The inequality can be written as \(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1}) \le -b_k b_{k+2}\).
Since \(b_{k+2} > -1\), we have \(-b_{k+2} < 1\).
So, \(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1}) \le -b_k b_{k+2} < b_k(1) = b_k\).
Thus, \(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1}) < b_k\). (Eq 2)

From (Eq 1): \(b_k^2+2b_k < b_{k+1}\). Since \(b_k>0\), \(b_k^2>0\), so \(2b_k < b_{k+1}\).
From (Eq 2): \(b_{k+1}^2+2b_{k+1} < b_k\). Since \(b_{k+1}>0\), \(b_{k+1}^2>0\), so \(2b_{k+1} < b_k\).

Combining these results: \(2b_{k+1} < b_k\) and \(2b_k < b_{k+1}\).
So \(b_k > 2b_{k+1} > 2(2b_k) = 4b_k\).
This means \(b_k > 4b_k\).
Since \(b_k>0\), we can divide by \(b_k\) to get \(1 > 4\). This is a contradiction.
Therefore, the initial assumption that \(a_k>1\) and \(a_{k+1}>1\) for some \(k \ge 2\) must be false.
So, for any \(k \ge 2\), at least one of \(a_k\) or \(a_{k+1}\) must be \(\le 1\).

Step 3: Prove \(a_{2022} \le 1\).
Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that \(a_{2022} > 1\).
Since \(2022 \ge 2\), we can apply the result from Step 2.
Consider \(k=2022\). Since \(a_{2022}>1\), it must be that \(a_{2022+1} = a_{2023} \le 1\).
(Because if \(a_{2023}>1\), then \(a_{2022}>1\) and \(a_{2023}>1\) would hold for \(k=2022 \ge 2\), which we've shown is impossible).
Consider \(k=2021\). If \(a_{2021}>1\), then along with \(a_{2022}>1\), this is a pair of consecutive terms greater than 1. Since \(2021 \ge 2\), this is impossible by Step 2.
So, if \(a_{2022}>1\), it must be that \(a_{2021} \le 1\).

So the assumption \(a_{2022} > 1\) leads to \(a_{2021} \le 1\) and \(a_{2023} \le 1\).
This means \(1-a_{2021} \ge 0\) and \(1-a_{2023} \ge 0\).
Therefore, their product \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) \ge 0\).

Now, let's use (Prop F*) again. Since we assumed \(a_{2022} > 1\), and \(2022 \ge 2\), (Prop F*) implies that one of its neighbours \(a_{2021}, a_{2023}\) must be strictly less than 1, and the other strictly greater than 1.
This means \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) < 0\).

The conclusions \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) \ge 0\) and \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) < 0\) are contradictory.
This means that the initial assumption, \(a_{2022} > 1\), must be false.
Therefore, \(a_{2022} \le 1\).

Let's briefly check what happens if \(k=1\). Is it possible that \(a_1>1\) and \(a_2>1\)?
In this case, (Eq 1) cannot be formed as \(a_{k-1}=a_0\) is not defined.
(Eq 2) for \(k=1\) (substituting \(k \to 1\) in \(b_{k+1}(2+b_{k+1}) < b_k\)) becomes \(b_2(2+b_2) < b_1\).
This is \( (a_2-1)(a_2+1) < a_1-1 \).
This does not lead to an immediate contradiction. For example, if \(a_1=7, a_2=2\), then \(b_1=6, b_2=1\).
Then \(b_2(2+b_2) = 1(3)=3\), and \(b_1=6\). So \(3 < 6\) is true.
Also, (Prop F*) applied to \(a_2>1\) implies that if \(a_1>1\), then \(a_3<1\).
So the sequence could start \(a_1>1, a_2>1, a_3<1\). For example, \(a_1=7, a_2=2, a_3=0.5\).
Check \(b_2(2+b_2)+b_1b_3 \le 0\): \(1(3)+6(-0.5) = 3-3=0\). This is \(0 \le 0\), which is true. So this sequence is possible.
However, the argument for \(a_{2022}\) only uses \(k \ge 2021 \ge 2\), so the case \(k=1\) is not needed for the proof regarding \(a_{2022}\).

The proof relies on Step 2 ("for any \(k \ge 2\), at least one of \(a_k\) or \(a_{k+1}\) must be \(\le 1\)") and Step 1 ("If \(a_{n+1} > 1\), then \((1-a_n)(1-a_{n+2}) < 0\)") . Both are solid. The combination of these two for \(a_{2022}\) leads to a contradiction if \(a_{2022}>1\).

Final check of logic:
1. Premise: \(a_{2022} > 1\).
2. From Step 2 (with \(k=2021\)): If \(a_{2021}>1\) and \(a_{2022}>1\), that's a contradiction because \(2021 \ge 2\). So \(a_{2021} \le 1\).
3. From Step 2 (with \(k=2022\)): If \(a_{2022}>1\) and \(a_{2023}>1\), that's a contradiction because \(2022 \ge 2\). So \(a_{2023} \le 1\).
4. From (2) and (3), if \(a_{2022}>1\), then \(a_{2021} \le 1\) and \(a_{2023} \le 1\).
5. This implies \(1-a_{2021} \ge 0\) and \(1-a_{2023} \ge 0\). So \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) \ge 0\).
6. From Step 1 (Prop F*), applied to \(a_{2022}\) (letting \(n+1 = 2022\), so \(n=2021 \ge 1\)): if \(a_{2022}>1\), then \((1-a_{2021})(1-a_{2023}) < 0\).
7. Points (5) and (6) are contradictory. Thus, the premise \(a_{2022}>1\) must be false.
8. Therefore, \(a_{2022} \le 1\).

problem:
Let \( p \) be a prime number and let \( s \) be an integer with \( 0 < s < p \). Prove that there exist integers \( m \) and \( n \) with \( 0 < m < n < p \) and

\[
\left\{\frac{s m}{p}\right\} < \left\{\frac{s n}{p}\right\} < \frac{s}{p}
\]

if and only if \( s \) is not a divisor of \( p-1 \).
solution:
Let $\{x\}$ denote the fractional part of $x$, i.e., $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$.
The given condition is
\[ \left\{\frac{s m}{p}\right\} < \left\{\frac{s n}{p}\right\} < \frac{s}{p} \]
Let $r_k = sk \pmod p$ be the remainder when $sk$ is divided by $p$. Then $\{sk/p\} = r_k/p$.
Since $0 < s < p$, we have $0 < s/p < 1$, so $\{s/p\} = s/p$.
The condition becomes
\[ \frac{r_m}{p} < \frac{r_n}{p} < \frac{s}{p} \]
Multiplying by $p$ (which is positive), this is equivalent to
\[ r_m < r_n < s \]
We are given $0 < m < n < p$.
Since $p$ is prime and $0 < s < p$, $s$ is not a multiple of $p$. Thus $s$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $p$, denoted by $s^{-1}$.
The values $r_k = sk \pmod p$ for $k=1, \dots, p-1$ are a permutation of $1, \dots, p-1$.
Note that $r_1 = s \pmod p = s$.
The condition $r_m < s$ implies $r_m < r_1$. This means $m \neq 1$.
Thus, we are looking for integers $m, n$ such that $1 < m < n < p$ and $r_m < r_n < s$.

Let $L_s = \{k \in \{1, \dots, p-1\} : r_k < s\}$.
The elements $r_k$ for $k \in L_s$ are precisely the set $\{1, 2, \dots, s-1\}$.
Let $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$. Then $r_k = x$ means $sk \equiv x \pmod p$. This implies $k \equiv xs^{-1} \pmod p$.
Let $s_0 = s^{-1} \pmod p$. Then $k_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ is the unique index in $\{1, \dots, p-1\}$ such that $r_{k_x} = x$.
The condition $m \neq 1$ means $k_x \neq 1$. If $k_x=1$, then $xs_0 \equiv 1 \pmod p$, so $x \equiv s \pmod p$. Since $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$, this is impossible. Thus $k_x \neq 1$ for all $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
So, $m, n$ must be of the form $k_x, k_y$ for some $x,y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
The condition becomes: there exist $x, y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$ such that $x < y$ (this is $r_m < r_n$) and $k_x < k_y$ (this is $m<n$).
Let $m = k_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ and $n = k_y = ys_0 \pmod p$. We need $x < y$ and $m < n$.
The condition $r_n < s$ means $y < s$, which is true since $y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.

The problem is therefore equivalent to proving that there exist $x, y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$ with $x < y$ such that $xs_0 \pmod p < ys_0 \pmod p$ if and only if $s \nmid p-1$.
This means that such $m,n$ do not exist if and only if for all $x,y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$ with $x<y$, we have $xs_0 \pmod p > ys_0 \pmod p$.
This latter condition means that the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ for $x=1, 2, \dots, s-1$ is strictly decreasing: $a_1 > a_2 > \dots > a_{s-1}$.

Let's analyze when the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ (for $x=1, \dots, s-1$) is strictly decreasing.
For $a_x$ to be strictly decreasing, we must have $a_{x+1} < a_x$ for all $x \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$.
$a_{x+1} = (x+1)s_0 \pmod p = (xs_0 + s_0) \pmod p = (a_x + s_0) \pmod p$.
So we need $(a_x+s_0) \pmod p < a_x$. This occurs if $a_x+s_0 \ge p$.
So, the sequence $a_x$ is strictly decreasing if and only if $a_x+s_0 \ge p$ for all $x \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$.
This means $\lfloor (x+1)s_0/p \rfloor - \lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor \ge 1$ for $x \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$.
Since $s_0 < p$, $s_0/p < 1$. Thus $\lfloor (x+1)s_0/p \rfloor - \lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor$ can only be $0$ or $1$.
(Specifically, $ (x+1)s_0 < xp+p \implies (x+1)s_0/p < x s_0/p + 1 $ if $s_0/p < 1$).
So we must have $\lfloor (x+1)s_0/p \rfloor - \lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor = 1$ for $x=1, \dots, s-2$.
Let $q_x = \lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor$. Then $q_{x+1} = q_x+1$ for $x=1, \dots, s-2$.
Since $s_0 \in \{1, \dots, p-1\}$, $q_1 = \lfloor s_0/p \rfloor = 0$.
Thus, $q_x = x-1$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$. (For $x=1$, $q_1=0$. For $x=2$, $q_2=1, \dots$, for $x=s-1$, $q_{s-1}=s-2$).
The condition $\lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor = x-1$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$ means that $(x-1)p \le xs_0 < xp$.
This must hold for all $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
For $x=1$, it means $0 \le s_0 < p$, which is true.
For $x > 1$, it implies $s_0 \ge \frac{x-1}{x}p$.
To satisfy this for all $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$, we must satisfy it for the largest value of $\frac{x-1}{x}$, which is when $x=s-1$.
So we need $s_0 \ge \frac{s-2}{s-1}p$.
Also, $s_0 < p$ is given by $xs_0 < xp$. (For $x=1$, $s_0 < p$).
So the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ is strictly decreasing if and only if $p > s_0 \ge \frac{s-2}{s-1}p = p - \frac{p}{s-1}$.
Let $s_0 = (tp+1)/s$ for some integer $t$. Since $0 < s_0 < p$, $0 < tp+1 < sp$. This means $tp+1 > 0 \implies t \ge 0$. Since $s_0 \ne 0$, $t p+1 \ne 0$. And $tp < sp-1 \implies t < s-1/p \implies t \le s-1$.
(If $t=0$, then $s_0=1/s$. This is an integer only if $s=1$. If $s=1$, then $s_0=1$. The sequence is $a_1=1$. There is only one term. The condition for $m,n$ does not apply as $x,y \in \{1, ..., s-1\}$ becomes empty set. If $s=1$, $r_m<r_n<1$ which is impossible as $r_k \ge 1$. Also $s=1$ always divides $p-1$. So the statement says: (impossible condition) iff $1 \nmid p-1$ (false). This holds.)
Assume $s>1$. Then $t \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
The condition for $a_x$ to be strictly decreasing is $p - \frac{p}{s-1} \le \frac{tp+1}{s} < p$.
$sp - \frac{sp}{s-1} \le tp+1 < sp$.
From $tp+1 < sp$: $t < s - 1/p$, so $t \le s-1$.
From $sp - \frac{sp}{s-1} \le tp+1$:
$s - \frac{s}{s-1} \le t + \frac{1}{p}$.
$s - (1+\frac{1}{s-1}) \le t + \frac{1}{p}$.
$s-1 - \frac{1}{s-1} \le t + \frac{1}{p}$.
Since $t$ is an integer and $s>1$:
$t \ge \lceil s-1 - \frac{1}{s-1} - \frac{1}{p} \rceil$.
Since $p \ge 2$ and $s \ge 2$: $\frac{1}{s-1} > 0$ and $\frac{1}{p} > 0$.
If $s=2$, then $t \ge \lceil 1 - 1 - 1/p \rceil = \lceil -1/p \rceil = 0$. But we know $t \ge 1$. $t \le s-1 = 1$. So $t=1$.
If $s=2$, $s_0 = (p+1)/2$. $s_0 \ge p-p/(2-1)=0$. Sequence $a_1=(p+1)/2$. It's strictly decreasing (vacuously true for $s-1=1$ terms). $s=2$ divides $p-1$ (if $p>2$, $p$ is odd). So $s=2$ implies non-existence.
If $s>2$, then $0 < \frac{1}{s-1} < 1$ (unless $s-1=1 \implies s=2$).
So $t \ge s-1$.
Combined with $t \le s-1$, we must have $t=s-1$.
So, the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ is strictly decreasing for $x=1, \dots, s-1$ if and only if $t=s-1$.
This means $s_0 s = (s-1)p+1$.
$s_0 = \frac{(s-1)p+1}{s} = \frac{sp-p+1}{s} = p - \frac{p-1}{s}$.
This expression for $s_0$ requires $s$ to be a divisor of $p-1$.
Let $c = (p-1)/s$. Then $s_0 = p-c$.
So, the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ is strictly decreasing if and only if $s|(p-1)$.

We can now prove the two directions of the statement.

$(\Rightarrow)$ Assume that there exist integers $m, n$ with $0 < m < n < p$ and $r_m < r_n < s$.
As shown above, this means there exist $x,y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$ with $x<y$ such that $k_x < k_y$, where $k_z = zs_0 \pmod p$.
This means the sequence $a_z = zs_0 \pmod p$ for $z=1, \dots, s-1$ is not strictly decreasing.
From our analysis, if the sequence $a_z$ is not strictly decreasing, it must be that $s_0 \neq p-(p-1)/s$.
This implies that $s$ is not a divisor of $p-1$.
This proves the forward direction. (Existence of $m,n \implies s \nmid p-1$).

$(\Leftarrow)$ Assume that $s$ is not a divisor of $p-1$.
Then $s_0 = s^{-1} \pmod p$ is not equal to $p-(p-1)/s$.
This means that the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$ is not strictly decreasing.
(The argument was that it is strictly decreasing iff $\lfloor xs_0/p \rfloor = x-1$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$, which happens iff $s_0 = p-(p-1)/s$).
Since the sequence $a_x$ is not strictly decreasing, there must exist some $x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$ such that $a_{x_0} > a_{x_0+1}$ is false, i.e., $a_{x_0} < a_{x_0+1}$ (since $a_x$ are distinct values as $x s_0 \equiv (x+1) s_0 \pmod p$ means $s_0 \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which is impossible).
Let $m = a_{x_0} = x_0s_0 \pmod p$ and $n = a_{x_0+1} = (x_0+1)s_0 \pmod p$.
Then $m < n$.
The corresponding remainders are $r_m = x_0$ and $r_n = x_0+1$.
We have $r_m = x_0 < x_0+1 = r_n$.
Since $x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$, $r_n = x_0+1 \le s-1$. So $r_n < s$.
Thus, $r_m < r_n < s$.
We also need to ensure $1 < m < n < p$.
$m = x_0s_0 \pmod p$. Since $x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$ and $s_0 \in \{1, \dots, p-1\}$, $m \neq 0$. So $m \in \{1, \dots, p-1\}$.
If $m=1$, then $x_0s_0 \equiv 1 \pmod p$, which means $x_0 \equiv s \pmod p$. This contradicts $x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$ (since $s \ge 2$ for $s-2 \ge 0$; if $s=1$ we already handled it, if $s=2$, $x_0 \in \emptyset$, this step applies for $s \ge 3$. Let's check $s=2$ later).
So $m > 1$. Similarly $n > 1$.
This construction provides the required $m, n$ when $s \ge 3$.

Let's check the edge cases:
- If $s=1$: $0 < s < p$ is $0 < 1 < p$. So $p \ge 2$. (If $p=2$, $s=1$).
The condition $r_m < r_n < s$ becomes $r_m < r_n < 1$. Since $r_k \in \{1, \dots, p-1\}$, this is impossible. So such $m,n$ never exist for $s=1$.
The statement becomes: (False) $\iff$ ($1 \nmid p-1$).
This means $1 | p-1$ must be true for the statement to hold. Indeed, $1$ divides any integer $p-1$. So the statement holds for $s=1$.

- If $s=2$: $0 < 2 < p$, so $p \ge 3$.
The condition is $r_m < r_n < 2$. This means $r_n=1$. So $r_m$ must be $0$ or a fraction, which is impossible as $r_m \in \{1, ..., p-1\}$. So such $m,n$ never exist for $s=2$.
The statement becomes: (False) $\iff$ ($2 \nmid p-1$).
This means $2 | p-1$ must be true. For $p \ge 3$ and $p$ prime, $p$ is odd, so $p-1$ is even. Thus $2 | p-1$ is true. So the statement holds for $s=2$.

The argument that " $a_x$ is not strictly decreasing $\implies \exists x_0$ such that $a_{x_0} < a_{x_0+1}$" holds for $s \ge 3$, as $(s-1) \ge 2$, so the sequence $a_1, \dots, a_{s-1}$ has at least two terms.
$x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$ is used. If $s=2$, this set is empty. If $s=1$, this set is empty.
The reasoning that $a_x$ is strictly decreasing iff $s|(p-1)$ is based on $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
If $s=2$, $x \in \{1\}$. The sequence is $a_1 = s_0$. It is trivially strictly decreasing.
In this case ($s=2$), $s_0 = s^{-1} \pmod p = 2^{-1} \pmod p$. Since $p$ is odd, $2^{-1}=(p+1)/2$.
$s|(p-1)$ is $2|(p-1)$, which is true for $p\ge 3$.
So for $s=2$, the sequence $a_x$ is strictly decreasing, and $s|(p-1)$ is true. This matches the equivalence.
So the non-existence of $m,n$ for $s=2$ is consistent with $s|(p-1)$ being true.

Therefore, the chain of equivalences holds for all $s$ with $0 < s < p$.
(Existence of $m,n$) $\iff$ (The sequence $a_x=xs^{-1}\pmod p$ for $x=1,\dots,s-1$ is NOT strictly decreasing) $\iff$ ($s \nmid p-1$).

Final check of the logic:
1.  The problem asks for $0 < m < n < p$ with $sk \pmod p < sn \pmod p < s$. As $s \cdot 1 \pmod p = s$, $m \neq 1$. So $1 < m < n < p$.
2.  Let $r_k = sk \pmod p$. We are looking for $1 < m < n < p$ with $r_m < r_n < s$.
3.  Let $s_0 = s^{-1} \pmod p$. For any $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$, let $k_x = xs_0 \pmod p$. Then $r_{k_x} = x$.
    Also $k_x \neq 0$. And $k_x \neq 1$, because $xs_0 \equiv 1 \pmod p \implies x \equiv s \pmod p$, which is impossible for $x \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$. So $k_x \ge 2$.
4.  The condition is equivalent to finding $x,y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$ such that $x < y$ (so $r_{k_x} < r_{k_y}$) and $k_x < k_y$ (so $m=k_x, n=k_y$ gives $m<n$). Also $r_{k_y} < s$ means $y<s$, which is true for $y \in \{1, \dots, s-1\}$.
5.  Thus, such $m,n$ exist if and only if the sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$ is not strictly decreasing. (If it's not strictly decreasing, then there must be some $x_0 \in \{1, \dots, s-2\}$ such that $a_{x_0} < a_{x_0+1}$. Then $x=x_0, y=x_0+1$ satisfy the conditions).
6.  The sequence $a_x = xs_0 \pmod p$ for $x=1, \dots, s-1$ is strictly decreasing if and only if $s_0 = p - (p-1)/s$. This requires $s$ to divide $p-1$.
7.  Therefore, such $m,n$ exist if and only if $s \nmid p-1$.

This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem:
Let \( p \) be a prime number and let \( s \) be an integer with \( 0 < s < p \). Prove that there exist integers \( m \) and \( n \) with \( 0 < m < n < p \) and

\[
\left\{\frac{s m}{p}\right\} < \left\{\frac{s n}{p}\right\} < \frac{s}{p}
\]

if and only if \( s \) is not a divisor of \( p-1 \).
solution:
Throughout the proof we write  

\[
r_k=\left\{\frac{s k}{p}\right\}=\frac{(s k)\bmod p}{p},\qquad 1\le k\le p-1 .
\]

Because \(\gcd (s,p)=1\), multiplication by \(s\) permutes the non–zero residues
modulo \(p\); hence the integers  

\[
(s k)\bmod p,\;k=1,\dots ,p-1
\]

are exactly the numbers \(1,2,\dots ,p-1\) in some order.

Define  

\[
\mathcal G=\{k\in\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\mid (s k)\bmod p < s\}.
\]

(The indices in \(\mathcal G\) will be called “good”.)  
Because each residue \(j\;(1\le j\le s-1)\) occurs exactly once,  

\[
|\mathcal G|=s-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall j\in\{1,\dots ,s-1\}\; \exists !\;k_j\in\mathcal G\;:\;(s k_j)\bmod p=j .
\tag{1}
\]

For these \(k_j\) we have \(r_{k_j}=j/p<s/p\).

The problem asks for two good indices \(m<n\) with \(r_m<r_n\);
in the language above we have to decide when the
sequence \(j\mapsto k_j\;(j=1,\dots ,s-1)\) is {\em not} strictly decreasing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  If \(s\mid(p-1)\) no such pair exists
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume \(s\mid(p-1)\) and write  

\[
t=\frac{p-1}{s}\quad(\text{so }p=1+st).
\]

For \(j=1,\dots ,s-1\) put  

\[
k_j=p-tj\qquad(1\le k_j\le p-1),
\]
then  

\[
s k_j=s(p-tj)=s p-(p-1)j\equiv j\pmod p .
\]

Thus each \(k_j\) is good and (1) gives \(k_j=p-tj\).
Because \(t>0\),
\[
j_1<j_2\;\Longrightarrow\;k_{j_1}=p-tj_1>p-tj_2=k_{j_2},
\]
i.e. the map \(j\mapsto k_j\) is strictly {\em decreasing}.
Hence for any two good indices the smaller index
carries the larger fractional part, so
no \(0<m<n<p\) can satisfy  

\[
r_m<r_n<\frac{s}{p}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  If \(s\nmid(p-1)\) a required pair always exists
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove the contrapositive:
suppose no pair \(m<n\) with \(r_m<r_n<s/p\) exists;
we show that this forces \(s\mid(p-1)\).

With the notation of (1) the absence of such a pair
means that  

\[
k_1>k_2>\dots >k_{s-1}.      \tag{2}
\]

Put  

\[
d_j=k_j-k_{j+1}\quad (j=1,\dots ,s-2),\qquad d_j>0.
\]

--------------------------------------------------
2.1  The differences \(d_j\) are all equal
--------------------------------------------------

From \((s k_j)\bmod p=j\) and \((s k_{j+1})\bmod p=j+1\) we get

\[
s(k_j-k_{j+1})\equiv j-(j+1)\equiv -1\equiv p-1\pmod p,
\]
so  

\[
p\mid s d_j+1\quad\text{for every }j.     \tag{3}
\]

Therefore \(s d_j+1=p q_j\) for some positive integers \(q_j\).
If \(d_a\neq d_b\) then from (3)
\[
p\mid s(d_a-d_b),
\qquad |s(d_a-d_b)|<s(p-1)<p^2,
\]
hence \(p\mid(d_a-d_b)\).
But \(0<|d_a-d_b|<p\), so \(d_a=d_b\).
Thus  

\[
d_1=d_2=\dots =d_{s-2}=d>0               \tag{4}
\]
and (3) gives  

\[
s d +1 = p q     \tag{5}
\]
for a fixed integer \(q\ge 1\).

--------------------------------------------------
2.2  The integer \(q\) equals \(1\)
--------------------------------------------------

By (2) and (4) we have  

\[
k_{s-1}=k_1-(s-2)d\ge 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(s-2)d\le k_1-1\le p-2.                \tag{6}
\]

Insert \(d=(p q-1)/s\) from (5) into (6):

\[
(s-2)\frac{p q-1}{s}\le p-2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(q-1)(s-2)\le \frac{p(s-2)- (p-2)s}{p}
            =\frac{s-p}{p}<1 .
\]

Because \(s\ge 2\), the left–hand side is an integer,
so it must be \(0\); hence \(q=1\).

--------------------------------------------------
2.3  Conclusion of the contrapositive
--------------------------------------------------

With \(q=1\) equation (5) reads \(s d = p-1\),
i.e. \(s\mid(p-1)\).

Thus “no admissible pair” implies \(s\mid(p-1)\);
the contrapositive says that if \(s\nmid(p-1)\)
then an admissible pair \((m,n)\) {\em does} exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Putting the two parts together
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We have proved

• If \(s\mid(p-1)\) no integers \(0<m<n<p\) satisfy  

\[
\left\{\frac{s m}{p}\right\}<\left\{\frac{s n}{p}\right\}<\frac{s}{p}.
\]

• If \(s\nmid(p-1)\) such integers must exist.

Hence the required pair \((m,n)\) exists
if and only if \(s\) is not a divisor of \(p-1\).

(The special cases \(s=1\) and \(s=2\) conform to the same statement:
\(1\) and \(2\) always divide the even number \(p-1\),
so the pair never exists, exactly as the theorem predicts.)

This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem: Let \( n \geq 2 \) be an integer, and let \(\{a_{1}, \ldots, a_{m}\}\) denote the \( m=\varphi(n) \) integers less than \( n \) and relatively prime to \( n \). Assume that every prime divisor of \( m \) also divides \( n \). Prove that \( m \) divides \( a_{1}^{k}+\cdots+a_{m}^{k} \) for every positive integer \( k \).
solution:
For brevity, given any $n$, we let $A(n)=\{1 \leq x \leq n, \operatorname{gcd}(x, n)=1\}$ (thus $|A(n)|=\varphi(n)$ ). Also, let $S(n, k)=\sum_{a \in A(n)} a^{k}$.

We will prove the stronger statement (which eliminates the hypothesis on $n$ ).
Claim - Let $n \geq 2$ be arbitrary (and $k \geq 0$ ). If $p \mid n$, then

$$
\nu_{p}(\varphi(n)) \leq \nu_{p}(S(n, k))
$$

We start with the special case where $n$ is a prime power.

## Lemma

Let $p$ be prime, $e \geq 1, k \geq 0$. We always have

$$
S\left(p^{e}, k\right)=\sum_{x \in A\left(p^{e}\right)} x^{k} \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p^{e-1}\right) .
$$

Proof. For $p$ odd, this follows by taking a primitive root $g$ modulo $p^{e}$. We will have

$$
S\left(p^{e}, k\right) \equiv 1+g^{k}+g^{2 k}+\cdots+g^{\left(\varphi\left(p^{e}\right)-1\right) k} \equiv \frac{g^{\varphi\left(p^{e}\right) k}-1}{g^{k}-1} .
$$

If $p-1 \nmid k$, then the denominator is not divisible by $p$ and hence the entire expression is $0\left(\bmod p^{e}\right)$. In the other case where $p-1 \mid k$, since $\nu_{p}\left(\varphi\left(p^{e}\right)\right)=e-1$, the exponent lifting lemma implies

$$
\nu_{p}\left(\left(g^{k}\right)^{\varphi\left(p^{e}\right)}-1\right)=\nu_{p}\left(g^{k}-1\right)+(e-1)
$$
and so the conclusion is true here too.
In the annoying case $p=2$, the proof is broken into two cases: for $k$ odd it follows by pairing $x$ with $2^{e}-x$ and when $k$ is even one can take $5$ as a generator of all the quadratic residues as in the $p>2$ case.

## Corollary

We have $\nu_{p}\left(1^{k}+\cdots+t^{k}\right) \geq \nu_{p}(t)-1$ for any $k, t, p$.

Proof. Assume $p \mid t$. Handle the terms in that sum divisible by $p$ (by induction) and apply the lemma a bunch of times.

Now the idea is to add primes $q$ one at a time to $n$, starting from the base case $n=p^{e}$. So, formally we proceed by induction on the number of prime divisors of $n$. We'll also assume $k \geq 1$ in what follows since the base case $k=0$ is easy.

- First, suppose we want to go from $n$ to $n q$ where $q \nmid n$. In that case $\varphi(n q)$ gained $\nu_{p}(q-1)$ factors of $p$ and then we need to show $\nu_{p}(S(n q, k)) \geq \nu_{p}(\varphi(n))+\nu_{p}(q-1)$. The trick is to write

$$
A(n q)=\{a+n h \mid a \in A(n) \text { and } h=0, \ldots, q-1\} \backslash q A(n)
$$
and then expand using binomial theorem:
\$\$\begin{aligned}

S(n q, k) \& =\sum_{a \in A(n)} \sum_{h=0}^{q-1}(a+n h)^{k}-\sum_{a \in A(n)}(q a)^{k} 
\& =-q^{k} S(n, k)+\sum_{a \in A(n)} \sum_{h=0}^{q-1} \sum_{j=0}^{k}\left[\binom{k}{j} a^{k-j} n^{j} h^{j}\right] 
\& =-q^{k} S(n, k)+\sum_{j=0}^{k}\left[\binom{k}{j} n^{j}\left(\sum_{a \in A(n)} a^{k-j}\right)\left(\sum_{h=0}^{q-1} h^{j}\right)\right] 
\& =-q^{k} S(n, k)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\binom{k}{j} n^{j} S(n, k-j)\left(\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^{j}\right)\right] .

\end{aligned}\$\$

We claim every term here has enough powers of $p$. For the first term, $S(n, k)$ has at least $\nu_{p}(\varphi(n))$ factors of $p$; and we have the $q-q^{k}$ multiplier out there. For the other terms, we apply induction to $S(n, k-j)$; moreover $\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^{j}$ has at least $\nu_{p}(q-1)-1$ factors of $p$ by corollary, and we get one more factor of $p$ (at least) from $n^{j}$.

- On the other hand, if $q$ already divides $n$, then this time

$$
A(n q)=\{a+n h \mid a \in A(n) \text { and } h=0, \ldots, q-1\} .
$$
and we have no additional burden of $p$ to deal with; the same calculation gives
$$
S(n q, k)=q S(n, k)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\binom{k}{j} n^{j} S(n, k-j)\left(\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^{j}\right)\right]
$$

which certainly has enough factors of $p$ already.

Remark. A curious bit about the problem is that $\nu_{p}(\varphi(n))$ can exceed $\nu_{p}(n)$, and so it is not true that the residues of $A(n)$ are well-behaved modulo $\varphi(n)$.

As an example, let $n=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7 \cdot 13=546$, so $m=\varphi(n)=1 \cdot 2 \cdot 6 \cdot 12=144$. Then $A(n)$ contains $26$ elements which are $1 \bmod 9$ and $23$ elements which are $4 \bmod 9$.

Remark. The converse of the problem is true too (but asking both parts would make this too long for exam).
author: human

problem: The points \(A, B, C, D\) lie, in this order, on a circle \(\omega\), where \(AD\) is a diameter of \(\omega\). Furthermore, \(AB = BC = a\) and \(CD = c\) for some relatively prime integers \(a\) and \(c\). Show that if the diameter \(d\) of \(\omega\) is also an integer, then either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
solution:
Let \(O\) be the center of the circle \(\omega\), and write \(R\) for its radius and \(d=2R\) for its diameter.  Since \(AD\) is a diameter, Thales’ theorem tells us that for any point \(X\) on the circle other than \(A,D\), the triangle \(AXD\) is right‐angled at \(X\).  In particular, \(\triangle ABD\) is right at \(B\) and \(\triangle ACD\) is right at \(C\).

Label the central angles
\[
\alpha = \angle AOB,\quad \beta = \angle BOC,\quad \gamma = \angle COD.
\]
Then \(A,B,C,D\) lie in that order on one semicircle \(AD\), so
\[
\alpha + \beta + \gamma \;=\;\pi.
\]
By the well‐known chord–central‐angle relation,
\[
AB = 2R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}=d\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}, 
\quad
BC = d\sin\frac{\beta}{2}, 
\quad
CD = d\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}.
\]
The hypothesis \(AB=BC=a\) and \(CD=c\) gives
\[
\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac a d,\quad
\sin\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac a d,\quad
\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}=\frac c d.
\]
Since \(\alpha/2\) and \(\beta/2\) lie in \((0,\tfrac\pi2)\), the equality of sines forces
\[
\frac\alpha2=\frac\beta2.
\]
Set
\[
x=\frac\alpha2=\frac\beta2,
\qquad
z=\frac\gamma2.
\]
Then
\[
2x+z=\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{2}=\frac\pi2,
\quad
\sin x=\frac a d,
\quad
\sin z=\frac c d.
\]
But \(z=\tfrac\pi2-2x\), so
\[
\sin z=\cos(2x)
=1-2\sin^2x
=1-2\Bigl(\frac a d\Bigr)^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac c d \;=\;1-\frac{2a^2}{d^2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
d^2-cd-2a^2=0.
\]
Because \(d\) is assumed an integer, the discriminant
\[
\Delta=c^2+8a^2
\]
must be a perfect square.  Write
\[
\Delta=k^2,\quad k\in\Bbb Z_{>0}.
\]
Then
\[
k^2-c^2=8a^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(k-c)(k+c)=8a^2.
\]
Since \(k\equiv c\pmod2\), both \(k\pm c\) are even.  Define
\[
u=\frac{k+c}{2}, 
\qquad
v=\frac{k-c}{2}.
\]
Then \(u,v\in\Bbb Z\) and
\[
uv=\frac{(k+c)(k-c)}{4}=\frac{8a^2}{4}=2a^2.
\]
On the other hand, solving the quadratic \(d^2-cd-2a^2=0\) shows
\[
d=\frac{k\pm c}{2}\;=\;\max\{u,v\},
\]
since geometrically the diameter exceeds each chord.  Thus
\[
u=d,\quad v=\frac{2a^2}{d}.
\]
We claim \(\gcd(u,v)=1\).  Indeed any odd prime dividing both \(u\) and \(v\) would also divide their product \(uv=2a^2\) and hence \(a\), and it divides \(u=d=(k+c)/2\) and hence \(c\); this contradicts \(\gcd(a,c)=1\).  Therefore \(\gcd(u,v)=1\).

Now \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime positive integers with
\[
uv=2a^2.
\]
By unique factorization, the only way two coprime integers can multiply to \(2a^2\) is that one of them is a perfect square and the other is twice a perfect square.  Since \(u=d\) is the larger factor, we conclude:

• Either \(d=u\) is itself a perfect square;  
• Or \(d=u\) is twice a perfect square, in which case \(2d\) is a perfect square.

This completes the proof.
author: llm

problem: The points \(A, B, C, D\) lie, in this order, on a circle \(\omega\), where \(AD\) is a diameter of \(\omega\). Furthermore, \(AB = BC = a\) and \(CD = c\) for some relatively prime integers \(a\) and \(c\). Show that if the diameter \(d\) of \(\omega\) is also an integer, then either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
solution:
Let the centre of the circle be \(O\) and let  

\[
\operatorname{diameter}(\omega)=d\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R=\tfrac d2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The central angles

Because the chords \(AB\) and \(BC\) are equal we have the equal
central angles  

\[
\angle AOB=\angle BOC=:2\theta ,\qquad 0<2\theta<\pi .
\]

(The inequality \(2\theta<\pi\) holds because every chord that is
strictly shorter than the diameter subtends a central angle strictly
smaller than \(180^{\circ}\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Expressing the given lengths

For every chord \(XY\) we have \(XY=2R\sin\frac{\widehat{XOY}}{2}\).
Hence  

\[
AB =BC =2R\sin\theta =d\sin\theta =a                    \tag{1}
\]

and  

\[
CD =2R\sin\frac{\widehat{COD}}{2}.
\]

Now  

\[
\widehat{COD}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{AOC}
             =\pi-(\widehat{AOB}+\widehat{BOC})
             =\pi-4\theta ,
\]
so  

\[
CD = 2R\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi-4\theta}{2}\Bigr)
    = 2R\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\Bigr)
    = 2R\cos 2\theta
    = d\cos 2\theta
    = c .                                          \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  A Diophantine equation for \(a,c,d\)

From (1) we obtain \(\sin\theta=\dfrac ad\).
Using the double–angle identity
\(\cos 2\theta = 1-2\sin^2\theta\) and (2) we get  

\[
\frac{c}{d}=1-2\bigl(\tfrac{a}{d}\bigr)^{2}
           =\frac{d^{2}-2a^{2}}{d^{2}},
\]
hence  

\[
cd=d^{2}-2a^{2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
d(d-c)=2a^{2}.                                       \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The two factors on the left–hand side are coprime

Put \(g=\gcd(d,d-c)=\gcd(d,c)\).  
Because \((a,c)=1\), the common divisor \(g\) must divide \(2\)
(otherwise it would divide \(a\) as well).  
Thus \(g\in\{1,2\}\).

Suppose \(g=2\).  
Then \(d=2m,\;d-c=2n\;(m,n\in\mathbb Z)\), so \(c=2(m-n)\) is even.
Equation (3) becomes  

\[
4mn=2a^{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;2mn=a^{2}.
\]

Hence \(a\) is even, write \(a=2k\ (\Rightarrow a^{2}=4k^{2})\).
We obtain \(4k^{2}=2mn\), i.e.\ \(2k^{2}=mn\); but the left side is
even while \(mn\) is odd (both \(m,n\) are odd because \(d,d-c\) share
no factor \(>2\)).  Contradiction.  
Therefore

\[
\gcd(d,d-c)=1.                                \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Consequences of coprimeness

Because of (4) the two factors \(d\) and \(d-c\) in (3) are coprime.
Their product equals \(2a^{2}\), which is twice a perfect square.
Hence every odd prime appears with an even exponent in each of the
numbers \(d\) and \(d-c\).  Consequently

    • each of \(d,\;d-c\) is of the form \(s^{2}\) or \(2s^{2}\);

    • they cannot both be even (otherwise they would have common factor
      \(2\)), so exactly one of them is even.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Finishing the argument

Case 1.  \(d\) is odd, \(d-c\) is even.  
Then \(d\) contains no factor \(2\); hence
\(d=s^{2}\) is a perfect square.

Case 2.  \(d\) is even, \(d-c\) is odd.  
Then \(d=2s^{2}\) for some integer \(s\), and therefore
\(2d=4s^{2}=(2s)^{2}\) is a perfect square.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Conclusion

In every possible configuration

\[
\text{either }d\text{ or }2d\text{ is a perfect square.}
\qedhere
\]
author: llm

problem: The points \(A, B, C, D\) lie, in this order, on a circle \(\omega\), where \(AD\) is a diameter of \(\omega\). Furthermore, \(AB = BC = a\) and \(CD = c\) for some relatively prime integers \(a\) and \(c\). Show that if the diameter \(d\) of \(\omega\) is also an integer, then either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
solution:
Let \(R\) be the radius of the circle \(\omega\), so its diameter is \(d = 2R\).
The points \(A, B, C, D\) lie in this order on \(\omega\). \(AD\) is a diameter of \(\omega\).
We are given \(AB = a\), \(BC = a\), and \(CD = c\). \(a\) and \(c\) are relatively prime positive integers (lengths must be positive). \(d\) is an integer.

Since \(AD\) is a diameter, \(\angle ABD\) and \(\angle ACD\) are right angles, as they are angles subtended by a diameter.
In \(\triangle ABD\), \(BD^2 = AD^2 - AB^2 = d^2 - a^2\). So, \(BD = \sqrt{d^2 - a^2}\).
In \(\triangle ACD\), \(AC^2 = AD^2 - CD^2 = d^2 - c^2\). So, \(AC = \sqrt{d^2 - c^2}\).
Since \(A, B, C, D\) are distinct points on the circle, we must have \(d>a\) and \(d>c\). This ensures that \(BD\) and \(AC\) are real and positive.

The quadrilateral \(ABCD\) is cyclic. We can apply Ptolemy's Theorem, which states that for a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of the products of the opposite sides is equal to the product of the diagonals.
The pairs of opposite sides are \((AB, CD)\) and \((BC, AD)\). The diagonals are \(AC\) and \(BD\).
So, \(AB \cdot CD + BC \cdot AD = AC \cdot BD\).
Substituting the known values:
\(a \cdot c + a \cdot d = AC \cdot BD\).
\(a(c+d) = \sqrt{d^2-c^2} \sqrt{d^2-a^2}\).

To eliminate the square roots, we square both sides of the equation:
\(a^2(c+d)^2 = (d^2-c^2)(d^2-a^2)\).
The terms \(d^2-c^2\) and \(d^2-a^2\) can be factored as differences of squares:
\(a^2(c+d)^2 = (d-c)(d+c)(d-a)(d+a)\).
Since \(d>c\), \(d+c\) is a positive quantity. We can divide both sides by \(d+c\):
\(a^2(d+c) = (d-c)(d-a)(d+a)\).
Now, expand \((d-a)(d+a)\) to \(d^2-a^2\):
\(a^2(d+c) = (d-c)(d^2-a^2)\).
Expand both sides:
\(a^2 d + a^2 c = d(d^2-a^2) - c(d^2-a^2)\)
\(a^2 d + a^2 c = d^3 - d a^2 - c d^2 + c a^2\).
Move all terms involving \(a^2\) to the left or simplify:
\(a^2 d + a^2 c - c a^2 + d a^2 = d^3 - c d^2\).
\(2a^2 d = d^3 - cd^2\).
Since \(d\) is a diameter of a circle, \(d \ne 0\). We can divide the entire equation by \(d\):
\(2a^2 = d^2 - cd\).
This can be rewritten as \(d(d-c) = 2a^2\).

We are given that \(a\) and \(c\) are relatively prime integers, and \(d\) is an integer.
Since \(a \ge 1\), \(2a^2 > 0\). Since \(d>0\), we must have \(d-c > 0\), so \(d>c\). This is consistent with our earlier observation.
Let \(g = \gcd(d, c)\). Since \(g\) divides \(d\) and \(g\) divides \(c\), \(g\) must divide \(d-c\).
Therefore, \(g = \gcd(d, d-c)\).
The equation is \(d(d-c) = 2a^2\).
Since \(g\) divides \(d\) and \(g\) divides \(c\), we can write \(d=gX\) and \(c=gY\) for some integers \(X,Y\) with \(\gcd(X,Y)=1\).
The equation becomes \(gX(gX-gY) = 2a^2\), which is \(g^2 X(X-Y) = 2a^2\).
We are given that \(a\) and \(c\) are relatively prime, so \(\gcd(a,c)=1\).
Since \(g\) is a divisor of \(c\), it must be that \(\gcd(a,g)=1\).
From \(g^2 X(X-Y) = 2a^2\), since \(\gcd(g,a)=1\) (and thus \(\gcd(g^2, a^2)=1\)), it must be that \(g^2\) divides 2.
As \(g\) is an integer, \(g^2\) must be an integer square. The only integer square that divides 2 is 1.
So, \(g^2=1\), which implies \(g=1\).
Therefore, \(\gcd(d,c)=1\).

Now we know that \(d\) and \(c\) are relatively prime.
Consider the factors \(d\) and \(d-c\) in the equation \(d(d-c)=2a^2\).
The greatest common divisor of these two factors is \(\gcd(d, d-c) = \gcd(d, c)\).
Since we have shown \(\gcd(d,c)=1\), it follows that \(d\) and \(d-c\) are relatively prime.

We have two relatively prime integers, \(d\) and \(d-c\), whose product is \(2a^2\).
Let \(d_1 = d\) and \(d_2 = d-c\). Then \(d_1 d_2 = 2a^2\) and \(\gcd(d_1, d_2)=1\).
Let \(a = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}\) be the prime factorization of \(a\). Then \(a^2 = p_1^{2e_1} \cdots p_k^{2e_k}\).
Since \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are relatively prime, they do not share any common prime factors. All prime factors of \(a^2\) (which are \(p_1, \dots, p_k\)) must belong entirely to either \(d_1\) or \(d_2\). The factor 2 must also belong to either \(d_1\) or \(d_2\).

There are two cases:

Case 1: The factor 2 divides \(d_1\).
Then \(d_1 = 2 \cdot P_1\) and \(d_2 = P_2\), where \(P_1 P_2 = a^2\).
Since \(\gcd(d_1, d_2)=1\), we have \(\gcd(2P_1, P_2)=1\).
This implies that \(P_2\) must be odd, and \(\gcd(P_1, P_2)=1\).
Since \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are relatively prime and their product \(P_1 P_2 = a^2\) is a perfect square, both \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) must be perfect squares. (If a prime \(p\) divides \(P_1\), then \(p^{2k}\) must be the full power of \(p\) in \(a^2\), so \(p^{2k}\) must divide \(P_1\). This applies to all prime factors of \(P_1\). Similarly for \(P_2\).)
So, let \(P_1 = x^2\) and \(P_2 = y^2\) for some integers \(x, y \ge 1\) (since \(a \ge 1\), \(d, d-c \ge 1\)).
Then \(a^2 = x^2 y^2\), so \(a=xy\).
In this case, \(d_1 = d = 2x^2\) and \(d_2 = d-c = y^2\).
We want to show that \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
Here \(d = 2x^2\). So \(2d = 2(2x^2) = 4x^2 = (2x)^2\).
Thus, \(2d\) is a perfect square. This case satisfies the condition.
We must also check that \(\gcd(d,c)=1\) is satisfied. \(c = d-(d-c) = 2x^2-y^2\).
\(\gcd(d,c) = \gcd(2x^2, 2x^2-y^2) = \gcd(2x^2, -y^2) = \gcd(2x^2, y^2)\).
Since \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=\gcd(2x^2, y^2)=1\), this means \(y\) must be odd and \(\gcd(x,y)=1\).
This ensures \(\gcd(d,c)=1\). Also, \(\gcd(a,c)=\gcd(xy, 2x^2-y^2)=1\) because \(\gcd(x, -y^2)=1\) (i.e. \(\gcd(x,y)=1\)) and \(\gcd(y, 2x^2-y^2)=\gcd(y, 2x^2)=1\) (i.e. \(\gcd(y,2)=1\) and \(\gcd(y,x)=1\)). These conditions are consistent.

Case 2: The factor 2 divides \(d_2\).
Then \(d_1 = P_1\) and \(d_2 = 2 \cdot P_2\), where \(P_1 P_2 = a^2\).
Since \(\gcd(d_1, d_2)=1\), we have \(\gcd(P_1, 2P_2)=1\).
This implies that \(P_1\) must be odd, and \(\gcd(P_1, P_2)=1\).
Similar to the first case, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) must be perfect squares.
So, let \(P_1 = x^2\) and \(P_2 = y^2\) for some integers \(x, y \ge 1\).
Then \(a^2 = x^2 y^2\), so \(a=xy\).
In this case, \(d_1 = d = x^2\) and \(d_2 = d-c = 2y^2\).
We want to show that \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
Here \(d = x^2\), which is itself a perfect square. This case also satisfies the condition.
Again, we check \(\gcd(d,c)=1\). \(c = d-(d-c) = x^2-2y^2\).
\(\gcd(d,c) = \gcd(x^2, x^2-2y^2) = \gcd(x^2, -2y^2) = \gcd(x^2, 2y^2)\).
Since \(\gcd(d_1,d_2)=\gcd(x^2, 2y^2)=1\), this means \(x\) must be odd and \(\gcd(x,y)=1\).
This ensures \(\gcd(d,c)=1\). Also, \(\gcd(a,c)=\gcd(xy, x^2-2y^2)=1\) because \(\gcd(x, -2y^2)=1\) (i.e. \(\gcd(x,2)=1\) and \(\gcd(x,y)=1\)) and \(\gcd(y,x^2-2y^2)=\gcd(y,x^2)=1\) (i.e. \(\gcd(y,x)=1\)). These conditions are consistent.

Both cases lead to the conclusion that either \(d\) is a perfect square or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
The initial assumption that \(a,c\) are positive integers means \(a,c \ge 1\).
If \(a=1, c=1\), then \(d(d-1)=2\), so \(d^2-d-2=0\), which factors as \((d-2)(d+1)=0\). Since \(d>0\), \(d=2\). Here \(d=2\) is not a square. \(2d=4=2^2\) is a square. This fits Case 1, with \(x=1, y=1\).
If \(a=3, c=7\), then \(d(d-7)=2 \cdot 3^2 = 18\). So \(d^2-7d-18=0\), which factors as \((d-9)(d+2)=0\). Since \(d>0\), \(d=9\). Here \(d=9=3^2\) is a square. This fits Case 2, with \(x=3, y=1\) (since \(a=xy\), and \(d-c=9-7=2=2y^2\)).

The proof has shown that, under the given conditions, the integer diameter \(d\) satisfies the property that either \(d\) itself is a perfect square, or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
author: llm

problem: Let \( ABC \) be a triangle, and let \( D, E, F \) be the feet of the perpendiculars from \( A, B, C \) to \( BC, CA, AB \) respectively. Let \( P, Q, R, S \) be the feet of the perpendiculars from \( D \) to \( BA, BE, CF, \) and \( CA \) respectively. Prove that \( P, Q, R, S \) are collinear.
solution:
Let \(ABC\) be any ( not necessarily acute ) triangle.  
Denote by  

• \(D\in BC,\;E\in CA,\;F\in AB\) the feet of the altitudes from \(A ,B ,C\),  
• \(P,Q,R,S\) the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from \(D\) to the lines \(BA ,BE ,CF ,CA\), respectively.

We must show that the four points \(P ,Q ,R ,S\) are collinear.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two right–angle circles through \(D\)

Because \(E\) is the foot of the altitude from \(B\), we have  
\(\angle BEA = 90^{\circ}\) ( \(BE\perp AC=AE\) ).  
Since \(D\) is the foot of the altitude from \(A\),  
\(\angle BDA = 90^{\circ}\) ( \(AD\perp BC=BD\) ).

Hence both \(E\) and \(D\) lie on the circle whose diameter is \(BA\); equivalently

  \(B,\,A,\,E,\,D\) are concyclic.                                               (1)

Similarly, \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\), so
\(\angle AFC = 90^{\circ}\); and we already have \(\angle ADC = 90^{\circ}\).
Consequently \(A,\,C,\,F,\,D\) are concyclic, the circle now having diameter \(AC\):

  \(A,\,C,\,F,\,D\) are concyclic.                                               (2)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Two Simson lines through \(D\)

A classical and well-known result (Simson’s Theorem) states:

 Simson’s Theorem.  
 For a triangle \(XYZ\) and a point \(T\) on its circumcircle, the projections  
 of \(T\) on the three sides \(XY,\;YZ,\;ZX\) are collinear.

We apply this theorem to the two circles found in Section 1.

a)  Circumcircle of \(B A E\)

With triangle \(BAE\) and the point \(D\) (which lies on its circumcircle by (1)),

 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(BA\) is \(P\);  
 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(BE\) is \(Q\);  
 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(AE\;(=AC)\) is \(S\).

Therefore Simson’s theorem gives

  \(P,\,Q,\,S\) are collinear.                                                   (3)

b)  Circumcircle of \(A C F\)

With triangle \(ACF\) and the same point \(D\) (lying on its circumcircle by (2)),

 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(AC\) is \(S\);  
 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(CF\) is \(R\);  
 • the perpendicular from \(D\) to \(FA\;(=AB)\) is \(P\).

Thus Simson’s theorem now yields

  \(P,\,R,\,S\) are collinear.                                                   (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion

Statements (3) and (4) show that the three points \(P\) and \(S\) lie on both
the line \(PQ\) and the line \(PR\).  Hence these two lines coincide, so

  \(P,\,Q,\,R,\,S\) are all collinear.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Remark on degeneracies

If \(ABC\) is right- or obtuse-angled, some of the feet \(E,F\) (and the points
\(Q,R,S\)) may lie on the extensions of the corresponding sides;  
Simson’s theorem is still valid for extended sides, and the above proof
goes through unchanged.

Hence, in every triangle \(ABC\), the four points \(P,Q,R,S\) are collinear, as required.
author: llm

problem: Find, with proof, the least integer \( N \) such that if any 2016 elements are removed from the set \(\{1,2, \ldots, N\}\), one can still find 2016 distinct numbers among the remaining elements with sum \( N \).
solution:
The answer is

$$
N=2017+2018+\cdots+4032=1008 \cdot 6049=6097392 .
$$

 Proof that $N \geq 6097392$ is necessary. To see that $N$ must be at least this large, consider the situation when $1,2, \ldots, 2016$ are removed. Among the remaining elements, any sum of $2016$ elements is certainly at least $2017+2018+\cdots+4032$.

гЂЋ Proof that $N=6097392$ does in fact work. Consider the $3024$ pairs of numbers $(1,6048),(2,6047), \ldots,(3024,3025)$. Regardless of which $2016$ elements of $\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$ are deleted, at least $3024-2016=1008$ of these pairs have both elements remaining. Since each pair has sum 6049, we can take these pairs to be the desired numbers.
